reads.title: The End of Rojava: Kurds in Northeast Syria Face an Uncertain Future Amid Integration With Damascus
reads.subtitle: Despite the formal dissolution of the SDF and the Kurdish-led autonomous zone, northeast Syria remains in a liminal state—not fully Syria, but not entirely separate, either.
reads.body:
Thank you again to all of our readers who donated to Huda Skaik, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, as she begins a journey to university in London. We met our goal in just a few hours thanks to your enormous generosity. We’re keeping the fundraiser open until Wednesday, and you can still give here:
Donate to support Huda
We also hope you’ll consider supporting our ongoing Gaza Journalist Fund, launched last year to help 29 Palestinian journalists cover the costs of shelter, transportation, and basic needs.
Please donate and share the campaign link: gazafund.dropsitenews.com.
Donate to the Gaza Journalist Fund

-
- A building in Qamishli, northeast Syria, bearing the name Kurdistan. September 9, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.QAMISHLI, Syria—Faded photographs of the dead line the walls of Fadia Ismail’s home in Hasake province, Syria—images of martyrs who died in the long quest for a Kurdish homeland.
Her son’s image is among them. Dalil was killed fighting ISIS in the flat desert of Al-Omar oilfield in 2017 when he was just 29. Dalil “died for Rojava,” she said in reference to the Kurdish-led political project in northeast Syria that gained de facto autonomy in 2012.
But now, as Syria’s president pushes to integrate the Kurdish community of the northeast into a unified Syria, the dream of Rojava as a self-governing Kurdish state has all but come to an end.
“All of our martyrs have been betrayed. All the blood we shed and for what?” she raged. “What did Dalil die for?”

-
- Fadia Ismail sits in her home in Gerbawi, Hasakeh with her husband under framed photos of martyrs from her family. September 9, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.On August 25th, the Autonomous Administration of North East Syria (AANES), also known as Rojava, and its military component, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), formally dissolved after more than a year of negotiations between the SDF and the new Syrian government led by Ahmed al-Sharaa. The talks ended when a surprise offensive by the government in January forced the SDF into accepting an integration agreement into a Syrian state. But many Kurds who spoke to Drop Site are fearful of rejoining a wider Syrian state that had previously marginalized and discriminated against them for decades under the Assad regime.
As the sun set on Gerbawi village in the countryside of Qamishli, Fadia and her husband enjoyed the cool twilight air on their porch. “There is no integration. This is the imposition of defeat,” she said as she swatted at flies landing on the brim of her teacup. “Alongside Dalil, how many other lives were lost to capture Al-Omar oilfield? We lost it overnight.”
“We have lost our chance at a better future.”
Subscribe to Drop Site or make a tax-deductible gift today.

## Kurdish Women Fighters
The SDF’s fighters now serve under the new Syrian flag and the senior leadership are to be given roles within the Syrian government. Mazloum Abdi, the SDF’s commander-in-chief, has been appointed as a special advisor to President Al-Sharaa.
However, their female counterpart, the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), who rose to prominence for their crucial role in the war against ISIS, are stuck in limbo, as Syria’s Ministry of Defense has refused to admit women into its ranks. The YPJ grew to become one of Syria’s most recognizable fighting forces, drawing global attention for its all female battalions that fought the Islamic State.
“Syrian law permits women to work in any position based on merit—except as combatants,” Mustapha Abdi, a senior member of the presidential team for the implementation of the integration agreement, told Drop Site News. “There is to be no female combat element within the Syrian military.”
The decision has left former YPJ fighters in limbo. In Hasake’s Khabour military hospital, Isiyan, 19, was recovering from a recent surgery. In January, with the SDF in full retreat ahead of the government’s offensive, Isiyan was ordered to get out of Raqqa, when her unit was ambushed on the road to Kobane. “I was hit by a Kalashnikov round that shattered the bones in my shoulder,” she said. “I lost a lot of blood.” She has been hospitalized since then, her days plagued by boredom and her nights by nightmares of what happened.

-
- Isiyan, 19, recovers from a battle injury in a hospital in Hasakeh as her comrades visit her. September 7, 2026. Photo by: Anagha Subhash Nair.Despite the attack, she is impatient to get back to her unit. “I miss my comrades,” she said. Isolated in hospital, she seemed unaware of the SDF’s dissolution. And like the rest of the YPJ, she had no sense of what her future would hold.
While integration into the Syrian military appears to be a red line for the government, Ruksan Mohammed, the YPJ spokesperson, said that, following the official dissolution of the SDF, YPJ leadership had met with officials from the Interior Ministry, and that “the possibility of integrating the YPJ as a special and organized force was emphasized.”
“We discussed how women can play an important role in protection of rights and society,” she told Drop Site. However, “no dates have yet been set for the upcoming meetings because we are waiting for a response from the Ministry of Interior.”
Before the dissolution of the SDF, as integration progressed in all other dimensions, the YPJ had largely found itself frozen out of talks, and according to Mohammed, were only afforded a single meeting with the government in April.
Abdi confirmed this, saying that the lack of any further meetings was because the YPJ “were offered non-combat roles, such as administrative office based work, which they refused.”

## Violence Targeting Kurds
The atmosphere is tense in northeast Syria following repeated incidents of violence targeting Kurds. Last Thursday, Sipan Hazni, a recently integrated Kurdish soldier was kidnapped and decapitated by Arab members of the Begara tribe. His killing set off the latest round of mass unrest, culminating in a riot and a fire at a prison in Kobane, which resulted in the deaths of seven detainees.
In Hasake city, the government’s decision to end SDF-era fuel subsidies has left the city cloaked in darkness. “People can’t afford the generator bills now, so they leave the lights off,” Musa Kiki, 65, said. “What kind of government is this?”

-
- Internal security forces stand in Qamishli during a protest in northeast Syria. September 10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.Kiki was attacked by the people who stole his home. He was part of the first convoy of Kurdish refugees returning to their homes in Serekaniye, a region from which he was displaced following Operation Peace Spring, an incursion by Turkey and the Turkish-backed Syrian National Army militia in 2019.
When he arrived back, he found his camera shop had been seized by a stranger and people were living in his house. “Honestly, I wish I had never tried to go back,” he said, stubbing out a thin cigarette. “The house had been ransacked. There were no windows or doors. The stairs were destroyed and someone had ripped out all the cables.”
“These people aren’t even from the area,” he added. “The person who took my home is from Deir Ez Zour, and my brother’s home is occupied by an Iraqi, imagine that.”
Despite the integration agreement stipulating the safe return of displaced peoples, under the protection of the Syrian government, Kiki and a number of other returnees were attacked by a group of armed men in the street.
“A large group of masked men came at us with clubs and knives, they were dragging people out of their cars,” he recounted. “One smashed the windshield of our car and the glass injured my grandchild.”
Ahmad Al-Hilali, the government-appointed deputy governor of Hasake, condemned the attacks, while Mahmoud Khalil Ali, the deputy head of Hasake’s internal security forces, announced the arrest of several perpetrators.
However, the government’s response did little to quell the simmering anger, with the attack setting off a night of rioting in Hasake province, during which protesters stormed Hasake city’s internal security headquarters and burned the recently hoisted Syrian flag. The following day, a security point of recently integrated SDF fighters was attacked, killing one and injuring three.
Kiki has little trust in the government. Although the occupant in his home has assured him that he would leave once he has found an alternative place to stay, “there is no way to ensure that,” he lamented. “If the government wanted they could go in and clear them out in a day, but they won’t.”
“Who can I complain to?” he added. “The government has done nothing for us.”

## Language and Kurdish Identity
The issues at play also extend to governance and, in a crucial way, to language.
Behind blastproof walls and multiple layers of security checks, Jihan Said Hisam is busy in her new role as the newly appointed head of Qamishli municipality. Until June, she had been negotiating with the government on behalf of the AANES, until her name was suggested for the position during talks. Now, she sits in front of a large Syrian flag speaking on behalf of that same government.
“I am optimistic for the future,” she said. “After 15 years of war, we can begin again and rebuild Syria.” Before the interview, her press office informed Drop Site that she wouldn’t be able to answer “political questions.”
Not long after the meeting, last Thursday, a large column of hundreds of children and young men and women, chanting and holding placards calling for the protection of Kurdish language, wound its way to the gates of the municipality building. Young boys attempted to scale the blast walls, but were pulled down and scolded by the armed guards.
After a few minutes, to the whistles and cheers of the awaiting protesters, Hisam made her way into the crowd to make an impromptu speech. “Although we are having a difficult time with the government, I urge you not to stop studying,” she railed. “Your education is vital and we still believe the government may reverse its decision.”
“I stand with you completely and I will work to raise your voices with Damascus,” she added.

-
- Jihan Said Hosam, head of the Qamishli municipality, speaks to protesters outside her office in northeast Syria. September 10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.Despite the formal dissolution of the AANES, the office of the Department of Foreign Affairs remains a beehive of activity. In a plush office inside, Ilham Ahmed greeted a number of different officials.
Until recently, she had been the co-president of the AANES, but following the dissolution, Ahmed is to become a member of parliament with a role on the Constitutional Committee, responsible for overseeing the drafting of Syria’s new constitution.
“We still don’t know how much power the constitutional committee will have,” she acknowledged. “Although we expect the parliament to play the standard legislative role in developing Syria’s institutions.”
While Ahmed spoke diplomatically, she admitted shortcomings in how negotiations are unfolding. “We feel that the issues aren’t really being taken seriously,” she explained. “Their approach is superficial and won’t lead to meaningful solutions.”
Despite that she recognized that the government has been willing to compromise on certain issues. “They initially offered us a deal which would have had Kurdish offered in school as an optional second language, akin to English,” she said. “We rejected this offer outright.”
“While we ultimately seek education in Kurdish, the outline of the integration file is yet to be finalized, so we remain optimistic,” she added.
As part of the integration agreement, Kurdish—the language of education for the last decade in northeast Syria while it was relatively autonomous—is set to be taught for three hours a week, alongside an additional hour of geography, history, or philosophy class in Kurdish. This is designed as a transitional settlement during the next academic year while a final settlement is yet to be agreed upon.
Last Wednesday, hundreds of children gathered in the streets and schoolyards of Qamishli. They chanted in Kurdish, demanding constitutional recognition for their language, and rejecting Damascus’s plans to return northeast Syria’s education system to Arabic.

-
- ​​People protest in Qamishli against a decision as part of SDF-Damascus integration that reduces the use of Kurdish language in education. September 10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.“I don’t speak Arabic well. I won’t be able to learn in it,” said Jihan Hafer, 14. “If they make us learn in Arabic, then I won’t come to school.”
“I’m scared for my future, that I will lose my chance for an education.”
Mustapha Abdi, a senior member of the government’s negotiating team, acknowledged that the agreed settlement didn’t go far enough. “To be honest, three classes a week is good in interior regions, but in Kurdish areas like northeast Syria, it is not enough completely,” he admitted.
He explained that while 1,400 schools are set to teach Kurdish, the government hopes “the number can also increase in the next year.”
“We have started now as a first step. We don’t want to make the step too big, so that the step succeeds,” he added.
Mezkil Hassan, a lecturer in Kurdish language at Rojava University, believes the policies are part of an effort to reverse a decade-long linguistic and cultural renewal that has taken place amongst northeast Syria’s Kurdish population.
“The Kurdish people have learnt that their existence is connected to their language,” explained Hassan. “This decision threatens the language and undermines Kurdish identity within Syria.”
Rojava University, founded in 2016 as a Kurdish language university, and only recently recognized by the Syrian government as part of the integration agreement, is set to switch teaching over to Arabic according to Hassan.
The Ministry of Higher Education did not respond to a request for comment.
Many Kurds fear a return to the Assad era, in which “the state did not recognize Kurdish identity as a legitimate part of Syrian culture,” explained Alexander McKeever, a researcher and author of the newsletter This Week in Northern Syria. “It viewed the Kurds as an alien population and so banned Kurdish-language instruction and cultural production.”
The Syrian government has sought to allay these concerns. In January, Al-Sharaa issued a presidential decree that recognized Kurdish as a “national language,” and annulled a controversial 1962 census that had effectively stripped citizenship from thousands of Kurds.
However, this decree doesn’t make Kurdish an “official” language nor one that is constitutionally protected. In fact, Syria is yet to draft its constitution.
Despite the formal dissolution of the SDF, northeast Syria remains in a liminal state—not fully Syria, but not entirely separate either. The individuals manning the checkpoints are no different than before, although some now wear the uniform of the government. While the flag of Syria’s government flies above public buildings, it is rare in the city streets, where the flags of Rojava and photos of martyrs remain ubiquitous.
The future of northeast Syria will not be determined by the change of flags or uniforms. After 15 years of governing themselves, those who sought to build an autonomous system are being asked to place their trust in a centralized state.
Whether that trust can be built will determine the success of integration and for the Kurdish community, it may come down to whether the new government can make them feel that there is still a place for them under Syria’s new flag.

reads.title: The Accelerating Collapse: Ukraine's Frontline Crisis and the Failure of Western Strategy
reads.subtitle: Marco | Independent Analyst ⚖️✓ *20 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction
The last 72 hours have marked a decisive inflection point in the Russo-Ukrainian war. The Russian Defense Ministry has broken its silence on multiple fronts, publishing a bulletin that confirms what independent analysts have been tracking for weeks: the pace of Russia’s advance is accelerating, and Ukraine’s defensive crisis is deepening beyond the point of sustainability.
This is not speculation. This is not propaganda. This is the documented, verifiable reality on the ground — corroborated by Ukrainian sources, Western intelligence assessments, and the admissions of senior European officials.

## The Frontline: A Systematic Collapse
The Russian Defense Ministry’s bulletin of 19 September is remarkable not for its rhetoric, but for its specificity. It confirms:

- Five settlements captured in a single day

- 670 square kilometers and 27 settlements seized in September alone — the fastest pace of advance this year

- Over 5,300 square kilometers and 220 settlements “liberated” since January 2026
The fighting is not limited to a single sector. It is systemic:

## Orikhiv: Street Fighting in the City Center
The Russian MoD confirms combat operations in the central quarters of Orikhiv. LNR expert Andrey Marochko reports the town is now divided roughly 50/50 between Russian and Ukrainian forces, with Russian troops entrenched on the southern and eastern outskirts. The capture of Novo Pavlovka and Novo Andrefka has effectively shut off the Ukrainian retreat route from the Orikhiv encirclement toward Zaporizhzhia.

## Dobropillya: Street Combat Confirmed
The Russian MoD reports street fighting underway in the central area of Dobropillya. This is the first direct Russian confirmation that its troops are inside the town’s core. The village of Dobropillya to the southwest has reportedly fallen, and Russian forces are advancing northward to encircle the remaining Ukrainian troops from the west.

## Lyman: The “Operation Vivaldi” Propaganda Collapse
The Russian MoD has publicly denied any Ukrainian counteroffensive in the Lyman area. It describes Ukraine’s “Operation Vivaldi” as a failed propaganda invention, claiming Russian forces are still clearing Krasnyi Lyman and Svyatohirsk of Ukrainian defenders.
The evidence supports this assessment. Ukraine has produced only two pieces of video footage purportedly showing success: Azov commander Andriy Biletskyi walking near a monastery, and a single flag-raising in one village west of the Nitrius River. Zelensky and the Ukrainian high command have said nothing about this supposedly successful operation.

## Kharkov: Cauldrons Fragmenting
The Ukrainian units encircled in the Kharkov region are being defeated. The two cauldrons established in that area are fragmenting — one at Alvatka has been cleared, the other has been divided into smaller pockets. Russian forces are advancing southward toward Veliki Burluk.

## The Human Cost: 27,000 Per Month
On 17 September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk made an admission that should have dominated every Western headline. Speaking in the Polish Sejm, he stated that Ukrainian military losses have reached approximately 27,000 killed and wounded per month — a figure he called a “sad record.”

> “Our partners from Ukraine told me that recently this has amounted to 27,000 killed and wounded every month. And these are, of course, unfortunately, in the saddest sense of the word, records in this regard.”
This figure aligns with Russian estimates. It is, by any measure, unsustainable. Even with tougher conscription measures, Ukraine cannot replace losses at this rate. The demographic math is inexorable.
Zelensky himself has acknowledged that Ukraine’s budget deficit is now of “cosmic dimensions.” One phone call to Ursula von der Leyen was enough to secure another €3.5 billion from the EU — apparently for drone production. But money cannot buy what does not exist: air-defense interceptors, radars, and artillery ammunition are in critical shortage.

## The Russian Response: Preparing for the Long War
On 18 September, Putin convened the Military-Industrial Commission and set out new priorities that reveal Russia’s strategic trajectory:

- Air-defense systems capable of destroying “any means of air and space attack”

- A broad range of unmanned and robotic systems — anti-drone weapons to combat drones

- Completion of the Rassvet orbital constellation — for real-time command and control of troops and weapons

> “It is necessary to fully complete the formation of the orbital constellation of spacecraft. This will enhance the capabilities of all types of space reconnaissance, navigation, satellite communications, and broadband internet access for the real-time command and control of troops and weapons.”
This is a direct response to the drone war — and a signal that Russia is preparing for a conflict measured in years, not months. Once the Rassvet system is complete, Russian drones, cruise missiles, and potentially ballistic missiles will be capable of being directed to targets in central and western Ukraine with unprecedented precision.

## The Diplomatic Failure: Three Attempts, Three Rejections
Over the course of September, the United States has made three separate attempts to persuade Russia to stop its offensive:

- CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow, meeting with intelligence chiefs Naryshkin and Bortnikov. The Russians disliked his menacing tone and sent him home after four hours.

- Witkoff and Kushner brought offers of economic cooperation — sanctions relief, business opportunities. Putin met them politely and rejected the offers. “No, thank you. We continue with the war.”

- Trump’s phone call to Putin — one hour of discussion, the same proposal: end the fighting, we lift sanctions. Putin politely said no.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, signed by Trump on 19 September, represents the fourth pressure point. But crucially, the law makes secondary tariffs on countries buying Russian oil discretionary, not mandatory. The discretion belongs to the President — and he has not pulled the trigger.
The United States does not have the weapons to force the Russians to stop. And all of the various strategies, schemes, and plans to force them to stop have failed.

## The Nuclear Dimension
In early September, Russia conducted three days of major nuclear drills involving 65,000 troops, 7,800 pieces of equipment, and over 200 missile launchers. The exercises included test-launches of ballistic and cruise missiles, with participation from aircraft, ships, submarines, and nuclear submarines.
Crucially, the drills also addressed “the joint training and use of nuclear weapons deployed on the territory of the Republic of Belarus.” Russia has deployed the nuclear-capable Oreshnik missile to Belarus, which borders NATO members Poland, Latvia, and Lithuania.
The ending of the New START agreement in February 2026 formally released the world’s two largest nuclear powers from a raft of restrictions. Russia has vowed to take a “responsible” approach — but Putin has also said that developing Russia’s nuclear forces is an “absolute priority.”

## The Strategic Picture: What This Means
The West’s great bet — the drone offensive of 2025-2026 — was designed to break the Russian economy, trigger a political crisis, and force Putin to the table. It has failed completely.
Russia absorbed the blow effortlessly. There is no evidence that the Russian economy has been unduly affected. There is no evidence of a political crisis. To the extent that the drone offensive has done anything, it has hardened Russian resolve rather than softened it.
Meanwhile, Russia has developed its own missiles and drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones are now rampaging across the skies of eastern, central, and southern Ukraine. Production rates have been increased to enormous dimensions. And Russia has been able to go onto the attack on a scale that totally eclipses anything Ukraine and its Western partners can muster.
The European response has been panic and hysteria — frightening their populations, trying to ramp up military production, sending more money to Ukraine, and begging the Americans to use every tool available to force Russia to stop. But there is no tool left that has not already been tried.
Meanwhile, the EU’s own sanctions regime is collapsing. On 18 September, the 27 member states failed to reach an agreement on extending individual sanctions against Russia. The sanctions were only extended for one week to allow for further negotiations. Slovakia and France are blocking the renewal, demanding changes to the sanctioned individuals list. The EU’s individual sanctions regime — asset freezes and travel restrictions targeting nearly 3,000 individuals and entities — is set to expire at midnight on Tuesday unless an agreement is reached.

## Verdict
The Russian advance is not a propaganda claim. It is a documented, accelerating reality. Orikhiv is being split in half. Dobropillya is under street assault. Kharkov cauldrons are fragmenting. Ukraine is losing 27,000 men a month and cannot replace them.
[The West is out of options. And it knows it.]
The drone offensive failed. The sanctions are discretionary. Diplomacy is dead. The EU cannot even agree to extend its own sanctions. And Russia is completing an orbital constellation that will give it real-time targeting capabilities across the entire theater.
One day — perhaps sooner than anyone expects — there will be recriminations in Western capitals about the failure to move forward with the Istanbul agreement and the Anchorage compromise. But by then, the deals will have been withdrawn.

reads.title: The Architecture of False Hope: Petraeus, the Hero Cult, and the War That Cannot Be Won
reads.subtitle: Marco | Independent Analyst ⚖️✓ *20 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction: The Function of the Hero
Every failing system needs a face that inspires confidence. Not a face that tells the truth — a face that makes the lie bearable.
In the architecture of Western strategic communication, General David Petraeus has served this function for nearly two decades. He is the decorated commander, the CIA director, the “hero of the surge,” the man who supposedly solved Iraq and was sent to replicate the miracle in Afghanistan. He is the man whose voice carries the weight of medals, not the weight of evidence.
And now, in September 2026, he is telling Ukrainians — a people losing 27,000 men a month — that there is still “a path to victory.”
This is not analysis. This is a mechanism. And it deserves to be examined not as a personal failing, but as a systemic one.

## Part I: The Record — A Pattern, Not an Incident
The problem with Petraeus is not that he was wrong once. It is that he has been wrong consistently, and that being wrong has never diminished his access to the microphone.

## Iraq, 2007 — The Credit He Did Not Earn
The narrative is well known: Petraeus arrived in Iraq, the surge was implemented, violence dropped, and the general became a legend.
The reality is more mundane. The Sunni Awakening — initiated by Sheikh Abdul Sattar Abu Risha and the Anbar tribes — preceded the surge. The tribes had already decided that Al-Qaeda in Iraq was their enemy, not the Americans. They made a tactical alliance with US forces to eliminate a common foe. Petraeus recognized the opportunity and exploited it. That deserves credit.
But then he did something else: he claimed the reduction in violence was the result of a counterinsurgency doctrine — of winning hearts and minds, of convincing Iraqis that their future lay with the coalition. This was false. As documented extensively at the time, the Iraqis were not persuaded by American values. They were making a temporary, pragmatic deal with the lesser evil. When the Americans left, the deal dissolved.
This pattern — mistaking a tactical truce for a strategic victory — is the first pillar of the Petraeus method.

## Afghanistan, 2010 — The Doctrine That Could Not Travel
In 2010, Petraeus went to Afghanistan to replicate the Iraq model. Analysts warned, publicly and in detail, that the conditions were not analogous: no Sunni Awakening, no tribal structure willing to break with the Taliban, no local partner capable of holding ground.
The warnings were ignored. The surge was implemented. The result was twenty years of war, trillions of dollars, thousands of American lives, and the return of the Taliban. Petraeus never accepted the failure. To this day, he argues that leaving was a mistake — that if it had been up to him, American troops would still be in Afghanistan today, in 2026, twenty-five years after the invasion.
This is the second pillar: the refusal to accept strategic defeat as a category.

## Ukraine, 2023 — The Prediction That Collapsed
Days before Ukraine’s summer counteroffensive, Petraeus told the BBC what would happen. He described combined arms operations: tanks protected by infantry, artillery suppressing the enemy, engineers breaching fortifications, air defense keeping Russian aircraft away, electronic warfare disrupting command and control, drones striking deep. He predicted Russian forces — “attrited” and exhausted — would “crack, crumble, and perhaps collapse.”
The counteroffensive failed. Ukraine lost tens of thousands of men and hundreds of Western vehicles. No breakthrough. No collapse. The same rhetorical device he now applies to Crimea — “the lights will go out, the water will stop, it will become a burden” — he applied to the Russian army in 2023. It did not happen.
This is the third pillar: the confidence to predict, and the absence of accountability when the prediction fails.

## Part II: The Current Claim — “There Is Still a Path”
In September 2026, Petraeus is again on the record. Ukraine, he says, can still win. The West should help “crush the Russian war economy.” He believes there is “a road to victory.”
This claim must be measured against the data we have compiled across our dossiers.

## Dossier #56 — Ucraina: The Demographic Reality
Ukrainian losses, as confirmed by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on 17 September 2026, stand at 27,000 killed and wounded per month — nearly 1,000 per day. This figure aligns with Russian estimates and has not been disputed by any Western government.
Ukraine has lost approximately half of its pre-war population — killed, displaced internally, or fled abroad. The mobilization is forced. Training is minimal. Men with no combat experience are sent to the front and killed within days. There is no rotation, no reconstitution, no strategic reserve.

## Dossier #82 — Droni e Fine Difese Aeree: The Material Reality
Ukraine’s air defense is collapsing. Patriot interceptors are depleted. Radar systems are being destroyed faster than they can be replaced. F-16s cannot be deployed near the front because Russian air defense and air superiority make it suicidal. The Ukrainian air force is effectively grounded.
Meanwhile, Russia is producing Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones at scale, and has begun deploying the Rassvet orbital constellation for real-time targeting. The drone war that the West bet on in 2025-2026 has not broken Russia. It has hardened it.

## Dossier #68 — Fronte Ucraino: The Operational Reality
Russian forces are advancing on multiple axes: Orikhiv, Dobropillya, the Kharkov cauldrons, the southern Donbas flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk conurbation. The Russian Defense Ministry reports 670 square kilometers and 27 settlements captured in September alone — the fastest pace of the year. Ukrainian counteroffensives, such as “Operation Vivaldi” in the Lyman area, have produced minimal territorial gains and no strategic effect.

## Dossier #13 — Dedollarizzazione: The Economic Reality
Twenty-one EU sanctions packages. Over 3,000 individual sanctions. The Russian economy has not collapsed. It has adapted. Trade with BRICS nations has shifted overwhelmingly to national currencies — 90% of Russia-BRICS trade is now in rubles, yuan, rupees, or other non-dollar currencies. Russia has reconverted its production capacity, developed new supply chains, and hardened its economy against external pressure.
The idea that “one more push” will break Russia is the geopolitical equivalent of chasing a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow.

## Part III: The Nuclear Dimension — The Unmentionable Fact
There is a fourth pillar to the Petraeus argument that is never stated but always present: the assumption that Russia will accept economic strangulation without resorting to its nuclear arsenal.
This assumption is not merely optimistic. It is strategically illiterate.
A nation with the largest nuclear arsenal on Earth — one that has explicitly revised its nuclear doctrine to allow for first use in response to existential threats — will not simply accept the destruction of its economy and the collapse of its state. If the West were to succeed in “crushing the Russian war economy,” the logical Russian response would not be capitulation. It would be escalation.
If America faced existential defeat, would it leave its missiles in their silos? Would it accept national destruction rather than use the weapons it built for exactly this scenario? No. No nation would.
This is not a controversial statement. It is the foundational logic of nuclear deterrence — a logic that has kept the world from great-power war for eighty years. To ignore it now, in the name of “helping Ukraine win,” is not strategy. It is denial.

## Part IV: The Ecosystem — Why the Microphone Never Moves
The most important question is not “Why is Petraeus wrong?” It is “Why is he still given a microphone?”
The answer lies in what we have documented in Dossier #99 — Propaganda UE and Dossier #89 — Controllo Media. The Western media ecosystem is not designed to produce accurate analysis. It is designed to produce narratives that sustain public support for policy. Petraeus is valuable not because he is right, but because he is reassuring. He tells audiences what they want to hear: that the sacrifice is not in vain, that victory is still possible, that the dead did not die for nothing.
This is the same mechanism that sustained the Afghanistan war for twenty years. The same mechanism that sustained the Iraq war after the WMD lies collapsed. The same mechanism that now sustains the Ukraine policy despite all evidence that it cannot succeed.
Dossier #110 — Strategia del Caos describes how fragmentation and confusion are used as instruments of power. The Petraeus phenomenon is a case study: the deliberate maintenance of a false narrative, sustained by a media ecosystem that rewards access over accuracy and confidence over truth.

## Part V: The Cost — Who Pays for False Hope
False hope is not a victimless crime.
Every month that Ukraine continues to fight on the promise of eventual victory, 27,000 more Ukrainians are killed or wounded. Every month, more territory is lost. Every month, more infrastructure is destroyed. Every month, the demographic catastrophe deepens.
And when the war ends — as it must, because it cannot continue indefinitely — the reckoning will come. As documented in Dossier #88 — Trappola di Zelensky and Dossier #107 — Mindichgate, the corruption, the offshore networks, the institutional warfare between NABU/SAPO and the Prosecutor General’s office — all of this will be exposed. Those who enabled the catastrophe, both in Kiev and in Western capitals, will face consequences.
Petraeus will not. He will write another book, accept another speaking fee, and be invited onto another panel. The microphone will be waiting.

## Verdict
David Petraeus was wrong about Iraq. Wrong about Afghanistan. Wrong about the 2023 counteroffensive. And he is wrong now about Ukraine.
[When a man has been catastrophically wrong three times, the burden is not on us to disprove him again — it is on the media to stop giving him a microphone.]
The real scandal is not that Petraeus says these things. It is that the system rewards him for saying them. False hope is a product. Petraeus is a salesman. And the currency is Ukrainian lives.

## Final Question
How many more Ukrainians must die before the West stops listening to the generals who lost Afghanistan?

reads.title: The greatest political con of our age
reads.subtitle: Why the West is really in decline – read the preface to The Fall of the West and watch the new book video
reads.body:
- Below is my preface to my new book The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It. you can get a copy here.
I’ve also included a sneak preview of the new book video. Let me know your thoughts!
Who holds power? How do they wield it, why, and to whose benefit? And when they fail, who is made to pay?
These questions have driven my writing from the beginning.
My first book, Chavs, looked at how working-class people suffered the costs of the Thatcherite economic experiment and, amid the wreckage, were mocked and demonized. My second book, The Establishment, turned to the perpetrators: a venal, self-insulating elite that rigged Britain’s political and economic order in its own interests, then escaped the consequences when that order began to fall apart.
This book tells a story of Western greed, power and hubris. It explores how the West has been sent into a tailspin by the elites who, some thirty-five years ago, once proclaimed its final triumph, and how their failure has today produced a global crisis. This crisis now affects us all, from those who live beyond the West’s increasingly militarized borders to its own citizens. Reporting it took me from Baghdad to Pittsburgh, Athens to Ramallah. Everywhere, I found a pattern that I had first encountered at home: elites whose decisions are driven by their own naked self-interest, and who protect themselves from the disastrous consequences of their own actions, presenting the world with the bill.
Share
We are encouraged to treat domestic and foreign policy as separate worlds. Factory closures, stagnating wages and decaying public services belong to one story; events in Afghanistan, Iraq, Russia, Palestine and the collapse of Western moral authority to another. But in fact, and as this book shows, they are not separate stories. The order that sucked wealth upwards at home imposed itself through brute force abroad. Distant wars came home as squandered resources, shattered legitimacy, repressive powers – and people displaced by violence, then demonized as the source of insecurity.
If we want to truly understand our crisis-ridden present, we need to pay attention to our history. Because while we might think that the likes of Donald Trump, Nigel Farage and Marine Le Pen are deviations from the political norm, if we look at the attitudes and actions of Western elites over time – and especially, as I argue here, since the collapse of the USSR in 1991 – we’ll see that there is nothing new under the sun. There is, rather, a through line of extreme ideas, normalized by the elites who have imposed them on us. Seen in this light, these figures are not aberrations: they are, to adopt a phrase from another deeply unstable age, morbid symptoms of an order in decline.
Which is why, in this book, I explore a number of flashpoints: from the West’s disastrous hubris of 1991 onward, when it truly believed it could rule the world, through the catastrophes of Afghanistan and Iraq, the financial crash of 2008 and the turbulent decades that followed, as the West’s rulers sought to impose the same economic model on their citizens again and again while expecting different results. The answer to every failure was more of what had failed. Throughout, as we’ll see, those same elites have forgotten their own ruinous history – or have deliberately chosen to ignore it, in the hope that we will do the same.
The idea that the West is in decline is fundamental to the political right. It blames the West’s ills on migrants, Muslims, refugees, trans people, and anyone else who can be cast as ‘other’. This narrative, which today infuses the discourse of Western politicians and the media, is a lie. And yet, the West’s decline is real – we feel it in our everyday lives – and there is no reason to expect it to be orderly or painless. We deserve to understand what truly caused it.
I wrote this book, then, to expose the greatest political con of our age. A deliberately inequitable, extractive economic model that stripped millions of security and comfort at home while unleashing blood and chaos abroad, foisted on us as established, unalterable fact, has brought the West and the wider world to crisis. What’s more, it has done this in a remarkably short period of time: a little under half a century. Yet our political and media classes have laboured to make this truth unsayable. Pointing to the wound, they protect those who inflicted it, along with the system that explicitly promises wealth and power to the few at the expense of the many. Having inflicted such extraordinary damage on the world and their own societies, those who rule the West have weaponized the resulting fear and fury to tighten their grip.
Much of what follows is bleak, because we have to confront the world as it is. But despair is not my intended conclusion. Humanity is capable of astonishing invention, creativity, solidarity and love, much of which has been suppressed by a political and economic order that has brought us to the edge. Only by understanding how we arrived here can we begin to imagine another, better future.
Order a copy here!

reads.title: Weekend Update #203: A Week Which Demonstrated Why Trump Is So Helpful To Russia
reads.subtitle: Operation Vivaldi; Russia Batters Ukraine At Range; Trump, Diesel And Ukrainian Energy Strikes.
reads.body:
Hi All,
This was a week which crystallized a number of things. When you add them all together, however, the key thing is that it demonstrated just how important the USA has become, through the Trump administration, in aiding the Russian war effort. This might have been hidden in all the distracting stardust being thrown in the air about the Graham Tariff Bill, or the recently announced (extremely weird) possible sale of some motley air defense capabilities to Ukraine (arrival uncertain and unknown). However, behind the stardust which the press seems too out of its depth to properly interrogate the reality is that the war has entered into a fascinating contrast.
Phillips’s Newsletter is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

On the land, where the Ukrainians were less reliant on the USA, it is the Ukrainians who are showing the initiative and dealing some substantial blows to Russian military strength. If what we are hearing about Operation Vivaldi is only partially true, the Ukrainians are continuing to advance in the combined operations of infantry and UAVs.

-
- Are Ukrainian Initiatives Paying Real Dividends Now?
In the ranged war, relying on Ukrainian sources, the Ukrainians are also showing some important strengths—when they concentrate on the right targets. However it is in their ranged campaign against the Ukrainians, aided enormously by the USA starving Ukraine of air defense (a great example of why relying on the weapons of another power is always so dangerous) that the Russians are being their most effective—and almost certainly will continue to be so for the upcoming winter.
Add it up, and what we see is that Russia’s area of initiative in the war has been enormously abetted by the USA and Donald Trump.
Share

Operation Vivaldi: Ukrainian Initiative On The Front Line
For weeks now there have been unconfirmed reports of an ongoing Ukrainian operation to push Russian forces back from outside of Lyman and, possibly, back into Luhansk. I’ve referred to this a few times, including in last weekend’s update. However, without formal Ukrainian confirmation, I did not want to say too much about it. At that point, we had some more general statements from Zelensky about Ukraine taking the initiative in the land war, but nothing specific.
This week, something changed and the Ukrainians started speaking specifically about their operation and even gave it a code name—Operation Vivaldi.
Vivaldi is being conducted, it seems, primarily by the 3rd Army Corps commanded by  Gen Andrii Biletskyi. Biletskyi confirmed this publicly on Sept. 15, saying the corps had launched Vivaldi under conditions of "maximum information silence." The name refers somewhat cheekily to Antonio Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons (shout out to Baroque music). That is because the Ukrainians are saying the operation has four stages—or “seasons” and we are only now in the first stage. Biletskyi also asked the public not to "give away the spoilers" because the operation still requires silence.
There was this excellent story in The Kyiv Independent, which quoted Biletskyi and which provides a good overview of what we know and, crucially, what we do not know about Vivaldi.
Since then there has been more information coming out from Ukrainian sources. Yesterday (September 19) there were some official statements released by the Chief of Staff and Deputy Commander of the Third Army Corps, Petro Horbatenko. You can read much of what he said in this report.
Horbatenko also described an ongoing operation making substantial progress.
“We will continue to make progress in a week. Accordingly, in the near future we will inform you about new details regarding the operation and new results regarding its success….We continue to move. What was announced is one figure, it will increase over time. New data on successes and liberated settlements will come, we just can't reveal and talk about everything yet. The enemy on this section is broken, disorganized. He is trying to transfer special forces units there to close the breakthrough, simply grinding them into "meat", without achieving any success,”
Horbatenko also confirmed that the Ukrainians are still in stage 1 of the four stages of Vivaldi. He, and others, have also spoken about 75 sq kms being liberated.
These latest reports also provided some detailed news about the military units involved, which are units of the 60th separate mechanized brigade, the 125th separate heavy mechanized brigade, the battalion tactical group of the 3rd assault brigade, the 3rd separate reconnaissance and 25th separate anti-tank battalions of the corps, the 66th separate mechanized brigade, the 85th tactical group of the 8th SSO regiment, the Artan special unit of the GUR, and the 10th border detachment "Dozor".
That is important as it shows the preparation the Ukrainians have put into this. This is a range of specialized units, all of which have seemingly been specially prepared for the operation.
And, not to reinforce this point every week, but it shows how the Ukrainians have been adapting their forces for the land war for a long time. In the Kyiv Independent story there was this description of how the Ukrainians are advancing in the modern battlespace and not suffering massive casualties.
Instead, territory is taken by small groups of infantry and assault teams that focus on concealment, while being supported constantly by drones that scan the battlespace, strike enemy targets and shelters, and drop supplies and ammunition to the teams on the ground.
This kind of extremely close and precise action, only possible if highly trained and motivated troops and drone forces can operate extremely well together. This minimizes the amount of time the attacking forces need to spend in the open, allowing them to move swiftly from point to point, take cover, and still be supplied.
It’s exactly what General Havrylov laid out as the intention 9 months ago—when the western media, led by its deeply flawed analytical community, was still saying Ukraine needed to draft more of its young population and send them to the front.
Now, with the Ukrainians keeping a lid on the specifics of the advance. Information about how much territory they have retaken is coming more from Russian sources than Ukrainian. And we need to be very careful with this. Rybar, a Russian source, has the Ukrainians crossing over into Luhansk Oblast.

-
- Ukrainian data also supports the idea that something significant is going on. There has been a notable comments on Russian tactics and casualties as part of the Vivaldi discussion. Deputy Commander of the 3rd Corps, Maksym Zhorin, talked about the lack of adaptation in the Russian military:
“In addition to the advance itself, we can say that during this operation a fairly large number of enemy officers were also destroyed and a fairly significant number of enemy personnel were taken prisoner. Perhaps, in recent years, this is the largest replenishment of the exchange fund that came from the Ukrainian side,”
Horbatenko was even more pithy on Russian losses, saying: “Russian tactics generally do not change. These are just meaty assaults.”
And Ukrainian claims of Russian casualties over the past week (this is for all fronts, not just Vivaldi) have spiked. The Ukrainian General Staff claimed 11,090 Russian personnel losses in the seven daily reports from 14 to 20 September 2026, an average of about 1,584 a day. Here is a breakdown.

-
- This is a crushing casualty rate, btw. If it were maintained for a month (30 days) it would be equal to 47,529. For 31 days we are talking over 49,000.
We must obviously be careful about not over-reacting to this. I dislike it intensely when people talk about a Russian “collapse” which makes it seem like the Ukrainians can start making swift advances. That still seems very unlikely in this battle space. Even large gaps in the line can be closed with drone forces and humans cannot survive for very long out in the open. So please rein such talk in.
However, the reality of this summer’s fighting seems to be this. Ukraine is demonstrating the capacity to take the initiative with new and better ways of fighting, which keep Ukrainian casualties down and ratchet Russian ones up. And the best thing about it is that the USA cannot help the Russians that much at this point—which is a major contrast to the next story.
Share

Russia Batters Ukraine At Range
The last week was actually a lighter week than the one before when it came to Russian ranged attacks on Ukraine. They launched attacks every night, but with a smaller number of systems than the seven days previously. Here is a table of the number of units attacking—mostly drones (which means Geran/Shaheds) from Sept 14-19. We do not have last night’s figures yet.

-
- This contrasts with the week before, when in one night alone there was a Russian attack with 453 drones.
The reality of the ranged war, even with these reduced attacks, remains the same however. Ukraine can do little to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. The attack on 17 September, for instance, the only example of the Russians making a large ballistic missile assault last week, saw the Ukrainians claiming that they could not intercept one of them. The Ukrainian Air Force listed only Shahed/Gerans and Banderols as being neutralized that night.
Note: Banderols are cruise missiles, not ballistic missiles.
And even with the reduced weight of attack, the Ukrainians were hit hard this week. The night of the ballistic missile attack saw Kyiv targeted, and possibly water infrastructure hit.
Indeed, this slower week could be a sign of the Russians stocking up for larger attacks in the fall and winter. They have a track record of doing that.
This is the reality. Ukraine, because of the US depriving it of Patriots. Even in the announcement yesterday that the US might be selling some air defense capability to Europe to pass on to Ukraine, there was no mention of Patriots. What was announced was some “possible” sale of deficient systems. Indeed, the press did not even know how to report what happened—as in this CBS report.
In a congressional notification, the State Department said that it made “a determination approving a possible Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Ukraine” for buying air defense development upgrades and related equipment and services.
According to the statement, the Ukrainian government requested to buy S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, as well as various launchers, counter-drone radars, trailers and spare parts.
My guess is that this is a political stunt by the Trump administration to look like it is doing something, when it is not. It will make no difference this winter.
And there we have it. Confirmation that, even on a relatively less damaging week, the big advantage that the Russians have is the one provided by the USA—which is doing nothing to help Ukraine in this vital area, and indeed is stringing the Ukrainians along and leaving them exposed.
Without this help, Putin and the Russians would be deprived of the strongest military card that they can play.
Share

## Trump, Diesel And Ukrainian Energy Strikes
Another area where the Ukrainians confirmed that they can be effective when not impeded in the USA, is their ongoing campaign against Russian fuel production. We have confirmation of that this week because Donald Trump came out and pleaded with the Ukrainians to do Putin a favor and stop attacking Russian refineries.
Things were so bad, that Trump begged once and lied twice—before the Ukrainians made it clear exactly what their position is. It was a fascinating “exchange” that started last Sunday (13 September). Then Trump said this to the press:
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia…We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting, that’s hurting the world.”
Even Trump has to know that it is his war with Iran that has so distorted the world oil market and done most of the work causing the steep rise in world diesel prices (which are pretty remarkable). One study is that the Iran War has caused three times the reduction in world diesel supplies as that caused by the Ukrainian campaign against Russian oil.
However, Trump decided to blame the Ukrainians and help Putin when discussing the issue publicly. And this was not all. On September 14, Trump doubled-down on his claim that the rise in diesel prices was Ukraine’s fault but, miraculously, claimed that he had gotten the Ukrainians and the Russians to agree to stop all energy attacks. He tweeted:
“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!…The World's Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran.”
It is still shocking how the President of the USA can just make up nonsense, spew it out, and some people will believe him.
We could see that this latest announcement was complete and total nonsense because on the subsequent days, both the Ukrainians and Russians went out and openly attacked energy targets. Overnight on 14–15 September, the Ukrainians hit the Syzran refinery and on Thursday 17 September a Ukrainian drone attack damaged an oil refinery at Yaroslavl (both refineries are still reportedly out of action).

-
- The Yaroslavl Refinery (Northeast Of Moscow) Is HitZelensky even openly contradicted Trump, in denying any deal had been reached. He said Ukraine might consider a deal, but as of now “Russia hasn’t stopped striking our energy sector… And our responses to them for this are tangible.”
It was a revealing exchange. As always for Trump, Ukraine is the baddies and Russia is to be protected. That will never change.
The more interesting thing is the confirmation of the seriousness of the Ukrainian campaign on Russian oil production. It is why this must be the key target of the Ukrainian ranged campaign. If the Ukrainians have no ability to defend themselves against Russian ballistic missiles because of the USA, the least they can do is not listen to the USA when the American president pleads with them to stop their most effective strategic campaign.
For now, they seem to have received the message.
Have a good rest of the weekend everyone.
Thanks for reading Phillips’s Newsletter! This post is public so feel free to share it.
