reads.title: The Saudis Fired a Chinese Missile. A Day Later Washington Blinked.
reads.subtitle: For two years Trump left the Riyadh ambassador chair empty. Within a day of the Saudi missile message, he rushed a nominee to the Senate. You read a signal by the move it forces, and this forced one.
reads.body:
Two days ago a video surfaced of a Chinese-made ballistic missile, allegedly fired by Saudi Arabia at the Houthis in Yemen. The missile either “crash-landed intact” or failed on impact, and that detail was the thing worth reading.
A missile that does not explode can be recovered, photographed, and passed around the world’s media. I wrote that this was NOT a “battlefield failure” but rather a “battlefield choice”. It was the choice to send a SIGNAL.
Riyadh, fed up with American inaction against the Ansarallah Houthis in Yemen, was telling Washington the loudest way it could that it has OTHER suppliers, OTHER options, OTHER patrons, if the United States will not act.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
An unexploded Chinese missile in a Saudi salvo is a sentence, and the sentence was: we do not have to wait for you.
How you confirm a SIGNAL, without the noise
You cannot confirm what a signal meant by asking. You confirm it by watching what the other side does next. A message that changes nothing was noise. A message that forces the other side to MOVE was received, understood, and taken seriously.
Leave a comment
Share
So the real test of the Saudi missile was never in the wreckage. It was in Washington’s response.

- If the United States shrugged, the missile was a coincidence and my read was wrong.

- If Washington moved, and moved fast, then the message had landed. Today Washington moved rapidly.
Subscribe now
Get 7 day free trial
Two years of an empty chair, filled in a day
The United States has NOT had a full-time, Senate-confirmed ambassador in Riyadh since the end of the Biden administration. For nearly two years, through the entire second Trump term and through this regional war, the most important American relationship in the Gulf has been run by “temporary American caretakers”. The chair at the top table in Riyadh sat empty, and Washington did not appear to mind.
Then, within a day of the Saudi missile message going viral and getting assessed by Washington, Trump moved to fill it. He nominated a new ambassador to the Kingdom and sent the nomination to the Senate. After twenty-plus months of leaving the post vacant, Washington suddenly needed its own voice in Riyadh, immediately.

-
- The speed is the answer to the question. Governments do NOT scramble a two-year-vacant nomination into a capital overnight for no reason. Something changed, and the thing that drove that change was likely the Chinese-made missile that landed in Yemen.
The selectivity is the harder tell…
Let me show you why I am confident in my reading, and I will do this by widening the lens and zooming out, because that is where my SIGNAL sharpens. Saudi Arabia was NOT the only Gulf capital Washington left without a confirmed ambassador.
The United States ran much of its Middle Eastern regional diplomatic bench empty through this war, posts sitting vacant or under caretakers across the Gulf. Of all of them, the one Washington rushed to fill first was the one that had just fired a Chinese-made missile to make a point.
Subscribe now
Give a gift subscription
Share
If Trump had filled every empty Gulf post at once, you could call it housekeeping and move on. He did not. He moved on the single capital that had just signaled it COULD look elsewhere. You do not rush a diplomat back into a relationship you ignored for two years unless that relationship just did something that alarmed you. The choice of which chair to fill first, and how fast, is the confession.
The exchange, move by move
Let me lay the sequence in order and the whole bargain is visible.

- First, Saudi frustration with American inaction against the Houthis. A client concluding its patron was not delivering.

- Second, the Chinese-made missile, fired and “conspicuously left intact”, a costly, deniable, unmistakable demonstration that Riyadh has another supplier and is willing to show it.

- Third, within 24 hours, Washington moving to put its own man back in the room after ignoring the relationship for the entire term.
The missile said, we can drift toward Beijing. The rushed nomination is Washington answering, please do not. Between a great power and its most important regional client, that is a complete exchange.
One side raised the cost of being taken for granted. The other paid, fast, to bring the temperature down.
Why this is the story under the headlines
The relationship this exposes is not the automatic partnership it is sold as. It is being renegotiated in real time, through signals and slights, and Riyadh just showed it holds more leverage than Washington likes to admit.
For decades the assumption was simple: Saudi Arabia needed American protection more than America needed Saudi cooperation. That assumption is what let Washington leave the ambassador’s chair empty for two years without cost.
The missile tested it and the rushed nomination answered it.
Riyadh now has a second patron it can gesture toward, a Chinese arsenal it can fire in public, and the demonstrated ability to make Washington jump. The dependence runs both ways now, and the Kingdom knows it.
That is what the episode reveals when you read the response instead of the rhetoric. When a client fires a rival power’s weapon to get your attention, and you answer by rushing back a diplomat you could not be bothered to send for two years, the client is not the one who blinked.

reads.title: A War Over Two Countries' Heating Is About to Reach Every European Power Bill. Here Is the Chain.
reads.subtitle: US diesel just passed six dollars. Every refinery Ukraine burns tightens global fuel, every Russian grid strike raises Europe's risk premium, and the reactors and refugee routes sit at the chain end.
reads.body:
The single most important variable in the Russia-Ukraine war this autumn is not a peace plan, a weapons package, or an election. It is the thermometer. It reads around 10 degrees Celsius (or 50 Fahrenheit) across much of the northern hemisphere today.
In roughly a month the first snow falls, and the winters in Russia and Ukraine are among the harshest inhabited places on earth. That temperature drop is what reshapes the war, because it turns heat and power from an economic asset into a survival requirement, and it hands both sides a target that was always there but never mattered this much. Here is what it forces, and why this winter is different from the three before it.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Get 7 day free trial
The shared vulnerability built into the concrete
Start with the physical weakness both countries carry, because it is identical on both sides of the line. Soviet urban planners built these cities around “combined heat and power” (CHP) plants, single facilities that generate electricity for the grid and pipe hot water straight into apartment blocks for heating.
It is efficient engineering and it is a structural liability when you are at war with a determined enemy. Both sides are determined. Knock out one CHP plant and you take the lights and the heat from tens of thousands of households in one strike. There is no distributed backup, because the system was never designed for one.

-
- This is an example of Combined Heat Power Plant used across many Soviet-influenced states to create warm water for city or district heating. This is the same system used in Russia and Ukraine now.Russia has exploited this against Ukraine for three straight winters, weaponizing the cold to break civilian morale, and it has already announced fresh mass strikes on Ukraine’s grid for this one. That much is the war people already know.
What changed: Ukraine can now answer in kind
Here is the shift that makes THIS specific winter dangerous in a way the last three were not. For three winters Ukraine COULD absorb the energy war but could NOT return fire. This year it can. Ukraine’s long-range drones and missiles have overwhelmed Russian air defenses repeatedly, forcing fuel rationing across Russia and setting refineries alight deep inside the country. More than 60 strikes on at least 24 Russian refineries have pushed Moscow to ban diesel exports and ration fuel at home, and US diesel has passed $6+ dollars a gallon on the knock-on effects.
The same Soviet-era CHP design that makes Ukraine vulnerable makes Russia vulnerable, and for the first time Ukraine has the reach to hit Russian heat and power the way Russia has hit Ukraine’s.
Zelensky has said it plainly: if Russia causes Ukrainian blackouts, Ukraine will respond in kind. The Kremlin understands the symmetry has arrived. So does Washington, which is why Trump is now publicly telling Zelensky to stop striking Russian energy. When the patron of one side starts begging the client to stop hitting the other side’s fuel, the strikes are working.

> SIGNAL, not noise is a reader supported platform, please consider becoming a paid subscriber if you find my work insightful or if it resonates with you.
Kindly sharing, like, and restack to help amplify this SIGNAL.
The order of effects

- The immediate effect is a race. As temperatures fall, each side has every incentive to take out the other’s heat and power before its own is taken. The value of a CHP plant as a target climbs with every degree that drops, so the tempo of energy strikes accelerates on both sides at once, and it accelerates fastest exactly when the cold is worst and the civilian cost is highest.

- The second-order effect is political, and it lands inside Russia for the first time. For three years the war was something that happened to Ukrainian civilians and to distant Russian soldiers. This winter the freezing and the blackouts reach Russian households too.

A Russian family without heat in January is a domestic political fact that three years of a faraway war never produced, and it changes the weather inside Russia in a way no battlefield map has. Putin has kept the war insulated from the ordinary Russian’s daily life. That insulation is what Ukraine’s reach now threatens.

- The third-order effect is that the campaign locks itself in. Energy strikes are cheap, deniable, and devastating, the best cost-exchange either side has found in four years of war. Once both are doing them at scale, neither can be the one to stop first, because stopping first concedes the winter to the other.

So the exchange runs until the thaw, not because anyone chooses it, but because the structure of the standoff removes the option of stopping. This is the systems trap underneath the whole winter: a self-reinforcing exchange that no single decision can end, because the first to lower its weapon loses.
The pause nobody is naming, and why it is not peace
Now the counterintuitive part, and it is the one most observers will misread. Do not be surprised if the energy strikes go quiet at some point this winter, and do not mistake that quiet for a step toward peace.
The Kremlin has been consistent that it does NOT want a ceasefire or a pause. It wants a full settlement that locks in its war aims. So any lull on the energy front is not diplomacy. Both sides need their own heat and grid intact to get their own people through the cold, so at the coldest moments they may tacitly hold fire on the one target that would freeze their own population too.
And if you read it through game theory like I do, this is not cooperation. It is mutual deterrence imposed by the season, the same logic that keeps two nuclear powers from a first strike, scaled down to a heating plant. A pause driven by shared vulnerability is not a move toward settlement. It is a ceasefire the weather enforces, and it breaks the instant one side calculates it can win the exchange, that it can take more of the other’s heat than it loses of its own. The quiet, if it comes, is the most fragile kind, held up by nothing but symmetry, and symmetry is exactly what a battlefield edge destroys.
The risks almost no one is pricing in
Follow the second and third-order effects outward and the tail risks come into view, the ones that turn a war over two countries’ heating into something continental.

- The first is nuclear. Ukraine’s grid instability threatens the cooling systems at facilities like Zaporizhzhia and Khmelnytsky, and cooling depends on external power. A strike near a reactor, by either side or by accident, in a winter when both are hammering the grid the plants draw from, is the tail risk that converts an energy war into a nuclear-safety emergency across the continent.

The colder it gets and the harder both sides strike the grid, the thinner the margin at the reactors becomes.

- The second is the refugee wave. A hard blackout winter pushes another surge of Ukrainians west, into a Europe already strained on migration and already bracing for its own high winter energy prices.

The people fleeing the cold arrive in countries getting colder and more expensive at the same moment, which stacks the pressure exactly where European politics is most brittle.

- The third is Europe’s own exposure, and it is the systems point that ties the whole thing together. Every refinery Ukraine burns tightens the global diesel market, which is why US diesel is already at a record and why Trump is publicly alarmed. Every Russian strike on Ukraine’s grid raises Europe’s power-risk premium.

A war fought over the heating of two countries reaches, through the energy market, into the utility bill of every European household in the coldest months of the year. The front line is in Ukraine. The cost lands in Berlin, Warsaw, and Rome, and it lands hardest when the cold is worst.
What this forces
Put the pieces together and the winter is not a lull the war takes. It is the weapon both sides are about to reach for. The temperature converts a dormant vulnerability into the decisive front, symmetry of reach turns it into a two-way exchange for the first time, the structure of the standoff locks that exchange in until the thaw, and the knock-on runs through the reactors, the refugee routes, and the European grid. The war is not winding down for winter. Winter is what escalates it.
Watch the thermometer, not the negotiating table. The negotiating table has been empty for months and will stay empty, because Moscow wants a settlement it cannot yet impose and Kyiv will not sign one that erases it.
The thermometer, by contrast, is about to move, and when it does, it moves both armies toward the same set of targets at the same time. The most dangerous phase of this war is not being decided by diplomats. It is being scheduled by the season.

reads.title: Mahmoud Khalil Sues Columbia University Over Persistent Anti-Palestinian Discrimination
reads.subtitle: Khalil and other graduates filed a federal civil complaint accusing Columbia University and SIPA Dean Keren Yarhi-Milo of Title VI violations.
reads.body:
- PWG students pose for a photograph after the press conference on Monday, September 14. Photo: Areeba Fatima.Mahmoud Khalil, Mohammed Ibrahim Zubairi, and other members of the Palestine Working Group (PWG) at Columbia’s School of International and Public Affairs (SIPA) filed a federal civil complaint on Monday accusing the university of failing to protect Palestinian, Arab, and Muslim students from doxxing and harassment. Columbia suspended PWG—the last remaining named student organization with “Palestine” in its name—in September 2025.
The complaint names SIPA Dean Keren Yarhi-Milo, who was born in Israel and served in Israeli intelligence during her mandatory military service, claiming she helped contribute to a hostile environment on campus by enacting discriminatory policies and ignoring repeated reports of severe and coordinated harassment against Palestinian, Arab, and Muslim students as far back as 2019.
Speaking to the press, Khalil said the university hired private investigators to investigate him, a Columbia graduate student, while he led negotiations between protesters and the university administration during the 2024 pro-Palestine campus encampments that called for the university to disclose and divest from Israel. In March 2025, ICE agents abducted Khalil from his campus residence despite his status as a permanent resident. He spent 104 days in a Louisiana immigration jail, missing the birth of his first child before he was released in June 2025 by a federal judge who ruled that his arrest and detention likely violated the Constitution. Since then, the university has reached out to him only once—to ask him to leave his campus housing.
“We are suing Columbia because of its blatant disregard for our safety and well-being,” Khalil told Drop Site News. “Columbia put us through hell over the past three years,” Khalil said the university administration joined pro-Israel groups in targeting the Palestinian movement on campus.
Campus Public Safety officers attempting to remove Mahmoud Khalil from campus just a few days before ICE abducted him from Columbia property. Video: Ibrahim Zubairi.
The suit is just the latest against Columbia’s administration over its policies around the pro-Palestine student encampments. Last month, a group of Palestinian students and faculty filed a lawsuit against Columbia alleging that the university engaged in “anti-Palestinian discrimination and fostered a hostile learning and work environment.” In February 2025, three students filed a complaint against the school administration for their suspensions related to their pro-Palestine activism on campus, claiming the university violated its own policies during the disciplinary process and that the university targeted the students for their views.
Don’t miss a story. Subscribe to Drop Site today:
Mohammed Ibrahim Zubairi, a SIPA graduate who succeeded Khalil as PWG president, was likewise accused of being intolerant and aggressive by other students after calling the U.S. deportation process violent. “An American, a white student, basically accused me of being aggressive and told me to check my violence at the door,” he said.
Zubairi told Drop Site News he was treated like he was not an “acceptable or tolerable Muslim on campus” because of his speech. The lawsuit also states another incident where Dean Yarhi-Milo directly expressed repulsion over Zubairi’s allegiance to Palestine despite not being from there.
Speaking to the crowd outside the university gates, Khalil asserted, “Dean Yarhi-Milo is not only a terrible administrator, is not only a failed dean but a manipulative one who weaponizes her identity to shield herself from legitimate concerns and criticisms.”
When students reported doxxing and harassment, according to the plaintiffs, Yarhi-Milo refused to acknowledge their complaints and instead accused them of destroying campus culture. While she was engaged in organizing rapid support for Israeli students and their gatherings, Palestinian students said they had to wait several weeks for approval despite repeated requests.
Yarhi-Milo serves on Columbia’s executive board and co-leads SIPA’s Institute of Global Politics (IGP) alongside former Secretary of State and Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton, according to the university’s website. In a conversation last year, Clinton recalled meeting a woman from the Israeli military’s Unit 8200 in October 2023 who told her she wanted to grow up to be like Yarhi-Milo.
Students say the institute’s policies reflect a longstanding pattern of prejudice against Arab and Muslim students on campus. Another IGP leader, Jacob Lew, told Israeli general Amos Gilead in a recorded conversation in June 2024, “We’re not of the view that there is a famine [in Gaza].” Lew has also repeated the claim that Hamas uses civilians as human shields.
Layla Saliba, a graduate of Columbia’s School of Social Work who now helps underprivileged New Yorkers find affordable housing and healthcare, told Drop Site that students faced hate crimes with no accountability from the administration. She said one student created a “nuke map” of Gaza and posted it publicly on social media. “They had a map of Gaza, and they listed specific locations that they thought should be targeted with nuclear bombs,” she said. “The same student also publicly stated that all Palestinian men over the age of twelve should be executed.”
Saliba continued,  “Students were having their hijabs ripped off, students were being called terrorists,” she said. “We had university professors publicly calling students terrorists on their social media platforms, doxxing students.”
In October 2023, students observed doxxing trucks displaying PWG members’ full names and photos on digital screens, labeling them “Columbia’s Leading Antisemites.” When PWG students reported the doxxing trucks to the Yarhi-Milo, she reacted with hostility and accused the students of being “harmful to campus culture.”
Bhavana Bellamkonda, another plaintiff and a former PWG board member, described a pattern of physical hostility and verbal abuse. Bellamkonda was doxxed by Accuracy in Media, a right-wing nonprofit that built a website revealing her name, photograph, and school.
During a Columbia alumni weekend in June 2024, she said, “We had a Columbia alumni yelling things at participants of the encampments, including saying that they hoped that participants of the encampment were raped.”
The suit alleges that a research assistant to Yarhi-Milo, called Bellamkonda, “our resident terrorist,” threatened her with physical violence for wearing a keffiyeh.

-
- Doxxing trucks spotted near Columbia University campus. Photos were presented in the case file.Khalil and other plaintiffs are demanding the full reinstatement of the Palestine Working Group as an officially recognized student organization, monetary damages (determined at trial), a jury trial, and a court injunction enjoining the university and the SIPA dean from discriminating against Arab, Palestinian, or Muslim students.
“This case is Mahmoud’s first opportunity to ask the court to offer accountability for all that he endured and all the discrimination that he faced,” said Brittany Finley, a civil rights attorney representing Khalil.
“While he was in ICE detention, [Columbia] kept targeting [PWG members]. They were scared, they were afraid because their friend had been picked up off campus property and put in an ICE detention center,” she said.
William Reynolds, another attorney representing Zubairi, Khalil, and the other plaintiffs, said he hopes the lawsuit will hold the university accountable for creating a hostile environment. “They were targeted disproportionately for their speech, they were disproportionately targeted for their ethnicity and their support of Palestine,” he said.
Speaking to the crowd outside the university gates, Khalil said, “President Mnookin, you must do the right thing and fire the disgraced dean of SIPA, Dean Keren Yarhi-Milo. What we are asking for is very simple: equal treatment.”

reads.title: Got Oxy? How Michigan’s Mike Rogers Helped Fuel the Opioid Crisis
reads.subtitle: The Republican Senate candidate spent 10 years in Congress as Pharma’s point man working to push prescription opioids.
reads.body:
As a reader-funded independent news outlet, we operate free from the influence of governments, advertisers, and corporate backers. This is essential to our mission: to report on what matters most, beholden only to the truth. In that spirit, we made a commitment to ensure that our journalism is free for everyone, not locked behind a paywall. But that means we rely on the voluntary support of our community of readers. Please consider making a tax-deductible donation to support our work today.

-
- Mike Rogers, candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas on September 10, 2026. Photo by Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images.Subscribe now
The last time Mike Rogers made a run for the Senate, his congressional record on opioids weighed him down. Although his Democratic opponent, Rep. Elissa Slotkin, mostly avoided the issue, surrogates like state Sen. Rosemary Bayer gave him no quarter, pounding the former Republican congressman and FBI agent. “Since 2021, one Michigander has died every four hours from opioid use, but in Congress, Mike Rogers was a leading advocate for increased access to opioids,” Bayer told a local reporter.
Now running for another open Senate seat, Rogers is again attempting to escape and rewrite his long and well-illuminated record on opioids. When the local news site Michigan Bridge asked the candidate if he “wished he had taken a different approach to the opioid issue while in Congress,” Rogers deflected, saying, “I understand that question is couched in a way that makes it sound terrible. I just disagree with the premise of the question.” Elsewhere he has sought to pre-empt discussion of his opioid record by decrying Democrats who are “spreading lies,” and by retroactively distorting and shrinking his work on the issue beyond recognition. “I voted to allow Americans who are suffering from debilitating pain to have access to the treatment they need to live comfortably, while keeping safeguards that prevent overprescription and addiction,” he said.
Rogers’ current Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, has been more aggressive than Slotkin, but is proving sloppy in the execution. He has mischaracterized Rogers as a former registered “lobbyist” for pharma and has anachronistically described his onetime signature bill, the Pain Care Policy Act, first introduced in 2003, as “the legislation that kicked off the opioid epidemic.”
But El-Sayed’s errors do not disturb the greater truth in the charges. It is a matter of record that Rogers spent most of his 12 years in Congress tied at the policy hip with opioid-producer front-groups dedicated to expanding “pain awareness” and “reducing barriers to pain care.” During his first four terms representing Michigan’s 8th District, Rogers staked his name to an industry wish-list to expand and loosen access to opioids. This advocacy was no one-off vote, but a strategic and persistent focus of his career, maintained throughout the prescription-opioid epidemic’s years of galloping growth.
The Rogers campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

-
- OxyContin pills, prescription only pain medication. Photo by Lawrence K. Ho/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images.

## “The 5th Vital Sign”
In 2001, the year Rogers entered Congress, 611 Michiganders and 5,528 Americans died by opioid overdose. These numbers signaled the continuation of a steady rise in fatal overdoses since the late-90s, with the sharpest spikes occurring in rural America. But even if one chose to downplay or ignore the troubling data, no public official could claim ignorance about a brewing national opioid crisis. During Rogers’ second month in office, the New York Times published a bombshell report on why “harried police detectives in dozens of rural areas in Eastern states are combating what they say is a growing wave of drug abuse involving a potent painkiller.” A few months after that, West Virginia’s attorney general filed the first lawsuit against Purdue Pharma for its marketing of Oxycontin, which the Food and Drug Administration soon slapped with a “black box warning.”
“In Michigan, we had a good sense that the dial was turning from heroin to overprescribed opioids by the early 2000s,” said Jonathan Stoltman, director of the Opioid Policy Institute in Grand Rapids, Michigan. “There were already janky local clinics in operation, and people were going across the border to pill mills in places like Toledo, Ohio. There were any number of data points where you could see what was happening—including Eminem songs.”
Yet in September 2003, with overdose deaths continuing to rise, Rogers held a press conference to announce his sole sponsorship of a bill called the National Pain Care Policy Act. His first signature piece of legislation, Rogers introduced the bill flanked by Dr. Dick Payne, director of the American Pain Society, an industry-funded group notorious for its 1996 advocacy of the concept of pain as the “the 5th Vital Sign,” considered a landmark development in the opioid crisis. Payne praised Rogers’ bill for tackling what he called “the leading health problem in America today.” The language used by both men tracked closely to the sales, educational, and lobbying lines of the same opioid manufacturers that underwrote the American Pain Society to the tune of $1 million in traceable funding during the early 2000s. Most of the group’s operating budget came from Purdue Pharma, whose CEO Richard Sackler described in private correspondence his company’s “good relationship” with the Society. Purdue and other opioid-makers also funded the American Pain Foundation, another multi-million dollar front group that “piloted mobilization strategies” and contributed to “strategic planning” for Rogers’ Pain Care Act, according to a presentation given at Purdue Pharma’s headquarters in September of 2004.

-
- An industry presentation from the American Pain Foundation, taking credit for “strategic planning” and lobbying on behalf of Mike Rogers’ legislation.Rogers’ bill arrived at a unique moment in the opioid crisis. Although the problem was spreading and garnering more urgent attention in the media, opioid producers and their sales teams were still living high on the hog and remained arrogant about their ability to keep the good times rolling. Industry executives, still years away from copping plea deals and signing billion-dollar settlements, believed they could keep expanding the opioids market while deflecting responsibility for the resulting public health emergency onto its victims. Rogers’ proposed Pain Care Act embodied this audacity. Supported by a Pain Society-funded radio and TV campaign, it sought to use the full might of the U.S. health bureaucracy to strengthen the intellectual and policy foundations of opioid normalization, access, and use.

## Reducing Barriers
Reflecting the urgency of what it called the nation’s “leading health problem,” Rogers’ bill gave the White House until June 2004 to convene a Conference on Pain Care, chaired by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, in order to “increase the recognition of pain as a significant public health problem” and “identify barriers to appropriate pain care [and] establish an agenda for action in both the public and private sectors that will reduce such barriers.” [Emphasis added.] The bill further called for a federally funded national awareness campaign to “educate consumers, patients, their families, and other caregivers [about] the right of patients to have their pain promptly assessed, appropriately treated, and regularly reassessed, and to have their treatment adjusted if needed.”
To help the public overcome any possible reticence in claiming their “right” to pain treatment, the campaign was to stress “the adverse physical, psychological, and financial consequences that can result if pain is not appropriately diagnosed or treated.”
Rogers’ bill did not specify a slogan for this campaign, but “Got Oxy?” would have been a catchy option.
To efficiently “reduce barriers” to pain treatment, the Pain Care Act proposed the creation of a National Center for Pain and Palliative Care Research—on par with the National Cancer Institute—that would manage six regional pain research centers. The new institutions would oversee an ongoing research program whose orbit of influence would include “schools, colleges, and universities, including schools of medicine and osteopathy, schools of pharmacy and pharmacology, schools of nursing, schools of dentistry, schools of physical therapy, schools of occupational therapy, and schools of clinical psychology, comprehensive health care centers and systems, and specialized centers of pain research or treatment.”
To get this infrastructure up and running, Rogers called for apportioning $40 million annually through 2007. Much of this money would be distributed as grants for professional school training programs focused on “applicable laws on controlled substances, including the degree to which misconceptions concerning such laws or the enforcement thereof may create barriers to patient access to appropriate and effective pain care.”
The flowchart at the center of Rogers’ bill was based on ideas that industry was at the same time promoting through its echo chamber of front groups and corrupt medical institutions and thought leaders. Expressed in a blizzard of proposals for restructuring the NIH, the thrust of the message was simple: medical guidelines were still too conservative in determining the conditions that merited prescription opioids. The Pain Care Act would rectify this by funding federal research centers to develop treatment options for “all types of pain and pain-related symptoms; and conditions for which no widely accepted treatment options are yet available.”
Sometimes the bill spoke of new “conditions,” and sometimes it spoke of new “populations,” but they were basically interchangeable. “In designing the public awareness campaign,” proposed Section V of the Pain Care Act, “the Secretary shall take into account the need to reach underserved populations who are disproportionately under-treated for pain,” including the elderly (Medicare Advantage programs) and veterans (the VA system).
A lawsuit filed by the state of Oklahoma against Johnson & Johnson in 2019 would uncover documents revealing that the industry did not depend on the passage of Rogers’ bill to target these “underserved populations.” An initiative organized by Janssen Pharmaceuticals, called the “Imagine the Possibilities Coalition,” ran unbranded campaigns to increase opioid use among the same populations named in Rogers’ bill, including veterans, children (through targeting school nurses and sports coaches), and the elderly.
Despite the industry-funded media campaign and the best expert testimony money could buy, the Pain Care Policy Act stalled in committee throughout 2004. But Rogers pushed on. He reintroduced the bill in 2005, as the number of Americans killed by opioids passed 16,000. When the bill died a second time, Rogers and his industry allies decided to regroup and reload, if not rebrand, before they tried again.

## An Epidemic of Addiction
Before introducing his bill a third time, Rogers co-sponsored another called the National All Schedules Prescription Electronic Reporting Act of 2005. The law, signed by George W. Bush in August of 2005, established a national prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) with the goal of identifying and stopping sketchy and unnecessary prescriptions. But the bill ignored the drug companies, who were already responsible for tracking their shipments, and who knew better than anyone when and where overprescribing was occurring.
PDMPs are “patient surveillance tools above all,” in the words of medical sociologist Elizabeth Chiarello, and serve to shift attention back to individuals, not the institutions that were driving the crisis in the 2000s. The companies understood this, and saved their lobbying fire to defeat every attempt that decade to enforce production caps and restrictive prescribing guidelines.
“The PDMP law did not address the supply-side of the equation, and by supporting it Rogers was still running cover for big pharma,” said Stoltman of the Opioid Policy Institute. “The data base was used to kick people unceremoniously off opioids after they were addicted, with no plan or attempt to move them into treatment. A lot of people think this was a big driver of the transition to heroin and the second wave of the crisis.”
To this day, Rogers points to his support for the PDMP Act as proof of his commitment to address the opioid addiction crisis. He has less to say about his other activities in the mid-2000s, such as his headlining the debut event of the Pain Care Forum, an industry front group hatched to rally support for the Pain Care Policy Act.
The Pain Care Forum announced itself to the world in a June 2006 briefing on Capitol Hill titled “The Epidemic of Pain in America.” In a now-familiar combo, the group was the brainchild of Purdue Pharma’s chief lobbyist in Washington, Burt Rosen, and deployed Rogers as its congressional face. Cosponsored by the American Pain Society, the Pain Care Forum was designed to build support for Rogers’ bill and reframe the spiraling opioid crisis as a familiar story of bad apples and addicts, rather than an epic tale of corruption and moral rot implicating drug companies, the house of medicine, Congress, and regulatory agencies responsible for protecting the public. At the Rogers event, speakers informed Congress that the “appropriate use of opioid medications like oxycodone is safe and effective and unlikely to cause addiction in people who are under the care of a doctor and who have no history of substance abuse.”
The Pain Care Forum would go on to spend $750 million amplifying this message and pushing for Rogers’ bill. This money was dispersed along a number of fronts, writes Chris McGreal in “American Overdose,” including “pushing policies, writing legislation, and funding elected officials in Washington, DC, and across the country to promote opioids and oppose curbs on prescribing.” When the covers were peeled back, McGreal writes, the forum was revealed to be little more than “a web of interwoven corporate interests and specialists in their pay.” Its donors were a murderer’s row of opioid producers, Purdue, Endo, and Abbott—Purdue’s main subcontractor in selling OxyContin.
With media support and coaching from multiple front groups, Rogers reintroduced the Pain Care Policy Act in 2007, only to see it die a third time. In 2009, he tried again with the co-sponsorship of California Democrat Lois Capps, a pharma favorite who had received $87,750 from Pain Care Forum backers since 2006, and Utah’s Orrin Hatch, who like Rogers had received at least $300,000 from drug makers during roughly the same period.
The law once again failed to clear the Senate, but its supporters saw opportunity in the impending passage of Obama’s healthcare reforms. After nearly seven years of defeat, they succeeded in stuffing a fair amount of Rogers’ bill into the Affordable Care Act of 2010.
The biggest elements involved the creation of two official committees: the Interagency Pain Research Coordinating Committee and a 18-member expert panel tasked with producing a study for the non-profit Institute of Medicine (IOM), which carried the imprimatur of the National Academies.
Because the drug makers had so thoroughly seeded the pain research ecosystem, both committees were staffed by influential figures drenched in industry largesse. The Interagency Pain Research Coordinating Committee featured at least five members with strong industry connections who would go on to oppose restrictions on opioid prescribing as “ridiculous,” “horrible,” and “shortsighted.” The IoM committee was also chock-o-block with recipients of heavy industry funding, including Richard Payne of the American Pain Society, and academic researcher Myra Christopher, whose chair was endowed with a $1.5 million grant from Purdue Pharma.

## The Opioid Lobby
The IoM released its report, “Relieving Pain in America,” in 2011, the year fatal opioid overdoses surpassed 17,000 and Purdue Pharma’s OxyContin revenues reached $3 billion.
The authors understood that it was no longer 2003, and the document contains an obligatory reference to the need to expand the menu of non-drug pain treatments. But the drug makers and their front groups embraced the study because it delivered a gilded, National Academies-blessed validation of a foundational industry estimate and talking point: that more than 100 million American adults lived with chronic pain, at an annual cost to the economy of $635 billion. According to McGreal, Purdue Pharma’s $150,000 campaign promoting “Relieving Pain in America” focused on these numbers. The wider opioid lobby also “swung its spotlight onto the headline figure of 100 million people in pain, claiming that this was the ‘real epidemic,’ not addiction.”
As summarized years later by the New York Times, the IoM’s 100 million figure “proved to be highly inflated [but] gave drugmakers another talking point for aggressive sales campaigns, primed doctors to prescribe opioids at an accelerating rate and influenced the Food and Drug Administration to approve at least one highly potent opioid.”
Some critics said as much at the time of the report’s release. Dr. Nathaniel Katz, a pain specialist who chaired various FDA advisory committees, blasted “Relieving Pain in America” as “a political statement” that translated “compassion for patients with pain…into a model for opiate prescribing.” Even at this late hour, however, it promised industry yet another boost, so long as the government was still asleep at the wheel. The FDA commissioner at the time, Margaret Hamburg, touted the IoM study’s numbers upon its release, only to be later named in a lawsuit alleging she and her husband profited directly from her approval of new drugs, including opioids, through their joint portfolio of pharmaceutical stocks.
The IoM report demonstrated that the industry’s investments—in politicians like Rogers, front groups like the Pain Society, and influential researchers and medical organizations like those represented on the new Pain commissions—could still pay dividends. But opioids were increasingly seen in exactly the light industry most feared: not as a criminal or legal issue, but as a full-blown public health crisis. Following the release of the controversial report, Rogers may have felt that his job was done, or realized that being the face of Pharma’s pain agenda was a bad thing for an ambitious politician to be. Whatever the cause, in 2011 he pivoted fully to national security and became chair of the House Committee on Intelligence, a post he would hold until 2015, when he left Congress to consult for tech and defense companies.
It was a well-timed parachute jump. Within months, the American Pain Foundation self-dissolved following the Senate Finance Committee’s announcement that it was launching an investigation into industry influence on opioid advocacy groups. (The American Pain Society would shutter its doors four years later.) In 2012, as Rogers was forcefully turning the page on his congressional career, 52,000 Americans overdosed on opioids, including 2,000 Michiganders.
By the time Rogers announced his first Senate campaign in 2023, the groups he’d worked with so closely during the 2000s were gone, but not forgotten. Their names routinely appeared in the $50 billion raft of opioid lawsuits being settled across the country.
“Rogers spent years in Congress pushing a bill that was clearly about training professionals to pump out more opioids, and worked behind the scenes with the companies that contributed to the crisis to get it passed,” says Stoltman of the Opioid Policy Institute. “At the end of the day, he was either stupid, an industry stooge, or both.”

reads.title: Supreme Court blocks Trump voting restrictions; UN Security Council to meet on Bab al-Mandab; Russia fires on Danish helicopter
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: September 15, 2026
reads.body:
- Fishermen motor past a commercial vessel anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandab on September 12, 2026. Photo by AFP via Getty Images.Tuesday, September 15, 2026 – Saudi-led coalition strikes kill three, including two children, in Yemen as fighting continues around Taiz. Ansarallah says Saudi Arabia launched 54 airstrikes on Yemen; Riyadh says attacks wounded 13 civilians. Saudi Arabia issues “potential danger” alerts across multiple areas, including Mecca. Ansarallah says it will halt attacks if Saudi ends Yemen campaign. AP: Repairs to key Saudi pipeline could take 3-5 weeks. UN Security Council to hold emergency meeting on Bab al-Mandab. Bloomberg: UK Prime Minister considering Saudi requests for a “range of military support” against Ansarallah. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claims downing of fourth U.S. MQ-1 drone over Hormuz. IRGC says supertanker exploded after hitting naval mine in Hormuz. Iran security chief: No talks with U.S. until Tehran’s conditions are met. U.S. watchdog confirms weapons shortages after months of war with Iran. U.S. Energy Secretary claims Hormuz oil flow tops 10 million b/d despite lower independent estimates. U.S. seeks forfeiture of $61 million in cryptocurrency tied to “Iranian military’s black-market oil sales.” Iran’s foreign minister to visit China Wednesday, days before President Xi Jinping’s U.S. trip. Israeli attacks kill at least three Palestinians in Gaza City and Jabalia. Israeli forces kill Palestinian man in occupied West Bank as settlers attack residents, steal livestock. Israeli strike that killed two Palestinians also damaged MSF bus and injured aid worker. Israeli restrictions force Gaza hospitals to place multiple premature babies in single incubators. World Health Organization to halt diesel supplies to more than 20 Gaza health facilities. UN: Hundreds of bodies recovered from Gaza rubble raise fresh war crimes concerns. Israeli forces kill 70-year-old teacher and destroy school in attacks across southern Lebanon during “ceasefire.” Lebanon says Israeli attacks caused up to $4 billion in damage, seeks Arab support for reconstruction. Supreme Court blocks Trump plan to overhaul mail-in voting ahead of midterm. Whistleblower report alleges DHS agents may have broken state laws in noncitizen voter hunt. Trump dismisses AI safety warnings as a “hoax,” rejects calls for guardrails. Rapper Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran’s stadium tour after pro-Palestinian remarks. Mitch McConnell returns to Senate. Department of Homeland watchdog: “Alligator Alcatraz” used small metal cages as “calming areas,” violating detention standards. ICE agents pepper-spray, detain two U.S. citizen teens en route to enlist in Marines. Mahmoud Khalil sues Columbia. Ukraine strikes Syzran refinery in Russia despite Trump claim of energy truce. NATO jets shoot down drone that entered Lithuanian airspace. Russian frigate fires flares at Danish military helicopter, narrowly missing aircraft. Hungary moves to repeal anti-LGBTQ+ restrictions. Turkish court orders detention of 16 in Izmir amid nationwide crackdown on LGBTQ+ group. Dutch farmers set fires and block roads in budget protest; sabotage incidents alleged. China tightens exit controls for citizens. World Food Program faces major Sudan funding shortfall as hunger crisis deepens. Pakistan-administered Kashmir internet shutdown continues past 100 days despite new government.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Yemen

- Saudi-led coalition strikes kill three, including two children, in Yemen as fighting continues around Taiz: Three people, including two children, were killed and two others wounded in Saudi-backed forces airstrikes on Dhubab and Maqbanah districts in Taiz governorate, according to the Ansarallah Health Ministry.

- Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces’ air operations against Ansarallah continued around Taiz on Tuesday, Al Jazeera reported. The Saudi-backed forces said warplanes struck an Ansarallah ballistic missile launch platform at Taiz airport and targeted positions and reinforcements in Khadir district, south of the city.

- Saudi Arabia issues “potential danger” alerts across multiple areas, including Mecca: Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense issued urgent “potential danger” warnings Tuesday for Jeddah, Yanbu, Taif, Jazan, Al-Ula, and Mecca, urging residents to seek shelter and follow official instructions.

- The alert in Mecca was the first issued in the holy city since recent clashes between Saudi and Ansarallah. Authorities later announced that the danger had passed, while urging residents to continue avoiding gatherings and filming.

- Ansarallah says Saudi Arabia launched 54 airstrikes on Yemen; Riyadh says attacks wounded 13 civilians: Saudi warplanes carried out 54 airstrikes over the previous 24 hours, targeting Taiz, Lahj, Al-Jawf, Marib, and Hajjah governorates in Yemen, Ansarallah’s military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Monday.

- Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Malki said Ansarallah launched ballistic missiles and drones at civilian sites in Khamis Mushait, Abha, and Taif in Saudi Arabia on Monday, wounding 13 civilians and damaging seven homes and two vehicles. Al-Malki said the coalition would take “all necessary operational measures” in response.

- Ansarallah says it will halt attacks if Saudi ends Yemen campaign: Senior Ansarallah official Mohammed Al-Bukhaiti told Sky News that the group is “ready for peace” and would end attacks on Saudi territory and shipping if Riyadh halted its airstrikes, lifted its blockade on Yemen, and stopped backing militias in Yemen fighting Ansarallah.

- “The Saudis have a lot more to lose than what Yemen has left to lose,” he said, describing the current policy as “a blockade for a blockade, an aggression for an aggression.”

- Al-Bukhaiti said Ansarallah does not have any plans to seize more territory, and said its recent advances along Yemen’s western coast “was the consequence of the Saudis moving their mercenaries inside Yemen to fight us.”

- He said Bab al-Mandab remains open to all shipping except Saudi vessels and that Ansarallah is currently targeting only Saudi ships.

- He also rejected Trump administration claims of direct talks, saying any communication is conducted through Oman.

- AP: Repairs to key Saudi pipeline could take 3-5 weeks: Repairs to Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline could take 3-5 weeks, two regional officials briefed on the damage told AP. The line may operate partially during repairs, but officials could not say how much crude would get through.

- The pipeline has been helping move roughly 4 million barrels of exports per day, about 4% of global oil demand.

- U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright struck a more optimistic note Monday, telling Bloomberg he expects the pipeline back “very soon.” Wright said he has been in close contact with his Saudi counterpart since the attack and may have “more of a time frame tomorrow” as officials finish assessing the damage.

- UN Security Council to hold emergency meeting on Bab al-Mandab: The UN Security Council will hold an emergency meeting Tuesday afternoon in New York to discuss the escalating situation in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Reuters reported, citing two French diplomats. The meeting was requested by France.

- The critical shipping route carried around 12% of global trade before fighting resumed this month. In recent days, Ansarallah seized most of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including Mayyun Island, which sits in the Strait.

- Meanwhile, foreign ministers from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), an East African regional bloc, are meeting in Djibouti to discuss developments in Bab al-Mandab and their security, humanitarian, and economic repercussions, particularly for East African countries bordering the Red Sea.

- Bloomberg: UK Prime Minister considering Saudi requests for a “range of military support” against Ansarallah: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham approved sending British military advisers as Riyadh reportedly seeks operational help to repel Ansarallah’s advance along Yemen’s Red Sea coast toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait and defend Saudi oil infrastructure.

- Bloomberg noted that the UK did not support Trump’s war on Iran and previously said it wants to avoid entering the conflict. But UK officials warn Ansarallah control of the shipping chokepoint could have a “catastrophic” economic impact.

## Iran

- IRGC claims downing of fourth U.S. MQ-1 drone over Hormuz: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it intercepted and destroyed a U.S. MQ-1 Predator drone west of the Strait of Hormuz.

- The MQ-1 is a surveillance and strike drone. Iranian state media said it was the second U.S. MQ-1 downed over the Strait within a day, and the fourth in several days. U.S. Central Command has not publicly confirmed the losses.

- IRGC says supertanker exploded after hitting naval mine in Hormuz; CENTCOM denies claim: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Monday that the supertanker El Gaia exploded after hitting naval mines while attempting to pass through a restricted zone south of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Mehr News Agency reported.

- The IRGC Navy said efforts to contain the fire failed and the tanker became fully engulfed in flames. It said warnings had previously been issued about the risks of using the “restricted” southern route.

- U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the account Monday, saying El Gaia had been “struck by an Iranian missile last month and rendered inoperable,” before being hit again by an Iranian drone over the weekend off Oman. CENTCOM said the tanker is currently being towed by a regional partner and called the IRGC’s account “another example of their lies and intimidation attempts.”

- Omani officials said the tanker is now being towed to an Omani port after a fire broke out in its engine room, Reuters reported. 23 crew members were evacuated, while two remain missing.

- Iran security chief: No talks with U.S. until Tehran’s conditions are met: Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran will not enter negotiations until its conditions are met, dismissing “mixed signals” from U.S. president Donald Trump.

- “Don’t get distracted by the U.S. president’s mixed signals—from ‘no negotiations’ to ‘we’re ready to talk.’ The stakes around oil and the straits have changed….No talks until Iran’s conditions are met. Period!” Rezaei wrote on X.

- His comments came after Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday that Iran “wants to make a deal, quickly and badly,” adding that he would determine whether the U.S. would engage and that “the concept of which we are open to.”

- U.S. watchdog confirms weapons shortages after months of war with Iran; Trump touts “Exquisite and Elite Weapons”: A U.S. government watchdog report released Monday confirmed strategic weapons inventory shortfalls and severe supply bottlenecks after months of war with Iran, with expert estimates cited in the report saying advanced missile and interceptor stockpiles could take up to three years to return to pre-war levels.

- The joint assessment by inspectors from the War Department, State Department, and USAID also detailed Iranian strikes that damaged or destroyed hundreds of structures at U.S. bases across eight Middle Eastern countries, as well as dozens of American aircraft and drones.

- Trump, meanwhile, said Monday that the U.S. is producing “more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History,” adding that defense factories are operating “24/7” while “building, on average, 4 to 5 largescale brand new Plants, each!”

- U.S. Energy Secretary claims Hormuz oil flow tops 10 million b/d despite lower independent estimates: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Monday that more than 12 million barrels of crude and oil products crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, with the seven-day average now above 10 million barrels per day (b/d) and rising.

- Wright told Bloomberg the ships are escorted and defended by U.S. forces, mostly transit at night, and travel with their AIS transponders switched off. He said his figures come from a daily government report listing every ship, its cargo, and its transit, and that his public Hormuz figure combines crude plus oil products.

- Independent tracker TankerTrackers puts the 7-day average for all flows exiting the U.S. blockade line at 9.87 million b/d.

- Kpler’s directly observed Hormuz flows of 5-7 million b/d are also lower than Wright’s figure, though its broader measure of Gulf regional exports from the blockade line is roughly 11.4 million b/d over seven days.

- U.S. seeks forfeiture of $61 million in cryptocurrency tied to “Iranian military’s black-market oil sales”: U.S. prosecutors are seeking the forfeiture of $61 million in cryptocurrency, alleging the funds are linked to the Iranian military’s black-market oil sales.

- “Today’s action demonstrates our determination to deprive the Government of Iran and its terrorist proxies of the illegal money they rely on to threaten the lives and safety of the citizens of the United States and elsewhere,” Deputy U.S. Attorney Sean S. Buckley said.

- Iran’s foreign minister to visit China Wednesday, days before Xi’s U.S. trip: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will make a one-day visit to China on Wednesday, September 16, for talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, China’s Foreign Ministry announced Tuesday.

- The two are expected to discuss bilateral relations and major regional and international issues. The meeting will be their second in-person talks in Beijing since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, and comes days before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, three Palestinians were killed and 27 injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,789 killed, with 174,798 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,375 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,686, while 831 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israeli attacks kill at least three Palestinians in Gaza City and Jabalia: At least two Palestinians were killed in an Israeli drone attack on the industrial area of Gaza City, according to Al Jazeera.

- In northern Gaza, a Palestinian man was killed by an Israeli sniper positioned on a high-rise crane while inside a displacement camp in eastern Jabalia.

- Israeli forces kill Palestinian man in occupied West Bank as settlers attack residents, steal livestock:

- Ramallah and Al-Bireh: Israeli forces shot and killed a Palestinian man during a raid on the Umm Al-Sharayet area of Al-Bireh on Tuesday, WAFA reported, bringing the number of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank since the beginning of 2026 to more than 100. In Deir Dibwan, east of Ramallah, Israeli settlers stole around 300 sheep and a horse from a Palestinian farm.

- Hebron: Israeli forces demolished an agricultural room, bulldozed Palestinian land, and uprooted trees in Khirbet Hamsa, west of Hebron. South of Yatta, Israeli settlers cut and burned the electricity cable supplying Wadi Al-Rakhim, cutting power to the area.

- Bethlehem: Israeli settlers attacked an elderly Palestinian man and his wife at their home in Abu Nujaym, southeast of Bethlehem, in the early hours of Tuesday, leaving both with bruises.

- East Jerusalem: Israeli forces demolished two Palestinian homes in Beit Hanina’s Al-Ashqariya neighborhood on Tuesday. In Hizma, northeast of Jerusalem, Israeli bulldozers demolished eight residential and agricultural structures, uprooted olive trees, and destroyed solar-energy systems. Meanwhile, Israeli settlers, under the protection of Israeli forces, established a new outpost on land in Khirbet Al-Alawneh in Beit Iksa—the second outpost established in the village in four months.

- MSF: Israeli strike that killed two Palestinians, also damaged MSF bus and injured aid worker: An Israeli strike on a vehicle in Gaza City on Sunday that killed two Palestinians and injured 13 others, also damaged a clearly marked Doctors Without Borders (MSF) bus carrying 10 humanitarian workers just two metres away, injuring one MSF staff member.

- MSF said Israeli forces have, once again, shown “blatant disregard for the safety of humanitarian and medical personnel.”

- Israeli restrictions force Gaza hospitals to place multiple premature babies in single incubators: Israel’s restrictions on incubators and oxygen entering Gaza left hospitals with major shortages, forcing staff to place two or three premature babies in one machine, AFP reported.

- Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis has no spare incubators; other hospitals are full and can’t accept transfers.

- Amid Israeli restrictions manufacturing shortages of food, medicine, and fuel, one in three pregnancies is high-risk and 70% of newborns are premature or underweight, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs says. Sharing incubators further raises the risk of death.

- WHO to halt diesel supplies to more than 20 Gaza health facilities, official says: The World Health Organization (WHO) will stop supplying diesel to more than 20 Gaza hospitals and health centers after September 19 due to a funding shortfall, Gaza Health Ministry Director General Dr. Muneer Al-Boursh said Tuesday.

- Al-Boursh warned the cutoff could shut down operating rooms and ICUs, disable ventilators and oxygen systems, and endanger newborns, dialysis patients, the wounded, and chronically ill. Ambulances and cold storage for medicines and vaccines could also be affected.

- UN: Hundreds of bodies recovered from Gaza rubble raise fresh war crimes concerns: UN human rights chief Volker Türk said Tuesday that the recovery of hundreds of bodies from buildings destroyed by Israeli attacks in Gaza has renewed concerns over violations of international humanitarian law, warning that the remains found so far could be “only the tip of the iceberg,” Reuters reported.

- Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 people remain buried under the rubble. This month alone, Palestinian Civil Defense crews recovered 96 bodies and remains from one site in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighborhood, including 58 children and 23 women.

- Türk called for international investigators to be granted access to Gaza to preserve evidence, adding that Israel has blocked the entry of heavy machinery needed to clear the rubble.

## Lebanon

- Israeli forces kill 70-year-old teacher and destroy school in attacks across southern Lebanon during “ceasefire”:

- Bint Jbeil: A 70-year old Lebanese teacher from Baraachit was shot and killed Monday by Israeli forces while raiding the town, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported. On Tuesday, Israeli forces struck near a UN peacekeeping forces position in Hanine.

- Nabatieh: In Kfartibnit, Israeli forces demolished the Martyr Mahmoud Fakih Public School, with aerial images released Tuesday showing extensive destruction from the blast. Lebanon’s Education Ministry condemned the demolition, which came on the first day of the new school year.

- Tyre (Sour): Israeli forces set fire to what remained of homes in the town of Al-Bayyada, south of Tyre, with plumes of smoke seen rising from the town on Tuesday. Israeli forces also carried out powerful explosions in Majdal Zoun. On Monday night, Israeli warplanes carried out two strikes on the town of Mansouri.

- Lebanese, Israeli ambassadors to meet in Washington as Rome talks postponed: Lebanon’s ambassador to Washington, Nada Mouawad, and Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter are set to meet Tuesday in Washington to discuss developments in Lebanon and implementation of the framework agreement reached in June, Anadolu Agency reported.

- The meeting comes after a round of Israeli-Lebanese negotiations scheduled for this week in Rome was postponed until October.

- Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Saturday that there are “no new negotiations with Israel at the moment,” reiterating Lebanon’s demands for an Israeli withdrawal, the return of prisoners and displaced people, and reconstruction.

- Lebanon says Israeli attacks caused up to $4 billion in damage, seeks Arab support for reconstruction: Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said Tuesday that Israel’s offensive has cost Lebanon between $3 billion and $4 billion and that the country lacks the resources to finance reconstruction without support from Arab allies.

- Addressing parliament, Salam said Lebanon had been “plunged into a war it did not choose,” adding that there would be no security or stability while fighting continues in the south.

- Salam said that restoring Lebanon’s ties with Arab countries had helped increase exports to several regional markets.

## U.S. News

- Supreme Court blocks Trump plan to overhaul mail-in voting ahead of midterm: The Supreme Court on Monday blocked a Trump administration plan to require the Postal Service to screen and restrict mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections, ruling the government was “unlikely to succeed on the merits” of the underlying case.

- The plan, rooted in an executive order President Donald Trump signed in late March, had drawn opposition from Democratic-led states, voting rights groups including the ACLU, and even several Republican secretaries of state, who warned that redesigning ballot envelopes so close to the election risked mass voter disenfranchisement.

- Whistle-blower report alleges DHS agents may have broken state laws in noncitizen voter hunt: A whistle-blower report provided to Sens. Chuck Schumer and Alex Padilla alleges that federal agents, under direction of top Homeland Security leaders, may have violated state laws while searching voter rolls for noncitizens as part of the department’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative.”

- The nearly 30-page account says agents were required to review at least 40 voters daily, and used personal data to pose as individual voters on state websites, a practice some states restrict to the voters themselves.

- The whistleblower also noted that the data upon which they based their decisions was potentially riddled with errors, including “alien identification numbers” which could possibly belong to presently naturalized citizens.

- Trump dismisses AI safety warnings as a “hoax,” rejects calls for guardrails: President Donald Trump on Monday rejected calls for AI safety regulations, calling concerns about the technology a “hoax”  on Truth Social and singling out Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei by name after Amodei published a 3,800-word open letter on Saturday calling for a slowdown in the development of A.I

- The pushback came as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called for a briefing with administration officials and former President Barack Obama urged Washington to draft concrete AI safety laws, while a recent NBC News poll found 70% of adults said they were more worried than excited about AI.

- Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, voiced skepticism that AI companies were sincere in requesting regulation, calling it “a bit of a Trojan horse.”

- Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran’s stadium tour after pro-Palestinian remarks, venues object: Macklemore has been removed from the remaining dates of Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour after venues told promoter Messina Touring Group they would not allow the rapper on the lineup, following onstage “Free Palestine” statements Macklemore made at two MetLife Stadium shows earlier this month.

- Macklemore alleged in an Instagram statement that Patriots owner Robert Kraft pressured Sheeran and rallied other stadium owners to issue an ultimatum, a claim Kraft’s representatives did not address, while groups including StopAntisemitism and the Israeli American Council had separately called for his removal. Several of the affected venues are publicly owned stadiums, where his removal could raise First Amendment questions.

- McConnell returns to Senate: Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) returned to the Senate floor Monday and cast his first vote since a June fall, voting to advance Matthew Byrne’s nomination as a federal judge in Ohio.

- McConnell, 84, said his recovery had been complicated by “lingering effects of childhood polio” and that he is not yet “back to 100%,” but pledged to be present for close votes, including Wednesday’s farm bill markup, where Republicans hold a slim 12-11 majority on the Agriculture Committee.

- McConnell, who is retiring at the end of his term, has faced repeated health scares in recent years, including a 2023 fall and several public freezing episodes.

- DHS watchdog: “Alligator Alcatraz” used small metal cages as “calming areas,”  violated detention standards: A Department of Homeland Security inspector general report found that Florida’s now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz” detention facility confined at least 79 detainees in 18-square-foot metal enclosures for up to nearly two hours, a practice the report called “unprecedented” and inconsistent with humane treatment standards.

- The report also found the facility failed to meet federal requirements for living space, food service, hygiene and recreation.
Gov. Ron DeSantis said Monday he had not read the report but defended the facility, while his communications director, Alex Lanfranconi, said the enclosures held “violent criminal aliens” and that officials “would make it even smaller if we could.”

- The findings add to scrutiny of the facility, which closed this summer after drawing legal challenges and cost the state more than $1 million per day to operate, with two guards there facing misdemeanor battery charges over an alleged assault on a detainee.

- ICE agents pepper-spray, detain two U.S. citizen teens en route to enlist in Marines: Two U.S. citizen teenagers were pepper-sprayed and detained for nearly eight hours by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents while on their way to file Marine Corps enlistment papers, after agents accused them of filming ICE arresting parents outside Santos Livas Elementary School in Alamo, Texas, Telemundo reported on Monday.

- One teen, Luis Ochoa, said agents told him “I don’t give a damn... your parents can’t help you now” after he stated he was a citizen, and video showed agents pulling the other teen from a car and punching him repeatedly while he lay on the ground.

- Ochoa’s mother said he is now reconsidering enlisting, asking how he could “serve a country that doesn’t even uphold their basic rights.”

- Mahmoud Khalil Sues Columbia: Mahmoud Khalil, a Palestinian activist and former Columbia graduate student who served as a spokesperson and mediator for the Gaza encampment, announced on Monday that he is suing the university after he was detained by ICE in March 2025

- The suit, filed with the school’s Palestine Working Group, also names Keren Yarhi-Milo, dean of the School of International and Public Affairs, and alleges systemic anti-Palestinian discrimination and retaliation.

- “Columbia laid the groundwork for my targeting by the Trump administration,” Khalil said. Immigration authorities jailed him for 104 days, and he missed his son’s birth, as Trump sought to deport him over his Palestine advocacy.
