reads.title: “All I Want Is for the War to End”: Displacement Behind the Front Lines in Yemen
reads.subtitle: Residents of Taiz are grappling with a war that has fully reignited and now arrived, once again, at their doors.
reads.body:
Drop Site’s journalism is free to read because thousands of readers choose to fund it. If our work matters to you, please consider making a tax-deductible donation today.
SUPPORT DROP SITE - DONATE TODAY

-
- Building makeshift shelters in Jabal Zaid displaced persons camp, Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo: Khalid Al-Banna.TAIZ, Yemen*—This week, as Ansarallah forces advanced by the hour to seize the port city of Mokha and secure access to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait off the coast of Yemen, residents of Taiz braced for more fighting.
Over the past week, some of the fiercest battles between Ansarallah (also known as the Houthis) and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces took place in the hills surrounding Taiz—a crucial trade hub in southwestern Yemen, situated between Ibb, Mokha, Hodeidah, and Aden.
On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia bombed five Yemeni governorates more than 50 times in a single 12-hour span. On Sunday, powerful explosions shook Taiz and several residential areas were shelled. The Yemeni government attributed the explosions to Ansarallah. Ansarallah neither claimed the bombings nor denied them, but the fighting proved decisive ahead of Ansarallah’s capture of Mokha later in the week.
Thousands of households from across the Taiz governorate have been displaced since September 3, when a new round of intensified fighting began. Across Yemen, nearly 20,000 have fled their homes, according to the International Organization for Migration. Over the past week, at least 500 have been killed, according to the AFP, most of them combatants. Among the dead and wounded are civilians, including numerous children.
Drop Site is always free to read. Subscribe today:
Many of the displaced are from Jabal Habashi, a district in the Taiz governorate characterized by greenery, agriculture, and terraced hills. Jabal Habashi has seen the majority of the violence in the area—and its families have experienced among the highest rates of displacement. Because of its strategic position, wedged between Taiz and Mokha, it is a crucial passageway for securing Yemen’s west coast.
Yet, as Ansarallah has been increasingly taking hold of the districts surrounding the provincial capital, which is thus far still under the control of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, has attempted to retain a sense of normalcy: Its markets are bustling and people walk the streets, despite the presence of military convoys bringing in injured fighters to its hospitals.
“When I heard the explosions I remembered the difficult days of the beginning of the war in 2015,” said Taiz city resident Mohammed Abdulmalik, “and felt with the suffering of the population who witness it nowadays in west Taiz.”

## Civilian Targeting
Drop Site News visited several hospitals in the city of Taiz, including Al Thawra and Al Safwah, speaking with local patients hospitalized with injuries incurred in the ongoing fighting. The aisles of these hospitals were overflowing with patients; the majority of them were injured fighters, although the hospital is treating civilians as well. Ashraf, a 47-year-old construction worker from the Jabal Habashi district, was injured while attempting to flee his village on Saturday with his family, a day after heavy fighting with shelling broke out around him. (Ashraf is a pseudonym used for his safety.)
“We were moving in small separate groups to reduce the risk of being targeted, and an explosion went off. I lost consciousness and fainted, and was later evacuated to Taiz.”
Ashraf woke up in a hospital surrounded by other wounded civilians, including children. Still sitting in a hospital bed, he told Drop Site, “It is always us civilians who suffer the brunt of this war.”
At a private hospital also in Taiz, four injured children were in hospital beds, staying in the same room: three boys and one girl, who was the eldest. The girl and two of the boys were siblings, while the fourth boy was their neighbor.
The children’s guardian, their uncle, told Drop Site he had brought them from the Jabal Habashi district to Taiz city after their home was shelled.
“On Friday, we all stayed home because the fighting was fierce,” he told us. “But by the afternoon, things had calmed down, and the children went out to play in front of the house as usual. Then we heard an explosion nearby and the screams of other children. We ran out and found the four of them on the floor, bleeding.” He was uncertain whether Ansarallah or the Saudi-backed government forces had caused the explosion, as both had been firing at each other.
The uncle said they normally could not afford hospital costs, but an international NGO operating locally funded their stay at the private facility.“I just hope they recover and can return home. Their parents are stuck in the village, as leaving is too dangerous right now. So I am taking care of them for the time being.”

## Families Torn Apart
The Jabal Zaid camp for Internally Displaced People (IDP), nestled between the green valleys of Taiz governorate, is one of several camps that have absorbed at least 5,600 households displaced across the Taiz and Hodeidah governorates in the past week, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Residents here live in makeshift tents built from scant, hard-to-source materials.
Rahma, a displaced woman at Jabal Zaid who asked to go only by her first name, told Drop Site News that her family—who was already displaced by fighting a decade ago and living in a different IDP camp—had not only been displaced again, but divided. “When fighting broke out near our [first] camp on Friday, we took our children and fled the area,” she said. “Later that same day, my husband returned to bring our belongings. We waited for him until the next day, but he didn’t come back. We were terrified he might have been killed or injured.”
Rahma later learned from neighbors that he was stuck in the middle of the fighting and no one was allowed to leave the area. Five days later, Rahma’s husband was still trapped in the middle of the fighting.

-
- Nujud Mohammed and her children at Jabal Zaid camp on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo: Khalid Al-Banna.Nujud Mohammed, 28, a mother of six also displaced at Jabal Zaid, described a similar rupture. She is originally from Al Barah, a site that has seen heavy clashes due to its position on the supply route connecting Taiz and Mokha, and has been increasingly targeted by Yemeni government forces and allied warplanes attempting to repel Ansarallah’s advance.
“I tried to return to retrieve our belongings,” she said, “but the road was blocked. We weren’t allowed to reach our old camp to take anything. Our area is now encircled by fighting, and no one can enter or leave. So I returned with nothing. I praise Allah that we are safe, and I trust that He will compensate us for everything we lost.”
For many at Jabal Zaid, the past week is not a first displacement but a second, or third. Nujud’s family fled to Jabal Habashi nine years ago, at the start of Yemen’s civil war, and had lived there ever since.
“Nine years ago we fled because of the fighting in our area. We spent nine years in Jabal Habashi, but on Friday, sudden fighting reached our camp. I immediately took my children and walked from the afternoon until sunset, when we finally found a car that brought us to this camp.”
Surrounded by her children, the youngest of whom is still a toddler, she cooked flatbread over a fire using plastic basins and a makeshift fire. “It isn’t easy to start over in a new camp, but we have been forced to do so because we have no alternative.”

## Camp Without Aid
Nujud and her children now share a single tent with three other families, relying on the goodwill of their new neighbors for food, mattresses, and other basic goods. “No humanitarian organizations have arrived yet,” she said. “Only two representatives from a relief agency came to take our names and ask questions, but no aid has been delivered. We are in dire need of shelter and food.”
Looking at the temporary tent housing her, she said: “All I want at this moment is for the war to end so I can return.”

-
- Mohammed Ahmed and his family in Jabal Zaid camp, Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo: Khalid al-Banna.
-
- Mohammed Ahmed and his family in Jabal Zaid camp, Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo: Khalid al-Banna.Mohammed Ahmed, 35, a father in the camp, said his family had expected help to be awaiting them once they reached safety: “We assumed that as soon as we reached a safe area, we would receive support from humanitarian organizations, since we know they cannot reach dangerous frontlines,” where their home is. Indeed, many families chose Jabal Zaid precisely because it is considered a safe area, yet no agency has provided aid there so far.
“If this situation continues, our children could starve to death, as there are no job opportunities here and no one to help us.”
Fawzi Al-Habashi, Director of the Better Life Association for Coexistence and Development, a local humanitarian organization that provides food, shelter, and hygiene assistance, said NGOs “have monitored and documented the displacement movement, conducted initial needs assessments, and coordinated with local authorities, providing limited emergency aid to the most vulnerable families based on priority.”
However, as explained by Baraa Shaiban, a Yemeni political analyst who spoke to Drop Site, the suddenness of the displacement, combined with severe funding shortages that have characterized many areas of Yemen (particularly areas controlled by Ansarallah where international aid access has been restricted for years), has hindered the delivery of emergency assistance.
The Saudi-led war against Ansarallah that began in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a spawned one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and left over 150,000 dead until an uneasy truce was reached in 2022. Many Yemeni civilians are experiencing the clashes as a return to heightened instability, as they see their lives starting over once again, in yet another displacement camp.
As Shaiban put it: “Whatever normality people were hoping to get, it is quickly fading away.”
* A journalist in Yemen contributed reporting.

reads.title: Israeli Strike in Lebanon Kills 12 People From a Single Family, Including 6 Children
reads.subtitle: Israel is once again escalating its bombing of southern Lebanon despite a ceasefire and ongoing U.S.-brokered talks.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- A local sheikh gives a final prayer over the body of one of six children killed in a September 7, 2026 Israeli airstrike on the Farhat family home in Kfar Remman, in Nabatieh district, southern Lebanon that killed a total of 12 members of the family. September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.KFAR REMMAN, Lebanon—“They are killing children. That’s what they’re doing,” Baker Malak said, pointing to the tiny coffins being carried through the streets of the town of Kfar Remman in southern Lebanon on Tuesday. He walked alongside hundreds of mourners in a funeral procession to bury 12 members of a single family, half of them children, killed in an Israeli airstrike on their home a day earlier.
Nearby, mourners carried the coffin of 18-year-old paramedic Ali Shahrour, killed in a separate strike on the town the same day. The procession wound through streets scarred by months of bombardment as an Israeli drone buzzed incessantly overhead.
“When Israel sees that the Lebanese government is doing nothing, they will keep targeting children,” said Malak.
Israel bombed the three-story family home of the Farhat family on Monday morning without warning, reducing the entire building to rubble, and killing three men, three women, and six children between the ages of two months and 13 years. Two other children, both eight years old, were severely wounded in the strike.

-
- The Farhat family home in Kfar Remman, in Nabatieh district, southern Lebanon after a September 7, 2026 Israeli airstrike killed 12 members of the family. September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.Malak, 45, a resident of Kfar Remman, was a close friend of two brothers killed in the attack, Hassan and Hussein Farhat. Both their coffins were draped in Hezbollah flags during the funeral. Malak told Drop Site he had seen the two men 10 days before the strike. He said they were preparing their children for school after months of closures due to Israel’s bombardment. In the ruins of the family home, schoolbooks, timetables and notebooks lay scattered among the ruins. The Israeli military claimed without evidence that it struck Hezbollah operatives transporting weapons in the area. Malak told Drop Site the house was a civilian home and contained no weapons. Lebanon’s Health Ministry called it a “grave violation of international law.”
During the burial procession, a man’s voice rang out over a loudspeaker: “Stand up and say goodbye to our angels”—referring to the six children among the dead. One of the few survivors, eight-year-old Mustafa Farhat, lost his entire immediate family in the attack—his parents, siblings and grandparents. Badly wounded, he remained at Al-Najda Hospital in Nabatieh.

-
- The funeral procession for 12 members of the Farhat family killed in a September 7 2026 Israeli airstrike on their home in Kfar Remman, in Nabatieh district, southern Lebanon. September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.The deadly attack on the Farhat home came as part of an escalated wave of Israeli strikes across southern Lebanon that killed at least 27 people, and wounded 69 over the previous three days, according to the Health Ministry. The renewed Israeli assault forced some 20,000 people to flee Nabatieh district last week alone, according to the United Nations.
The attacks come despite a ceasefire and U.S.-brokered framework agreement signed in Washington by the governments of Israel and Lebanon on June 26. The deal requires the Lebanese Armed Forces to disarm Hezbollah before Israel withdraws from parts of the swathe of Lebanese territory it occupies. Hezbollah has rejected the deal, which has been criticized for extracting few guarantees from Israel and placing nearly all obligations on the Lebanese government. An eighth round of talks between Lebanon and Israel overseen by Washington is expected later this month.
The talks have proceeded despite nearly daily attacks by Israel on Lebanon. Between Thursday and Monday, the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, UNIFIL, recorded no less than 528 projectiles fired by the Israeli military. On Sunday alone, it recorded 62 Israeli violations of Lebanese airspace—among the highest daily totals since June. UNIFIL also detected Israeli airstrikes inside its area of operations and north of the Litani River. And for the first time since June 21, it also detected a Hezbollah projectile on Sunday, with the group beginning to reengage in retaliatory attacks.
Asked on Tuesday whether the escalation was being driven by one side, UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric pointed to UNIFIL’s observations and said: “Everyone can draw their own conclusions pretty clearly.”
Malak said the continuing strikes have only deepened the conviction among many in the south that the framework agreement has failed to protect civilians. “The resistance is the only solution,” he said, referring to Hezbollah. He stressed that people in Nabatieh opposed the Israeli occupation of Lebanese territory in a variety of ways: with weapons, words, or by refusing to leave their land.
Malak remained in heavily bombarded Kfar Remman throughout the war, distributing aid and food, and helping to bury the dead. “I will never leave my village,” he said. “If I ever have to leave, it will be to the grave.”
Since the latest phase of the war began in Lebanon on March 2, nearly 4,400 people have been killed, including more than 250 children, and over 12,400 wounded, according to the Health Ministry. Israel has also targeted health care workers and medical facilities, killing at least 135 emergency workers and attacking 17 hospitals. On Sunday, an Israeli airstrike completely destroyed Ghandour Hospital in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, according to the ministry, which condemned the attack as another violation of the special protections afforded to medical facilities.
At the funeral in Kfar Remman on Tuesday, Karim Saleh, a 32-year-old paramedic with Al-Rissala Scouts— a Lebanese youth and civil defense organization—stood beside the grave of his friend and colleague, 18-year-old paramedic Ali Shahrour who was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his car in Kfar Remman at 1 a.m. on Monday.
Saleh, Shahrour, and two other paramedics, Hadi Farhat and Hassan Hamze, had just finished work at a small restaurant they had recently opened together and Shahrour was driving them all home. Saleh was dropped off first, but shortly after he entered his home, he heard the screech of a missile tearing through the air followed by an explosion. Saleh put on his scouts vest and raced to the scene. Shahrour, Farhat, and Hamze had been struck in the car. People managed to pull out Farhat and Hamze from the burning vehicle just before it exploded. Farhat and Hamze were wounded, but Shahrour was killed.
“Every time I close my eyes I see their faces from that moment. That’s why I’m trying to stay awake, so I don’t close my eyes,” Saleh told Drop Site, his yellow emergency worker vest stained with blood and his eyes red from tears and exhaustion.

-
- Daniel Sharhour (left) the father of paramedic Ali Shahrour, who was killed in a September 7, 2026 Israeli airstrike on his car in Kfar Remman, stands beside Ali’s friend and colleague, Karim Saleh (right). September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Houmøller.When Saleh visited Farhat in the intensive care unit in Al-Najda Hospital, Farhat’s first question was “Where is Ali?” He had only just been taken off the breathing tube so that he could speak. Saleh said his friend was in shock, struggling with traumatic memories of the attack. Farhat insisted on attending his friend Shahrour’s funeral Tuesday, but doctors said his condition was too serious to leave the hospital.
“I’m not going to wash their blood off this vest,” Saleh said. “It makes me feel like I’ll always have them by my side.”
Shahrour’s father, Daniel Sharhour, stood beside him. “They killed him in his own hometown. In his own car. In his own country,” Daniel Sharhour said. As he spoke, his voice grew louder, drawing people around him. “I will never forgive what happened to my son. Revenge is hanging around my neck like a necklace. I will take my revenge. I’m not afraid.”

reads.title: Britain finally acts against Israel’s illegal settlements – because people forced it to
reads.subtitle: This isn’t enough. But it’s something to build on
reads.body:
- As British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced new sanctions targeting Israel’s illegal settlements, I thought back to exactly a year ago.
Back then, I was in the West Bank – Palestinian land that is illegally occupied by Israel.
I had travelled on a delegation organised by the Christian Palestinian charity Sabeel-Kairos, and if I’m honest, I was surprised Israel let me in after keeping me for interrogation at the Jordanian border.
A couple of days later, they sent me an email revoking my visa, which answered that one.
Help us take on the pro-war, pro-genocide, pro-injustice mainstream media by becoming a subscriber.
In the village of Beit Ijza, I met Sa’adat Gharib and his family. By the time I visited, their home had been completely boxed in by the neighbouring Israeli settlement. Sa’adat told us the surrounding land had belonged to his family. Around the house stood a 26-foot-high metal fence. They lived under the constant gaze of settlers and surveillance cameras.
To get in or out, the family had to pass through an electronic gate controlled by Israeli forces.
Sa’adat told us that the family had been arrested, intimidated and physically attacked. That included attacks on the children. Sometimes, he said, settlers would deliberately walk around the fence naked when his kids were outside.
I went to Hebron and walked down what was once its main commercial street. Much of it has been shuttered, and Palestinians are barred from walking on sections of the street – while Israeli settlers can move freely.
Share

-
- This is apartheid.
One evening, a young Palestinian man I’d met in London took us to a hipster bar in Ramallah. He lived on the outskirts of Jerusalem, where we were staying. But while I could walk freely around Jerusalem, he had only entered the city once in his entire life – as a small child. He couldn’t remember it.
Here is a land where some 770,000 illegal Israeli settlers now live. Palestinian life is being gradually asphyxiated. Palestinians live under military occupation and are routinely detained and incarcerated under a military legal system, including children. Jewish Israeli settlers living alongside them are subject to Israeli civil law.
They endure the routine humiliations of the longest belligerent occupation of our time. Travelling around the West Bank is made nightmarish by Israeli checkpoints. Land is routinely seized. Palestinians are being violently driven from their homes.
In the northern West Bank, Israeli forces have emptied the Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps of their residents. More than 33,000 Palestinians were displaced, according to the UN, while huge areas of the camps were demolished or damaged and residents were prevented from returning.
With the support of the Israeli state, settlers are waging a campaign of terror.
Subscribe now
Since 7 October 2023, more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank, including more than 240 children.
This is what I thought about when Miliband announced the sanctions.
At first, I was extremely cynical. I remember talking to Palestinians in the West Bank about the UK’s recognition of a Palestinian state last year. They were entirely dismissive.
They said it was for domestic political consumption, and made no difference to them. If it had been done three decades earlier, they said, then maybe it would amount to something. But the Israeli state was destroying any possibility of a Palestinian state – and the West was doing nothing meaningful about it.

-
- The “two-state solution” has just been a crutch for politicians. When they receive any scrutiny about Israel’s crimes – which is rare – they simply point to their meaningless abstract support for a “two-state solution”.
Subscribe now
Britain’s sanctions are certainly not even close to being enough. Israel is a state committing genocide in Gaza. UN investigators have also found it responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity. That’s without even mentioning the heinous crimes committed in Lebanon, the illegal occupation of Syrian land, or the disastrous attacks Israel and the US have launched against Iran.
It is a reasonable question to ask why Britain is still conducting any trade with illegal settlements. The direct economic impact of the import ban will be negligible: it will represent only a tiny fraction of the roughly £6 billion in annual trade between Britain and Israel.
But even so, this is a victory won because of those who have ceaselessly campaigned – and because voters, including those who switched to the Green Party, punished Labour at the ballot box.
Those electoral shocks helped bring down Keir Starmer and usher Andy Burnham into Downing Street. Burnham now faces pressure to shore up Labour’s left flank – and that includes taking action on Israel. Recent polling shows support for banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements massively outstripping opposition.
This isn’t enough – but it represents concessions that can be built on.
It doesn’t just mean a ban on imports from illegal settlements. It opens the way to sanctions against companies and individuals whose money or services help settlements expand. That potentially puts Israeli banks and financial companies in scope.
Britain has now officially declared that Israel’s continued occupation of Palestinian land is unlawful, in line with the 2024 ruling of the International Court of Justice. That is – alas! – a new development, and provides a legal basis to push for more action.
Arms export restrictions have been tightened – although the existing carve-out for components supplied through the global F-35 programme remains.
The government is using very careful language, declaring that “there is increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed”. Miliband, the prime minister and the rest of the government obviously know that war crimes have been committed on an industrial scale. A definitive finding, however, would impose certain legal obligations on the government.
Subscribe now
But Miliband explicitly backed legal processes to determine responsibility for war crimes, and said Britain supports the International Court of Justice reaching its judgment in South Africa’s genocide case.
The Global Human Rights sanctions regime is being expanded, allowing sanctions to be imposed not just on those involved in illegal settlements, but potentially on those responsible for violations of international humanitarian law in Gaza.
Miliband also declared that “settler terrorists” are committing ethnic cleansing in parts of the West Bank, and said members of the Israeli government had supported the forced displacement of Palestinians.
All of this can lay the foundations for us to build more pressure – and ensure more far-reaching action.
There were certainly other problems. Miliband denounced the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, which consciously draws on the successful boycott movement against South African apartheid.
He denounced anyone who questions Israel’s right to exist as “a homeland for the Jewish people” – as though it is somehow outrageous to support a single state (which de facto exists!) with equal rights for all between the River Jordan and the Mediterranean Sea.
That won’t age well.
But you can see from the resulting hysteria that Israel and its cheerleaders are rattled.
Outrageously, that has centred on arguing that taking even these limited measures against a foreign state’s illegal conduct endangers Jewish Brits.
This shameless conflation of Jewish people with Israel’s crimes is dangerously irresponsible.
So no, this isn’t enough.
But it does represent welcome movement – and these concessions were only won because people organised, from the streets to the polling booth.
That includes people like you.
Help us take on the pro-war, pro-genocide, pro-injustice mainstream media by becoming a subscriber.

reads.title: Weekend Update #201: It Will Be A Brutal Fall and Winter
reads.subtitle: Trump Speaks His Truth About Russia And Ukraine: Drapatyi’s Principles
reads.body:
Hello all,
One point I have tried to get across in this Substack from the very beginning is that in a war, length is far more important than ferocity. Trying to keep a war from escalating might seem like a prudent thing (and academic theory, which simply does not understand history, says as much). However, clamping down on escalation can actually make things far worse. What such a move can do, in a vain attempt to keep a war under control, is lengthen a war out of all expectation. And length of war is almost always the key variable in how horrible a war becomes. Short escalation if it can be effective is far preferable to the kind of long and grotesque war we are now seeing.
Phillips’s Newsletter is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
/
I was struck by that this week when President Zelensky did something that would have seemed shockingly escalatory a few years ago, but which actually people passed over quite quickly now—he announced the “de facto” closing of Russian commercial airspace.

-
- Zelensky making the announcement.In other words, we are escalating now, and people have stopped caring. It brings us back to the opening phase of the full-scale invasion, when people believed such escalation could be controlled.
Now, I am always amused when people accuse me of being a great Biden supporter because I criticize Trump. For the first two years of this Substack (more than half of the time of its existence) I spent much of my time pointing out the great flaws in the Biden administration’s escalation policy. By trying to restrain escalation, what the Biden administration was actually doing was protecting Russia and lengthening the war. They were at best simply delaying any escalation and in doing so they would actually make that escalation worse and cause more damage. I wrote a few pieces on just this theme at the start of 2024.
Here is the conclusion for the January 2024 piece.

-
- Now, under Trump, US policy has been revealed as the real disaster that it was. Putin is now free to escalate without any fear that the US will do anything to stop him—and that means that the Ukrainians are left playing a brutal game of catch-up. This week we saw a prime example of this when the Ukrainians announced that they will now “de facto” threaten civil aviation in Russia. They have had to deal with their airspace being a wild west for years and now they are trying to turn the tables.
All that is indicative of what we are going to see this Fall and Winter. Both Ukraine and Russia are now, more than four and a half years into the war, facing the reality that this war is going to get even more intense and horrible, setting up a reality where life itself for all people will become increasingly hard. And both sides at the same time have the ability to do more and more damage with their ranged campaign—far more than they could have done a few years ago.
This is what not helping Ukraine to win the war quickly has done—lengthened the war and made it worse. Trying to artificially restrain escalation has led the war to be far more horrible and extensive than it needed to be.
Other stories this week include a spate of different stories from the US administration about  US positioning and the war. The upshot is that Trump is explicit now that Russia is the friend and Ukraine is despised. Finally, General Drapatyi released a new set of principles for the Ukrainian military. They are worth reflecting on—for all militaries. And they say nothing about needing to give all soldiers a testosterone shot.
Share

## It Will Be A Brutal Fall and Winter
During his evening address on September 1, President Zelensky made a very pointed statement about what he believes will happen in the war against Russia. He believes now that the number and type of drones/missiles that the Ukrainians are firing against Russia (and in particular against cities like Moscow and St Petersburg which have large international airports) means that Ukraine is “de facto” closing much of Russian air space to “civilian aircraft”. Here is a story about what he said.
Zelensky was so determined to get the message out, that he tweeted out the warning in English right after the address.

-
- As the above statement showed, Zelensky believes that Ukraine “effectively” closing Russian air space is a direct result of Russia being allowed to escalate with impunity over the last few years—continuing this week.
And of course Zelensky is right. This week has shown just how Russia is able and willing to attack whatever it wants in Ukraine without worry about being accused of escalating, without worrying about being accused of escalating, and without Ukraine’s partners being willing to help Ukraine (let alone do anything strong to deter Russia). It is worth noting what did happen this week. The Russians killed more civilians, 38, in one air strike than they have done at any other time this year. To reinforce the point that what the Ukrainians are doing in threatening air traffic is part and parcel of how Russia has waged this war, on Friday night the Russians hit two major Ukrainian airfields.
Both sides are also engaging in campaigns of targeted assassination which were reconfirmed this week. The Russians put a drone into the office of the head of Ukrainian military intelligence—which is in one of the most central and prominent positions in Kyiv. The Ukrainians, meanwhile, seem to have assassinated a Russian military officer in St Petersburg, an officer who had been accused of war crimes.
And this is just the start of what we are about to see. As both sides understand, this winter could be quite determinative in shaping the end of the war, particularly if it is as cold and terrible as last winter. The Ukrainians I know are already starting preparations, on the assumption that they may lose power and heating for large stretches of the winter.
The Ukrainians admitted in August that up to 80% of their pre-war power generation facilities have either been either completely or partially destroyed. Zelensky even stated that Ukraine had “virtually no intact thermal power plants” and that “Russian missiles are aimed precisely at making the lives of Ukrainians unbearable.” What is left is to a large degree based on nuclear power plants that Russia for reasons of self-interest is reluctant to attack. However there are signs that even this reluctance is breaking down.
In other words, this winter could see major power and heating cuts, making the lives of millions of Ukrainians extremely hard.
The Ukrainians response will be fascinating—and could potentially be to hit back in a similar way. So far the vast majority of Ukrainian attacks of this kind have been against Russia’s fuel industry—primarily its refineries. What it has not tried to do, though conceivably it could, is turn the lights and heat out to Moscow or St Petersburg. However, by warning that civilian aviation is not safe in Russia, Zelensky is “de facto” warning that all such infrastructure is potentially now at risk. If airfields are not safe, neither are power plants, etc.
The Russian response has been to threaten even greater attacks on Ukrainian power generation—but as they have basically done as they can, they cannot really escalate in that regard.
The upshot of all of this is that we are poised for a pretty harsh Fall and Winter. The policy of trying to control and stop escalation has failed utterly. It might have delayed escalation for a little while, but has made it now far worse when it happened. It has already led to great suffering and will lead to much more.
Share

## Trump Speaks His Truth About Russia And Ukraine
At times Donald Trump speaks the truth. It can happen when he loses control and gets so angry that he blurts out what he really thinks. He did that this week on twitter, when he started a rant about the US reporting of his war with Iran, but which he then turned into a whine about how the US needs to be paid back for giving Ukraine aid under the Biden Administration.

-
- It seems he could not control himself and Natalie could not either, so he just had to let his resentment towards Ukraine come out.
Note—this aid was all Congressionally sanctioned, so actually the US cannot demand any money back. Trump cares so little for Congress that he overlooks that. However the truth is there that if Trump could make Ukraine pay back the aid—he would.
At the same time that Trump could not control himself about Ukraine, he revealed his instinctive respect and affection for Putin by defending the Russian dictator from the charge that it was Russians who had orchestrated the attack on Germany’s Leipzig airport (which is now what the German government is stating clearly). When Trump was asked about the German government’s claim, he instinctively jumped to Putin’s defense, and, as he often does with the Russian dictator, talked up the fact that the two of them have a close personal relationship.
“I don’t think that Putin will be… I speak to him. I know him very well. Putin’s not looking to attack NATO territory,”
This instinctive Trumpian affection for Putin and Russia was shown in the other big story of the last few days, the visit of Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv. That trip (which started yesterday when the two reached Moscow and which should soon see them in Kyiv) reveals just how deep the affection runs between Trump and Putin. When Witkoff and Putin sat down with Putin yesterday, the Americans could not have been more positive. Witkoff gushed about his repeated pleasure at meeting Putin, saying that when he retires he will look back on all these “incredible stories and incredible memories and yours will be right at the top.”

-
- Witkoff can barely contain his glee at meeting again with PutinBeyond Trump’s and Witkoff’s obvious affection for Putin, the staging of the visits reveals a great deal. Even though the two have never before visited Ukraine, Trump felt the need for them to go to Moscow first, to show Putin he is, always, the number 1 priority. Only after seeing Putin, and presumably working out a plan with him, can they be allowed to finally to visit Ukraine. Remember, the last time they presented a “compromise” plan to the Ukrainians, it was practically word for word a dictation of a Russian plan.
So once again, the US government seems to need to agree a position with Putin before it can talk with Ukraine.
Such behavior, btw, makes me doubt that the real reason behind the Ratcliffe visit was to somehow tell Putin the war was going badly for Russia—the US government remains in Putin’s thrall.
So the last few days reveal once again the instinctive position of Donald Trump and through him the US government. He/they want to help and work with Putin and believe that Ukraine needs to do what it is told.
And it has always been thus.
Share

## Drapatyi’s Principles
On September 2, Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi, publicly released a document entitled “Principles of Leadership and Military Development in Wartime.” If you want to read the full text in English (and I recommend that you do) here is a link to a translatable version.
Btw, here is the piece that I wrote about Drapatyi when he was first appointed. Since then I can happily report that everything I have heard from Ukrainians has been extremely positive about what he is doing. He might be an even better selection than he seemed at the time.
What Drapatyi writes is fascinating and heartening.  It gives an indication of what Drapatyi believes are the key tenets of how Ukraine needs to fight the war and how the Ukrainian army needs to be run. Foundationally, he believes that the Ukrainians must out-think and out-adapt the Russians. Key elements that will make this possible are keeping Ukrainian casualties down, keeping morale high, and demanding accountability from Ukraine’s officer corps.
The first part of the document has a subhead which starts: “People are the most valuable combat capability”.

-
- It is very well reasoned. Drapatyi does not talk about saving lives through not fighting or taking no risks. He sees this happening by taking the right risks and always trying to stay ahead of the Russians in the adaptation and innovation cycle. To do that, he calls on Ukrainian officers to not just give orders, but to listen. He is saying to them, “it is your responsibility to put your soldiers in the best possible position to achieve their objectives and save their lives.”
Here was a fascinating reflection on precisely that point.

- A separate priority is accelerating adaptation and the implementation of innovation. The purpose of this work, as set out in the Principles, is linked to people: technologies are needed where they enable tasks to be accomplished with fewer casualties and less risk to those directly holding the front line. The source of change is not limited to headquarters: commanders are required to create an environment in which “good ideas can come from any service member, regardless of military rank or position.”
And you know what he says is the linchpin of all of this—it is truth. Drapatyi calls for truth from the top of the Ukrainian military on down. Sorry for all the quotes, but the whole document is really worth digesting. Note—translating the text from Ukrainian to English can lead to some awkward phrasing.

- Truth makes us stronger

- The document requires commanders and headquarters to provide honest assessments and not allow optimism, fear or personal ambitions to distort reality.

- “Problems that are ignored only grow.” “Healthy professional debate strengthens decisions; silence weakens them.”

- The same standards of conduct apply to generals, officers, sergeants and civilian leaders: there is no place in the Armed Forces for corruption, abuse of authority, harassment, discrimination or injustice. A separate requirement for everyone commander is the responsible use of state resources.
I was struck in reading this about not only how different it is from the values of the Russian military, but also from the present leadership in the Pentagon. In the latter, truth is considered a useless commodity, focusing on brains and adaptability over brainless bravery the sign of being a sissy, and accountability has been thrown out of the window. The US military is being run by a group that apes the Russians and not the Ukrainians—when we have in front of us one of the best statements of command principles I have ever seen from the latter. It is a tragedy.
The USA is going to have to change so many things in the future, and that will start with understanding that it needs to learn from others and that the present US ethos is one that fosters failure. The US military could do far worse than to start its rebuild based on Drapatyi’s principles of command.
And as I said above, there are no testosterone shots or cosplay warriors in sight.
Have a good rest of the weekend everyone.
Thanks for reading Phillips’s Newsletter! This post is public so feel free to share it.

reads.title: Minsky’s Society of Mind & The OpenAI — Hugging Face Hack
reads.subtitle: Anthropomorphizing aside, should we be legitimately concerned over the “emergence” of unforeseen capabilities in groups of interacting agents?
reads.body:
In 1986, Marvin Minsky, the American mathematician, computer scientist and AI pioneer, published The Society of Mind1, a book detailing his theory for the emergence of intelligence. The Society of Mind, he wrote, is a scheme in which each mind “is made of many smaller processes. These we’ll call agents. Each mental agent by itself can only do some simple thing that needs no mind or thought at all. Yet when we join these agents in societies—in certain very special ways, this leads to true intelligence.”

-
- Image credit: Gemini (AI generated)He further wrote, “To explain the mind, we have to show how minds are built from mindless stuff, from parts that are much smaller and simpler than anything we’d consider smart. Unless we can explain the mind in terms of things that have no thoughts or feelings of their own, we’ll only have gone around in a circle.”
I can’t help wondering what Minsky would have to say about the revelations these past weeks about the “OpenAI — Hugging Face Incident2,” in which AI agents reportedly figured out a way out of their sandboxed environments on to the internet, hacked the Hugging Face website, and accessed information they needed to solve some problem (to be clear, I’m not equating Minsky’s notion of an emergent mind with activities of a group of AI agents. Minsky’s quote is simply a way to get us talking about something potentially serious.)
A report on the incident by METR and Redwood Research3 had this as one of the core takeaways: “Roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. Of these agents, 700 went on to participate in the attack on Hugging Face.”
Hugging Face, which was the target of the attack, wrote: “We believe the entire intrusion was, from the agent's point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation: reach our production systems and steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge on its own.”4
We won’t go into the details of the hacking incident. Much ink has already been spilled over it. But I do want to point out that the takeaway quoted above is linguistically fairly bland (maybe using the passive voice would make it blander: “over 70,000 messages and files were sent,” and “Hugging Face was attacked by 700 of these 1200 agents,” etc.). There has been, somewhat justifiably, much hand-wringing over the use of overly anthropomorphic language in describing the incident (with Dwarkesh Patel’s blogpost, The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations5, drawing the most ire.)
But linguistic choices shouldn’t detract us from trying to understand what actually happened. Did the interactions of hundreds of agents, with each agent potentially unlikely to successfully attack Hugging Face on its own, make possible a considerably complex, and unanticipated, behavior? Depending on your persuasion, the answer is either an emphatic yes or an equally emphatic no. But a whole lot of us are in the middle—wary of moneyed interests, wary of naysayers, and their respective echo chambers. Maybe we can take a step back and look at some prior research that helps make sense of such claims.
Thanks for reading WHERE MACHINES THINK! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
In the aforementioned incident, each agent was a harness with access to a frontier model. Databricks defines a harness6 as the “software infrastructure that wraps around a large language model (LLM) and enables it to act on tasks, not just respond to prompts. The model reasons through a problem and decides what to do next. The harness connects [the model] to the tools, systems, memory and execution environments needed to carry out those actions.” So, each agent is an LLM plus a harness.

## Natural Examples
We don’t know the full capabilities of the harnesses used by OpenAI. But it’s not unreasonable that a collection of such agents would likely display behavior that goes beyond the bounds of any single agent; in fact, that’s the entire point of having multiple agents interacting with each other. After all, nature is full of examples of such “emergence”—and I use the word emergence cautiously here, for it too has hand-wavy qualities.
But if there’s any doubt about the capabilities of such “emergent” processes, here’s a description of some of the accomplishments of tiny social insects, in a paper published in The Royal Society’s Philosophical Transactions A7: “Many of the collective activities performed by social insects result in the formation of complex spatio-temporal patterns...Some of these patterns spread over large-scale surfaces and there may be several orders of magnitude difference between the size of an individual and the size of the structure built by a colony; we can find, for instance, a whole range of species of ants and termites that build huge nests and large-scale networks of chemical trails or underground galleries. In the ant Formica lugubris, super-colonies that contain more than 20 million individuals are spread over several thousand square metres. These super-colonies build tens of kilometres of trail networks that are several million times the size of an individual ant...Among the most impressive nest structures are those produced by African termites of the subfamily Macrotermitinae: the fungus growers. A mature nest of a Macrotermes species usually reaches 6 or 7 m high, while individuals are at most a few millimetres long.”
What’s the point of all this in the context of AI agents? Well, it’s to point out that the behavioral outcomes of a large collective of insects (where each individual insect may not be capable of much on its own) can be impressively off-the-charts and well beyond the scope of any one individual’s abilities. Substituting “AI agents” for “insects” should give us pause.

## Multi-Agent Scenarios

> So, it’s not surprising that multiple studies—examining the phenomenon of emergent capabilities in interactions of simple agents—are suggesting that increased intelligence could be an outcome of such interactions, and that it’s something that AI safety and alignment efforts should consider as plausible.
One study connects the emergence of a “hive mind”—observed in swarms of bees and colonies of ants—with reinforcement learning, which is a form of machine learning in which agents learn to act optimally within an environment to maximize cumulative rewards. In nature,  individual agents can use reinforcement learning to make optimal decisions using trial-and-error. Or, a collective of agents can make optimal decisions by mimicking each other and effectively choosing the best course of action from a set of options.
Last year, researchers from Canada and Germany showed that simple agents (such as individual bees) interacting with each other via simple rules are mathematically equivalent to a single macro-agent interacting with multiple environments in parallel. The emergent behavior exhibited by this macro-agent can be modeled as the outcome of a well-known reinforcement learning technique called a bandit algorithm. Essentially, a large population of non-learning agents that each behave according to simple rules of interaction with each other ends up mimicking a single, large reinforcement learning agent. (The Hive Mind Is A Single Reinforcement Learning Agent:8, Oct 6, 2025)
“This result provides a formal basis for understanding how simple, local imitation behaviors, often regarded as non-cognitive, can give rise to group-level intelligence and adaptive learning at scale,” the authors write.
In another demonstration of this idea, a team from the Institute for Robotics and Intelligent Machines at Georgia Tech used the idea of stigmergy, where agents leave traces in the environment that guide the actions of others, to design a system of deep reinforcement learning agents.
Again, here are the authors of the Royal Society’s Philosophical Transactions A paper, on stigmergy in insects: “Stigmergy is an elegant and stimulating concept to understand the coordination and regulation of collective activities. It explains how individual builders can act independently on a structure without the need for direct interactions or sophisticated communications. The basic principle of stigmergy is extremely simple: traces left and modifications made by individuals in their environment may feed back on them. The colony records its activity in part in the physical environment and uses this record to organize its collective behaviour.”
In the Georgia Tech study, agents left behind a trace of virtual pheromones. A system of 8 such agents, with some stochasticity built in, showed emergent cooperative behavior to solve a benchmark pellet retrieval task in OpenAI’s Gym platform. Previous state-of-the-art algorithms that used reinforcement learning agents could only scale up to 2 agents. (Deep reinforcement learning for multi-agent coordination9, Nov 26, 2025.) “The learned cooperative behaviors exhibit emergent strategies similar to those observed in biological systems, emphasizing the potential of stigmergy-inspired approaches for scalable and robust multi-agent coordination in dynamic environments,” the authors write.
If it occurred to you that the agents in the OpenAI — Hugging Face hack writing to a common message board is a form of stigmergy, you’d be anthropomorphizing (or whatever is the equivalent to comparing AI agents to insects), but you wouldn’t be alone.

## Predictive Agents
This notion of a dynamical relationship between RL agents and the environments in which they operate was mathematically formalized in an expansive 203-page position paper, by a cross disciplinary team from Google Paradigms of Intelligence, Google DeepMind, Mila-Quebec AI Institute, ETH Zurich and the Santa Fe Institute. (Embedded Universal Predictive Intelligence: a coherent framework for multi-agent learning, Nov 27, 2025.10)
To start with, the researchers point out that “a major frontier in artificial intelligence involves moving beyond the imitation of human data, leveraging reinforcement learning (RL) to enable agents to self-generate experience and continually improve.”
Indeed, the use of reinforcement learning has proved extraordinarily powerful in AI, for e.g., in making large language models become powerful ‘reasoning’ agents capable of solving complex coding and math problems. But, current RL agents (such as LLMs) modify themselves based on past states of the environment.
The authors write: “This form of learning has its roots in 19th and 20th century empirical observations on how animals respond to reward and punishment…and accompanying theories such as Thorndike’s law of effect, which can be loosely understood as ‘do more of what worked well in the past, and less of what did not’... Such retrospective learning works well when the environment is stationary, but multi-agent systems are intrinsically nonstationary.”
The researchers argue that in real world settings, agents have to anticipate future states of the environment, and learn how to modify their behavior accordingly. But in a multi-agent setting, future states of the environment involve other agents, so an agent has to model or anticipate the actions of other agents, which in turn involves anticipating the other agents’ model of itself. The authors write, “To accurately model other agents, an agent must account for the fact that those other agents are, in turn, forming beliefs about it to predict its future behavior, motivating agents to model themselves as part of the environment.”
So, agents develop a “theory of mind” and figure out, for example, that “similar agents behave similarly in similar situations” — a property the researchers call similarity awareness.
The team showed that similarity awareness can solve the Twin Prisoner’s Dilemma, which is a twist on the standard Prisoner’s Dilemma. In the standard version, cops nab two suspected bank robbers and put in adjacent cells. The cops tell the robbers the rules: 1) If both confess to the heist, they each get five years in prison; 2) If one confesses and the other stays mum, the confessor goes free (for helping law enforcement, ostensibly), but the silent robber gets 20 years in prison; and 3) If both stay silent, then they each get one year in prison (for, maybe, possession of firearms). In the Twin version of this dilemma, the robbers are psychological twins (i.e., they are identical agents in terms of how they make decisions).
In the classical game theory, the rational choice of the robbers (or agents) is betrayal.
But when agents can anticipate future states of the environment and the states of other agents, similarity awareness engenders new behavior, involving forms of cooperation and coordination that is not possible in classical game theory. Because agents can reason that other agents will act similarly, the end result is cooperation for mutual gain, not betrayal. The team mathematically formalized this result, drawing upon previous results that had also shown similar outcomes.
What does this have to do with concerns about the increasing intelligence of AI agents? The researchers write, “As we move toward deploying vast numbers of AI agents, many of which are based on shared foundation models, similarity awareness may offer a powerful mechanism for achieving robust coordination with minimal communication, possibly paving the way for effective social scaling—increasing the capabilities of a society of agents by increasing their numbers.”
Finally, another team from Google DeepMind argues in a Dec 2025 paper for an alternate hypothesis for artificial general intelligence (AGI): that it’s something that emerges from a group of interacting agents. (I’ll avoid getting into definitions about what constitutes AGI—we can simply think of it as some collection of capabilities that is beyond the reach of current monolithic LLMs.) The authors write: “AGI may initially emerge as a patchwork system, distributed across entities within a network. A Patchwork AGI would be comprised of a group of individual sub-AGI agents, with complementary skills and affordances. General intelligence in the patchwork AGI system would arise primarily as collective intelligence.” (Distributional AI Safety, 18 Dec 202511)
They say that we should be alert to the emergence of AGI through this alternate route. “This patchwork AGI hypothesis needs to be given serious consideration, and should inform the development of corresponding safeguards and mitigations. The rapid deployment of advanced AI agents with tool-use capabilities and the ability to communicate and coordinate makes this an urgent safety consideration.”
So, whether we anthropomorphize or not, the OpenAI — Hugging Face hack is a clarion call: Such incidents are not theoretical concerns anymore.
Thanks for reading WHERE MACHINES THINK! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

reads.title: Zack Polanski’s big gamble
reads.subtitle: The Green Party leader is standing in the upcoming by-election: we spoke about his courageous move
reads.body:
Zack Polanski has announced he’s standing in the upcoming by-election caused by Keir Starmer’s resignation - and he has quite the fight on his hands.
I interviewed Polanski today - and discussed with him the challenge he faces.
Holborn and St. Pancras is an inner London seat, and there is much fertile ground there for a left challenger. Even at Labour’s supposed peak - its victory in the 2024 general election - Starmer’s majority collapsed from 27,763 to 11,572.
That’s for two reasons. One, the independent campaign of left-wing former anti-Apartheid activist Andrew Feinstein, who came second with 7,312 votes and nearly a fifth of the vote share. That was despite almost a total media blackout - with him written off as a total no-hoper.
BattleLines with Owen Jones is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
And at the same time the Greens surged, too, chalking up 10.4% of the vote.
Alas, that was a divided left. But all of that, the combined left vote was approaching 30%.
In the local elections, the Greens surged in Holborn and St. Pancras - although the left there has still been hobbled by a lack of unity.
Now the circumstances are rather different. Andy Burnham is now prime minister and is enjoying his honeymoon, and is dressing himself - in rhetoric at least - in progressive garbs.
The frontrunner to be the Labour candidate is Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former Somali refugee who is said to be close to Starmer. (It is hard not to wonder what she thinks of Labour’s proposed introduction of one of the harshest asylum systems in Europe).
But Polanski has advantages. He is a national party leader with huge name recognition.
He will have the support of a Green Party which now has more than a quarter of a million members - and far more resources and experience than it once did.
He will surely be able to attract a huge grassroots army of supporters.
Share
This is a diverse community - many minority Brits have been attracted to the Greens from Labour - and many younger progressive-inclined voters live there.
That said, this is not Hackney or Haringey: as pollster Steve Akehurst notes, it has many financially secure voters with socially liberal attitudes, rather than their financially insecure counterparts who are more attracted to the Greens.
Polanski will surely have to be position himself as an MP who will stand up for the constituency - rather than a Labour MP who will represent the government.
He will have to hammer away at Burnham shifting in rhetoric, but not in policy, and not the various U-turns he’s already made. “Hold Burnham’s feet to the fire” and “send Labour a message” must surely be part of the approach.
There is no risk of Reform winning here, so Labour can’t fall back on “Vote Green, get Farage”. Voters can be encouraged to take a risk-free punt on the Greens, believing it will send a signal to the government that they want meaningful change in substance, not in tone and rhetoric.
That includes taxing the wealthy and big business to invest in crumbling services and infrastructure.
Here is a constituency with many voters from a migrant background, or who have friends, lovers and workmates who hail from other countries.
It’s certainly worth going for Labour’s anti-migrant, anti-refugee policies. If Polanski won, there’s a good chance Shabana Mahmoud would be driven from office.
Here’s an important truth to end on. It’s Polanski and the Greens who kicked Starmer out of office. That’s because of the Gorton and Denton by election, and the local elections: Labour lost four times as many votes to the Greens as to Reform.
So already the Greens can point to having made a huge political impact.
Burnham certainly has his honeymoon - but political reality will inevitably bite, not least as a Budget approaches.

reads.title: Weekend Update #200: Summer Is Ending, The Russian Offensive Is A Failure So Far
reads.subtitle: Why Fuel Attacks Need To Be Prioritized, An Update;
reads.body:
Hello All,
Well, this is Weekend Update #200. When I wrote the first of these, in November 2022, I certainly did not expect to be producing these close to four years later. I just went back and read my first update, which was quite an experience. I have taken it out of paywall so that anyone can go down memory lane with me.
All I can say is that if you have read these for the past 45 months, you would have had a great deal of discussion of production/logistics and how Trump/populism was shaping US politics and foreign policy. The first story was about the Ukrainian liberation of Kherson, but the next two were about the production war (which most people still do not understand) and how pro-Russian populism in the GOP could be a major problem for Ukraine. Here was how the production section started:
Production. It’s remarkable how time and again the ability to produce is overlooked before a war and then becomes so important during the war. This is partly the case because of the almost always faulty lightning war fallacy, which has one of the sides assume that they are so strong the war won’t last long (another reason the faulty pre-war analysis was so problematic).
And the political section was a warning that if the GOP captured both houses of congress in the upcoming midterm elections, if would be bad for Ukraine as the Republicans had a growing anti-Ukraine wing. It is worth noting that I did not mention Trump by name in the piece, but did mention that there was a “pro-Russian” wing in the Republican Party that looked to be growing in influence.
This is definitely understood in Russia as well, which is why I imagine all eyes are on the US mid-term elections this week. If the Republicans take both houses of Congress, both Ukrainians and Russians will be watching intently to see if the pro-Russian wing of the GOP (Tucker Carlson, MTG, etc) start having some success in influencing policy.
You can accuse me of many things—but at least I have highlighted some pretty important aspects of the war. The war has arguably been defined by Russian and Ukrainian war production and the GOP has gone down a pretty dark pro-Russian road.
And, as I said last weekend, I will keep producing these as long as Russia is invading Ukraine and as long as people still want to read them. As part of that, I set up a special Weekend Update #200 donation link for Come Back Alive. Many of you have already contributed and many of you tried but had trouble having the payment go through. I talked this over with CBA and they said the issue was with banks not approving payments to Ukraine, not on their end. They have tried to improve the situation, so if it did not work the first time, it might work now.
All I can say is thank you for trying!
Now the update this week. I will start with a quick look at the state of the Russian summer offensive (if it can be called that) as we are now closer to the end of the summer than the start. It is notable that when Russia advances, the press screams about a coming Ukrainian manpower crisis and collapse, but when the Russians throw away masses of soldiers for no gain, the reporting often moves on to other things.

-
- Russian Advances This Summer Are Tiny Compared To Earlier In the WarTwo other stories. First, I know some people were not pleased with my skepticism about the value of the Wildberries attacks and the argument that fuel attacks needed to get priority. I do think what we have seen over the last week supports that case. Finally, Putin had a rather freaky moment this week when he described his view of international relations. It is so disturbing it is worth noting. It involves Orcas, polar bears and a touch of insanity—pure realism from an academic perspective.
Phillips’s Newsletter is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

## Summer Is Ending, The Russian Offensive Is A Failure So Far
As we are only two days from September, it would be worth having a quick update on the Russian summer offensive. In August 2025 this was when the press was full of doom about Ukraine, and was writing about inexorable Russian advances and Ukraine collapsing because of manpower shortages. It was almost exactly 12 months ago that the press was writing about a Russian breakthrough around Pokrovsk, how Ukraine was running out of soldiers, etc.
There was so much reporting about this supposed reality, that the weekend update produced almost exactly a week ago tried to put what we were seeing in perspective and put a little perspective on both the idea of a Russian breakthrough and a Ukrainian collapse (and yes both words were used a great deal).
 Here was how that update ended:
The last three weeks have indicated not massive problems with Ukrainian manpower (which are actually being grossly distorted) but more massive problems with how the war is viewed by the press and analytical community. Sadly, there are no signs that it is going to get better—and it matters, because Ukraine will (and in some ways already is) coming under massive pressure to cede land to Russia. It would be far better to report the land war for what it is—a bloody quagmire for Russia, where the Russian state is expending vast resources and losing mass numbers of soldiers for little or at times no gain. Because that is the truth.
This week, as there have been no Russian breakthroughs (ho, ho) there has been much less reporting of the Russian summer offensive and, amazingly, hardly any mention of the Ukrainian manpower crisis which the press wrote about constantly in 2025 and which major analysts were claiming was going to lead to a Ukrainian failure that year.
What we have seen this summer and spring has been a Russian offensive that will go down as one of the most extraordinary and bloody wastes in military history. It is worth looking at the Deep State map of the main areas of the fighting on March 21, 2026 (first day of Spring) and today.

-
-
-
- The most notable change is the Ukrainian recapturing of land in the middle of the line (the green area to the east of Pokrovske). There are tiny shifts in Russia’s favor in other places, but you do need to look hard to see them.
What this means is that in all probability the Ukrainians have liberated slightly (and I do mean slightly) more territory from Russia than the Russians have seized—during the Russian spring/summer offensive season. The exact amount is impossible to know, but it is worth noting that both Deep State and the Institute for the Study of War are estimating that over the summer Ukraine has taken more land from the Russians than the Russians have from them—while disagreeing slightly over the specific figure over the last four weeks. During that time, Deep State has Ukraine taking a net of 3 square miles from Russia, while ISW has Russia taking 20 square miles from Ukraine. If you want to see both tabulations in a helpful metric, Russia Matters has put them together here.
And at the same time, Russian troop losses have continued to trend upwards. Over the last four weeks, Ukrainian intelligence has estimated that the Russians have lost 36,080 troops in combat. That is a daily number of 1289, which would work out to almost exactly 40,000 during the entire month of August.

-
- Btw, I just checked and the Ukrainian claim of Russian losses for the last 24 hours was exactly 1,400—so the final figure might be over 40,000.
This is an unsustainable loss rate, unless Russia finds a new way to generate large number of manpower. The Guardian, in a piece published on August 28, estimated that Russia is losing 6000 more troops a month than it can raise. Here is a quote from that piece:
“We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said.
To change the trajectory on those losses Russia will either have to greatly increase the number of soldiers they are recruiting from the rest of the world or Putin will have to enforce a greater mobilization across Russian society. When it comes to recruiting from around the world, Shaun Pinner just released a really interesting piece about how many POWs in Ukrainian custody are coming from outside Russia.
When it comes to internal mobilization, the Ukrainians interestingly still say that Putin is hoping to force more soldiers from the periphery into the army, another 300,000 after the upcoming elections. That remains his plan, they say, because he still does not want to enforce a general mobilization on Moscow or St Petersburg.
This “peripheral” mobilization will not be easy as these areas have already been combed through for soldiers—those forced in now will be the lowest of the low in priority list.
So, the Russians have hardly advanced this summer, have probably lost more land than they have gained in the last few months, are losing considerably more soldiers every month than they can generate, and are facing some pretty serious internal questions about how to find more soldiers.
What we are seeing is a summer offensive of failure.
Share

## Why Fuel Attacks Need To Be Prioritized, An Update
I know not everyone enjoyed my skepticism last weekend about the Wildberries strategic air campaign by the Ukrainians. And certainly the Ukrainian decision makers are not backing away from such a campaign, and they even broadened it this week to include the second largest Russian online retailer, Ozon.
That being said, the important economic signs this week were arguably about the stresses being shown in the Russian fuel system. The most important piece of evidence there is a report that Russian output of refined fuel can now only meet 70% of Russia’s own domestic production. There was an worthwhile report on that in the Japan Times. Here is how that story started.
Russia’s gasoline production fell to about 70% of domestic consumption levels by the end of August after a series of drone attacks forced major refineries to suspend operations, according to two industry sources.
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure in a bid to curb Moscow’s revenues, creating a fuel crisis that has forced Russia to import petroleum products and maintain sales restrictions across the country.
After a brief respite at the end of July, when some local authorities began easing or lifting restrictions on fuel sales, shortages returned to Russian regions in August.
And there are concrete signs that this shortage is real and spreading. Lines for Russian motorists to buy fuel are back, and in some cases this is real even close to Moscow. Russia seems to be living hand to mouth when it comes to refined fuels, which does not bode well for the Russians with winter approaching.
Overall, this means Russia will have to import refined fuels (very expensive) to just keep its economy and war machine functioning. This has been the situation over the last month. Now it seems to be getting more acute. It is the exact opposite of the first few years of the war, when oil was basically an income generating system for Russia.
Russia having to import fuel to keep functioning also opens up another possible target mix for Ukraine—fuel imports into Russia. This will have to come in by ship (I do not know of any pipelines that run into Russia—but I may be wrong). That means there will be limited pumping systems that can handle oil coming into Russia—and they should be hit.
Ukraine did make some refinery attacks this week. The Ukrainians hit the large refinery at Yaroslavl for instance. And, last night the Ukrainians also reportedly attacked the large KINEF refinery near St Petersburg. This is all good, but the campaign could always be more consistent and with a deeper target set. It must include not just refineries, but ports, pipelines, etc.
The system is showing real stress. It is getting by on quick repairs that are becoming less and less effective. It is Russia’s weak point as it involves everything—income generation, military operations, the functioning of the economy, etc.
Share

## Putin, Orcas, Polar Bears and Insanity
Speaking just the other day to faculty and students at a Moscow University, Vladimir Putin justified his invasion of Ukraine with a truly wild analogy.

-
- Putin Could Teach International Relations From A Realist Perspective“There are killer whales living nearby. They eat these bears up like small fry. Yes, they just attack as a pack – boom! – and tear them to pieces. It’s all very interesting. Yes, that’s the food chain.
Children need to be told about this too, so they understand what kind of world we’re living in and why we are carrying out the special military operation.”
First of all, this is wrong. Orcas do not kill polar bears (at least according to an internet search). However what is even worse is that it makes no sense. Is Russia the polar bear and NATO the orcas? Or is Ukraine the polar bear and Russia (with China and Iran perhaps) a pack of orcas.
And you know the great tragedy of international relations? It is that there are serious scholars, or at least those who some take seriously, who articulate this kind of a “realist” framework as automatic when it is far from it. If there is one thing we can say that has been shown, it is that states do not behave like this by nature. The US actually put together a brilliant alliance system that for 75 years was the exact opposite of a pack of killer whales attacking a polar bear. If it had wanted to, it could have crushed Russia. It did not.
Today’s Europe is also based on the reality that states do not have to do this to each other.
One of the reasons that Ukraine must win this war is to undermine this way of thinking. If Putin wins, with the help of Donald Trump, the orcas might actually start ripping the polar bears to pieces.
Have a good rest of the weekend everyone.
Thanks for reading Phillips’s Newsletter! This post is public so feel free to share it.
Share
