This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- New traffic plan for Hormuz: Iran and Oman agreed on a basic traffic plan for a safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Foreign Ministry announced on Monday, stressing that the route remains closed as long as the U.S. continues its attacks and maintains its blockade. Technical points are still under discussion.

- Regarding the issue of charging ships for transiting the Strait, spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said that Iran would “naturally” assess charges for the “services” it renders, though no decision was announced on the matter.

- Talks with the U.S. are still not happening. “We are not having negotiations with the United States,” Baghaei insisted. “Exchanging messages is natural and occurs through intermediaries,” but Tehran’s immediate focus, he maintained, remains the negotiations with Oman.

- Qatar backed up Iran’s reports of an impending deal. Majed Al-Ansari, a spokesperson for the Qatari Foreign Ministry, said on Tuesday that negotiations between Oman and Iran on the future of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz had reached an “advanced stage” and were at a “critical juncture.”

- Al-Ansari said Qatar’s focus, as a mediator to the U.S.-Iran talks, is the opening of the waterway “at the earliest opportunity.”

- Trump claims the Strait is open and under full U.S. control: U.S. President Donald Trump claimed in the Oval Office on Monday that the U.S. had swept the entire Strait of Hormuz of mines, and that it was “open” and “100%” under U.S. control.

- WSJ: U.S. fires on ship in the Gulf of Oman: U.S. forces fired on a Panama-flagged vessel early Tuesday after it reportedly attempted to bypass Washington’s naval blockade of Iranian ports, according to the Wall Street Journal. Maritime security firm Vanguard separately reported that the Panama-flagged container ship Vela Nova was struck by a missile fired from a helicopter while traveling westbound through the Gulf of Oman, about 71 nautical miles off Pakistan, sparking a fire that was later extinguished. All 17 crew members were accounted for, with no immediate reports of casualties.

- Iran accuses U.S. of “compulsive addiction to sanctions” after Treasury threat: Baghaei, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, criticized renewed U.S. sanctions threats on Tuesday after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke of “suffocating” Iran through economic pressure.

- In a post on X, Baghaei charged Washington of a “compulsive addiction to sanctions,” arguing that the U.S. turns to sanctions whenever it is “incapable of pursuing diplomacy” and escalates them when they fail to produce results. “This is no longer ‘policy’—it is ‘habit,’” he wrote, warning that U.S. officials risk undermining their “remaining chances” of finding a way out of the current crisis.

- Trump demands “compensation” from Iran, cites USS Cole attack carried out by Al-Qaeda: Responding to Iran’s demand for compensation for damage inflicted during the U.S.-Israeli war that began on February 28, Trump said Monday that Washington would likewise demand “compensation” from Tehran for U.S. soldiers and Iranian protesters he says Iran has killed, including the families of those killed in the USS Cole attack, which was carried out by Al-Qaeda.

- “Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, also citing “thousands” killed in combat.

- Trump added that Iran “should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza.”

- Trump claimed that 52,000 protesters had been killed in Iran over the past five months, raising his previous figure of 32,000 and far exceeding the roughly 7,000 deaths verified by HRANA and 5,000 verified by a UN special rapporteur.

- Khamenei shuffles military leadership: Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued decrees formally appointing six senior commanders across Iran’s armed forces, the IRGC, and the Basij, consolidating a wartime command structure that had operated on an interim basis for months, according to Al Jazeera and The National.

- Khamenei named Ahmad Vahidi the IRGC commander-in-chief. His predecessor was killed on February 28. He tapped Hossein Taeb to head the Basij, a paramilitary volunteer force operating under Iran’s IRGC.

## Yemen

- Four crew members killed in Bab Al-Mandab: Four crew members were killed in a suspected Ansarallah attack on the Egyptian-owned cargo vessel Tihamah in the Bab Al-Mandab Strait on Tuesday, Reuters reported. Ansarallah has not claimed responsibility for the attack.

- Saudi’s Jizan refinery closed until end of month: Saudi Aramco postponed the reopening of its Jizan refinery to August 30, after a second Ansarallah attack hit the facility, Reuters reported.

- Jizan, which produces 400,000 barrels of petroleum per day, particularly gasoline and diesel, has been struck twice since late July. It was anticipated to restart production on August 15 before a strike on Sunday.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, one Palestinian was killed after succumbing to wounds sustained in earlier attacks, and one was injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,387 killed, with 174,257 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,259 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,146, while 807 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel continues its assault on the occupied West Bank with 504 attacks in one week: Israeli forces and settlers continue to escalate attacks on the occupied West Bank, with 504 reported attacks in the past week alone, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.

- Hebron: Israeli authorities ordered the demolition of an elementary school and several homes in Masafer Yatta on Tuesday, WAFA reported. In the Bedouin community of Yatta, Israeli forces demolished a Palestinian house and filled in a water well.

- Ramallah: An Israeli attack on the village of Al-Mughayyir wounded six Palestinians on Tuesday, two of whom were women and three of whom were children, with Israeli forces firing tear gas on the village inhabitants as they plowed their fields, according to WAFA.

- Jenin: Israeli authorities summarily demolished 12 warehouses in Anza on Tuesday, WAFA reported. On Monday, an Israeli military court sentenced Ata Rmeilat-Abu Rmeileh, a 67-year-old Fatah official from Jenin, to 42 months in prison and fined him more than $1,650, after detaining him without charge for nearly 3 years and with his health deteriorating.

- Nablus: Israeli forces injured six Palestinians during an incursion into Burqa on Tuesday morning, two of whom were children. In Tal, Israeli forces conducted a raid on Monday before demolishing the home of Farouq Ramadan, a Palestinian who, while being attacked late last month, grabbed a settler’s gun before being shot dead by Israeli settlers.

- East Jerusalem: The Jerusalem Governorate announced on Tuesday plans by Israeli authorities to build 650 new settlement units on 27 dunums of land in East Jerusalem near Umm Tuba.

- Israeli government greenlights “Green Rafah”: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz quietly approved infrastructure work for “Green Rafah,” a residential zone on the Israeli-controlled side of Gaza’s Yellow Line, Israeli Army Radio reported on Monday.

- Netanyahu’s office has advertised “Green Rafah” as a pilot project backed by the UAE and has said it would offer temporary housing to Palestinians “free” of Hamas’ influence. Palestinian workers at the site will be subject to intense Shin Bet scrutiny, and strict rules have been announced for residences at the site.

- Drop Site previously reported on plans for a “residential” zone for Palestinians in Rafah that would contain and control its residents through biometric surveillance, checkpoints, monitoring of purchases, and more. Read here.

- Israel is holding the bodies of 1,700 Palestinians to use as bargaining chips: Israel is holding the remains of approximately 1,700 Palestinians for possible use in future exchanges, Haaretz reported, citing two security sources, despite no Israelis being held captive by Palestinian resistance groups.

- Shin Bet chief David Zini and the Israeli military reportedly support retaining the bodies in case Israelis are captured or disappear in the future.

- Many of the bodies are held in freezers in military facilities. At least 13 of the bodies are of Palestinian citizens of Israel, the paper noted.

- Former UN official says body must “clean house”: Former UN human rights official Craig Mokhiber said on Monday that the UN must “clean house” after a Drop Site investigation revealed senior UNICEF official Yahav Lichner repeatedly shared confidential UN information with Israeli officials during his time at the UN Population Fund in 2014 and 2015.

- Lichner later served as a senior aide to Sigrid Kaag while she coordinated Gaza aid. Kaag subsequently led the UN presence in Palestine and now sits on the executive board of the U.S.-Israeli “Board of Peace.”

- Lichner was reportedly placed on administrative leave following the publication of Drop Site’s investigation.

- MSF doctor discusses malnutrition in Gaza: James Smith, a doctor for Doctors Without Borders (Médecins sans Frontières) working in Gaza, described the “slow and cumulative effect of…manufactured deprivation” in the Strip to the UK’s Channel 4 on Monday, as Israel continues to restrict the entry of life essentials into Gaza. “Every month still, approximately 3,000 children are being admitted into acute malnutrition programs,” Smith noted. His full interview is available here.

- VIDEO: The family of 13-year-old girl killed in Khan Younis: Drop Site contributor Mohamed Ahmed spoke with relatives of Saba Al-Hashash, a 13-year-old Palestinian girl killed in Khan Younis on Saturday. “Last Thursday was the anniversary of her sister’s death, and today the second sister was martyred,” one told Ahmed. Al-Hashash’s mother said her daughter was shot as she went to recite the Quran. “Everyone in the mosque was a child, no older than 15, along with their teacher,” she told Drop Site. “Why target children? Don’t they know where they’re shooting?” Watch Ahmed’s video reports here and here.

## Lebanon

- Israel strikes ambulance, wounds two, and sets fire to fields in southern Lebanon despite ceasefire:

- Israeli forces set fire to fields and orchards in Sarda and Wazzani in the Marjayoun district on Tuesday, Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) reported.

- In Nabatieh, Israeli drones dropped explosive and incendiary materials around the General Security center, the Imam Ali Mosque and the vicinity of the Lebanese army barracks in Nabatieh Al-Fawqa, igniting fires that were later extinguished by Civil Defense and local firefighting teams.

- A separate Israeli drone strike in Nabatieh wounded two people, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry. The ministry said Israel struck the area a second time after an ambulance crew from the Al-Rissala Association arrived to assist the wounded, damaging the ambulance.

## U.S. News

- Primaries in six states, including Wisconsin, Minnesota, and South Carolina:

- Progressive Francesca Hong, a chef and state lawmaker, faces Milwaukee County executive David Crowley in Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary. Hong, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is the frontrunner in the race, despite party efforts to back several of her opponents, including former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who dropped out two weeks before the election, and current Lt. Gov Sara Rodriguez, who dropped out earlier.

- In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and Rep. Angie Craig are vying for the Democratic nomination to replace outgoing Sen. Tina Smith. Craig, whose career-long support from AIPAC has complicated her more recent votes for resolutions blocking weapons funding to Israel, holds a narrow lead over Flanagan—who has received the endorsement of Sen. Bernie Sanders—according to the latest poll.

- Editor’s note: This has been corrected to amend an earlier version which said Sanders endorsed Craig instead of Flanagan.

- In the race to replace Craig, progressives Matt Little, a former state senator, and Kaela Berg face Matt Klein, a pro-Israel physician who has received over $2.5 million from 314 Action, which supports scientists and doctors running for public office and sometimes operates as an AIPAC cut-out. Drop Site’s Julian Andreone and Ryan Grim wrote about this race here.

- Ten Republicans in South Carolina are running to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, including his sister Darline Graham, who Gov. Henry McMaster appointed to complete her deceased brother’s term, and who received Trump’s endorsement in the primary. Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman are also seeking the nomination, along with former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford and businessman Mark Lynch. A majority in the primary is needed to avoid a late August runoff. Lynch, who previously challenged Graham, is running as the only candidate to reject AIPAC money.

- Trump administration prepares executive order to overhaul childhood vaccine schedule: The Trump administration is preparing an executive order, obtained by The Washington Post and dubbed “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations,” that would divide vaccines into three categories and push for children’s immunizations to be administered at separate medical visits rather than in combined doses. The order is expected to be signed as soon as Monday.

-  In the draft, vaccines against 11 diseases, including measles, polio, and whooping cough, would remain recommended for all children, while others such as hepatitis A and B, meningococcal disease, influenza, and coronavirus would move to a “shared decision-making” category between parents and doctors.

- The order also calls for developing alternative vaccine adjuvants to aluminum, which some FDA officials have said is not feasible on a practical timeline.

- The move follows a January administration effort to reduce recommended childhood vaccines that a federal judge blocked in March, and dovetails with Trump’s reported concerns about the debunked links between vaccines and autism.

- State Department says it revoked more than 175,000 visas under Trump: The State Department said Monday it has revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals during Trump’s second term.

- Most of the visas were rescinded as a result of criminal allegations against their holders, though several visas were rescinded from people accused of celebrating the assassination of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, and others were revoked from people accused of ties to the Cuban and Iranian governments.

- Rep. Ilhan Omar demands answers after ICE agent found outside her town hall with mismatched plates: Rep. Ilhan Omar sent a letter Friday to a DHS field office after local police discovered an ICE agent sitting outside her Richfield, Minnesota town hall in a car with mismatched license plates, HuffPo reported on Monday, a practice that DHS had claimed was discontinued and which violates state law.

- The Homeland Security Investigations employee said she was conducting an undercover drug operation before a supervisor call led her to leave the scene.

- Omar wrote that the incident “raises serious and uncomfortable questions” and “emphasizes many Americans’ growing concern that the Trump administration uses ICE to surveil political opponents.”

- Google co-founder has spent more than $100 million fighting California billionaire tax proposal: Google co-founder Sergey Brin has donated an additional $20 million to Build a Better California, bringing his total spending against the state’s proposed billionaire tax to more than $100 million, Tech Crunch reported, as he seeks to avoid an estimated $13.3 billion tax payment.

- California’s Prop 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of roughly 200 billionaires in the state to help fund healthcare programs.

- Other tech figures including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, and venture capitalist Peter Thiel have taken steps to avoid the assessment, though Jensen Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia, has said he would be “perfectly fine” paying the tax, which voters will decide on in November.

- Private intelligence firms selling surveillance dossiers on AI, data center critics: Private intelligence firms including RANE Network, Kroll, and Liferaft are marketing dossiers and monitoring services on critics of artificial intelligence and data centers, framing grassroots opposition to server farms and AI expansion in counterterrorism-style language, according to documents obtained by The American Prospect.

- RANE offered the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission a tailored assessment of “anti-technology sector sentiment” in March 2025 and later held a webinar warning of threats from protesters including creatives, environmentalists, laid-off workers, and civil liberties advocates.

- The commercial offerings coincide with “anti-tech extremism” memos from federal agencies.

- Read the full report from The American Prospect here.

- Pentagon official says U.S. “digging in” to Asia: Elbridge Colby, Undersecretary of Defense for Policy, said in a speech in Manila Monday that the United States is not disengaging from Asia but rather “digging in” to maintain a favorable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific.

- Colby said maintaining a balance of power favorable to the U.S. in the region required a “posture of deterrence by denial” in the area from Japan, through Taiwan and the Philippines, and down to Borneo.

- He also pointed to what he characterized as a growing U.S. military commitment in the region, though he called on U.S. “allies and partners” to increase their defense spending. “We are looking for partners, not protectorates,” he said.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- Over 11,000 more people displaced in Sudan over two days, IOM says: More than 11,000 people were displaced from villages in Sirba locality, in Sudan’s West Darfur near the border with Chad, over two days of escalating fighting between the Sudanese army and the RSF, the UN’s International Organization for Migration said on Monday. Most of those displaced crossed into Chad, while others sought refuge around El Geneina, West Darfur’s capital.

- 7.4 magnitude earthquake kills at least 111 in western Colombia: A 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia Monday, killing at least 111 people and damaging roughly 1,600 buildings, including 61 that completely collapsed, according to the Associated Press.

- The earthquake’s epicenter was in the Choco region, with destruction reported in the cities of Cali, Pereira, Quibdo, and Manizales.

- Colombia’s Geological Service called it the country’s strongest quake recorded this century.

- The U.S. State Department announced $15.5 million in emergency aid Monday night, with Mexico, El Salvador, and Chile also offering assistance. The disaster follows two earthquakes that devastated neighboring Venezuela in late June, killing more than 6,300 people.

- Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad, brother to death in absentia: A Syrian court sentenced ousted President Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher, a former commander in the country’s military, to death in absentia on Tuesday for crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during Syria’s 14-year civil war.

- Judge Fakhareddine al-Aryan, delivering the verdict at Damascus’s Fourth Criminal Court in a session aired live on state TV, said Assad “used state agencies to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity,” marking the first sentences against Assad or his inner circle since his family’s five-decade rule ended 20 months ago.

- The brothers fled to Russia after the government’s fall in December 2024 and received asylum there.

- Libya declares maximum emergency after third drone strike hits largest functioning refinery: Libya’s National Oil Corporation declared a “maximum state of emergency” around the Zawiya refinery, west of Tripoli, after three drone attacks in roughly 48 hours, Anadolu reported. The state oil company warned it could declare force majeure and shut down operations if the attacks continue.

- Monday’s strike hit a tank containing an estimated 4.5 million liters of gasoline, igniting a massive fire before the tank collapsed, according to Reuters.

- An early Saturday strike punctured a naphtha tank, causing a contained chemical leak. Another drone struck the complex’s desalination plant, damaging its main pipeline and a storage tank.

- Libya’s Ambulance and Emergency Service said Tuesday there were no “serious injuries” from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation.

- No group has claimed responsibility for the attack with the 120,000-barrel-per-day facility repeatedly being caught in fighting between rival armed factions amid the instability that has gripped Libya since the NATO-backed overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

- Turkish parliament passes limited amnesty bill for PKK militants: Turkish lawmakers voted 468-88 on Monday to pass a “terror-free Turkey” law offering limited amnesty to Kurdish PKK fighters who lay down their weapons, the country’s first legislative step toward ending decades of conflict.

- The bill comes 18 months after jailed PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan urged his followers to disarm, and was backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s ruling AKP party and the pro-Kurdish DEM party.

- It suspends prosecutions and sentences for five to 10 years and is expected to lead to the release of about 3,500 PKK-linked detainees in an initial phase, though it excludes those involved in “serious crimes .“

- The law makes no mention of Ocalan’s own case. The PKK warned in a Sunday statement that excluding Ocalan would leave many provisions of the bill a “dead letter.”

- Returning Kurds attacked in Syria: The return of displaced Syrian Kurds to their northeastern hometown of Ras al-Ain was suspended Monday after a first group of roughly 2,500 returnees was attacked by “armed groups,” The New Arab reported.

- A security official in Hasakeh province said several attackers were arrested and trips were “temporarily suspended as a precautionary measure” until safety could be ensured.

- The attack sparked protests in nearby Qamishli, where demonstrators attempted to breach security headquarters.

- Nearly 100,000 people from the Ras al-Ain area have applied to return home since Turkish-backed forces seized the territory from Kurdish control in 2019.

- Iraq forms new military command to secure southern border after militia attacks on Saudi Arabia: Iraq has established the Al-Badiya Operations Command to strengthen security in its southern desert border region following attacks by Iran-aligned militias against Saudi Arabia, Iraqi sources told The New Arab on Monday. The move is aimed at preventing Iraqi territory from being used for cross-border strikes or drawing retaliation onto Iraqi soil.

- Military sources said Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the command after Iraqi intelligence reports identified security gaps that pro-Iranian armed groups exploited to transport drones and launchers through Iraq’s Al-Muthanna desert.

- Saudi Arabia struck targets in Iraq it said were linked to attacks on its oil facilities in late July.

- Russia’s top court bars antiwar Yabloko party from parliamentary elections:  Russia’s Supreme Court ruled Monday to bar Yabloko, the only officially registered party opposing Moscow’s war in Ukraine, from next month’s parliamentary elections. The pro-Kremlin nationalist party Rodina had filed suit alleging Yabloko received undeclared campaign support, including from Western sources.

- Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov called the case an “unconstitutional attack on freedom of thought” and said the party would appeal, as about 100 supporters gathered outside the courthouse.

- The party has been backed by exiled opposition figures including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of assassinated Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny. It was polling at just 3% earlier this year, short of the 5% threshold needed to win seats.

- Seven Uzbek citizens killed in drone attack on Russia’s Tatarstan region: Seven Uzbek citizens were among those killed in a drone attack in Russia’s Tatarstan region Monday, the Uzbek consulate in Kazan said. The Ukrainian attacks in the region killed 13 people on Monday.

- Between two and three million Uzbek citizens work in Russia, with Uzbekistan’s economy partly reliant on remittances from migrant workers.

This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Trump on Iran: “We are low-keying it”: President Donald Trump signaled Sunday that he is prepared to let economic pressure on Iran mount rather than launch a new military offensive, telling Axios the U.S. is “low-keying it.” “We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money,” Trump said.

- Trump also pointed to oil prices falling to slightly above $75 a barrel as easing the war’s impact on U.S. consumers. “It will work out. It always works out. It’s like a chess game,” he said.

- Iran FM says no current negotiations with U.S., but Oman agreement is close: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran is not currently negotiating with the U.S., and negotiations would not resume until Washington ends its violations of the memorandum of understanding and compensates Iran for the commitments it breached.

- Araghchi did say, however, that the two sides continue to exchange messages through intermediaries, though he insisted that this is “not called negotiation.”

- On Saturday, Araghchi said that Iran and Oman are “very close” to an agreement on a new legal and navigational framework for the Strait of Hormuz, stressing again that an agreement with Oman would not fully reopen the Strait.

- Six demands to open the Strait: Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who served until this weekend as Supreme National Security Secretary, articulated Iran’s six demands to reopen the Strait, calling on the U.S. to end all threats to the country, permanently end “war and aggression” against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq, lift the U.S. blockade of Iran, remove its naval and air forces from the area, pay for damages caused by its attacks, lift sanctions on Iran, and unconditionally release its frozen assets.

- Iran’s terms, Axios noted on Sunday, were the prerequisite for a nuclear deal “until several weeks ago.” Now, they are the prerequisite for the Strait reopening.

- WSJ: Trump hints he will end Iran war with Strait reopening: U.S. President Donald Trump told aides he may walk away from the Iran war without a nuclear deal if Tehran fully reopens the Strait of Hormuz, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday. Trump said he would lift the blockade if Iran fully reopens the strait, but disputes remain over other demands, including reparations, frozen assets, and waivers for Iranian oil exports, the report says.

- Vessel struck off the coast of Hormuz: A vessel was struck on Saturday by an unknown projectile near the Strait of Hormuz, 18 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations. The vessel and crew were reported safe, and there was no environmental damage. Oman’s Foreign Ministry condemned attacks on transiting vessels and warned about their potential to derail its ongoing negotiations with Iran over the Strait.

- U.S. sneaking millions of barrels of oil through southern Hormuz lane, official tells Axios: An unnamed U.S. official told Axios on Sunday that “around 8 million barrels of oil are going out of the Gulf every night” through Hormuz’s southern lane in coordination with the U.S. military.

- The reporting has not been independently confirmed. Far lower amounts of oil have been suggested by available tracking data, with the maritime tracking firm Kpler reporting a total of nearly 16.9 million barrels moving west-to-east through Hormuz from August 1 to August 7.

- FT: U.S. blockade has halted Iranian exports of crude from Kharg: Iran’s crude exports appear to have stopped due to the renewed U.S. naval blockade, with no tankers loading at Kharg Island for at least a week, the Financial Times reported on Sunday.

- Kharg handles nearly 90% of Iranian crude exports and has been idle since July 31. Iran is still receiving revenue from earlier cargoes reaching Asia, including 26 Iranian-flagged tankers near Malaysia, but that income could dry up within weeks under a blockade. Empty tankers are also unable to return, while storage levels indicate Iran has begun cutting production, the report noted.

- Vance says the U.S. is still “in the middle of the game” in war with Iran: In a Sunday interview with Fox News, U.S. Vice President JD Vance said that the U.S. characterized the war with Iran as not presently near a resolution, saying that the U.S. was “in the middle of the game,” and that it intends to leverage its economic, military, and diplomatic advantages to “get the best outcome for the American people.”

- Vance said the administration’s immediate priority is “getting as much oil and gas out of the Middle East” as possible.

- He said Washington expects Gulf exports to return to prewar levels once the Strait reopens under a new agreement. He also claimed that Iran had told the U.S. it will neither impose tolls nor fire on commercial vessels, and that Iran is “hurting” and looking to get out of the conflict.

- Pentagon orders U.S. defense companies to speed up weapons production: The Pentagon issued a memo on Wednesday ordering U.S. defense companies to dramatically speed up the production and delivery of weapons and ammunition, as the five-month war with Iran depletes American arsenals.

- In the memo, Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg gave contractors a maximum of 21 days to submit plans to “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules”  for critical weapons.

- The U.S. has burned through much of its stockpile of long-range precision missiles in the war. The Post reported the military fired more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles in the first month of the conflict alone, faster than manufacturers can replace them, alarming some Pentagon officials.

- Mohsen Rezaei appointed to lead Iran’s Supreme National Security Council: Iran named former Revolutionary Guard commander Mohsen Rezaei as head of its Supreme National Security Council, according to state media. Rezaei replaces Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who was appointed after Ali Larijani was killed by an Israeli strike in March.

## Yemen

- Saudi and Saudi-backed forces shell areas in Saada and Taiz: Four civilians, including two children and two women, were wounded when artillery from Saudi-backed forces struck a home in Wadi Hansh in Taiz, Yemen on Saturday, according to an Ansarallah media official. Separately, Saudi artillery shelled Tabara village in Ghamr district of Saada governorate, Al-Masirah reported.

- Ansarallah-aligned governors in Hodeidah and Lahj urged residents to reject recruitment by Saudi-backed forces, warning them against becoming “fuel for the Saudi war.”

- Yemen’s UAE-backed Southern Armed Forces claim drone strikes on Ansarallah: The Emirates-backed southern Armed forces said Saturday they struck Ansarallah positions across three fronts in northern Dhale governorate. The Southern Armed Forces claimed “heavy losses” in personnel and equipment but provided no casualty figures.

- Fires reported at two major Saudi Aramco energy sites: Two fires were reported at two Saudi Aramco sites on Saturday.

- Satellite fire-monitoring data showed a major thermal event at the Berri Gas Plant near Jubail on the Gulf coast. The extent of damage and cause remain unclear.

- Separately, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry confirmed that a fire broke out at dawn at a facility belonging to Aramco’s Jizan refinery on the Red Sea coast. Aramco crews extinguished the blaze and no injuries were reported. Ansarallah claimed the attack.

- Ansarallah launches assault on Red Sea port, killing seven: Ansarallah struck the government-held Red Sea port of Al-Mokha on Yemen’s western coast with ballistic missiles and drones on Sunday.  The “National Resistance Forces,” aligned with Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, claimed four troops and three civilians were killed and 30 wounded, with a pier, buildings, and stored food damaged.

- Oman works to contain oil spill near protected marine reserve: Omani authorities are working to contain an oil spill covering around 390 square kilometers near the Hallaniyat Islands, more than a month after the tanker Caroline Bezengi, carrying roughly one million barrels of Russian oil, ran aground in waters off the country’s southern coast, according to Oman’s state news. The spill threatens environmentally sensitive areas, including coral reefs, turtle nesting grounds, and marine habitats around the Hallaniyat Islands marine reserve.

- The cause of the incident has not been determined, though British maritime security firm Vanguard previously reported explosions aboard the tanker off Yemen’s Mukalla coast on June 6 that caused flooding and disabled its main engines.

## Palestine

- Netanyahu formally rejects U.S.-backed Gaza roadmap: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu formally rejected a U.S.-backed 15-point Gaza roadmap announced by President Trump at the end of July, saying Israeli forces would not withdraw until Hamas was “fully disarmed” of heavy and light weapons.

- He said Israeli forces would continue military “operations” in Gaza against what Israel labels “threats” to its forces and civilians.

- Netanyahu also ruled out a Palestinian state in either the occupied West Bank or Gaza.

- “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said, in a reference to the U.S.

- Last week, Israeli ministers and security chiefs discussed resuming attacks on Gaza to signal that Israel rejects the U.S.-backed 15-point phase 2 roadmap accepted by Hamas, according to the Times of Israel. The report follows a lull in Israeli airstrikes over the past several days, though shootings by Israeli troops have continued, killing and wounding Palestinians. During the meeting, one minister reportedly described the roadmap as a “diplomatic October 7.”

- Hamas reaffirms commitment to 15-point plan: Hamas said in a Sunday statement that it remains committed to the 15-point Gaza roadmap agreed upon with mediators and supervised by the U.S.

- It reiterated that its priorities are an end to Israeli attacks, Israel’s withdrawal from the Strip, the reopening of crossings and the entry of aid and shelter materials.

- Senior Hamas official Basem Naim said about the group’s position that it “expects the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons.”

- Mladenov defends Israel, claims no troops beyond Yellow Line: Nickolay Mladenov, High Representative of the Gaza Board of Peace, said on Sunday that Israeli forces would begin a phased withdrawal only after all weapons in every sector of Gaza—including heavy, light, police, and personal arms—are surrendered and “rendered unusable,” contradicting the plan originally released by the Board and agreed to by Hamas. The plan includes a parallel process of storage of “heavy weapons” by the Palestinian resistance alongside a phased withdrawal by Israel.

- “Nobody is required to do anything, last of all Israel,” before this happens and is verified, he said. In the same remarks, Mladenov falsely claimed that, “currently,” Israel had no “beyond the Yellow Line.” The original demarcation left Israel controlling roughly 52% of Gaza. Israeli officials now say forces control around 70%.

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, six Palestinians were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,386 killed, with 174,256 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,258 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,145, while 807 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israeli attacks kill 13-year-old girl, wound several Palestinians across Gaza: A 13-year-old Palestinian girl was killed on Monday after succumbing to wounds sustained when Israeli forces shot her on Saturday in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis, southern Gaza, WAFA reported. Several Palestinians were also wounded by Israeli fire in Jabalia, northern Gaza, early Monday, while Israeli artillery shelled multiple areas across Khan Younis, Al-Bureij, and Beit Lahia.

- Israeli attacks on Gaza over the weekend:

- Israeli forces shot and wounded three Palestinians in Khan Younis on Saturday morning, according to WAFA.

- Israeli forces shot and killed a young Palestinian man near Deir al-Balah in central Gaza on Saturday.

- On Sunday, Israel shelled the Al-Bureij and Jabalia refugee camps, Israeli tanks fired on Gaza City, and the Israeli navy bombarded the coast near Al-Bureij, Khan Younis, Rafah, and Gaza City.

- Israel shot and wounded three more Palestinians, including a child, on Sunday evening, opening fire in the central Khan Younis neighborhood of Al-Najjar and the western Al-Dahra neighborhood, according to WAFA.

- Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank:

- Nablus: An Israeli settler attack on the town of Beit Furik, east of Nablus, injured two Palestinian men on Saturday, WAFA reported. Israeli soldiers shot and wounded another Palestinian youth on Monday morning during a raid on the Balata refugee camp, detaining five others.

- Jenin: Israeli forces stormed the town of Ja’bad, in the Jenin governorate, on Saturday, sealing off its entrance and raiding dozens of homes, detaining several Palestinians in the process, according to WAFA. Israeli forces began bulldozing Monday Palestinian land between Marka and Qabatiya, south of Jenin, to establish a military post and build a settlement road. Forces also seized agricultural land and bulldozed the surrounding area.

- Hebron: Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians in a mosque in the town of Idhna on Saturday, an assault for which Israeli soldiers provided cover. During the attack, soldiers detained seven Palestinians, including the imam of the mosque. A separate settler attack in Wadi al-Rakhim on Saturday evening injured six Palestinians, one of whom was shot, according to WAFA. On Sunday, Israeli forces opened fire on a shepherd while he was grazing his flock in Idhna, killing three sheep and injuring several others.

- Bethlehem: Israeli forces deployed sound bombs and tear gas canisters during a raid on the Dheihesh camp on Saturday evening, inducing several cases of suffocation, WAFA reported. Additional attacks were reported in the villages of Za’atara, Ash Shawawra, Dar Salah, and Al ‘Ubeidiya on Saturday evening.

- Ramallah: Israeli forces fired tear gas into a Palestinian home during a Saturday evening raid in al-Mughayyir, leaving several members of the family, including children, struggling to breathe. Simultaneous raids were reported in the nearby villages of Turmus ‘Ayya and Abu Falah, and in the villages of Beit ur al-Tahta and Jiljilyya.

- On Monday, Israeli forces detained Mahmoud Shalato, a former Palestinian detainee from the town of Aboud after raiding his home and ransacking its contents. Shalato has spent 10 years in Israeli prisons. Also on Monday, Israeli settlers attacked the Al-Kaabneh Bedouin community near Al-Taybeh, after attacking the same community last Thursday, injuring three members of a Bedouin family.

- Al Aqsa mosque stormed again: As many as 133 Israelis illegally stormed the Al-Aqsa mosque on Sunday under the protection of Israeli police, WAFA reported. Israeli Knesset member Zvi Sukkot raided the Nour Al-Huda School in the Shuafat refugee camp in occupied East Jerusalem, filming inside and placing signs reading “Closed” on the school’s doors.

- Israel seals off Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh: The Israeli army declared the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank a closed military zone on Monday claiming it’s to prevent escalating settler attacks in the area, according to Israeli broadcaster KAN. The order bars Israelis and foreigners, including activists and journalists, from entering the area. Settlers attacked Taybeh, one of the few remaining Christian-majority Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank, on Friday.

- Israel acknowledges death of Palestinian prisoner after years: Israel acknowledged on Sunday that Palestinian prisoner Ehab Diab, 36, died in custody, the Palestinian Prisoners’ Affairs Commission announced, nearly two years after Diab was detained.

- Diab was arrested on December 12, 2023. The commission believes he died on September 18, 2024, after roughly nine months of reported torture in Israeli custody.

- Families protest Israel’s restrictions, medical assault on the Strip: Palestinian families gathered in Gaza on Saturday to protest Israel’s medical attacks on Gaza, describing their experiences watching their loved ones die from treatable illnesses as Israel blocks the entry of medicine into the Strip and restricts patients from leaving for treatment.

- Dr. Saleh Sheikh al-Eid, head of oncology and hematology at Nasser Medical Complex, said three to four cancer patients are dying each day. More than 18,500 patients require medical evacuation from Gaza, according to the WHO.

- Ben-Gvir renews order banning family visits for Palestinian prisoners: The Palestinian Prisoners’ Club announced on Sunday that Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir renewed an order barring families from visiting Palestinian prisoners, warning that their complete isolation enables torture, starvation, and “slow killing.”

- The renewal came shortly after Israel’s Supreme Court ruled the continued ban on International Committee of the Red Cross visits unlawful.

- Palestinian Journalists Syndicate documents 108 Israeli attacks on journalists in July: The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate documented 108 attacks by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinian journalists and media workers in July. There were 58 cases of brief detentions and reporting restrictions, 12 cases in which journalists were targeted with stun grenades and tear gas, 11 attacks by settlers including physical assaults and threats, and six cases of beatings, with four journalists sustaining injuries from shrapnel while covering events in Gaza.

## Lebanon

- Israeli violations continue on Monday despite “ceasefire”: Israeli forces carried out a large explosion between Markaba and Rabb Thalathin in the Marjayoun district on Monday, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA). Israeli forces advanced into the western outskirts of Mais Al-Jabal in the Marjayoun district, as artillery shelling targeted a home. Forces set fire to a number of homes in Khiam in the same district. Israeli soldiers carried out a large explosion between Kfar Tibnit and Arnoun in the Nabatieh district, and another explosion in Zawtar Al-Sharqieh on Monday.

- Israeli forces bombard southern Lebanon, demolish homes, and target workers over weekend:

- Israeli forces carried out attacks across southern Lebanon, with troops advancing toward Kfar Shuba as artillery struck Mays Al-Jabal, al-Mansouri and other areas. Israeli forces also targeted residential homes in Mays Al-Jabal.
A video released Saturday reportedly showed Israeli forces firing toward the director and staff of the Bint Jbeil water department as they were conducting maintenance on the water network in Aita Al-Jabal.

- Israeli artillery struck Kfar Rumman, the Ali Al-Taher hill, Al-Mansouri, the outskirts of Mayfadoun, Tallousa, Bani Hayyan, and Wadi al-Slouqi on Sunday.

- Israeli forces demolished civilian homes and infrastructure in Zawtar Al-Sharqiyah, Al-Mansouri, Hadatha, and Sarbin.

- Israeli forces also dropped incendiary devices in Ain Al-Tineh, setting fires in the area.

- Report: Israel conditions survival of Sunni Lebanese village on excluding displaced Shiites: Residents of Kfarshouba, a predominantly Sunni village in southern Lebanon, were told the town would be spared from destruction only on condition that they don’t shelter any displaced people from neighboring Shiite villages, The National reported. Israel has destroyed at least 60 villages across the predominantly Shiite south, forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands and blocking their return.

## U.S. News

- Senate confirms Todd Blanche as attorney general: The Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general early Saturday in a 50-49 vote, with Republican Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski joining every Democrat in opposition after a contentious confirmation fight centered on Blanche’s controversial settlement of President Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS.

- Blanche, who had been serving in an acting capacity since Trump fired Pam Bondi in April, won over the decisive vote of Republican Senator Bill Cassidy after formally rescinding in writing the proposed $1.776 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” and narrowing tax audit immunity for Trump and his family.

- Trump names Will Scharf as White House counsel: President Donald Trump announced Sunday that Will Scharf, currently his staff secretary, will replace David Warrington as White House counsel next month.

- Scharf, a former personal defense lawyer for Trump, worked on the Supreme Court case which granted immunity to Trump for actions taken while he was president. He also ran unsuccessfully for Missouri attorney general in 2024.

- Rep. Max Miller defies party pressure, will stay in race despite abuse allegations: Rep. Max Miller, the Ohio Republican accused of physically abusing his ex-wife and young daughter, will not withdraw from his re-election race despite mounting pressure from his own party.

- President Donald Trump personally called Miller last week to urge him to reconsider his odds, Sen. Jon Husted publicly called him unfit for office, and Sen. Jim Banks called his actions “deeply troubling.”

- Miller will face Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker, in November.

- Rep. Ed Case defeats progressive challenger in Hawaii Democratic primary: Rep. Ed Case, a moderate Democrat from Hawaii, defeated progressive state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole in Sunday’s Hawaii primary.

- Federal judges allow TPS termination for Myanmar, South Sudan migrants: Two U.S. district judges rejected efforts to preserve Temporary Protected Status for migrants from South Sudan and Myanmar, prompting the Department of Homeland Security to confirm the protections were halted effective August 7. The decisions will affect about 4,200 migrants, according to Reuters.

- Judge Patti Saris of Boston and Judge Matthew Kennelly of Chicago issued the rulings following a June Supreme Court decision that ended TPS protections for Haitian and Syrian migrants.

- Palestinian students and faculty sue Columbia University for discrimination: A group of Palestinian students and faculty are filing a lawsuit against Columbia University today alleging that the university engaged in “anti-Palestinian discrimination and fostered a hostile learning and work environment.”

- The plaintiffs—Hadeel Assali, Bahia Munem, Mahdi Sabbagh, Maryam Alwan, and Layla Saliba—allege that since October 2023, Columbia University failed to protect Palestinian students, faculty, and staff from harassment, threats, and doxxing targeting Palestinians on campus, while aggressively disciplining pro-Palestinian students, increasing surveillance of their speech and activities, and subjecting them to unequal treatment.

- “We are bringing this case because Columbia failed in its basic duty to ensure a safe and equitable environment,” the plaintiffs said in a joint statement. “Instead of protecting us, the University contributed to discrimination and harassment of its Palestinian community and created a climate of intimidation, fear, and hostility.”

## Other International News

- Ukrainian strike targeting refining plant kills 13 in Russia: A Ukrainian drone attack on Nizhnekamsk in Russia’s Tatarstan region killed at least 13 people, including a child, and injured 39, according to Russian authorities.

- Ukraine said the strike targeted Tatneft’s TANECO refinery, about 800 kilometers east of Moscow.

- The attack comes amid an intensified Ukrainian strike campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, which has contributed to fuel shortages in parts of the country.

- In separate incidents three people were killed and 37 wounded in a Russian attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, while authorities in Russia’s Belgorod said five were ​killed and 25 wounded by another Ukrainian drone attack.

- U.S. backs Philippines in new South China Sea dispute: The State Department accused China of using a “national nature reserve” designation around the Scarborough Reef maritime area as a pretext to strengthen its territorial claims.

- The statement said that the designation was coercion by Beijing and reiterated support for the Philippines in its claim over disputed maritime waters which have been the site of naval clashes in recent months.

- The dispute stems from a 2016 international tribunal ruling that rejected Chinese claims to the waters.

- Mass graves discovered in Sudan: Mass graves containing the bodies of 25 civilians, including women, children, and hospital staff, were discovered in Kurmuk after the Sudanese military recaptured the town, Sudan Tribune reports. Kurmuk’s commissioner said the victims were executed by the RSF near Jebel Fankat.

- The RSF and an SPLM-N faction seized the Ethiopian border town on March 8 before the military retook it on July 8.

- U.S. drone crashes in Djibouti: A U.S. Air Force MQ-9A Reaper drone crashed near Chabelley Airfield in Djibouti on Sunday. Chabelley Airfield is a heavily restricted desert base and serves as the central hub for American unmanned intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance flights across the Horn of Africa and the southern Red Sea. The cause is currently under investigation.

- U.S. and Ecuador conduct joint operation: Ecuadorian and U.S. forces carried out a joint operation in Ecuador’s northern border province of Esmeraldas, Ecuador’s Defense Ministry announced Friday, deploying troops in riverine areas and destroying a clandestine site allegedly used by drug-trafficking groups.

- The operation comes a few days after U.S. Southern Command announced it was replacing Joint Task Force-Southern Spear with a new Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere, which it said would “secure the region and defeat all threats.”

- U.S.-Ecuador joint military operations began in March under the U.S. campaign against “narco-terrorists.”

- Attacks in Congo kill 21: At least 21 civilians were killed in attacks attributed to Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels in Mambasa territory, in eastern DR Congo’s Ituri province, overnight Friday and into Saturday, Drop Site’s Africa correspondent Godfrey Olukya reported.

- “21 bodies have so far been discovered,” a local police officer said, warning that the toll remains provisional because villagers are still missing. Local leaders said they had warned authorities about an ADF presence days before the attack but received no help and no response.

- The ADF was formed in Uganda in 1995, originally seeking to overthrow President Yoweri Museveni, before relocating into eastern Congo amid military pressure. The group later pledged allegiance to ISIS in 2019 and has carried out repeated massacres of civilians.

reads.title: Chartbook 465 The Last of the Magicians: Thomas Mann, John Maynard Keynes and the Alchemy of Bourgeois Liberalism
reads.subtitle: An essay by Adam Tooze and Stefan Eich
reads.body:
> The new, socialized world, the world of planning and co-operation, will come; humanity will get rid of unnecessary sufferings that are a disgrace to intelligence; and this will be achieved by a great and sober effort that has already enrolled under its banner all who have turned their backs upon a cult of musty, obscurantist, petty bourgeois sentiment. It will come; for a rational outward order of things in keeping with the present stage of human enlightenment must be created, or, if the worst happens, will be produced by violent convulsions. Only then can the heart reassert its rights with good conscience. The great sons of the bourgeois age, those whose capacity for spiritual growth raised them above the level of their class, are living proof of the fact that there are in the bourgeois nature infinite potentialities, unlimited potentialities for self-liberation and self-conquest. Our time summons the middle class to remember these innate powers and to take their stand upon them intellectually and ethically. The right to power is contingent upon the conviction that one has a historic mission to perform. If any class refuses to do this, or is too weak, it will have to step aside, abdicate power, and make way for a type that knows none of the inhibitions and ties of atavistic sentiment, which, one cannot but fear at times, may render the European middle class unfit to guide the body politic and economic into a new world.
Without doubt, the credit that history is still willing to accord to the bourgeois republic to-day—a short-term credit, indeed—rests upon the faith not yet lost that democracy also has that ability which its increasingly powerful enemies claim as their own: the ability to undertake our guidance into the new age. It is not by staging celebrations for its great sons that the middle class proves itself worthy of them. The greatest of these, Goethe, hails it:
Turn your backs upon dead trappings,
Let us love what is alive!
Whose words are these? We are in the spring of 1932. The themes are familiar. The appeal to the educated middle class standing at a turning point. The idea of living on borrowed time.
The obvious suspect is John Maynard Keynes. And yet this is clearly not Keynes. For one, if this passage was by Keynes, it would be very well-known. But it is also a little too bombastic, too European in its evocation of class categories and the reference to Goethe would be out of character too.
In fact, it is the text of a speech written by Thomas Mann speaking on the centennial of the death of his great literary hero Goethe on March 22, 1932.
Nevertheless, the resemblance in contemporary diagnosis between Keynes and Mann is intriguing. In continuation of the thought begun in Chartbook 463, it is fascinating to explore the parallels and divergences between two of the most famous liberal intellectuals of the period from the 1920s to the 1940s.

-
-
Was there contact between them? Not, as far as we know, in direct terms. So what follows is not intellectual history but speculative juxtaposition. Nevertheless, the connection is not merely imaginary.
Mann can hardly have not known about Keynes. No educated German could have been ignorant of The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919). Indeed Mann’s diary records him reading excerpts from the book in February 1920 and delighting at the portrayal of Wilson. As one would expect, Mann invokes “Keynes’s book” as a household term.

-
- Conversely, after the critical success of Buddenbrooks (1901) and The Magic Mountain (1924), the Bloomsbury group must surely have had views about Mann, who went on to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929.
And yet there is no evidence that Keynes ever read Thomas Mann. He was far more interested in Ibsen plays and Russian ballet than contemporary continental novels. It is a remarkable and perhaps telling missed connection, one that points to the relatively hermetic nature of much of middle class culture, particularly in early twentieth-century Britain.
After all, their preoccupations were deeply aligned.
Both were fundamentally interested in the fate but also the role and responsibility of the social elites inherited from the nineteenth century in the twentieth century.
Keynes’s opening to the Economic Consequences of the Peace could have come straight out of a Mann novel, except that in Mann it would have been tongue in cheek.
As Mann himself later remarked in a talk at Princeton given in 1939, Zauberberg, his great novel looking back at bourgeois life in the pre-1914 period, was only imaginable under conditions of “intact” capitalism.
For Keynes, the underlying stakes were nothing less than “civilization,” a term loaded with promise and anxiety. The force of The Economic Consequences of the Peace had after all come from treating the pre-war European order as an astonishing and fragile achievement.
In “My Early Beliefs,” the memoir Keynes read to his Bloomsbury friends in September 1938 in the midst of the Sudeten crisis, Keynes looked back on the confident rationalism of his pre-war youth and judged it “disastrously mistaken.” What he and his friends had missed was the existence of “irrational springs of wickedness in most men.” “We were not aware that civilisation was a thin and precarious crust erected by the personality and the will of a very few, and only maintained by rules and conventions skilfully put across and guilefully preserved.” It is this startling confession about the precarity of civilization that underpins Keynes’s quest for renewal and reinvention.
For the young Mann, by contrast, the same term was very nearly a slur. During World War I, and then most explicitly in his Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man (1918), he had built a whole metaphysics out of pitting “civilization” against Kultur. Civilization was the shallow, sociable, rationalizing West: epitomized by the Enlightenment, France, democracy, “literature,” even politics as such. Kultur, by contrast, was a peculiarly German thing: arising from the soul, endowed with depth, and expressed in music, form, art, indeed in the daemonic. “The difference between Geist and politics,” Mann wrote, “contains that between culture and civilization, between soul and society, between freedom and the franchise, between art and literature.” Culture was where the enchantment lived.
Having drawn this map in which enlightenment rationalism was neatly separated from the magical realm culture, within a few years he redrew it.
Already by the early 1920s Mann had dissolved the binary. In his extraordinary speech “Von deutscher Republik” (On the German Republic) given in October 1922, which startled his admirers on the right, Mann declared himself for the Weimar Republic and simultaneously insisted this was no mere recantation of his earlier beliefs. Instead, he announced by way of the unlikely duo of Novalis and Whitman “the identity of humanity and democracy,” the first being “only a classicistically old-fashioned name for the second.” Kultur and civilization, the German romantic and the American democrat. The antitheses on which his wartime Reflections had rested were now to be reconciled through the republican state and under the heading of humanity. By 1932, summoning the bourgeoisie to “guide” society into a rational new order, Mann speaks in almost exactly the civilizational register the author of the Reflections had ridiculed. That intellectual and political migration is what lets Mann’s Goethe speech begin to sound like Keynes.
By the early 1930s, theirs was thus a shared question: How do we make modern civilization work under conditions that are both affluent and yet fraught?
Like Mann, Keynes had a deep sense of inherited ideas as both powerful and out of step with the world. The profound sense that the old order was taking itself down to ruin and had to be reinvented in order to be saved, is common to both of them.
Both of them were reluctant but realistic exponents of modern democracy.
The working class as the unexpected but essential ally against bourgeois philistinism, in favor of modern intellectual and cultural progress – Mann and Keynes also agree on this.
Most fundamentally, both situated their contemporary interventions and historical reflections within a historical schema of transition.
Mann’s 1932 Goethe speech was the warrant for Georg Lukács’s claim that Mann was the “last great critical realist”. Like the modernists of his generation – Woolf, Joyce, Proust – Mann was caught up in the exploration of inner life. Under conditions of late capitalism, Lukács argued, nothing else was possible. But unlike his contemporaries, Mann remained rooted in a broader, overarching view of history, precisely the socio-economic trajectory set out in his Goethe speech: towards “(t)he new, socialized world, the world of planning and co-operation”. This meant that Mann’s Zauberberg (as argued in the last Chartbook 463) is not just a case study of subjective disorientation, but truly a structural account of the drifting apart of subjective time and objective history. This was for Lukács (and for Adorno’s btw) the essential hallmark of “realism” under conditions of late capitalism.
Taking up the Lukácsian reading, would it be too far-fetched to suggest that Keynes, in his own domain, was accomplishing something similar?
If Mann (as read by Lukács) was the last great critical realist because he accounted in grand architecture of his novels for the disintegration of the classic unity of subjective time and objective historical development, was Keynes, in his General Theory (1936), not trying to do something similar for the domain of political economy? Was Keynes not corralling the dispersed fragments of a late-nineteenth-century coherence into a new and more general framework, an intervention that was both radical and at the same time an act of preservation, not to say conservation?
Keynes’s basic diagnosis was that the old properties of a well-functioning market economy and with it the self-confident subjectivity of bourgeois identity, consumption, and personal freedom were no longer in evidence. Conservatives might insist that the only way forward was a hard-faced return to the nineteenth century. But for Keynes that amounted to a form of denial. The other great experiments of the age, the new model of 1920s Soviet civilization, as well as the distasteful centralized authoritarian regimes of Italian fascism and German Nazism, were at least able to reckon with the rupture.
But liberalism had no reason to abandon itself to this bad set of choices. If it actually occupied the space of sex-life-death – i.e. biopolitics, Mann’s preeminent domain – and at the same time situated its economic policy within an enlightened macroeconomics, framed not as a “special” case but by a “general theory” – what Mann’s novels did in narrative terms – liberalism could regain its agency and vindicate the special role of the educated elite as guiding all of society into a better and more civilized future. As both Mann and Keynes insisted, liberalism need not be shy, it need not concede the future to the fascists, so long as it put itself on the historical front foot. It must demonstrate its capacity to “guide”, as Mann put it in his Goethe speech.
That also meant accounting for one’s own vantage point in addressing a bourgeois audience. Like Keynes, Mann inhabited the contradictions of this bourgeois perspective with preternatural ease, as Lukács already observed in his essay “In Search of Bourgeois Man,” written in 1945 in honour of Mann’s seventieth birthday. Describing Mann as “the last great bourgeois writer,” Lukács highlighted his “dialectically complex attitude to the middle class.”
If we think of economics and the novel as two distinctively modern “technologies” of sense-making in bourgeois society, and if those apparatuses first took on their consolidated “classic” shape for the first time in the early nineteenth century, then both Mann and Keynes found ways to update and translate those technologies into the Age of Extremes. So, Keynes’s macroeconomic stands in relation to its Marshallian forebears, as, according to Lukács, Mann’s novels stand in relation to their nineteenth-century predecessors.
But if this parallelism is illuminating there is another deeper motif that it may unlock.
What, after all, is the pivot we are using for this speculative exercise? A speech commemorating the dominant figure of modern German culture, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749-1832).
For Mann’s sense of history (and for Lukács’s reading of Mann as a historical thinker and writer) it is not just the crisis of World War I that is key. It is not by accident that in the midst of the crisis, in 1932, Mann should return to Goethe as his essential anchor point, straddling the Sattelzeit (Koselleck) between the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Furthermore, by way of Goethe’s own historical vista, Mann opens to the seventeenth century and the age of alchemy supposedly overcome by enlightenment rationalism. Hence the figure of Dr Faustus.
Geoff Mann (no relation) has recently given us a brilliantly illuminating reading of Keynesianism, also in terms of the Sattelzeit, but in his case by way of Hegel. This is inspired less by any specific indebtedness of Keynes to Hegel, than by Geoff Mann’s productive wrestling with Marxist readings of Keynes – above all that of Toni Negri.
In rewriting Keynes as the theorists of the thermidor, Geoff Mann gives us a tour de force in every sense of that phrase.
Our reading of Keynes in light of Thomas Mann suggests an alternative, less conservative, speculative history. On our reading, the historical depth to Mann and Keynes’s liberalism would be provided not by Hegel and his visions of the state, but by figures of bourgeois genius like Goethe and, on Keynes’s side, his great heroes of the seventeenth and early eighteenth century.
Thomas Mann’s reading of the late Goethe is worth quoting at length:

> This bold, dream-like anticipation of a new society to succeed the bourgeois order is as remarkable, as impressive, as the old man’s growing interest in engineering projects of utopian scope, his enthusiasm for undertakings like the cutting through of the Isthmus of Panama. He talks of these things insistently and goes into detail as if they were of more importance to him than all the poetry in the world, and that is true, in the last analysis. His optimistic delight in the scientific side of civilization, affecting communications particularly, need cause no surprise in view of the end of Faust, who experiences his highest moment in the realization of a utilitarian dream, the draining of a swamp—a peculiar affront, indeed, to the one-sidedly aesthetic and philosophical trend of the age! In the same way, Goethe was astonishingly indefatigable in his old age in discussing the possibilities of joining the Gulf of Mexico with the Pacific, and in expatiating on the incalculable effects of such a feat upon the whole world, civilized and uncivilized alike. He wanted the United States to undertake the work, and his fancy dwells upon the prosperous cities that would spring up one after another along the Pacific coast, where nature had so felicitously prepared the ground for man by making good harbors. He could hardly wait for that to come about—that and the joining of the Danube and the Rhine, a perfectly staggering project, to be sure, along with a third very great project, the Suez Canal for the English. “To see all that,” he exclaims, “might make it worth while to hold out on this earth for another fifty years.” He cast his eyes over the earth, refusing to stop short at the borders of his own country; his enthusiasm for the future was vast enough to take in the whole world; and the quickening of life, the joys and sorrows, of foreign nations affected him as did those of his own people. His was an imperialism of love—the imperialism of an august mind risen above barriers of nationality, a mind that cherished liberty particularly under its aspect of greatness. It is the same trait that we have already seen in his heralding of a world literature. In setting itself to create a utopia of applied science, the bourgeois outlook expands to world-wide proportions; it turns into “communism,” taking that word in a sufficiently broad, undogmatic sense. This is an enthusiasm of a sober sort. But what we need to-day is the sobering of a world that is dying from the strangle-hold of emotional survivals. Who was it who said that the Germans should be prohibited from using the word “Gemüt” for fifty years? It was Germany’s greatest poet. The middle-class man is lost and is doomed to be swept aside in the era that is approaching unless he can succeed in ridding himself of the fatal sentiment and life-sapping principles that still govern his thinking. He must bravely espouse the future. It is idle to scorn reason and hold to a stubborn cult of atavistic feeling which, in present conditions, appears utterly blind and senseless—a kind of desperate, malignant, murderous sentimentalism.
It is as though Thomas Mann is reading Goethe by way of Keynes’s “Economic Possibilities of our Grandchildren”, which had been published in June 1930.
Which suggests the question – riffing this time on Geoff Mann rather than Thomas Mann – are all true Keynesians not so much descendants of Hegelian, as children of Goethe?
A textbook description of the Weimar classicism shaped by Goethe and Schiller in the transition from the eighteenth to the nineteenth century, would describe it as the synthesis of rationalism of the Enlightenment with the romantic, “animal spirits” of Sturm und Drang, a decidedly “Keynesian” formulation. An argument for Goethe over Hegel could be made simply on grounds of precedence and preeminence. By the late eighteenth century, Goethe was a cultural star of quite different proportions than Hegel. Whereas Hegel was an awed spectator of Napoleonic history, Goethe was on the young Bonaparte’s bedside table. As Emperor, Napoleon received Goethe for a personal audience in October 1808. Indeed, as Napoleonic historian Nicolas Broussard remarks:

> Hegel opens his lessons on Roman history by reporting the famous bit of conversation between Goethe and Napoleon: “One day he was conversing with Goethe about the nature of tragedy. He expressed then the opinion that the modern tragedy was differing from the old one essentially in that we do not have fate any more of which men will succumb and that in the place of the ancient Fatum has appeared politics. It should thus be used as the modern destiny for tragedy, as the power of circumstances to which the individual has to bend to.” (Lectures, p.215).
Once again this is a chain of intellectual association without textual warrant in Keynes himself. The point of making it is to answer Geoff Mann’s brilliant Marxo-Hegelian reading by way of Negri with one derived from Thomas Mann by way of Georg Lukács.
Keynes, himself, might very well have been bewildered by either chain of association. After all, he situated himself self-consciously in the tradition of English political thought that descended from Hobbes and Locke. His most charged points of identification lay with figures the “nineteenth century” had flattened and which Keynes set about disinterring.
The first was Thomas Robert Malthus, almost exactly Goethe’s contemporary and, in Keynes’s insistent phrase, “the first of the Cambridge economists.” What Keynes prized in Malthus was precisely what the nineteenth century had discarded. Malthus was the road modern political economy had failed to take, defeated and buried by Ricardo. For the discipline had refused to build on Malthus the “inductive and intuitive investigator,” the mind that stayed close to the texture of experience. Instead, Ricardo’s more abstract intellectual constructions proved victorious. The triumph of the cleaner, colder system produced a science remade in the misleading image of purified reason. Keynes presented his own task as revealing why the subsequent century of Ricardian dominance had been a “disaster,” stuck in an “artificial groove.”
To recover Malthus was to reopen the groove, to insist that the ancestor the nineteenth century had buried was the richer mind who had come to economic questions “by the best of all routes,” beginning as a philosopher and moral scientist, passing through history, and only then arriving at theory, as Keynes put it the biographical essay he finally published in 1933 he made the stakes plain. To describe that arrival Keynes reached for a startling image of transformation: “from being a caterpillar of a moral scientist and a chrysalis of an historian, he could at last spread the wings of his thought and survey the world as an economist.” It is an image of magic and metamorphosis: a shapeshifting creature that leaps from one fixed form into another, unrecognisable and more alive.
This was exactly the image Keynes would reach for again, on a far grander scale, when he turned from Malthus to a stranger and even more charismatic ancestor, reaching back past the eighteenth century into the seventeenth: Isaac Newton.
In 1936, Keynes, a long admirer of Newton, purchased the scientists’ unpublished manuscripts at a Sotheby auction. He reportedly paid £3,000 or around £200,000 today adjusted for inflation. As Keynes was surprised to discover, the manuscripts he had purchased reflected Newton’s extensive interest in the subject of alchemy. By Keynes’s own estimation, Newton scribbled perhaps a million words in notes on alchemical matters. As Keynes came to realize, Newton was not just the first of the scientists, but the last of the magicians.
In the remarkable commemorative essay that he penned for December 1942 the anniversary of Newton’s birth, Keynes started by apologizing for the fact that “The war has deprived me both of leisure to treat adequately so great a theme and of opportunity to consult my library and my papers and to verify my impressions … .” He then went on:

> “I believe that Newton was different from the conventional picture of him. But I do not believe he was less great. He was less ordinary, more extraordinary, than the nineteenth century cared to make him out. Geniuses are very peculiar. Let no one here suppose that my object today is to lessen, by describing, Cambridge’s greatest son. I am trying rather to see him as his own friends and contemporaries saw him. And they without exception regarded him as one of the greatest of men. In the eighteenth century and since, Newton came to be thought of as the first and greatest of the modern age of scientists, a rationalist, one who taught us to think on the lines of cold and untinctured reason. I do not see him in this light. I do not think that any one who has pored over the contents of that box which he packed up when he finally left Cambridge in 1696 and which, though partly dispersed, have come down to us, can see him like that. Newton was not the first of the age of reason. He was the last of the magicians, the last of the Babylonians and Sumerians, the last great mind which looked out on the visible and intellectual world with the same eyes as those who began to build our intellectual inheritance rather less than 10,000 years ago. Isaac Newton, a posthumous child born with no father on Christmas Day, 1642, was the last wonderchild to whom the Magi could do sincere and appropriate homage.”
What is extraordinary about this essay, as about Thomas Mann’s rereading of Goethe in 1932, is its historical creativity. Keynes summons a new Newton, one freed from the encrustations of the nineteenth century. One that is both stranger and yet also more alive, freed from the wax works and thus present in the twentieth century. As one contemporary remarked, Keynes described Newton as “Copernicus and Faustus in one, and doubtless he thought he resembled them both”.
Ultimately, this is what makes Keynes and Mann kindred spirits: the ambition not only to rethink the position of the twentieth-century bourgeoisie, and its politics of liberalism in relation to the tensions of their moment, but also to give that politics a new history in the grandest sense.
I love putting out Chartbook. I am particularly pleased that it goes out for free to thousands of subscribers around the world. But, writing this newsletter takes a lot of work.
