reads.title: As the Board of Peace Cosplays Diplomacy, Israel Once Again Ramps Up Killing in Gaza
reads.subtitle: After Hamas agreed to a roadmap for implementing the next phases of the Gaza “ceasefire,” Israel escalated its assault on Gaza and the Board of Peace backtracked.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- Ahmed Abu Al-Kas (right) at the site of an Israeli airstrike that targeted Al-Sousi tower in Gaza City on August 2, 2026. Photo by Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto via Getty Images.Story by Abdel Qader Sabbah, Mohamed Ahmed, Sharif Abdel Kouddous, and Jawa Ahmad
GAZA CITY—Ahmed Abu Al-Kas was sifting through the debris of an apartment in the Al-Sousi Tower in western Gaza City in the aftermath of a pre-dawn Israeli airstrike on Sunday that killed a pregnant woman, her husband, and their five-year-old son. Among the broken concrete, strewn blankets, children’s toys, and backpacks lay the body of an unborn baby, curled in a fetal position and covered in grey dust. Al-Kas watched as another man picked up the tiny figure with a hand towel and gingerly placed it on a pile of blankets.
He had been nearby when the bombing happened. “All of a sudden, we heard the sound of an explosion. We started running and we came next to the tower,” Al-Kas, 32, told Drop Site News later that day. “I broke down the door and went in with the other young men. I found body parts scattered everywhere. Over there, I found a small child. I shined my flashlight into the other part of the apartment, and found that half of it had collapsed. Since this morning, I’ve been searching through the rubble for the body parts left behind overnight. While searching, I found this baby.”
The force of the blast had apparently torn the baby from the mother’s body. Al-Kas was distraught. “I found a baby thrown from its mother’s womb,” he said. “His mother was torn apart, and I found [the baby] just like this.”
The attack on the family home in the Al-Sousi Tower came on one of the deadliest days in Gaza in recent weeks, with at least 18 Palestinians killed, according to the Gaza Health Ministry—just as President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace was claiming that an agreement had been reached on a new phase of “the ceasefire.”
Remnants of the munition found at the site appeared to be from an Israeli weapon, likely a suicide drone—a type of highly precise attack drone—that has been used frequently in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, according to Trevor Ball, an analyst with Armament Research Services (ARES) and a former U.S. army explosive ordnance disposal specialist, after reviewing images provided by Drop Site.

## Ahmed Abu Al-Kas and others remove debris and body parts after a strike on a residential tower in Gaza City on August 2, 2026. Video by Mohamed Ahmed.

The surge in Israeli attacks came in the wake of a deal with Hamas, first announced by Trump on Thursday, on a roadmap for implementing the next phases of the Gaza “ceasefire.” Shortly after Trump’s announcement, mediator countries said Hamas had, “for the first time,” formally committed to “an actionable plan for relinquishing all its weapons.”
The following day, Hamas said it had engaged “responsibly and positively” with mediators’ proposals but stressed that implementation of the deal would only proceed if Israel fulfilled all of its obligations under the first phase of the October 2025 agreement. The group said discussions over handing over its heavy weapons were conditional on a permanent end to Israeli attacks, a full Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, early recovery and reconstruction, the entry of a Palestinian technocratic committee and international forces, the dismantling of Israel-backed armed militias, and progress toward Palestinian self-determination and an independent Palestinian state.
While Tel Aviv did not initially issue a formal response, Israeli officials were quickly quoted in the press saying they rejected the deal as the escalated weekend assault began.
On Saturday, at least six Palestinians were killed in a series of airstrikes, including one targeting the area of Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir al Balah, damaging an adjacent medical storage facility and destroying essential medical supplies as well as a number of tents sheltering displaced families.
“We went to sleep under a [new ceasefire deal]. Trump announced a ceasefire and things were going in the right direction.…We slept peacefully and happily, thinking that the situation would get better from the next day onward,” Fatima Sharab, who was displaced from her home and living in a tent near Al-Aqsa Hospital, told Drop Site. She said she was woken up at around 2 a.m. on Saturday morning with instructions to flee the area before it was bombed.
Sharab stood among shredded tents and belongings that littered the ground next to a massive crater in the sand. “The camp here is made up of tents and a warehouse for kidney medications for dialysis patients. So what was the problem? What did we do wrong?” She added, “You can’t even tell where your own tent was or where your belongings are. Today, we have no shelter. I don’t even know what to say anymore.”

## The aftermath of an Israeli strike near Al-Aqsa Hospital in Deir al-Balah on August 1, 2026. Video by Abdel Qader Sabbah.

According to the director of Al-Aqsa Hospital, Raed Hussein, the warehouse that was targeted on Saturday was the main one of four the hospital established in coordination with the World Health Organization to help deal with a storage crisis. “This warehouse contained all the solutions and equipment needed for kidney dialysis,” Hussein told Drop Site. “We were shocked to wake up today and find that this warehouse had been targeted…Over the past three years, supplies have never been fully available, and when they do arrive, they come only in limited quantities. So you can imagine the consequences of this attack.”
The heavy assault continued the next day when an Israeli missile slammed into Al-Thawra street in western Gaza City, killing a child and a bridegroom in his tent.
“He was preparing his tent for his wedding, then he was torn apart in it,” said Rasem Asaliya, 35, an eyewitness. “They said there would be a ceasefire, no more strikes, no more assassinations. But they struck anyway.”
The torn, blood-spattered tent barely stood upright next to a small crater where the missile struck. “They are still attacking us and our children. Nothing has changed. They’re liars. They broke their word,” said Mohamed Yassin, 37, who rushed to the site in the aftermath of the attack. “All the news we’re hearing [about a new deal] is a lie. This isn’t news; it’s all false propaganda.”
On Monday, three countries that have served as mediators—Qatar, Egypt, and Turkey—issued their first joint statement condemning the Israeli attacks. They denounced Israel’s targeting of healthcare facilities and medical infrastructure, and the killing of civilians, including women and children, calling the attacks “a flagrant violation of international law and international humanitarian law.”
At the same time, Nickolay Mladenov, the High Representative of Board of Peace, along with other board members, met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The board issued a statement shortly afterwards saying “Israel and the Board of Peace share a common understanding of the ultimate objectives.” The statement clarified a series of measures that contravened the board’s own roadmap, saying Hamas must first fully disarm before Israel took any steps. “Contrary to inaccurate reports, we note that the withdrawal of the IDF [Israel Defense Forces] beyond the Yellow Line will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators. This applies to light weapons, heavy weapons, and the tunnels alike,” the board said.
In his first public comments on the agreement on Tuesday, Netanyahu flatly rejected the deal. “They sent us a draft. We did not agree. It is not our draft. We sent our comments,” he said in a video posted on social media. “We’re not withdrawing from our current lines until Hamas is totally disarmed.”
Since the “ceasefire” agreement went into effect nearly 10 months ago, Israel has violated the terms of the deal on a daily basis. Over 1,250 Palestinians have been killed, including over 300 children, in routine airstrikes, shelling, and shooting. Israel has not allowed in the agreed upon levels of humanitarian aid and life essentials, blocked the entry of reconstructions equipment and shelters, refused to fully open the Rafah border crossing, and has gradually pushed in its ground troops further westward from what was supposed to be an initial line of withdrawal of 53% of Gaza to now controlling nearly 70% of the enclave.
The pace of killing has been gradually increasing. Gaza’s Health Ministry recently noted that 152 people were killed during the month of July, including 21 children, marking the highest monthly death toll recorded since the beginning of 2026 in what has been a steady escalation over the past few months.
The official death toll since the beginning of Israel’s genocidal assault in October 2023 has now topped 73,300 with over 174,200 injured. Thousands more are missing and trapped under the rubble. Denied proper equipment and resources, Civil Defense crews have been unable to properly retrieve the bodies.
Over the weekend, first responders managed to complete intensive efforts to recover the remains of 112 Palestinians, including 40 children, killed in one of the deadliest single incidents of the genocide—an Israeli attack on a residential block in the Sabra neighborhood of Gaza City on November 22, 2023 that killed over 300 members of the Hassayna and Abu Sharia families in what Amnesty International called “a chilling illustration of a pattern of Israeli attacks wiping out entire multi-generational families.”
A mass funeral ceremony was held on Tuesday for the 112 retrieved bodies in what was understood to be the largest funeral in Gaza’s modern history. The bodies, wrapped in Palestinian flags, were carried on stretchers through the destroyed streets of Gaza City before being laid in rows on the ground for the funeral prayer. They were then brought to a nearby cemetery to be laid to rest.

## A mass funeral ceremony in Gaza City for the remains of 112 Palestinians retrieved from under the rubble after an Israeli attack on a residential block in the Sabra neighborhood in November 2023. Video by Abdel Qader Sabbah.

“This overwhelming scene reminds us of the crimes and attacks committed by the Israeli occupation, and its brutality and criminality against these families,” Fares Affana, the Civil Defense Director of Ambulance and Emergency Services in North Gaza told Drop Site. “This massacre is one of the largest carried out in the Gaza Strip. We could hear the cries and screams of the wounded from beneath the rubble of such massacres. Some were wounded and still alive. But because of our lack of equipment, we couldn’t reach them.”
Another mourner watched as the martyrs were carried through the streets. “Those whose bodies were recovered from beneath the rubble and debris embody for the world the devotion to the Palestinian cause,” he said. “This is not a funeral for one family alone. It is a funeral for all of Gaza.”
Sami Vanderlip edited the videos for this report.

reads.title: Trump denies munitions shortages, vows to jail leakers; Israeli settler charged with killing Palestinian; Senate holds Fauci in contempt
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: August 6, 2026
reads.body:
- Dr. Anthony Fauci is sworn in during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on July 29, 2026. Photo by Alex Wroblewski / AFP via Getty Images.Thursday, August 6, 2026 – Iran-Oman deal on Hormuz “on verge of being finalized,” deputy foreign minister says. U.S. President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance talk Iran negotiations. U.S. redirects 48 vessels as part of Iran blockade. Pakistan Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif headed to Saudi Arabia. Iran arrests 21 for allegedly spying on its military. U.S. removes sanctions on Iraqi airline. Ansarallah announces “wide military operation” amid missile and drone attacks on Saudi-backed forces. Ansarallah claims two strikes on Saudi tankers. Israel shot sixth-grader in Gaza tent classroom, UN confirms. Israel releases 24 Palestinian detainees into Gaza. Israel continues attacks on the occupied West Bank. Israeli authorities beat Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya in detention, break his ribs. Arab and Islamic countries condemn Israeli violations in Gaza; Israel army chief says attacks will continue. Board of Peace awards first building contract in Gaza for military base. In rare move, Israeli prosecutors charge settler in killing of Palestinian activist Awdah Hathaleen. Israeli attacks wound eight in southern Lebanon as UNIFIL reports 113 projectiles launched. Rights groups condemn Israeli strike that killed Lebanese journalist as a war crime. Senate committee votes to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt. Trump maintains frequent contact with Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, WSJ reports. Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed opposes “unconditional” U.S. military aid to any country, including Israel. Trump-appointed judge ran D.C. public relations firm for months after taking bench, ex-employees say. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services backlog surges to 7.5 million. Government Accountability Office report finds DOGE overstated federal savings claims. Senate Democrats probe South Korean firm’s $2 million payment to Trump company. Michigan Democratic congressional candidate William Lawrence pledges to vote for Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker. Explosive-laden drone found near Ukrainian cargo plane in Germany. North Korea fires short-range ballistic missile. Nigerian military rescues 308 kidnapping victims. Flavio Bolsonaro names Congressman Alfredo Gaspar as running mate. UN experts warn of “silent Gaza” in Cuba amid U.S. pressure campaign. Iraqi government says armed groups could face terrorism charges after deadline. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney defends International Criminal Court.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Iran-Oman deal on Hormuz “on verge of being finalized,” deputy FM says: A deal on the Strait of Hormuz between Oman and Iran is “on the verge of being finalized,” Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iran’s IRNA news agency on Thursday,  saying that the two countries had come to an agreement on nearly all issues, including the location of entry and exit routes for maritime traffic.

- Gharibabadi said that the “new model” for managing traffic through the Strait would have large parts of the shipping route going through Iran’s territorial waters, and a smaller portion passing through Omani territorial waters.

- Existing temporary routes, including one near Iran’s Larak Island and another southern route near Oman, would be closed.

- Iran condemns U.S. “breach of promises,” claims U.S. ready to return to MOU commitments: Gharibabadi also discussed Iran’s view of the U.S. on Thursday, saying that Iran distrusts the U.S. after its “breach of promises and commitments” under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.

- The deputy foreign minister said that a return by the U.S. to its obligations under the MOU would be a necessary condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but not a sufficient one.

- He claimed that Iran had received messages that the U.S. was “fully prepared to return to its commitments” under the June memorandum, including the immediate cessation of military operations.

- Trump, Vance talk Iran negotiations: U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance publicly addressed the state of negotiations with Iran on Thursday.

- Speaking in Las Vegas, Trump said he’d “rather make a deal with Iran,” because he doesn’t “want to kill people.” In the same remarks, he repeated an earlier claim that the U.S. was preparing to launch “the biggest attack since World War II” before Iranian officials asked for negotiations.

- Trump also rejected reports of diminishing U.S. stockpiles in a Truth Social post on Thursday, saying that the Pentagon possessed “massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” and that more were being manufactured “as needed.” He said that those “leakers” who had claimed otherwise were being “hunted down” and that “long term jail sentences” would be pursued against them.

- Trump confronted War Secretary Pete Hegseth during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David last week demanding to know why he had apparently been misled about severe U.S. munitions shortages, according to the Washington Post. Trump reportedly said he believed the issue “had been fixed.” The shortages, particularly of long-range guided missiles and air-defense interceptors, have been one reason Trump has held back from authorizing additional large-scale strikes on Iran in recent days, one source told the outlet.

- Vance, interviewed by Laura Ingraham on Fox News, said diplomatic negotiations with Iran were “going to be messy” and would “take some time.”

- He also called his Iranian counterparts “extraordinarily difficult people” and blamed the failures on Iran’s “fractured system,” divided between moderates and hardliners who, he claimed, had pushed the country back into war.

- Vance told Ingraham that he was happy to “own” the negotiating effort, and played down reports that his recent meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had turned hostile. “He didn’t confront me. We had a nice and frank conversation,” Vance said of the talks.

- U.S. redirects 48 vessels as part of Iran blockade: The U.S. military announced on Wednesday that it had redirected 48 commercial vessels while enforcing its naval blockade of Iran, disabling two and boarding two.

- The statement from CENTCOM also claimed that the U.S. Navy had assisted in more than 1,000 transits over the course of the last three months.

- The maritime tracking firm Kpler announced on Wednesday that maritime risk remained “elevated” around the Strait of Hormuz.

- Only two vessels transited the Strait on Wednesday, down from eight the previous day, according to Kpler.

- Pakistan PM headed to Saudi Arabia: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif is scheduled to visit Saudi Arabia on Thursday to discuss consolidating Pakistan-Saudi Arabia bilateral relations and exchange views on developments in the region with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

- The Pakistani delegation includes the country’s deputy prime minister/foreign minister, the chief of army staff, the chief of defence forces, as well as other ministers.

- Regarding the U.S. war on Iran, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi told a weekly press briefing that Pakistan was “still engaging with other countries” and that it was aiming its diplomatic efforts at “a comprehensive and sustainable solution regarding the Strait of Hormuz.”

- Iran arrests 21 for allegedly spying on its military: Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence announced on Thursday that it had arrested 21 people in the southeastern Kerman Province accused of providing military intelligence to the Israeli spy agency Mossad, according to state broadcaster IRIB.

- U.S. removes sanctions on Iraqi airline: The ⁠U.S. ⁠lifted “counterterrorism” sanctions ⁠on at least one airline and several aircraft it previously accused of having ties to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), according ⁠to details ⁠posted to ⁠the U.S. Treasury Department’s website on Thursday.

- One of these airlines is Fly Baghdad, according to the website.

- The U.S. also removed sanctions on two Iraqi individuals on Thursday, whom it accused of close ties to the IRGC, or the previously sanctioned airline.

## Yemen

- Ansarallah announces “wide military operation” amid missile and drone attacks on Saudi-backed forces: Several casualties were reported after suspected Ansarallah missile and drone attacks targeted camps belonging to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government Emergency Forces in the Marib and Hadramout governorates on Thursday.

- Local media reported that ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones struck military camps in Marib and Hadramout, causing multiple casualties.

- The Emergency Forces said the attacks resulted in “human and material losses” but did not release an official casualty toll.

- Separately, forces said they shot down an Ansarallah drone over the city of Marib after it entered the city’s airspace.

- An Ansarallah spokesperson said the group would soon announce details of a “wide and qualitative military operation,” but did not specify whether he was referring to the reported attacks.

- Ansarallah claims two strikes on Saudi tankers: Ansarallah military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed on Wednesday that the group had conducted two strikes on Saudi oil tankers over the course of the previous 24 hours, and that it was continuing to enforce its blockade of the kingdom’s shipping on both the “south and north of the Red Sea.”

- Saree said the group struck the Saudi oil tanker Daisy in the Gulf of Aden with a ballistic missile, damaging it and forcing it to turn back. The attack followed a similar one on Tuesday on the Saudi oil tanker Wafa.

- Saree also vowed that the group would let no Saudi tanker pass until “our people’s legitimate demands are met, and the siege on them is lifted.”

- Oil spill from suspected Russian shadow fleet tanker threatens Oman’s coast: An alleged Russian shadow fleet tanker stranded off Oman’s southern coast is leaking oil across an estimated 600 square kilometers, raising the risk of a major environmental disaster, according to AFP. Satellite imagery reviewed by AFP showed an expanding oil slick near al-Qibliyyah Island, with Greenpeace warning the impact could be “severe and long-lasting.” The Caroline Bezengi, which Kpler data indicates loaded one million barrels of Russian crude in May, has been adrift since explosions near Yemen on June 6 disabled its engine and steering, according to maritime security firm Vanguard Tech. The cause of the blasts remains unclear.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, one Palestinian was killed after succumbing to wounds sustained in an earlier attack, and five were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,382 killed, with 174,236 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,255 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,125, while 806 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel shot sixth-grader in Gaza tent classroom, UN confirms: Israeli forces shot and wounded a sixth-grade student inside a classroom tent in Gaza City on August 4, the UN confirmed on Wednesday. A day earlier, Israeli forces destroyed the last remaining school in Beit Lahia in what had been a four-school compound.

- Israel releases 24 Palestinian detainees into Gaza: Israeli authorities released 24 Palestinian detainees back into Gaza on Wednesday. They arrived at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, with at least one carried in on a stretcher, and immediately hospitalized.

- Israel continues attacks on the occupied West Bank:

- Qalandia: Israeli forces continued their siege of Qalandia refugee camp and the nearby city of Kafr Aqab for a second day on Thursday, arresting dozens of Palestinians, including a woman with a broken leg after breaking down her door and assaulting her family members, according to WAFA. Soldiers entered dozens of homes in the area, issued demolition threats against businesses, and prevented ambulances from attending to the wounded. Israeli soldiers were also reported to have targeted journalists operating in the area, with one reporter physically assaulted by Israeli soldiers and others facing down stun grenades, according to Al Jazeera.

- The Palestinian Red Crescent said on Thursday that it had treated 16 Palestinians injured by Israelis during the military operation.

- The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society reported that more than 60 residents of Qalandia were detained and interrogated, including women and children. Israeli soldiers beat detainees during interrogations, used restraints, and threatened detainees with retaliation, according to the group, while vandalizing and seizing property.

- Nablus: Israeli settlers attacked and injured three Palestinians in Beit Furik, near Nablus, in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday, according to WAFA. Settlers also diverted water in the area on Wednesday, redirecting water pumps used by Palestinians to their settlement outpost. Israeli forces conducted a separate raid on the Askar refugee camp, east of Nablus, on Thursday.

- Jenin: Israeli soldiers continued on Thursday to raze land and uproot olive trees in the villages of Zububa and Arabuna, near Jenin, WAFA reported.

- Hebron: Israeli settlers set several homes on fire in the Khirbet Al-Tuba community in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday, leaving women and children suffering from smoke inhalation. The Palestine Red Crescent Society said its crews treated six people, including three women, for bruises sustained in the attack. The Israeli military also demolished a home in the village of Birin, near Hebron, on Thursday morning, after raiding the area.

- Al-Bireh: Israeli soldiers seized three homes in Al-Bireh on Wednesday evening, storming the neighborhood in which they were located and forcing their inhabitants out at gunpoint.

- Kfar Qasim: Israeli authorities demolished a home in Kfar Qasim, a Palestinian town in Israel, WAFA reported on Thursday morning.

- Israeli authorities beat Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya in detention, break his ribs: Israeli authorities severely beat Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya on July 27, breaking his ribs as part of what the Palestinian Prisoners’ Media Office called his “most difficult day.”

- The office reported the doctor, who suffers from heart disease and high blood pressure, has experienced a serious deterioration in his health.

- Abu Safiya has spent 21 days in solitary confinement during his time in Israeli prison. He has been detained without charge since December 27, 2024, after Israeli forces seized him while he was working as the director of the Kamal Adwan Hospital during attacks on northern Gaza.

- Arab and Islamic countries condemn Israeli violations in Gaza; Israel army chief says attacks will continue: Arab and Islamic countries including Qatar, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt issued a joint statement on Thursday condemning the ongoing Israeli violations in the Gaza Strip, including “the targeting of healthcare facilities and medical infrastructure, attacks on civilian infrastructure, and the continued loss of civilian lives, including women and children.”

- The ministers warned the violations “threaten to derail the political process, reignite the cycle of escalation, and further deepen the humanitarian catastrophe in the Gaza Strip” despite the Palestinian factions’ acceptance of the roadmap.

- Israeli army chief Eyal Zamir said in a statement on Thursday that the Israeli military would continue “proactive” operations in Gaza, claiming that the army had “significantly weakened Hamas” and “changed the security reality” in Gaza.

- Board of Peace awards first building contract in Gaza for military base: The Board of Peace has issued its first construction contract in Gaza to build a rudimentary 150-person military outpost to house Moroccan troops, according to the Guardian. The contract, which has not yet been finalized, was awarded to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company that has previously carried out work with the U.S. government in countries such as Iraq. The base is 100 meters by 120 meters and is intended to house a contingent of Moroccan troops, who would rotate from a base in Israel, the Guardian said, citing a source familiar with the matter.

- In rare move, Israeli prosecutors charge settler in killing of Palestinian activist Awdah Hathaleen: Israeli prosecutors have filed charges against Yinon Levi, the Israeli settler who shot and killed prominent Palestinian community leader and activist Awdah Hathaleen in the village of Umm al-Khair in the occupied West Bank in July 2025. Levi was charged with reckless manslaughter, which holds a lesser punishment than murder. Other charges include armed trespassing and malicious damage to property. Israeli rights group B’Tselem said that the charges against Levi mark the first time since Oct. 7, 2023, that an Israeli has been indicted for the death of a Palestinian in the West Bank. During that period over 1,100 Palestinians have been killed in attacks by Israeli soldiers and settlers. Read Drop Site’s coverage of the killing of Awdah Hathaleen here.

## Lebanon

- Israeli attacks wound eight in southern Lebanon as UNIFIL reports 113 projectiles launched:

- Israeli attacks on the district of Tyre (Sour) in southern Lebanon wounded at least eight people and forced many residents to flee their homes, according to the Lebanese National News Agency, with drone and jet strikes hitting Burj Shemali on Thursday.

- Additional Israeli strikes hit the towns of Burj Shemali and Al-Mansouri, according to the NNA.

- Israeli forces also shelled Majdal Zoun, Al-Mansouri, and Haddatha on Thursday morning, and fired at the coastal Al-Hamra area in Bayt Al-Sayyad.

- UNIFIL said Thursday that its peacekeepers continue to observe daily Israeli violations of Lebanese airspace and military activities on the ground, adding that the 113 projectiles launched by the Israeli military on Wednesday were the highest daily total recorded by the mission since June 21.

- Israeli settlers attempt incursion into Lebanon: A group of about 15 Israeli women affiliated with a settler movement illegally crossed into southern Lebanon on Wednesday, according to The Times of Israel.

- The Israeli military claimed that it located most of the group and escorted them back into Israel.

- The women are reportedly part of the Uri Tzafon Movement, a group which seeks to establish Israeli settlements in southern Lebanon.

- Rights groups condemn Israeli strike that killed Lebanese journalist as a war crime: An Israeli strike which killed Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and injured photojournalist Zeinab Faraj in southern Lebanon in April amounted to a war crime, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and Legal Agenda said in separate reports on Thursday that all concluded Israeli forces deliberately and directly targeted the two women despite knowing they were civilians.

- The organizations also found that Israeli forces delayed rescue efforts for hours, dropping stun grenades near Lebanese Red Cross personnel and firing on ambulances, potentially contributing to Khalil’s death.

- They called for a war crimes investigation and accountability, with Human Rights Watch urging states to halt arms sales to Israel and impose targeted sanctions on Israeli officials responsible for ongoing violations.

- “The impunity enjoyed by Israeli forces for the killing of journalists and other civilians in Lebanon over the past three years has enabled the Israeli military to continue with its unlawful air strikes, including direct attacks on civilians,” Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Heba Morayef, said. “It is well past time that the international community impose a comprehensive arms embargo on Israel.”

- At least 15 journalists have been killed by Israel in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to the UN human rights office. Read Jeremy Loffredo’s report on Khalil’s killing for Drop Site here.

## U.S. News

- Senate committee votes to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt: A Senate committee voted 8-7 Thursday to hold Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute for Allergy and Infectious Diseases, in contempt of Congress. During a hearing last week before the Government Affairs Committee, chaired by Sen. Rand Paul, Fauci repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right and declined to answer questions. Paul said he would refer the matter to the Justice Department for potential prosecution.

- Separately, three state attorneys general, led by Florida AG James Uthmeier, announced on Wednesday that they were subpoenaing Fauci over allegations that he “profited” from the recommendations he gave during the Covid-19 pandemic.

- Fauci, who left government in 2022 and received a preemptive pardon from President Joe Biden, has denied Paul’s allegations that he hid information from the public regarding the possible laboratory origins of Covid-19.

- Sen. Ron Johnson claimed Wednesday that he had obtained a copy of Fauci’s government phone and years of his personal diary entries from the Trump administration’s Department of Health and Human Services.

- Trump maintains frequent contact with Fed Chair Warsh, WSJ reports: President Donald Trump has spoken repeatedly with Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh since Warsh took the job less than three months ago, seeking his counsel on issues including the Iran war and artificial intelligence’s economic effects, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal.

- One source cited by the paper said Trump has not raised interest rates directly since Warsh’s confirmation. Communication between presidents and Fed chairs has typically been choreographed to avoid the appearance of political influence over rate decisions.

- Democrats on the Senate Banking Committee have pressed Warsh for more disclosure about his contacts with the president.

- El-Sayed opposes “unconditional” U.S. military aid to any country, including Israel: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, outlined his stance in an interview with CNN. “I’m opposed to unconditional military aid for any country. That is Israel, yes, but that’s also Egypt, where my family immigrated from. That’s Pakistan, that’s Saudi Arabia, that’s UAE,” El-Sayed said.

- “There are Leahy laws against dealing arms to countries who are engaged in human rights abuses, and I don’t want to fund a foreign military that does genocide, apartheid or has taken us to a war we don’t need to fight,” he added. “I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Jewish Israelis and Palestinians alike.”

- Abdul El-Sayed made clear that his opposition to unconditional aid for foreign governments extends to defensive military technology, including Israel’s Iron Dome system. “I don’t believe that there’s really a difference between offensive or defensive weapons, and I also don’t believe it’s my responsibility to buy defensive weapons for a foreign government when our kids are defenceless against schools that have been underfunded for a very, very long time,” he said.

- Trump-appointed judge ran D.C. PR firm for months after taking bench, ex-employees say: Jennifer Mascott, a Trump-appointed judge on the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals, remained deeply involved in operating the Washington public affairs firm Adfero for at least six months after her October 2025 confirmation, according to Politico.

- Mascott oversaw the firm’s staffing, business development, and client relations while working out of its office weekly, according to several former employees and clients.

- Mascott inherited ownership of the firm from her late husband, Jeff Mascott, in 2023. After taking over the historically nonpartisan firm, she brought on consultants with strong Republican ties, and longtime clients departed, an arrangement sources said drove staff attrition and ultimately led the two-decade-old firm to shut down on June 30.

- Judicial ethics experts told Politico that Mascott’s situation falls into a gray area under rules generally permitting judges to maintain family businesses, though they noted that it could veer into illegality if it interferes with her “judicial duties.”

- USCIS backlog surges to 7.5 million: A work slowdown at the Trump administration’s immigration offices has pushed the backlog of citizenship, green card, and work permit applications to an unprecedented 7.5 million people—or more than 12.1 million when including asylum and humanitarian cases—according to the latest agency data cited by Axios.

- Processing times for naturalization applications have doubled to about 10 months since June 2024, while more than 1.3 million “Dreamers” have waited over six months for work authorization renewals, up from 556,000 two years ago.

- GAO report finds DOGE overstated federal savings claims: The Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that the U.S. Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) Service, the cost-cutting group led by Elon Musk, consistently overstated its claimed savings, taking credit for lease cancellations initiated before the group existed and reporting contracts as terminated when they were not, according to The Washington Post.

- Of the $110 billion in contract, grant, and lease savings the GAO examined from DOGE’s $215 billion “Wall of Receipts”” investigators found more than half of the $61 billion in claimed contract savings was either not actually terminated or could not be corroborated.

- 108 of 264 leases DOGE listed were already in the process of termination before the group formed, according to the GAO report, which is set for release today.

- Senate Democrats probe South Korean firm’s $2 million payment to Trump company: Senate Democrats Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Andy Kim demanded Wednesday that South Korea’s Base Group explain a $2 million payment to President Donald Trump’s holding company made while the firm’s key investment, Korea Aluminium, faced a Commerce Department tariff dispute, writing that the transaction “raises significant concerns about pay-to-play politics and the potential for bribery.”

- “If Base Group were attempting to buy influence with President Trump in an effort to secure lower tariffs or special-interest exemptions for Korea Aluminium, it would be a particularly egregious example of Trump Administration corruption,” Sen. Warren wrote.

- The payment, which the Trump Organization claimed was related to the development of a golf course and which was disclosed in Trump’s June financial filing as a “nonrefundable development fee,” came shortly before Commerce issued a preliminary finding to impose a 105% tariff on Korea Aluminium’s exports.

- Newly nominated Lawrence pledges to vote for Jeffries for Speaker: Progressive candidate William Lawrence, elected on Tuesday as the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 7th congressional district, pledged to vote for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker if elected, reversing a position he held earlier during his campaign.

- Lawrence, backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, follows Brad Lander, who announced after his election in June that he would vote for Jeffries.

- Other DSA-backed candidates, including Darializa Avila Chevalier, Melat Kiros, and Chris Rabb, have refused to commit to voting for Jeffries if the Democrats retake the House in November.

- Lawrence faces a highly contested general election, with his race against Republican Rep. Tom Barrett consider

reads.title: Abdul El-Sayed leads anti-war sweep in Michigan; Israel raids Qalandia refugee camp; Russian strikes kill 17 in Kyiv
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: August 5, 2026
reads.body:
- Michigan Democratic Senate primary winner Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a press conference in front of the Spirit of Detroit statue on August 05, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images.Wednesday, August 5, 2026 – Iran’s talks with Oman about the Strait of Hormuz in final stages, have “nothing to do” with the U.S. Qatari Foreign Minister: Multinational effort underway to reach diplomatic resolution to Iran War. Report: Iran demands say over inbound and outbound Hormuz traffic. Iraq in Hormuz talks with Iran, Iraqi official says. At least 56 executed in Iran since March, UN human rights chief says. Ansarallah claims attack on Saudi tanker. Israel’s assault on Gaza continues. Israel carries on with attacks in the occupied West Bank. Israeli military probe says soldier may have killed settler in Tal attack. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he has “disagreements” with President Donald Trump over the Gaza plan. Israeli abuse of Palestinian “doctor of the poor.” Israeli Knesset committee approves around 110 million dollars for settlement expansion. Israel orders evacuation, launches strikes after explosion kills soldiers in south Lebanon. Primary results from Michigan, Missouri, and Kansas. ICE arrests hit record 51,000 in July. Trump administration refunds $100 billion in “liberation day” tariffs. Appeals court rules Environmental Protection Agency cannot block $20 billion in climate grants. Rep. Chuck Edwards drops re-election bid after Ethics Committee recommends censure for sexual harassment. Democrat Julian Beaudion withdraws from South Dakota Senate race. AP: Trump administration has detained more than 50 relatives of active-duty troops in immigration crackdown. Russian barrage on Kyiv kills at least 17. Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return to Bangladesh despite death sentence. U.S. revokes visa of Brazilian ambassador. Brazil downgrades diplomatic ties with Argentina after President Javier Milei’s latest insults of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Mass jail break, armed clashes kill three in cities west of Tripoli. Malaysia says it won’t repatriate Rohingya refugees to Myanmar if their lives are at risk. Ceuta seeks transfer of 1,100 unaccompanied minor migrants to mainland Spain.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Tehran’s Hormuz talks with Oman in final stages, have “nothing to do” with U.S.: Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Wednesday that Iran and Oman have agreed on the geographic parameters of a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz and are in the final stage of preparing a joint announcement, provided “certain third parties” do not interfere.

- An agreement on shipping arrangements between Iran and Oman through the Strait of Hormuz would not immediately reopen the waterway, a government source told Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, saying that the ongoing talks have “nothing to do” with the U.S. The source told the broadcaster that the waterway would remain closed as long as “U.S. violations” continue.

- Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely restricted on Tuesday, with just eight vessels transiting the waterway for a second consecutive day, according to shipping data firm Kpler. Prior to the war, roughly 130–140 ships typically passed through each day.

- Qatar FM: Multinational effort underway to reach diplomatic resolution to Iran War: Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al-Ansari said on Tuesday Doha is coordinating with Oman, Pakistan, and GCC states to broker a U.S.-Iran diplomatic resolution and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

- He called mediation efforts “ongoing” and said a draft of a possible agreement was being circulated among the relevant parties, adding that the talks have reached “very progressive stages.”

- Report: Iran demands say over inbound and outbound Hormuz traffic: Iran is demanding control over ships entering the Strait of Hormuz and oversight of outbound traffic, with the power to intervene if necessary, under a temporary reopening plan being discussed with Oman, a senior Iranian source told Reuters on Tuesday.

- Outbound vessels would travel between Iran and Oman, with Oman granting exit clearance after notifying Tehran, Reuters reports.

- The source told the outlet that Iran has already compromised from its initial demand for full control in both directions and is unlikely to shift further.

- Iraq in Hormuz talks with Iran, Iraqi official says: Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair said on Tuesday that the country is in talks with Iran over the “smooth flow of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz,” expressing hope for a breakthrough in the coming days, according to a statement carried by the Iraqi News Agency.

- Iraq exports roughly 95% of its crude through the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the major OPEC producer heavily exposed to the disruption caused by the waterway’s effective closure.

- The talks come days after Iraq signed a separate agreement with Turkey to maintain northern crude exports to the Mediterranean through the Ceyhan pipeline, bypassing the Gulf.

- At least 56 executed in Iran since March, UN human rights chief says: Iran has executed at least 56 people on national security-related charges since March 19, including 27 in cases linked to mass anti-government protests in January, according to United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk, with over 100 others at risk of execution on similar charges. “I am alarmed by the rise in executions and death sentences issued in Iran since March, and that capital punishment continues to be used to instill fear among the population and suppress dissent,” Turk said in a statement. He added that executions for drug-related offenses are also continuing “at an alarming rate.”

## Yemen

- Ansarallah claims attack on Saudi tanker: Yemen’s Ansarallah movement announced on Tuesday that it had struck the Saudi oil tanker Wafa with ballistic missiles in the northern Red Sea, off Yanbu, claiming a direct hit as part of enforcing its maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, though neither the Saudis nor major maritime tracking firms confirmed the incident.

- Ansarallah said its forces have now targeted eight Saudi oil tankers since the blockade began on July 22, adding that 29 Saudi tankers have been prevented from continuing their voyages and forced to turn back in the Red and Arabian Seas.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, two Palestinians were killed after succumbing to wounds sustained in earlier attacks, and one was injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. Two bodies were also recovered from beneath the rubble.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,381 killed, with 174,231 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,254 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,121, while 804 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel’s assault on Gaza:

- Israel struck and wounded a Palestinian child on Wednesday morning, west of Khan Younis, according to Shehab News.

- Israeli artillery shelled an area northeast of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza on Wednesday, WAFA reported, and also fired on the northern areas of Al-Bureij refugee camp.

- In the southern Gaza Strip, Israel shelled areas southwest of Khan Younis.

- Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank:

- East Jerusalem: A large force of Israeli soldiers raided Qalandia refugee camp, north of Jerusalem, on Wednesday morning, conducting searches and raids, and detaining several Palestinians. Israeli soldiers distributed leaflets stating that “a large-scale operation” in the camp was underway, according to Quds News Network. The Palestinian Red Crescent said its crews in the camp have so far treated eight people who were assaulted. The army operation comes one week after Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz issued instructions to occupy another Palestinian refugee camp under the model of the army invasions of the Jenin, Tulkarem, and Nur Shams camps in early 2025 that Human Rights Watch said amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity. In a separate attack in the town of Al-Ram, Israeli soldiers shot a young Palestinian man in the foot, according to the Red Crescent.

- Bethlehem: Israeli forces raided the town of Beit Fajjar on Tuesday evening, firing tear gas and sound bombs. In Nahalin, west of Bethlehem, Israeli settlers began demolitions on three Palestinian homes.

- Jenin: Israeli forces detained four Palestinians in several raids on the Jenin governorate on Wednesday, seizing one home in the area and converting it into a military barracks. Settlers bulldozed Palestinian land and uprooted olive trees in nearby Ajja, receiving support from the Israeli military, according to WAFA.

- Tubas: Israeli settlers attacked a water pipeline in Yerza, East of Tubas, on Wednesday, according to WAFA, the eighth attack on this pipeline since the beginning of July.

- Galilee: Israeli forces demolished a Palestinian home in Al-Ba’na in Galilee on Wednesday, forcing evacuations from the area, and detaining the home’s owner and his brother when they attempted to resist the operation.

- Israeli military probe says soldier may have killed settler in Tal attack: An Israeli military investigation published Wednesday found that friendly fire may have killed Israeli settler Benayahu Mellet during a deadly settler attack in the occupied West Bank village of Tal last month, The Times of Israel reported. Four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed during the attack after around 20 settlers, some of them armed, stormed the village. The incident sparked a large-scale Israeli military operation across the occupied West Bank. According to the probe, Mellet died shortly after a Palestinian wrestled a rifle from another Israeli, though the military said it could not determine whether he was killed by Palestinian fire or by Israeli troops because his body was buried without an autopsy.

- Netanyahu says he has “disagreements” with Trump over the Gaza plan: After meeting with “Board of Peace” representative Nickolay Mladenov on Tuesday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Israeli media that he had “disagreements with President Trump” concerning “the recent agreement with Hamas.”

- Netanyahu maintained, contrary to the roadmap published by the board, that Hamas “must be disarmed and the Gaza Strip [be] demilitarized before moving to the reconstruction phase.”

- During the meeting, Mladenov reportedly urged Netanyahu to halt Israeli attacks on Gaza, two sources told the AP.

- Following the meeting, Hamas called for clarifications from the board, the AFP reported, voicing “unease” over Mladenov’s statement after he met with Netanyahu. The statement, a Hamas official said, “focused solely on the issue of weapons and failed to address the occupation’s obligations,” which include an end to all Israeli attacks on Gaza.

- Israeli abuse of Palestinian “doctor of the poor”: Israeli prison guards have beaten a 71-year-old Palestinian doctor, tear-gassed his overcrowded cell, and denied him vital medication, according to testimony published by Haaretz on Tuesday.

- Dr. Mazen Al-Rantisi, nicknamed the “doctor of the poor” because of the free and low-charge medical care he provides Ramallah-area residents, was imprisoned by Israeli forces during a raid on June 21, and was indicted for chairing a health nonprofit previously outlawed by Israel.

- Al-Rantisi told a lawyer from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel this week that guards force blindfolded prisoners to walk bent over, beat him and other detainees during repeated raids, and fired tear gas into their cells. Younger prisoners surround him during the beatings in an effort to shield him.

- Israel withheld all of his regular prescriptions for his first 10 days at Ofer Prison and continues to deny him one medication. His requests to see a doctor have been ignored, and his lawyer said he has lost significant weight.

- Drop Site video dispatch from mass funeral in Gaza: 44 children and 37 women were among 112 members of the Al-Hasayna and Abu Sharia families laid to rest at a mass funeral in northern Gaza after Civil Defense crews recently recovered their bodies from beneath the rubble. Drop Site contributor Abdel Qader Sabbah shared footage from the funeral and spoke with attendees.

- “The first house was bombed, so they fled to a second house, then to a third, searching for somewhere safe to hide,” family elder Nahed Al-Hasayna told Drop Site. “These were all children and women, peaceful and innocent. For what crime were they killed?”

- Fares Affana, director of ambulance and emergency services for Civil Defense in northern Gaza, told Drop Site that Israeli attacks had systematically destroyed Gaza’s rescue capacity, leaving crews unable to reach people trapped beneath collapsed buildings. “We could hear the cries and screams of the wounded from beneath the rubble….But because we lacked equipment, we could not reach them,” he said, adding that many remained trapped for days until they died.

- Watch Sabbah’s full report here.

- Israeli Knesset committee approves around 110 million dollars for settlement expansion: The Israeli Knesset Finance Committee held a special session Tuesday during the election recess to approve 335 million shekels (~$110 million) for settlement expansion, which would raise the Israeli Settlement Ministry’s budget for the year to a record 821 million shekels (not including the 944 million shekels it has committed for future settlements).

## Lebanon

- Israel orders evacuation, launches strikes after explosion kills soldiers in south Lebanon: Israel launched a wave of attacks across southern Lebanon on Wednesday after two Israeli soldiers were reportedly killed and others wounded after an explosive device detonated inside a building in Majdal Zoun, a village in southern Lebanon that is partially occupied by the Israeli military, according to Israeli media.

- Following the explosion, the Israeli military claimed Hezbollah had violated the ceasefire and ordered residents of Al-Mansouri to evacuate north before carrying out two airstrikes on the Mashaa al-Mansouri area south of Tyre (Sour). Israeli artillery also shelled the outskirts of Majdal Zoun, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA).

- An Israeli airstrike struck the rooftop of a prayer room at the Tebnine cemetery, killing one person and wounding 11 others, according to NNA.

- Israeli forces also dropped illumination flares over the heights of Kfar Reman, which NNA said were intended to ignite fires, while troops set fire to forested areas and fruit orchards in Houla, with the flames spreading to homes in the town’s western neighborhoods.

- Israel has continued carrying out near-daily attacks in Lebanon despite the U.S.-brokered ceasefire. On Tuesday night, Israeli forces carried out another large-scale demolition in Hadatha in Bint Jbeil district and a drone struck the same location twice in the Roueiss neighborhood of Nabatieh Al-Fawqa, according to NNA.

## U.S. News

- Primary results:

- Abdul El-Sayed beat Rep. Haley Stevens in Tuesday’s Michigan Democratic Senate primary, overcoming over $60 million in outside funding, mostly from pro-Israel groups, and late endorsements of Stevens from current Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and prominent national Democrats like Rep. James Clyburn. El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers in the November general election. If elected, he will be the first Muslim-American to serve in the U.S. Senate.

- State Rep. Donavan McKinney prevailed over incumbent Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar in their Detroit-area primary contest, despite Thanedar’s backing from AIPAC and cryptocurrency interests. McKinney, a 34-year-old endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, is now the heavy favorite to represent the safely Democratic district.

- Progressive William Lawrence defeated two moderate candidates in his Democratic primary in the Lansing Area. Lawrence, a climate organizer endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rashida Tlaib, will face incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Barrett, rated one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents in this cycle, in the general election to represent Michigan’s 7th district in the House.

- Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in Missouri’s 1st Congressional District Democratic primary, repeating his 2024 win over Bush, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. AIPAC spent about $3 million on Bell’s behalf, less than the $8 million he received in 2024, when he was one of the largest beneficiaries of AIPAC spending nationwide.

- Missouri voters rejected a Republican-backed measure that would have required a majority in each of the state’s eight congressional districts, rather than a simple statewide majority, to pass citizen-sponsored constitutional amendments, preserving a tool voters have used to pass measures including Medicaid expansion, marijuana legalization, and an abortion rights guarantee. Opponents, including a state real estate association and abortion rights groups, noted the measure would have set the highest such threshold among the 18 states allowing citizen-led constitutional amendments and that none of the four amendments Missouri voters passed since 2020 won in all eight districts.

- Rev. Adam Hamilton, pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, won Tuesday’s Democratic Senate primary in Kansas, according to The Associated Press, setting up a challenge against Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 100 years. Though Kansas has not factored into Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate, Hamilton is viewed by some as a talented fundraiser and has some political tailwinds, including the recent re-election of a Democratic governor and an electoral victory for abortion rights in 2022.

- Kansas voters rejected a Republican-backed ballot measure that would have required state Supreme Court justices to be popularly elected rather than appointed by the governor, dealing another setback to lawmakers seeking to overturn a 2019 court ruling that established a constitutional right to abortion in the state. Kansas Republicans had campaigned for the measure by arguing that the state Supreme Court had failed to represent the “will” of the state’s voters, but told anti-abortion groups that the referendum was aimed at challenging the state’s abortion laws.

- Abbas Alawieh won his Democratic primary to represent the Dearborn area in the state Senate. Before his work on behalf of the “Uncommitted” movement, which attempted to hold the Democratic Party accountable for its failures on Gaza. Alawieh previously served as a congressional aide to Reps. Andy Levin, Rashida Tlaib, and Cori Bush. If elected, he will be the first Arab-American to serve in Michigan’s state Senate.

- ICE arrests hit record 51,000 in July: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested 51,000 people in July, the largest single-month total in Department of Homeland Security history, according to sources familiar with the data cited by ABC News.

- ICE has particularly ramped up its campaign at American airports, with 30 people detained at airports in July, according to the data.

- Trump administration refunds $100 billion in “liberation day” tariffs: The Trump administration has paid out about $100 billion, or 60% of the $165 billion collected, in refunds of “liberation day” tariffs since the Supreme Court struck down the emergency powers used to impose them earlier this year, according to a report U.S. customs officials gave judges at the U.S. Court of International Trade on Tuesday.

- Customs and Border Protection said in a Tuesday court filing that more than $128 billion has been “accepted for processing,” indicating that more refunds are imminent.

- Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas) noted that the refunds go almost exclusively to companies, and are not seen by consumers. “Every single cent of these refunds should go back to American consumers,” he said on X.

- Appeals court rules E.P.A. cannot block $20 billion in climate grants: A divided 10-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld an injunction Tuesday barring the Environmental Protection Agency from terminating $20 billion in climate grants under the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, ruling that recipients should have access to the funds while their case proceeds. If the E.P.A. does not appeal to the Supreme Court within seven days, the ruling will effectively reinstate the Biden-era program, which E.P.A. Administrator Lee Zeldin sought to kill, using as his pretext unsubstantiated allegations of waste and fraud against eight climate groups.

- Rep. Chuck Edwards drops re-election bid after Ethics Committee recommends censure for sexual harassment: Rep. Chuck Edwards, a North Carolina Republican, withdrew from his re-election campaign early Wednesday after the House Ethics Committee recommended censure after finding he sexually harassed two female staffers and created a hostile work environment.

- The House is expected to vote on censuring Edwards after the August recess. Edwards said in a post on X that he would complete his current term.

- Democrat Julian Beaudion withdraws from South Dakota Senate race: Julian Beaudion, the Democratic nominee for South Dakota’s Senate seat, withdrew from the race Tuesday after months of vowing to stay in, clearing the way for a one-on-one contest between independent Brian Bengs and Republican incumbent Mike Rounds, The Washington Post reported.

- South Dakota becomes the third state where Democrats have opted not to field a Senate candidate, following Nebraska and Idaho, a strategy that gained traction after independent Dan Osborn came within seven percentage points of winning Nebraska’s 2024 race.

- Beaudion said he would not endorse either Bengs or Rounds and accused Bengs, without naming him, of “intimidating threats to drop out of this race.”

- AP: Trump administration has detained more than 50 relatives of active-duty troops in immigration crackdown: More than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty U.S. service members have been detained under President Donald Trump’s second-term immigration crackdown, with at least six deported, according to an Associated Press investigation published on Wednesday.

- The detentions, which experts say reverse decades of bipartisan practice protecting military families and even Trump’s own first-term policy, have disrupted deployments and left troops without childcare, including Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, whose wife was detained outside a Walmart, and Air Force Tech. Sgt. Wendy Gbeve, whose father was deported to Mexico despite a pending legal status application.

- DHS said in a statement that “military service alone does not automatically grant lawful immigration status,” even as Army and National Guard recruiters continue advertising immigration benefits like “military parole-in-place” to potential enlistees.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- Russian barrage on Kyiv kills at least 17: Russia struck Kyiv and surrounding areas with 24 ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles, and 115 drones early Wednesday, killing at least 17 people, according to Al Jazeera, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the strikes hit warehouses, a brewery, and construction supply sites.

- Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s supply of air defense missiles is three times lower than in 2025 and that missile interceptors “could have saved the lives of those killed today.” Reuters reported that U.S. officials are discussing options to replenish Ukraine’s depleted Patriot stockpiles, including allowing domestic component manufacturing.

- Separately, Ukraine struck a Wildberries warehouse in Russia’s Tula region and an oil refinery in Bashkortostan on Wednesday.

- Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return to Bangladesh despite death sentence: Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, 78, said in a video address on Wednesday that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December after two years in exile in India, despite a death sentence handed down against her.

- Hasina, who was ousted following a violent crackdown on protests in 2024, made the announcement alongside her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, and other leaders from her Awami League Party.

- She said the exact date of her return would be announced “when time comes.”

- U.S. revokes visa of Brazilian ambassador: The United States revoked the visa of Brazilian Ambassador to Washington Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti. The move comes after Brasília stalled the approval of the incoming U.S. envoy and refused visas for two U.S. State Department officials over concerns of political meddling. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defended the move by openly accusing the American diplomats of seeking to interfere in the October vote and cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s electoral system. State Department officials indicated the ambassador’s credentials could be reinstated once Brazil accepts Washington’s choice for the post.

- Brazil downgrades diplomatic ties with Argentina after Milei’s latest insults of Lula: Brazil will handle relations with Argentina at the chargé d’affaires level after Argentine President Javier Milei again insulted Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, calling him an “ex-convict,” a “thief,” and “corrupt”  in recent interview on Argentine television, a Brazilian government source told Reuters on Tuesday.

- Brazil’s ambassador to Argentina, Julio Bitelli, who had already been recalled last month after Milei criticized Lula while campaigning alongside opposition candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, will not return to Buenos Aires.

- Milei and Lula have not held an official bilateral meeting since Milei took office in December 2023.

- Mass jail break, armed clashes kill three in cities west of Tripoli: Detainees staged a mass escape from a jail in Surman, near Tripoli, on Tuesday as armed clashes between rival groups erupted in the nearby cities of Zawiya and Surman, killing three civilians and injuring several others, Reuters reported.

- The origin and cause of the clashes remained unclear.
Zawiya, located 40 kilometers west of Tripoli, is home to Libya’s largest functioning oil refinery, which urged workers to avoid the areas of fighting.

- Surman’s Mayor Mohamed Abu Snina described the humanitarian situation as “very bad” but said relative calm had returned to the city after a neutral force was deployed to the area.

- Malaysia says it won’t repatriate Rohingya refugees to Myanmar if their lives are at risk: Malaysia will not proceed with repatriating 5,000 Rohingya refugees to Myanmar if their lives are found to be at risk, government spokesman Fahmi Fadzil said Wednesday.

- Fahmi said Myanmar’s junta government is ready to receive the refugees but that Malaysia’s foreign and home ministries are still reviewing the plan before proceeding.

- Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government sought the handover after unrest between the Rohingya refugees and Malaysians, in response to which Rohingya schools were shut down, and some refugees were evicted from homes in Penang or briefly detained after gathering outside the UNHCR building in the country’s capital.

- Ceuta seeks transfer of 1,100 unaccompanied minor migrants to mainland Spain: Local leaders in Spain’s Ceuta are seeking the transfer of roughly 1,100 unaccompanied minors to mainland Spain after 72,000 migrants arrived in the enclave in one week, Reuters reported on Tuesday.
