-
- Funeral prayers for JAAC leader Sardar Umar Nazir’s brother Usman Nazir, led by their brother Siddique Nazir. Photo from the Facebook page of Hamza Naseer.Early on the morning of July 9, 2026, men from a paramilitary force known as the Pakistan Rangers began raiding homes in the village of Gehl Topi, a few kilometers from the city of Rawalakot in Pakistan-administered Kashmir—known locally as Azad Kashmir.
It was four weeks after protests over electoral reform erupted in Azad Kashmir, and a curfew was in place. The local mosque announced over its loudspeaker that the Rangers, who operate under military authority, had entered the village, and a crowd began gathering.
The armed men opened fire on the crowd, according to one eyewitness and another person who has family members in the village. Hassan Zohaib, who was present at the scene, said his cousin, Muhammad Nasir Khan, 39, was killed. Khan, a night caretaker at a government-run school, who had walked downhill along the Link Road to see why people were gathering. When the Rangers opened fire, a bullet entered Khan’s side, tore through his rib cage, and exited his neck. “We rushed him to the Rural Health Center in Chitra Topi, but there were no doctors or paramedical staff, and the blood loss was too severe. He could not survive,” his cousin, Hassan Zohaib, told Drop Site News.
Khan has four children; the eldest is ten. The same day, Zohaib’s family buried a second relative killed by military gunfire in the same village, a 22-year-old named Wajid Siddique. “I am not sure what kind of ammunition they are using, because he was shot in his lower abdomen, which was blown away, and he died instantly,” Zohaib said. “We could not even take him to the hospital.”
Neither Siddique’s nor Khan’s death has been reported in the local press, which is subject to intense censorship and has not been allowed to report on the violent crackdown in Kashmir. For eight weeks now the demonstrations in Rawalakot—a city just 40 kilometers away from the disputed Line of Control with India that has become an epicenter of the movement—have been met with live-fire by Pakistani security forces, mass arrests, and a siege of the city.
Local officials and hospitals have not shared an official tally of total civilians killed. On July 2, Amnesty International estimated at 40 killed before regional elections began on July 2. Locals who spoke to Drop Site said that number is a significant undercount.
Despite the violent crackdown, civilians have continued to demonstrate against local authorities and the Pakistani military. In a video circulating on social media this week, a travel vlogger identified as Aqeel says to the camera, “The streets of Rawalakot are drenched in blood. They are shooting our brothers with the bullets they purchase with our taxpayer money,” as gunshots are audible in the background.
Harris Qadeer, editor of the local newspaper Roznama Jeddojehad, told Drop Site that he has documented 89 deaths in Rawalakot and Mirpur as of July 28 by collecting first-hand accounts of funerals, burials, and death records maintained by a civil society group that has been leading the protests.
“Forty-five people were killed before July 27, and a list of their names was compiled by consulting their family members. An additional 37 people were killed on July 27 and 28,” he said. On Monday, Qadeer added, paramilitary forces killed 22 more civilians, as well as another 13 the next day.
The region has remained under curfew and a complete internet blackout since June 5, 2026. No food or medicine has entered and grocery store owners are not allowed to open for business. Regular announcements from loudspeakers of local mosques declare that any civilian violating curfew, including women and children, will be shot without hesitation.
“Armed officers torture anyone who attempts to open for business and a majority of the rations present inside the stores were confiscated by the officers for their own use,” Qadeer said. Local residents of Rawalakot are only able to bring negligible amounts of food and groceries from their relatives in nearby villages.
“Patients can still not access any medicines and those who could afford to move had to move to Rawalpindi and Islamabad where they are forced to live in hotels,” he added.

## Escalating Repression
Protests in Azad Kashmir began in early June over electricity tariffs, wheat prices, and accusations of bribery and corruption by local government officials, led by the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC). JAAC, a coalition of local traders, civil society members, and political activists, has been organizing demonstrations in Kashmir for the past three years.
But the core demand from the protesters centers around the allocation of 12 reserved seats in the local assembly for Indian Kashmiri refugees living in Pakistan, which the authorities accepted in September 2025, but backed out as the region approached election day. Within a few weeks, the protests evolved into a Kashmir-wide call for electoral reforms.
The 12 seats sought by locals are reserved for refugees who left Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir for Pakistan after the partition of the subcontinent in 1947, which also includes their descendants. These people settled in various parts of the country and are now registered to vote in Pakistan’s four other provinces rather than in Pakistani administered Kashmir.
Civil society activists including the JAAC argue that this system takes local governance issues out of the hands of those actually living in Azad Kashmir. Those eligible to run on these seats are not residents of Kashmir and, JAAC argues, therefore do not represent the concerns of locals. Pakistan’s military establishment and the central government have historically used these seats to sway votes in favor of policies that go against the interest of Kashmiris.
JAAC circulated a charter of demands with 38 points that formed the bedrock of negotiations between the chief organizers of the protest movement and the Chairman of the Overseas Pakistanis Forum (OPF), Syed Qamar Raza Shah, who is believed to maintain a close relationship with Pakistan’s military chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir.
The group is demanding reforms to the system of  of assembly seats, elimination of bribery and corruption in government departments, provision of interest-free loans for the youth, elimination of false charges against protesting civilians, and medical treatment for protesters injured by armed forces among others.
In a recent video statement published on JAAC leader Sardar Umar Nazir’s Facebook page, he reiterated the demand for electoral reforms. “This election that’s ongoing right now is being carried out at gunpoint,” he said. “We will not create obstacles for this election but we, as JAAC, declare these fraudulent and farcical.” He further invited all residents of Muzaffarabad to reject the elections and continue protesting on the streets of Kashmir.
Pakistan’s military junta has shown little tolerance for the protests. The JAAC was designated as a terrorist organization by the government in June. Since then the Pakistan Rangers, along with other security forces working under the Pakistani Army and officials working for the district administration, have been carrying out regular “flag marches”—sending processions of 20 to 25 vehicles carrying masked men, mounted with machine guns, through villages around Rawalakot with sirens blaring.
“They’ve spread so much fear and intimidation into the hearts of the residents in that region, to a common village man it is an unbelievable sight,” said Zohaib. “As soon as ten or more people gather just to see what’s going on, they open fire at them.”
On June 4, a trader was shot during a confrontation with law enforcement officers. The next day, family members took the body to Combined Military Hospital (CMH) in Rawalakot for a post-mortem examination. The request for an examination was denied, enraging locals who began gathering outside the hospital.
On June 5, the AJK government issued a notification declaring JAAC a proscribed organization under the First Schedule of the Anti-Terrorism Act 2014, citing “terrorism” and conduct “prejudicial to peace and security,” listing 147 members of the civil society group as a members of a terrorist organization.
Then, late on the night of June 6, JAAC organizers returned to Rawalakot from a meeting in Khaigla, eight kilometers from the city. Unidentified men opened fire, killing Shahzaib Habib, an activist who worked closely with the JAAC leadership.
The following night, clashes broke out in Rawalakot between supporters of JAAC and the police, resulting in the deaths of seven civilians and three police officers, according to the police commissioner of Poonch, Sardar Waheed.
The local government then imposed a legal measure banning all public gatherings and suspending cellular service across the region. That measure has remained largely in place since.
“Three people were killed in my village on the same day, there is no access to the internet and barely any access to cellular services. It is impossible to tell how many people have been shot dead by the paramilitary forces so far,” said Zohaib.
Several government employees have been fired, and pensions have been seized for several retired military officers who were accused of participating in the protests.
On July 9, JAAC called for a region-wide strike to close markets, businesses, educational institutions and public transport. Protesters established a sit-in at Drek, a suburb on the outskirts of Rawalakot, among six other protest venues, while Pakistan Rangers and Frontier Constabulary (FC) forces were deployed en masse. More than 45 civilians were killed in the violent crackdown that followed.
On July 27, as Mirpur division voted, the JAAC marched into Rawalakot city, defying the region-wide curfew. The two days that followed were the deadliest in terms of civilian casualties. Members of the FC and the Rangers situated themselves on rooftops to try to quash any protests in the street. Reports emerged that security forces had shot civilians indiscriminately, including those who had no part in the protest.
Shehreyar Zulfiqar, born and raised in Rawalakot, moved to Lahore in 2018 and regularly visits his family. He now speaks to his mother by phone every three days, on a line that has become increasingly unreliable. His family lives within a 100 meter distance from the hospital and has witnessed much of the repression up close. His neighbor Farrukh Aziz, who ran a grocery store, was shot dead on July 27.

-
- Right to left: Farrukh Aziz, shopkeeper; Abdul Aziz (father of Uzair Aziz); Uzair Aziz (PAF squadron leader); Osama Jameel (PhD student).“He was not a part of the march, he had nothing to do with the political atmosphere in the city. He was only grabbing groceries from his own store for his family members,” Zulfiqar told Drop Site News. “Snipers killed him with a headshot, they were perched atop a nearby building and they killed him when he was on his way back home.”
Usman Nazir, the brother of JAAC leader Umar Nazir, was also killed on July 27 when the Rangers opened fire on protesters in Rawalakot.
In the same neighborhood, an officer of the Pakistan Air Force (PAF), squadron leader Uzair Aziz, lives with his family.
His father Abdul Aziz, who was a school teacher at a local high school, and his brother were also shot by armed officers in the streets of Rawalalot as the two were on their way back home. “His father passed away and his brother is severely injured,” said Zulfiqar. “They have not even returned his father’s dead body to their family. And this is not even a civilian, this man leads a squadron in the air force.” Aziz’s family, Zuliqar added, were not involved in the protests; his family has lived in Rawalakot for four generations.
In one of the many videos from the scenes of protest on the ground, a young student is seen reciting Sarfaroshi Ki Tamanna, an Urdu poem written by Bismil Azimabadi, which roughly translates to “The desire to sacrifice our lives is now in our hearts; let us see how much strength is in the arms of our executioner.”

That student was Osama Jameel, a geology PhD scholar at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, and a member of the Jammu Kashmir National Students Federation (JKNSF), a group that has been aligned with the JAAC for the better part of a decade. On July 28, he was gunned down at Chinar Chowk, while marching towards Muzaffarabad.
Omer Khan, a member of the JKNSF was privy to the negotiations between the government and JAAC from a year ago. “They had signed an agreement and accepted the demands, including the one about 12 assembly seats after eight civilians were killed in September 2025,” he said. “When elections came closer, they backed out of every promise they made because they [the military establishment] have been using these seats to install their own leadership in the Kashmir assembly, overturning the democratic choice of the people of Kashmir.”

## “They Have Subjected Us to Collective Punishment”

-
- Thousands of residents gathered in Drek, Rawalakot on July 23, 2026. Photo from the Facebook page of Hamza Naseer.Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khwaja Asif has labeled the protesters as enemies of the state and ruled out any possibility of future negotiations with the JAAC. On Tuesday, Asif told reporters, “There will be no dialogue with the protesters. I bracket them with India. I put them in the same category as India and consider them as enemies of Pakistan.”
The crackdown has triggered a major backlash in the Kashmiri diaspora, including in London where more than 1.5 million Kashmiris from Pakistan live and where thousands gathered in a massive demonstration against the violence this month.
JAAC activists on the ground are now planning to conduct a march to enter Rawalkot on Saturday in defiance of the siege, before continuing in a planned procession onwards to Muzaffarabad, the capital of Azad Kashmir.
Qadeer, the local journalist in Azad Kashmir, was forced to relocate his family members to the city of Rawalpindi in Punjab. He told Drop Site that the situation has become unbearable for journalists and activists still attempting to document conditions inside the province.
“No journalist is allowed to move, in fact no journalist is acknowledged as a member of the press even if they have a card identifying them as such. Everyone with video recordings in their phones are forced to delete them,” Qadeer explained. “They torture everyone attempting any journalistic activity. They have beat me up in public as well.”
He added, “They are punishing us all indiscriminately, they are subjecting us to collective punishment and they want to make an example out of us. They are using battle-grade weapons, the violence is senseless.”

reads.title: Gaza deal remains conditional on Israel; Earthquake-level explosions in Lebanon; 60,000 migrants cross from Morocco into Spanish territory
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: July 31, 2026
reads.body:
- Hundreds of migrants have attempted to swim from Morocco to the Spanish city of Ceuta in North Africa, Spain on July 30, 2026. Photo by Marcos Moreno/Anadolu via Getty Images.Friday, July 31, 2026 – U.S. resumes strikes on Iran. Iran hits U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain. Over 4,000 children killed or injured in Iran war. Pakistan trying to broker more negotiations, Foreign Ministry says. Egypt, Iran respond to Wednesday attack on Egyptian port. Iraqi government denies it approved U.S.-Saudi strikes. U.S. tags more Iranian firms with sanctions. Tanker traffic through Hormuz is increasing, Bloomberg reports. Britain arrests British-Azerbaijani man on suspicion of spying for Iran in Cyprus. Report: Saudi Arabia prepares offensive against Ansarallah. Fourteen countries back Saudi-led Red Sea naval coalition. Chinese-linked ships transit Bab Al-Mandab openly as most vessels go dark. Lloyd's underwriters restrict war-risk cover for Saudi-linked ships. Israel kills six in Gaza. Hamas agrees to second phase of Gaza ceasefire, says implementation hinges on Israel. Drop Site obtains roadmap documents on Gaza governance, weapons. Israel continues its attacks in the occupied West Bank. Palestinian says he was tortured while in Israeli custody. Israeli demolitions in southern Lebanon generate seismic waves the equivalent of a 3.8-magnitude earthquake, despite “ceasefire.” Lebanon's Aoun seeks Turkish backing for U.S.-brokered framework with Israel. Mandela Barnes drops out of Wisconsin Democratic governor's race. A third of Democrats now identify as democratic socialists, CNN poll finds. ExxonMobil and Chevron post combined $26.5 billion in second-quarter profits amid Iran war oil surge. New York sues Kalshi, alleging prediction market platform runs “illegal gambling operation.” 60,000 cross from Morocco into Ceuta after border breach. Russia’s Africa Corps killed eight civilians in Mali air strike, HRW reports. Attack on police checkpoint kills 11 officers in northwest Pakistan. Cuba details plans to open state economy to private industry. Milei signs decree allowing Argentina to expel foreigners who “spread hate” about the country. Brazilian Supreme Court authorizes probe into President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s son. Sudanese air force launches heavy strikes on RSF positions across Kordofan. Ukrainian drone sets Wildberries warehouse ablaze. Nepal’s Prime Minister calls for calm after Hindu-Muslim clashes leave three dead. At least 32 miners killed in Balochistan coal mine explosion. British police arrest 77 at rally in support of Palestine Action.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- U.S. resumes strikes on Iran: The U.S. restarted its campaign of strikes against Iran Thursday following an Iranian missile attack on a U.S. base in Jordan on Wednesday, with strikes reported across Iran’s south and southwest.

- U.S. strikes on Qeshm Island on Thursday killed a taxi driver, his wife, and their 2-year-old child, Iranian media reported.

- Three members of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were killed in U.S. strikes on Thursday, the group announced.

- Footage circulating online appeared to show missiles being launched from Kuwait, despite the insistence of the government to the Wall Street Journal earlier this week that it had not allowed missiles to be launched from its territory.

- Separately, CENTCOM claimed on Thursday evening that U.S. forces had redirected 24 commercial vessels, disabled two, and boarded two, as part of their naval blockade on Iranian ports that began mid-July.

- Iran hits U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait:

- Iran responded by attacking bases in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain, with Friday attacks reportedly targeting aircraft shelters, satellite communication systems, and equipment storage facilities at the Ahmed Al-Jaber base in Kuwait and the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain. Kuwait’s Defense Ministry said it detected and destroyed Iranian drones in Kuwaiti airspace.

- The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed a missile strike on the Al-Azraq air base in Jordan on Thursday “completely destroyed” three U.S. F-35 fighter jets and badly damaged three others, according to a statement carried by Iranian state media.

- The IRGC also reported that its strikes on Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait destroyed two drone hangars and a fuel depot for military aircraft and helicopters, according to Tasnim. U.S. CENTCOM denied this, though satellite imagery appeared to show damage to a hangar.

- The Chinese embassy in Kuwait reported that a vehicle working for a Chinese company was struck during Iran’s Thursday strikes on the country, killing its Nepalese driver, though it did not identify Iran as the party responsible for the strike in its statement.

- In the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday it targeted two oil tankers attempting to pass with U.S. military “air support.” The IRGC claimed the two tankers were “targeted and stopped,” while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and turned back.

- Over 4,000 children killed or injured in Iran war: More than 4,000 children have been killed or injured across six countries since the Iran war began five months ago, according to UNICEF. In Iran, 386 children have reportedly been killed and 2,117 children injured. “As war reverberates in Iran and neighboring countries, children continue to be killed and maimed in the places where they should be safest – their homes, schools and communities,” Abdul Fofana, UNICEF Acting Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said in a statement. “Parties to the conflict should not normalize the suffering of children, who remain at the sharpest end of conflicts they did not start and have no power to stop.”

- Pakistan trying to broker more negotiations, FM says: Tahir Andrabi, a spokesman for Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry, told reporters Pakistan is making “every effort to bring all parties back to the Islamabad memorandum,” and has urged them to fully honor their commitment to hold technical talks under the deal, according to BBC Persian.

- Egypt, Iran respond to Wednesday attack on Egyptian port: Egypt’s government confirmed that a U.S.-owned Floating Storage Regasification Unit, the Energos Winter, sustained significant damage from a drone attack at Egypt’s Damietta port on Wednesday. Fire also engulfed a separate vessel, the Gaslog Salem.

- The government said its security committee was assessing the situation and reviewing potential responses.

- The Winter is a floating terminal that receives super-chilled liquefied natural gas from transport tankers and converts it back into its gaseous form to feed national energy grids. FSRUs like the Winter play a critical role in supplementing Egypt’s national power grid and managing domestic energy demand.

- Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi responded to Wednesday’s drone attack by warning that it may be an Israeli “false flag” operation.

- Iraqi government denies it approved U.S.-Saudi strikes: Iraqi government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi said on Thursday that Baghdad had no prior knowledge of the joint U.S.-Saudi attacks on Iraqi territory, directly contradicting President Donald Trump’s earlier claim. The strikes killed at least 20 members of the Iran-backed Popular Mobilization Forces. Prime Minister Mohammed al-Zaidi subsequently postponed a planned trip to Saudi Arabia.

- Iran thanks Jordan for “cooperation” after public letter calling for U.S. to leave: An open letter demanding the immediate withdrawal of U.S. forces was signed by more than 200 prominent Jordanians. The letter said the roughly 4,000 U.S. troops in Jordan expose the country to “security, political, and economic risks that serve no national interest,” according to the New York Times.

- Iran’s armed forces publicly thanked “the people of Jordan” on Thursday for their “cooperation” and for providing useful information from inside U.S. bases on Jordanian soil.

- Iran has previously claimed that it has operational support within Jordan.

- U.S. tags more Iranian firms with sanctions: The U.S. Treasury Department announced on Thursday that it would be sanctioning Mahan Air, one of Iran’s largest airlines, along with individuals and companies in China, India, Russia, and Iran accused of keeping the carrier flying.

- The Treasury accused Mahan of “enabling” the IRGC while “presenting itself as a civilian carrier,” and alleged that it facilitated the movement of drones and weapons for the group.

- Tanker traffic through Hormuz is increasing, Bloomberg reports: A Thursday report from Bloomberg claimed that oil-tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is picking up again after slowing earlier this month, despite this week’s intensification of strikes.

- The report outlines a “transfer system” involving smaller or regional vessels, often sailing with transponders off, which work to move crude out of the Persian Gulf and which bring that crude to larger ships for international transport.

- Over the past seven days, the maritime tracking firm Kpler recorded 18 tankers exiting the Strait of Hormuz, five of which were linked to Iran, carrying an average 1.86 million barrels per day.

- Britain arrests British-Azerbaijani man on suspicion of spying for Iran in Cyprus: Rashad Sultanov, a 44-year-old dual British-Azerbaijani national from Islington, north London, was arrested in Cyprus on July 17 on suspicion of surveilling Britain’s RAF Akrotiri base and passing information to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, London’s Metropolitan Police announced.

- The IRGC threatened earlier this month to strike British bases used by U.S. forces against Iran, and an Iranian-type Shahed drone caused slight damage at Akrotiri on March 2, after which Britain excluded the base from its defensive agreement with Washington.

## Yemen

- Report: Saudi Arabia prepares offensive against Ansarallah: Saudi Arabia is reportedly preparing for a major military offensive against Yemen’s Ansarallah by sea and possibly by land, in an effort to break their pressure on Saudi oil exports through the southern Red Sea, according to The Guardian.

- Saudi forces have reportedly begun withdrawing from eastern Yemen and concentrating troops for a possible assault on Ansarallah-controlled Al-Bayda governorate in central Yemen.

- Fourteen countries back Saudi-led Red Sea naval coalition: Fourteen countries, including Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan, backed a Saudi-led maritime coalition aimed at countering Ansarallah’s blockade of regional shipping routes. Saudi Arabia’s Defense Ministry said the coalition would expand military coordination across the Bab Al-Mandab Strait, Red Sea, and Gulf of Aden. The United States, whose participation analysts call essential, is not among them.

- Chinese-linked ships transit Bab Al-Mandab openly as most vessels go dark: Two Chinese-linked cargo vessels passed through Bab Al-Mandab on July 30 without evasive maneuvers, GPS manipulation, or disabling their AIS signals, according to maritime intelligence firm Windward.

- Windward said the movements support reports of a case-by-case safe-passage arrangement between China and Ansarallah, with Iran informed.

- Twelve vessels traveled “dark” during the same period amid Ansarallah threats to target Saudi-linked tankers and export infrastructure.

- Lloyd’s underwriters restrict war-risk cover for Saudi-linked ships: Leading Lloyd’s underwriters, including Ascot and Navium, told brokers they would cancel or restrict war-risk and cargo coverage for vessels with Saudi links, following Ansarallah’s July 20 maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, the Financial Times reported.

- The squeeze leaves Saudi Arabia caught between disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea embargo, with Yanbu, currently its main outlet for crude exports.

## Palestine

- Israel kills six in Gaza: Israeli strikes on Gaza Thursday killed six Palestinians, including two children, and wounded several others.

- An Israeli strike on Gaza City Thursday morning killed two Palestinians and wounded at least 10 others, WAFA reported.

- A separate drone strike in Jabaliya, north of Gaza, killed another Palestinian and wounded several more.

- Israeli warplanes struck a tent sheltering displaced people in the Al-Mawasi area west of Khan Younis, killing two Palestinians, including a child.

- An Israeli missile struck a residential apartment in central Gaza, killing a child and injuring several others.

- Hamas agrees to second phase of Gaza ceasefire, says implementation hinges on Israel:

- The Board of Peace and mediator countries announced Thursday that Hamas had agreed to a detailed roadmap for implementing the next phases of the Gaza ceasefire. The mediators said Hamas had, “for the first time,” formally committed to “an actionable plan for relinquishing all its weapons,” followed by an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza.

- In a Truth Social post, President Donald Trump hailed what he called a “HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas.”

- Hamas said Friday that it and other Palestinian factions had engaged “responsibly and positively” with mediators’ proposals for the second phase of the ceasefire but stressed that implementation cannot proceed unless Israel fulfills all of its obligations under the first phase of the October 2025 agreement.

- The group said discussions over its heavy weapons are conditional on a permanent end to Israeli attacks, a full Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, early recovery and reconstruction, the entry of the National Committee and international forces, the dismantling of Israel-backed armed militias, and progress toward Palestinian self-determination and an independent Palestinian state.

- Drop Site obtains roadmap documents on Gaza governance, weapons: Drop Site obtained a document outlining the framework Hamas and other Palestinian factions’ agreed to for Gaza’s governance and the handling of resistance weapons.

- Heavy weapons, military production sites, weapons depots, and tunnels would be inventoried and stored only after Israel halts attacks, withdraws from Gaza, and allows the entry of life essentials.

- The process would proceed alongside a phased Israeli withdrawal and a decommissioning of Israel-backed armed militias. No weapons would be handed over to Israel or any non-Palestinian party, and the National Committee would ultimately become the sole Palestinian body responsible for storing and controlling weapons in Gaza.

- The document says the framework is intended to support “a credible path toward realizing Palestinian self-determination and the establishment of the Palestinian state.”

- On governance, the document states the National Committee would assume responsibility for Gaza’s civil administration, ensure the continuity of public institutions and services, and restore the rights of public employees who were dismissed or forced into retirement in accordance with Palestinian law.

- The Committee would also conduct a comprehensive financial and administrative audit of Gaza, work to protect and recover public assets, and gradually repay up to $400 million in debts owed to suppliers and contractors over three years.

- Israel has yet to officially agree to the deal: Israel has not publicly agreed to the proposal and has made no official comment yet. An Israeli official told Reuters on condition of anonymity: “Israel demands the complete disarmament of Hamas, including the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarization of the strip as a precondition for ‌any process.” National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir posted in Hebrew on X: “The draft agreement published by the ‘Peace Council’ is not acceptable to Israel.…The targeted killings in Gaza must continue, encouraging emigration must happen, Israel must win.”

- Israel continues its attacks in the occupied West Bank:

- Nablus: A Palestinian man was shot in the neck by Israeli soldiers on Thursday, following an attack on his vehicle. Israeli forces shot a Palestinian man in the abdomen in Al-Juneid on Friday. Forces tear-gassed several Palestinians, including children. The Israeli military was accompanying settlers who had initiated an attack in the area. In the village of Burin, Israeli settlers set fire to agricultural land and burned down several olive trees.

- Bethlehem: Israeli forces raided the Solomon’s Pools tourist area on Friday, declaring the site to be a “closed military zone” and forcing visitors to leave the site at gunpoint, WAFA reported. Earlier, an Israeli military convoy stormed into the city, raided a house, and detained a Palestinian man.

- Ramallah: Israeli forces attacked the Qaddura refugee camp, ransacking the headquarters of the camp’s Popular Committee and releasing tear gas, and detaining one of the camp’s residents.

- Palestinian says he was tortured while in Israeli custody: Rizq Shakarneh, 47, from Nahhalin west of Bethlehem, told WAFA he suffered fractures and multiple injuries from torture during his eight days in Israeli detention, after being arrested following the demolition of homes and structures in his town.

- He said Israeli forces starved and denied him necessary medical treatment despite pre-existing health problems, and CT scans conducted after his release Wednesday evening reportedly revealed rib fractures, bruises and head injuries.

- Drop Site interviews family of Palestinian man detained and mocked by Israeli soldiers in viral photos: Drop Site’s Mohamed Ahmed spoke with the parents of 22-year-old Mahmoud Al-Drimli, who identified him as the blindfolded Palestinian man in a viral photograph showing two female Israeli soldiers smiling as they pose beside him.

- Mahmoud disappeared on November 2, 2024. His family said they had received no information about him until recognizing him in the image.

- “The moment I saw the picture, my heart was at peace, and I was happy. But at the same time, when I saw him in that state, my heart broke,” his mother said through tears.

- Watch the full interviews with Mahmoud’s parents here.

- Israeli soldiers walk off Sde Teiman base in protest of order to remove battalion signs glorifying hazing: Fourteen soldiers of the Givati Brigade’s Tzabar Battalion who took part in a mass desertion on Thursday have been sentenced to 30 days in military jail and permanently dismissed from combat duty, according to the Israeli military.

- Around 100 soldiers from the battalion walked out of the Sde Teiman base without authorization on Thursday—leaving behind their military equipment and weapons—after their commander ordered battalion signs to be removed and destroyed.

- Sde Teiman is the notorious military detention and torture site where Israel has held Palestinians seized en masse from Gaza without charge or access to lawyers. There is extensive documentation of severe beatings, systematic rape and sexual abuse, and other forms of torture there.

- The soldiers did not walk off the base in protest of the torture of Palestinians at Sde Teiman or of combat duty in the genocide in Gaza but rather because they argued the signs that were ordered taken down—which portrayed or related to hazing practices inflicted by older troops on younger ones—represented a long-standing battalion tradition.

## Lebanon

- Israeli demolitions in southern Lebanon generate seismic waves the equivalent of a 3.8-magnitude earthquake, despite “ceasefire”: Israel carried out a series of large-scale demolitions, shelling attacks, and artillery strikes across southern Lebanon late Thursday and Friday, despite the U.S.-brokered ceasefire, Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) reported.

- Shortly after midnight, Israeli forces carried out massive explosions in the Nabatieh district around Yahmar al-Shaqif, Arnoun, and Kfartebnit. The explosions, centered near Beaufort Castle, shattered windows and damaged homes in Qlayaa, while Lebanon’s National Center for Geophysics said the blast generated seismic waves equivalent to a 3.8-magnitude earthquake.

- Israeli forces demolished caves and homes around Al-Mansouri and Majdal Zoun in the Tyre (Sour) district on Friday. Forces also shelled Talousa in the Marjayoun district.

- Israeli troops fired illuminating shells at Ali Al-Taher hill on the outskirts of Nabatieh Al-Fawqa, “deliberately igniting” fires in the area, according to the NNA.

- Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri condemned the attacks, saying the 700 tons of explosives that generated tremors equivalent to an earthquake should “awaken national and human conscience” to Israel’s “machinery of destruction.”

- Lebanon’s Aoun seeks Turkish backing for U.S.-brokered framework with Israel: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun traveled to Ankara on Thursday to meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, seeking Turkey’s support for a U.S.-brokered framework agreement Lebanon signed with Israel in Washington on June 26.

- Aoun, who faces domestic opposition to the deal from Hezbollah and Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, told Turkey’s Anadolu Agency that implementation depends on “a complete Israeli withdrawal simultaneous with the deployment of the Lebanese army” and an international mechanism to verify compliance from both sides.

## U.S. News

- Mandela Barnes drops out of Wisconsin Democratic governor’s race: Former Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes announced that he is exiting the Democratic primary for governor. The state’s primary is August 11.

- Democratic socialist and state Rep. Francesca Hong now faces Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who re-entered the race earlier this month with the endorsement of outgoing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.

- A Marquette University Law School poll released on Wednesday showed that Hong had the support of 38% of Democratic primary voters, and Crowley had only 7%, with 34% of voters remaining undecided and 16% preferring the now-withdrawn Barnes.

- A third of Democrats now identify as democratic socialists, CNN poll finds: About a third of Democrats and Democratic-leaning adults identify as democratic socialists, according to a CNN poll conducted by SSRS.

- The poll found democratic socialists tend to be younger, more likely to be extremely motivated to vote, and are also much more likely to be critical of Israel, with 48% saying they’d be enthusiastic about a candidate who wants to cut U.S. support to Israel, compared with 20% of non-democratic socialists.

- ExxonMobil and Chevron post combined $26.5 billion in second-quarter profits amid Iran war oil surge: ExxonMobil and Chevron reported combined second-quarter earnings of $26.5 billion, with Chevron posting record net income of $12.2 billion and ExxonMobil reporting $14.5 billion, as crude and petrol prices surged following the U.S. and Israeli attack on Iran in February.

- Exxon chief financial officer Neil Hansen said further price increases are possible if the Strait of Hormuz is closed to tanker traffic.

- Hansen told the FT that the “pain point” regarding oil prices was not with crude, which he said is trading within its historical ranges, but with products such as petrol and diesel, which have seen their prices surge as production capacity diminished.

- New York sues Kalshi, alleging prediction market platform runs “illegal gambling operation”: New York state announced a lawsuit against the prediction market platform Kalshi on Friday, with Attorney General Letitia James alleging the company is operating illegally by accepting wagers without registering with the New York State Gaming Commission.

- The lawsuit seeks a permanent injunction, restitution to users, and financial penalties against the company, which is based in New York City.

- WSJ reports on Trump’s fundraising focus, nightly calls for multimillion dollar donations: President Donald Trump has personally directed a fundraising operation that has taken in more than $800 million since he returned to office, according to a Wall Street Journal report published on Thursday, with the president nightly calling his fundraiser Meredith O’Rourke to press companies for donations ranging from $5 million to $50 million toward projects including his presidential library, a White House ballroom, and political committees.

- Companies including SoftBank, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta Platforms have made multimillion-dollar contributions, and executives told the Journal that donations appear linked to access and favorable regulatory treatment.

- “What can I do to help you?” Trump has told donors at multiple events, according to attendees. “What do you need?” he reportedly asked a group of CEOs at an event he hosted in Florida. The full report from the WSJ is available here.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- 60,000 cross from Morocco into Ceuta after border breach: At least 41 people have died trying to reach the Spanish territory of Ceuta after breaching the border from Morocco with some 60,000 migrants entering the enclave in the past 24 hours.

- Ceuta, along with Melilla—another autonomous ‌Spanish city in North Africa—represents the European Union’s only land border with Africa. Migrants cross into Ceuta by land and sea, with people often swimming from the Moroccan town of Fnideq three miles away. Many of those who died drowned, while others were killed in a stampede to cross the border fence.

- Moroccan security forces clashed with thousands of people on the Moroccan side of the border as they tried to cross, using water cannons and firing warning shots into the air.

- Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez travelled to Ceuta on Friday and called the crossings  “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity.” Spain’s Ministry of Interior said some 25,000 people were returned from Ceuta to Morocco so far on Friday.

- According to the AP, authorities in both Ceuta and Madrid, linked the mass influx of migrants to a recent decision by Spain’s Supreme Court that ruled migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported, unlike those who cross by land or climb the border fence. Sánchez said migrant smugglers misinterpreted the ruling, triggering the surge.

- Russia’s Africa Corps killed eight civilians in Mali air strike, HRW reports: Africa Corps, the Russian paramilitary group that has largely replaced the Wagner Group in Africa, killed eight civilians, including three children, in a June 15 air strike on the village of Kyrnia in Mali’s central Mopti region, Human Rights Watch said Friday.

- The rights group noted no fighters from the al-Qaeda-linked group Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimin were believed to be killed in the strike despite the group controlling the village.

- Russian mercenaries have backed the Malian government’s fight against JNIM and the Azawad Liberation Front, a Tuareg separatist group. The two rebel groups joined forces to launch nationwide, coordinated attacks on government installations starting in April.

- Attack on police checkpoint kills 11 officers in northwest Pakistan: An ambush on a police checkpoint in the Hangu district of Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province killed at least 11 police officers and injured 28 others late Wednesday.

- The attackers reportedly used explosive-laden quadcopters before storming the post near the Afghan border. Security forces said they killed 15 of the attackers in a subsequent hours-long gun battle.

- No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, though it follows a suicide bombing claimed by the Pakistan Taliban that killed 27 people in nearby Tank district last week.

reads.title: Trump and NYT Say There’s a Russian Spy Base in Cuba. Turns Out, It’s a School.
reads.subtitle: Belly of the Beast found no evidence of an active Russian intelligence base, much less the sort of extensive equipment described by the NYT.
reads.body:
- This abandoned watchtower is one of the few structures left from the Lourdes spy base in Cuba. Photo: Reed Lindsay.This story was written in collaboration with Belly of the Beast, an independent media outlet that covers Cuba and U.S.-Cuba relations. You can support their work on Patreon.
Since U.S. President Donald Trump imposed an executive order in January threatening tariffs on any country that ships fuel to Cuba, major media outlets have descended on the island to report on the resulting prolonged blackouts, collapsing hospitals, and piles of uncollected trash.
Far less attention has been paid to the rationale the administration offered for imposing the blockade in the first place.
The executive order states that Cuba represents a “national emergency” and poses an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to the United States, stringing together a kitchen-sink list of familiar allegations, including accusations that Cuba sponsors terrorism and aligns itself with “dangerous adversaries” of the United States, such as Iran, Hamas, Russia, and China.
More specifically, the order claims that “Cuba hosts Russia’s largest overseas signals intelligence facility, which tries to steal sensitive national security information of the United States.”
For two months, the allegation that Cuba was hosting a major Russian spy base was largely ignored by U.S. media outlets. Then, on March 24, The New York Times published an article by Michael Crowley claiming not only that the Russian spy base exists, but that it “bristles with antennas and other eavesdropping equipment” capable of spying on the U.S. Central Command, the satellite launchpads of Cape Canaveral, and Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence.
Crowley pinpointed the location: a former Soviet base on the outskirts of Havana called Lourdes that was “temporarily shut” by Vladimir Putin in 2001 but was reopened in 2014, according to the Times.
There is just one problem with this story: the base isn’t there.
The State Department did not respond to a request for comment. Belly of the Beast also sent requests to The New York Times and to Michael Crowley but received no response.
Today, Lourdes (also known as Torrens) is home to Cuba’s University of Computer Sciences (UCI). The reporting team at Belly of the Beast spent the better part of two days walking the campus, searching the grounds, and speaking with students, faculty, and workers. We found no evidence of an active Russian intelligence base, much less the sort of extensive equipment described by the Times.
“Do I look like a Russian spy?” laughed Malcolm Jarrozai, a 40-year-old art professor who has been teaching at UCI and living at a residence on campus since 2006. “It’s truly laughable that these kinds of claims are being made and that major outlets like The New York Times give them a platform and allow them to be used to justify policies against Cuba.”

-
- Malcolm Jarrozai, an art professor at the University of Computer Sciences, speaks with Belly of the Beast journalist Liz Oliva Fernández. Photo: Alfredo Lazcano ValeraSubscribe now

## The Rise and Fall of Lourdes
Construction of a Soviet signals intelligence (SIGINT) facility in Cuba began as early as 1962, even before the Cuban Missile Crisis. By the 1980s, U.S. intelligence said Lourdes was “the USSR’s largest and most valuable base outside the Soviet Union for intelligence collection against the United States.”
In a 1983 televised address, President Ronald Reagan cited Lourdes as evidence of the Soviet threat to argue against proposed congressional budget cuts to defense spending. Reagan said the 28-square-mile base was manned by 1,500 Soviet technicians and had grown by 60 percent in the previous decade. Two years later, the Departments of State and Defense estimated there were as many as 14,700 Soviet personnel in Cuba, including 2,100 at Lourdes.

-
- A photo of the wall of the Russian base known as Lourdes with satellite dishes in the background, before the base was dismantled. Photo: Rafael Torrabas.
-
- A map of the Lourdes base released by the U.S. government. Photo: Federation of American ScientistsEven after the fall of the Soviet Union, the Lourdes base remained in place to the consternation of neoconservatives and Cuban-American hardliners. In 1998, Jane’s Intelligence Review wrote that Lourdes remained “the greatest single overseas GRU [Russian military intelligence] asset” and provided 60-70 percent of Russian electronic intelligence data on the United States. Two years later, a congressional report noted that there were still more than 1,500 Russian engineers, technicians and military personnel at the base.
In January 2001, the hardline anti-Castro lawmaker Rep. Ileana Ros-Lehtinen (R-FL) introduced a bill that would have prohibited forgiveness of Russian government debt until Lourdes was shuttered. Ten months later, Ros-Lehtinen, for whom Marco Rubio served as an intern in the early 1990s, got her wish.
On October 17, 2001, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin announced that Russia would abandon Lourdes. U.S. President George W. Bush congratulated Putin for taking down a “Cold War relic” and hailed the news as “another indication that the Cold War is over.”
But other U.S. politicians have had a harder time letting go of the Cold War.

-
- The Lourdes intelligence facility featured massive satellite dishes until Russia dismantled them when it closed the base between 2001 and 2002. Photos: Rafael Torrabas.

## From Russia to China
The closure of Lourdes didn’t end talk of foreign spy bases in Cuba. Even before the Russians finally handed the base over to Cuban authorities in August 2002, El Nuevo Herald published an article claiming that Lourdes had been replaced by a Chinese base at Bejucal, a town about seven miles away.
But allegations that China was using Cuba to spy on the United States did not become a national news story until 2023, when The Wall Street Journal reported that the two countries had reached a “secret agreement” for China to establish a spy base in Cuba. The Journal, citing anonymous officials “familiar with highly classified intelligence,” said China had agreed “in principle” to pay Cuba “several billion dollars to allow it to build an eavesdropping station,” and described the agreement as a “brash new geopolitical challenge” that has “sparked alarm” in the Biden administration.
A year later, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) released a report that used commercial satellite imagery to identify four locations in Cuba, including Bejucal, “where China is most likely operating” its alleged spy bases.
The report, which was part of CSIS’s “Hidden Reach” program to expose China’s influence around the world, provided no evidence that the alleged spy bases in Cuba, even if real, were being operated by China. CSIS recently acknowledged there was “no clear publicly available evidence” proving China’s presence at Bejucal.
“The report pulls the rumors and speculation in only one direction—to support its preordained conclusion that Chinese intelligence capabilities are expanding in ways threatening to U.S. interests, with Cuba’s full support,” said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst who also served as the nation’s top intelligence officer on Latin America. “That’s bad analysis.”
Belly of the Beast attempted to visit three of the four locations identified in the CSIS report. They appeared to be Cuban military installations but we found no evidence of heightened security or Chinese personnel.
At one site, the guard posts appeared abandoned. Part of the facility’s perimeter was lined with a rusty fence. Another section was bordered by trees. The main entrance was guarded by an elderly Cuban woman who was an unarmed civilian employed by Cuba’s Vigilance and Protection Corps (CVP), a state agency that provides security services at schools, hospitals, stores, and hotels.
At another site, antennas draped in ivy and a dirt-covered satellite dish could be seen from the street.
“That’s laughably old technology,” said Armstrong after viewing video footage from two of the facilities. “It’s sort of an insult to the Chinese if you’re going to say that this is the future of their intel collection against the United States.”
CSIS claimed the fourth location, near Santiago de Cuba, was being used to construct a circularly disposed antenna array (CDAA), a Cold War-era technology that has become largely obsolete. The report itself acknowledges that Russia and the United States have abandoned most of their CDAAs.
A CSIS update to the report published last month said construction had “largely ceased” and there was no indication the site was operational.
The CSIS report made no mention of a Russian spy base beyond noting that Lourdes had operated during the Cold War.
But Lourdes had nonetheless resurfaced in the news in 2014 amid heightened U.S.-Russian tensions, when The New York Times reported that Russia had plans to reopen the base, citing a Russian newspaper and Russian parliamentarians who “appeared to confirm the report.” The next day, Putin said Russia had no such plans.
Not much was heard about the purported spy base until Trump’s executive order revived the narrative that the Russians had returned to Cuba, though Rubio did mention Lourdes at a 2016 Republican primary debate against Trump in Miami: “Here’s a good deal…Cuba kicks out the Russians from Lourdes and kicks out the Chinese listening station in Bejucal.”
In June testimony before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Rubio was asked for evidence supporting Cuba’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.
“Cuba continues to host a pretty substantial collection of intelligence sites on behalf of the Chinese and the Russians,” he said.

## From Spy Base to Cuba’s Silicon Valley
Cuban engineer Rafael Torralbas first stepped foot on the Russian base in April 2002. Torralbas and two other colleagues were tasked with creating a university within a matter of months.
“We had the challenge of receiving the installations being left behind by the Russian officials,” said Torralbas. “There were huge [satellite dish] antennas, and I witnessed the process of dismantling them. There was technological equipment connected to the antennas, which we never saw. We knew it had been there, but the Russian officials had dismantled it all and they handed over the buildings completely empty.”
Torralbas said the Russians removed “absolutely every antenna” along with everything else, including furniture and curtains. The Russians hauled the base’s equipment home in six Antonov An-124 Ruslan cargo plane flights, according to Torralbas.
On September 23, 2002, one month after the last Russian left Lourdes, the University of Computer Sciences held its first classes on the grounds of the old base, which is located just two miles from Havana’s José Martí International Airport.
In the following years, some of the Russian buildings were torn down, while others were repurposed. The apartment buildings housing the Russian personnel and their families were converted into residences for students and professors. A daycare center became a center for medical technology. A supermarket was turned into a library.
Torralbas now serves as the president of the Havana Science and Technology Park, an innovation hub on the UCI campus that he says was inspired by Silicon Valley. Founded in 2020, the Technology Park serves as an incubator for Cuban tech startups, most of them private companies (despite claims to the contrary by hard-line politicians in Florida, Cuba’s private sector has been thriving in recent years). The park also provides technological support to foreign and state-run companies.
Torralbas says the idea that Lourdes was reopened “could only exist in the mind of the person who made up that news.”
“At no time, in this university, has anything existed that is not school buildings, students, computer science development centers, postgrad programs, that is, the normal activities of a university,” he said. “It’s shocking to me that someone in the intelligence community in the United States, with access to satellite images, could claim that a [spy base] exists here now.”

-
- The University of Computer Sciences, which occupies the grounds of the former Russian base known as Lourdes, has graduated thousands of students since it was founded in 2002. Photo: Alfredo Lazcano Valera

## Hunting for Russian Spies
We spent hours walking around UCI’s expansive tree-lined campus and drove around the perimeter, looking for any signs of signals intelligence or military installations. The security presence was minimal. We moved around freely and nobody seemed to care who we were or what we were doing. There was a guard at the entrance and two others in a far corner of the campus, where they watched over what appeared to be a side entrance—a partially closed door made of corrugated metal. The guards, who were unarmed, said they worked for a state-run security company. There were no military checkpoints.
According to Torralbas, more than 80% of the buildings on the campus were built since the Russians left 24 years ago. New classroom buildings, computer labs and research centers now occupy land where Soviet antennas once stood.
The only remnant of the old base we came across was a crumbling watchtower near the perimeter of the campus. It was impossible to ascend as its metal ladder had long since rusted away, leaving a small piece still visible at the top.
As for The New York Times’ claim that the re-opened Lourdes “bristles with antennas”—we ultimately found two mobile phone antennas belonging to ETECSA, the state telecommunications company.

-
- One of the only antennas that is visible at the university. University staff say it is a mobile phone antenna owned by Cuba’s state-run telecommunications company. Photo: Reed Lindsa“We’re in a rural area, so this is the only way we can have service for phone calls, text messages, internet, and everything else,” explained Héctor González, a UCI graduate who now works in its communications department. “The antennas that were here [under the Russians] that were dismantled were different. They were enormous satellite dishes that you can see in some old photos, giant radars many meters high. These are just ordinary mobile network antennas.”
The campus was mostly deserted. There are more than 2,500 undergraduate students currently enrolled at UCI, but only a handful were on campus.
The oil blockade has ground Cuba’s public transportation to a halt. In February, with students and professors unable to get to class, Cuba’s universities shifted to remote and hybrid instruction, suspending most in-person classes.
“It’s a shame our students aren’t here today,” said Aylín Estrada, a UCI graduate and now a university dean who guided us around one of the newer school buildings, which has dozens of classrooms. “Normally these hallways are full of students, smiling, learning.”
“Those buildings over there used to be for the people who worked [on the base],” said Franklin Quintana, a 37-year-old software developer, pointing to faded green five-story apartment buildings that now house university staff.
Quintana, who recently returned to the university to work as a software developer, shook his head when asked about the spy base.
“It’s a false justification. There’s no other way to understand it,” he said.
“Rubio should come and look for it himself then. Look for it and prove it’s here,” said 68-year-old Estrella Luque, a school administrator whose daughter and son graduated from UCI and are now professors. “Cuba isn’t a threat to anyone. I don’t think anyone with two brain cells to rub together believes that.”
After watching her children study and later teach at the university, Luque said she was sad to see the campus without students.
“They can say we’re a failed state if they want…but no one can ignore or deny the impact of the blockade,” said Luque. “A country like this little island, which has virtually no natural resources—we’re not a major oil-producing island or a country with abundant resources—if you don’t let oil in, naturally everything starts to fall apart. That’s what’s happening to us. But here we are. We keep going.”
Leave a comment

reads.title: Nigel Farage's raging hypocrisy over Zack Polanski
reads.subtitle: Consider what Farage has said - and what he has defended
reads.body:
- Nigel Farage and Reform are exposing themselves as massive, raging hypocrites - again - this time over the furore surrounding Zack Polanski briefly accepting a collaboration post on Instagram.
Farage is desperately trying to distract you from the undeclared £5 million personal gift from a Thailand-based crypto donor, and from donations linked to the convicted fraudster George Cottrell. Indeed, the latest Guardian headline about Cottrell has just dropped:

-
- So Farage is playing a very obvious game: look over there!
BattleLines with Owen Jones is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

## Here’s the TL;DR of what actually happened
Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party, briefly accepted a collaboration request on Instagram.
For those unfamiliar with the feature, someone can tag you as a collaborator on their post. If you accept, the post also appears on your own grid.
This particular post was a carousel containing several photographs. All but one were innocuous campaign-style pictures. The first showed Polanski at an event called Green Space in Bristol.
Anyone who has looked at Polanski’s Instagram account knows that he accepts collaboration requests en masse. I don’t think that is a good idea - not least because it leaves you vulnerable to exactly this sort of thing - but I’ll come back to that.
Several photographs into the carousel, there was an image of someone wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with the words “We’re Only Making Plans for Nigel”, alongside a man operating a French Revolution-style guillotine.
The words are a reference to Making Plans for Nigel, the song released by the English rock band XTC in 1979, which has often been linked to Farage for obvious reasons.
When Polanski became aware of the image, he immediately removed himself from the collaboration and said accepting it had been a mistake.
Share
But all hell broke loose.
Former Reform chair Zia Yusuf tweeted:

-
-
No. Zack Polanski did not “post” the photograph. He accepted a collaboration containing a series of images, the first of which was an entirely ordinary photograph of him speaking at an event. When he noticed the offending image several slides in, he removed himself.
Nor does the photograph actually call for Farage’s beheading. It does not make any demand at all. It is obviously crude satire. There is no shortage of jokes involving Madame Guillotine in British political culture. Let’s be serious here.
Subscribe now
Yusuf went on:

-
- This bloke needs to seriously calm down. He is always so hysterical. It is completely one-note. At least Donald Trump occasionally intersperses the derangement with some levity.
And, again, it is a lie. Polanski did not post a threat to kill anyone.
Yusuf then declared:

-
- Demanding that the leader of another political party be arrested over an Instagram collaboration request he accepted by mistake is not a serious response. It is unhinged.
Subscribe now
Farage then posted a video with the caption:
He went on Sky News demanding that the Metropolitan Police take action.
Again, let’s spell out what we are talking about: Polanski accepted a collaboration containing a series of photographs. The first showed him speaking at an event. Several photographs later came an image of someone wearing a very edgy satirical T-shirt. When Polanski realised, he removed himself from the post.
That is the basis on which Farage and his outriders are demanding consequences - and, in Yusuf’s case, police custody.
Subscribe now

## The hypocrisy is staggering
This is the same Nigel Farage who said in May 2017:

> “If they don’t deliver this Brexit that I spent 25 years of my life working for, then I will be forced to don khaki, pick up a rifle and head for the front lines.”
#Brexit... I will be forced to don khaki, pick up a rifle and head to the front lines\" \n\nif he was not white and had a muslim name, he’d have been arrested. ","username":"Munir566","name":"Munir A Hussein","profile_image_url":"https://pbs.substack.com/profile_images/1198247079824515084/75ckm3jT_normal.jpg","date":"2019-04-13T17:30:01.000Z","photos":[{"img_url":"https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uMU1!,w_1028,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:best,fl_progressive:steep/l_play_button_usfui2,w_88,e_colorize:0/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F__ss-rehost__tw-video-preview-7_1117117714965913602.jpg","link_url":"https://t.co/bzhjeX53Vo"}],"quoted_tweet":{},"reply_count":4,"retweet_count":7,"like_count":13,"impression_count":0,"expanded_url":null,"video_url":"https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1117117714965913602/pu/vid/176x320/959cLvqGDBlDnNxT.mp4?tag=8","video_preview_media_key":"7_1117117714965913602","belowTheFold":true}" data-component-name="Twitter2ToDOM">This was less than a year after the Labour MP Jo Cox was shot and stabbed to death during the referendum campaign.
This is the same Farage who said Reform would “take the knife” to the civil service.
The same Farage who called for “pure, cold rage” after the conviction of the murderer of Henry Nowak, with riots taking place just hours later.
But more to the point, Farage and Reform came to the defence of Lucy Connolly, a childminder jailed after the nationwide riots and pogroms of August 2024, portraying her as a free-speech martyr.
After the horrific Southport murders - committed, to be absolutely clear, by a British-born British citizen - Connolly tweeted:

-
- The “bastards” she was referring to were asylum seekers.
Subscribe now
And during the riots, people really did attempt to set fire to hotels containing asylum seekers. The country was in the grip of a violent, fascist uprising.
Farage nevertheless declared:

> “I want to make it absolutely clear: Lucy Connolly should not be in prison.”
He added:

> “While she should not have said what she said, understand there were millions of mothers at that moment in time after Southport feeling exactly the same way.”
Richard Tice, Reform’s deputy leader, visited Connolly in person and called her a “political prisoner”.
When she was released, Farage tweeted:
He even took her case to the United States.
Connolly was then platformed on the main stage of Reform’s September 2025 conference, introduced as “Britain’s favourite political prisoner” and publicly embraced by Farage himself.
So let’s get this straight.
A woman explicitly called for hotels containing asylum seekers to be set on fire not long before violent mobs went on to do exactly that. Farage and Reform turned her into a martyr, defended her, visited her in prison, took her case overseas and gave her a starring role at their party conference.
But Zack Polanski accidentally accepts an Instagram collaboration containing a crude piece of satire several photographs in - and Farage demands that he “face the consequences”, while Yusuf calls for him to be taken into police custody.
This is not a principled stand against violent rhetoric. It is a desperate attempt by Farage to distract from his own scandals - one which has instead exposed the grotesque hypocrisy of him and his party.
Indeed, the Metropolitan police have declared that no action will be taken against Polanski because the threshold for criminal action hasn’t been met.
Subscribe now

## Polanski should change his social-media strategy
I do think Zack Polanski should alter his relationship with social media - and I say that as someone who is terminally online.
As a leader, constantly reposting other people’s material drowns out your own message. It also leaves you vulnerable to bad-faith attacks and accidental shares of material you have not properly checked.
Look at Zohran Mamdani’s social media. It is very disciplined. He posts sparingly and sticks closely to the key messages he wants to communicate at any given moment.
Polanski would benefit from taking the same approach.
But that does not change the absurdity of this attack. Nor should anyone allow Farage’s theatrical outrage to obscure the obvious reason he is promoting it.
He wants you looking anywhere but at him.
