reads.title: Data Centers Divide Democrats in Michigan Primary
reads.subtitle: Senate candidates offer conflicting visions over the role of A.I. and corporate power.
reads.body:
The article below is part of Drop Site’s ongoing collaboration with Barn Raiser to put a focus on rural politics with a newsletter running through November.
SIGN UP HERE

-
- A demonstrator at an April rally in Traverse City, Michigan, holds a sign emblematic of the growing data center resistance. (Miles MacClure)Story by Miles MacClure
Over the past year, dim, windowless, gargantuan warehouses have taken center stage in rural Michigan. The data centers draw ire for consuming vast energy resources to fuel an artificial intelligence boom viewed with increased skepticism. They have spiked utility bills, guzzled the region’s fresh water, occupied large tracts of land, and emitted a hum so constant that some residents have sued over excessive noise.
The projects have sparked renewed civic engagement in rural areas and small towns—stories that inspire David and Goliath comparisons. Residents ignite with fury upon finding out their local elected officials have made deals in the dark to bring data centers to town. They come out in force to city council meetings, zoning hearings, and protests in an effort to confront the power of major utility companies and multinational tech corporations with billions of dollars at their disposal.
This growing opposition has forced Michigan’s elected officials to reconsider the wisdom of the state’s 2024 decision to hand out tax breaks to data center constructors.
Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former Wayne County public health official running in the August 4 Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, told Barn Raiser that the corporations building data centers aren’t straightforward about their development plans.
“There’s been so little transparency on the part of the corporations themselves and the part of the utilities,” he said. “It has raised the hackles of folks who’ve learned not to trust a lot of these bigger corporations when they tell them everything’s going to be okay.”
El-Sayed is locked in a fierce contest that has accentuated divides within the Democratic Party. El-Sayed, whose parents immigrated from Egypt, has pledged not to accept corporate PAC money, has called for eliminating arms sales to Israel and supports universal health care and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) is a vocal supporter of Israel who has accepted money from corporate PACs, outside groups like the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and has the support of Democratic party leader Sen. Chuck Schumer. Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, a third challenger in the race, suspended her campaign July 5.
An April Emerson College poll shows data centers could be among the deciding issues in the election. Emerson’s poll of 519 likely Michigan primary voters found that a majority, or 55%, opposed data centers being built in or near their community, versus 27% who supported them. Opposition to data centers was much higher among likely Democratic primary voters, with 63% opposed versus 45% among likely Republican primary voters.
Dark money spending and support for Israel remains another flashpoint in the campaign, gaining national attention. The Associated Press reported AIPAC and its affiliated groups have spent close to $30 million backing Stevens, which is their largest investment ever in a single race.
In January, El-Sayed released a terms of engagement proposal for data centers, which includes a guarantee for local jobs, a freeze on consumer electricity rate hikes and community benefit agreements. In recent weeks, he has shown support for a system of federal oversight and public ownership of AI companies, a proposal first advanced by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has endorsed El-Sayed.
Stevens has not laid out any similar positions. At a Democratic primary debate in July, Stevens connected data center construction with job creation, saying it will put Michigan “on the forefront of innovation and manufacturing,” but she has also called for protecting Michiganders from data center costs.
In an email statement to Barn Raiser, Stevens wrote, “When it comes to data centers and AI infrastructure, my top priority is making sure costs don’t go up for Michigan families and that we are protecting good-paying union jobs. We cannot allow utility companies like DTE to pass new costs onto consumers while these projects move forward.”
Stevens did not answer the question regarding Michigan residents’ concern about AI potentially resulting in less jobs.
“ Part of the problem with our politics is too often corporations are buying and selling politicians in the first place. In the case of DTE, our local utility, they’ve given to 93% of state legislators,” said El-Sayed, referencing McMorrow, who eventually dropped out. DTE was McMorrow’s top donor in her 2022 state Senate reelection campaign. El-Sayed’s current opponent, Stevens, has received money from DTE since her first U.S. House reelection campaign in 2020.
McMorrow was among the 38 state senators to vote for a Senate bill that exempted hyperscale data centers from sales and use taxes on their equipment. The bill was signed into law by Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in 2025.
In hindsight, El-Sayed said a more extensive review process should have occurred before state legislators approved laws to entice data center development in the state.
“I think we should have spent a bit more time to hold the particular utilities accountable ahead of laying out the red carpet, as our state has done,” he said.
Data centers have split support amongst unions and their endorsements. The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has over 400,000 members nationwide, endorsed El-Sayed in June. In an April press conference with Bernie Sanders and other labor leaders, UAW president Shawn Fain compared AI to NAFTA because of the risks it poses to workers and communities. “The same greedy corporate power brokers today want us to believe that killing millions of jobs in the name of AI will be a good thing, and the working class knows better,” he said. Several of the building trades unions, on the other hand, view data centers as a catalyst for job creation, with many, including Plumbers Local 98 and Pipefitters, Steamfitters, Refrigeration & Air Conditioning Service Local Union 636, having endorsed Stevens.
Michigan’s chapter of the AFL-CIO, the nation’s largest federation of labor unions, has not made an endorsement in the Senate race. In June, the AFL-CIO released a policy agenda for the next five years. It included demands that data centers and AI infrastructure be “built by and run on union labor,” while requiring that “data centers pay their fair share of costs and taxes” and that working-class families and communities “are protected and included every step of the way, including regulations over water and power use.”
Construction workers may be the only local residents who stand to benefit from the data center boom. A Citizens Research Council of Michigan report on data centers found that the economic benefits of data centers largely occur during the construction phase and concluded that the projects aren’t long-term drivers of economic development. In June, Bloomberg reported that data centers account for 2.3% of all construction spending in the United States.
In a July debate, El-Sayed and Stevens clashed over their approaches to AI and data centers. El-Sayed reiterated his community engagement plan and added, “I think we have to be serious about the fact that these pose real dangers,” he said. “And the people who are pushing them are the richest, most powerful corporate CEOs in the history of our economy.”
Stevens did not speak directly to citizens’ concerns about AI but pledged to entice data centers to pay for utilities and rate increases. “I also want to secure Michigan being on the forefront of innovation,” she said in a statement to Barn Raiser.
Michigan state Rep. Dylan Wegela (D-Garden City) voted against the tax breaks for data centers when the Michigan House of Representatives voted on the bill in 2023. Wegela had concerns about the environmental impact of data centers from the beginning, he said, but hadn’t anticipated the magnitude of the pushback against using hyperscale facilities to drive AI developments.  
“I think there are a lot of concerns with that industry right now and concerns about what the technology, unregulated as it is now, might do to working-class people,” Wegela said. “And I think that is one of the many reasons this is becoming so controversial now.”
For Wegela, data centers are an issue that unites people across party lines. “In areas that these data centers are coming to, you have these coalitions of people on the left and the right coming out to fight together against data centers,” he said. “That’s working class versus Big Tech.”
That coalition of residents was on display on a sunny Saturday morning in Traverse City, Michigan. About 40 protesters showed up to oppose data center construction across Michigan, one of several anti-data center protests that took place across the state on April 11. At the Traverse City protest, attendees brought signs decrying data centers and signs in support of Lake Michigan’s freshwater supply. Speakers voiced their opposition to AI in schools and expressed skepticism about the number of local jobs that data centers would generate.

-
- Ryan Wagner, the Kalkaska County GOP party chair, speaks at an anti-data center rally in April in Traverse City, Michigan. (Miles MacClure)Ryan Wagner, the Kalkaska County GOP party chair, appeared alongside Mitch Distin, who helped organize the protest and is running as a Democrat for state representative in Michigan’s 104th district.
Wagner voiced his discontent with the Make America Great Again movement after continuous campaign promises broken by the Trump administration, like financial gain for working-class Americans, and he found common ground with Democrats seeking to maintain natural resources and oppose AI companies. “I feed my kids off this land. I don’t want Big Tech to poison it,” Wagner told the crowd.
In November, a company called Rocklocker—a subsidiary of oil and gas company Reefworks—proposed building a data center in rural Kalkaska County, just east of Traverse City, on 1,440 acres of land owned by the Michigan Department of Natural Resources. But community backlash was fierce. At meetings to discuss the proposal, residents didn’t buy the economic benefits claimed by Rocklocker and they were wary of the environmental impact.
“The scientific literature is abundantly clear that none of the benefits are distributed or trickle down to local communities, they’re the ones who ultimately pay the price for data centers,” Distin told the protestors. “The only people who are benefiting from this are big tech CEOs and the legislators.”
If a data center is abandoned by a company, it’s unclear who will be responsible to pick up the pieces. “What happens if the company goes bankrupt?” said Wegela. “You’ve seen factories across the state for the automotive industry and cities have been on the hook for cleaning those up or maintaining those. And I just think these are things that aren’t being talked about enough.”
“Democrats should be leading the opposition to unchecked data center growth,” said Michelle Deatrick, chair of the DNC Climate Council. “That’s not because we oppose technology, it’s because we believe growth needs to serve the public interest, it needs to serve the people, and that’s in both the short and the long term.”
One tactic used by local organizers has been to implement moratoriums. For instance, residents in Livingston County, north of Detroit, successfully pushed Howell Township to approve a six-month moratorium on data center projects, including the $1 billion, 1,077-acre data center proposed backed by Meta, which owns Facebook.
Michigan State Rep. Jennifer Wortz, a Republican in the 35th District, introduced a bill in February that would place a moratorium on data center construction across the state until April 2027.
Towns, counties, cities, and states across the country are deciding how to respond. An analysis from The Information found more than 300 bans or moratoriums across the United States. (Datacenterbans.com has an interactive map and updates a tracker on data center policy around the country.) On July 14, New York enacted the nation’s first statewide one-year moratorium on data center construction following an executive order signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul. Maine nearly became the first state to do so in April, when the state legislature passed a moratorium, but Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat, vetoed the bill.
As communities sour on data center projects, they’re also turning away from AI. A Quinnipiac University poll from March 2026 found that 81% of millennials were concerned about AI. The poll also found that 55% of Americans believe AI will do more harm than good, up from 44% in April 2025.
“ I don’t know if everybody in the public space has connected that the data center and the AI fight is one and the same,” said Wegela.
In the workplace, AI is meeting resistance. Futurism reported that some workers are intentionally sabotaging their employer’s AI deployments. Fears over the direction of AI are also turning violent. In April, a Houston man traveled to San Francisco and hurled a Molotov cocktail at OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s house.
“The fear and anxiety about AI is justified,” Altman wrote on his blog in the wake of the attack. “We are in the process of witnessing the largest change to society in a long time, and perhaps ever.”
Kyle Blomquist, an architect running for Congress in Michigan’s rural 1st congressional district, said the data center tax breaks handed out by Michigan should be repealed. “I’m surprised by the fact that our state has decided to incentivize the location of data centers in the state through these various different tax abatement programs and cuts,” said Blomquist.
When Michigan first legalized medical marijuana, local governments had to set ordinances about marijuana store zoning before any business was allowed to set up shop. Blomquist said he would have liked to see a similar process play out with data centers.
Instead, the Wild West of data center growth has exposed a need for towns and counties to update their zoning ordinances. Many of the towns where data centers have been proposed have never had such large developments set up shop before.
“ I would’ve liked more caution with the data centers, more along those lines where you give the communities the opportunity to set their own conditions as to whether or not they want them located there at all,” said Blomquist. “Instead, it’s kind of a free-for-all.”
Miles MacClure is a writer based in Traverse City, Michigan. This story was first published by Barn Raiser, whose coverage was supported by a grant from the Lumpkin Family Foundation.

reads.title: U.S.-Saudi strikes kill 20 Iraqi fighters; Israeli settler attacks in West Bank “hitting an all-time high”; Cholera outbreak in Sudan
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: July 29, 2026
reads.body:
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Iran launches missiles toward U.S. base in Jordan: Iran launched ballistic missiles toward a U.S. base in Jordan on Tuesday evening and Wednesday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps confirmed, with U.S. and Jordanian military officials claiming that the missiles were intercepted.

- After an initial announcement by the U.S. that it had shot down a series of missile attacks on Tuesday evening, the Jordanian military said it had intercepted 5 missiles on Wednesday morning.

- In a statement confirming the attacks, the IRGC said that the attacks targeted Muwaffaq Salti Air Base and the headquarters of the U.S. military’s Central Command in Jordan and warned that they would continue as long as U.S. threats and actions against Iranian interests persist.

- In remarks to Fox News, Trump said, “We’re going to beat the fuc*ing sh*t out of them. We’ll be hitting them hard,” adding that Iran was “going to get a beating,” in response to the attack. He said U.S. troops had only minutes to respond before intercepting the missiles. Trump also said that Washington would “let them keep talking” regarding the possibility of future negotiations with Tehran.

- Iranian state television reported Wednesday that U.S. warplanes carried out airstrikes on an area near the Iraqi border in northwestern Iran, saying a location in the border region of Piranshahr came under “hostile U.S. airstrikes.” Earlier, the semi-official Fars news agency quoted the crisis management chief of West Azerbaijan province as saying a “hostile missile” struck an uninhabited area in the same region, causing no casualties.

- U.S.-Saudi Strikes across Iraq kill at least 20 PMF fighters: Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) said joint U.S.-Saudi airstrikes killed at least 20 of its fighters and wounded 32 others in attacks across seven provinces, in one of the biggest escalations in the region in weeks.

- The PMF, an Iraqi state-integrated paramilitary body with factions close to Tehran, said the strikes hit its positions in Baghdad, Wasit, Nineveh, Basra, Kirkuk, Karbala, and Diyala, damaging buildings, vehicles, and equipment.

- U.S. Central Command and Saudi Arabia confirmed the joint operation, saying it targeted “Iran-backed” militants in retaliation for attacks on U.S. troops and Saudi oil facilities, with CENTCOM saying it hit “logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq.” Trump claimed the overnight strikes were carried out in coordination with the Iraqi government.

- Earlier on Tuesday, Saudi Arabia said its air defenses had  intercepted and destroyed additional drones targeting petroleum facilities in the Eastern Province and Riyadh, following separate attacks reported Monday and Tuesday. Riyadh blamed Iran-aligned militias operating from Iraqi territory.

- Iraq’s National Security Council, chaired by Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi, condemned the U.S.-Saudi strikes, calling the attack “an unacceptable aggression,” the Iraqi News Agency reported. The council said the strikes came while Baghdad was communicating with U.S. and Saudi officials to address concerns over attacks on Saudi territory. It announced a comprehensive security plan to “confront any violation of Iraq’s sovereignty” and stressed that responding to such attacks is “the exclusive responsibility of the Iraqi government and its constitutional institutions.”

- Iraqi militias deny responsibility for Saudi attacks: The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella of “resistance axis”-aligned factions, denied involvement in the drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities that Riyadh has blamed on Iraq on Tuesday, calling the accusations “fabrications.”

- The group said the claims were meant to mask Saudi Arabia’s “inability to respond to the painful Yemeni strikes,” and warned that any “foolish action” by the kingdom would meet a “harsh response.”

- Yemen’s Ansarallah has separately claimed the attacks on Saudi, with spokesman Yahya Saree saying they targeted crude facilities in the kingdom’s east.

- Netanyahu visits Trump: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday for a closed-door meeting, which lasted roughly an hour and a half and was described by White House officials as “positive and productive.” At the meeting’s conclusion, Netanyahu said he had finished “one of the best conversations I’ve ever had with a president of the United States, our friend Donald Trump.”

- After their meeting, Netanyahu was interviewed by Fox News’ Sean Hannity, and said about the U.S.-Israel war on Iran that he was “skeptical” of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and that Israel would respond “with terrific force” if attacked by Iran.

- He said he and Trump “see…eye to eye” on this, and were both committed to preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.

- Trump struck a different tone when he was interviewed by Fox News on Tuesday, telling Fox & Friends that he was frustrated that his plans to discuss intelligence regarding an alleged nuclear facility at Iran’s “Pickaxe Mountain” with Netanyahu were leaked. “I don’t need [Netanyahu] to tell me that,” he said, expressing a similar frustration that Netanyahu insisted that the U.S. “stay involved” in the war.

- Iranian deputy FM on Hormuz, U.S. blockade, and Iran’s nuclear program: Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, outlined Tehran’s strategic position during an appearance on Iranian state television on Tuesday.

- Iran insists, Gharibabadi says, on control of the Strait of Hormuz, which it says will “never return” to the prewar status quo. “If the Strait of Hormuz returns to its previous arrangements, our success in the war will not be complete.”

- Iran will keep the Strait closed unless Oman agrees to a new arrangement handing Tehran control over the waterway’s shipping lanes, Gharibabadi said. Gharibabadi also noted that Iran is prepared to keep the Strait closed, even if it means war resumes, and that it would never recognize the southern shipping lane that the U.S. and Oman have proposed and attempted to establish.

- He warned the U.S. against its present strategy of imposing a naval blockade on the country, saying that it would not force any concessions on Iran’s part, and said that any European warship approaching the Strait would be considered a legitimate military target by Iran.

- On the nuclear issue, Gharibabadi said Iran is effectively operating as if it were no longer a member of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), adding that it rejects inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency and other international agencies as long as the war continues. “The other side should not think Iran will remain in the NPT forever. All options are on the table,” he said.

- Traffic still impacted through Hormuz, though no new attacks reported: The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said on Tuesday that the regional maritime threat level in the Gulf remained “Severe,” but reported no newly confirmed attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz during the past 48 hours.

- Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains well below normal, with most transits continuing through the northern Iranian-controlled corridor.

- JMIC said IRGC harassment of merchant vessels, including hailing, drone overflights, and surveillance, persists, while many ships continue sailing with AIS switched off after earlier attacks.

- The maritime tracking firm Kpler counted only seven total transits through Hormuz yesterday (another firm, Windward, counted five).

- Iran’s IRGC Navy said on Tuesday that it targeted and stopped three oil tankers that continued along what it called an unsafe and illegal route despite repeated warnings.

- Iran demands restitution over Ukrainian strike on ship Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tuesday he had been assured by his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, that a Ukrainian attack on an Iranian commercial ship was “unintentional” and that Kyiv was not seeking escalation.

- Araghchi called any attack on Iranian citizens or interests “unacceptable” and demanded “restitution for losses.”

- The Ukrainian strike on Saturday killed one Iranian sailor and wounded another, according to Iran’s Foreign Ministry.

## Yemen

- Ansarallah reports successful downing of Saudi reconnaissance drone: Yemen’s Armed Forces, the military wing of the Ansarallah movement, said on Wednesday that it shot down a Saudi Karayel reconnaissance drone while it was carrying out “hostile operations” over the Saada governorate in northern Yemen, near the Saudi border.

- The Karayel-SU is a Turkish-designed military drone used for surveillance, intelligence gathering and target identification, though it can also carry guided weapons.

- Spokesperson Yahya Saree said the drone was downed and asserted that Yemeni forces would continue “defending the country’s sovereignty” by responding to any further attacks.

- China holds direct talks with Ansarallah for Bab Al-Mandab access: China held direct talks with Yemen’s Ansarallah movement to secure safe passage for Chinese tankers through the Bab Al-Mandab Strait after the group announced it would target vessels calling on Saudi ports, Reuters reported on Tuesday.

- Chinese officials are reportedly clearing tankers individually with Ansarallah, while informing Iran of each transit.

- At least four China-bound tankers have made the passage since the blockade was announced.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, two Palestinians were killed—one in a new attack and one due to wounds sustained in earlier attacks—and 29 were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,335 killed, with 174,052 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,209 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 3,943, while 803 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israeli attacks on Gaza kill one, wound 29: Israeli attacks across the Gaza Strip on Tuesday killed at least one Palestinian and wounded 29 others, according to the Palestinian news agency WAFA.

- An Israeli attack on the Al-Balata Market in the Nuseirat refugee camp killed a Palestinian man and wounded 20 others.

- An Israeli drone struck the roof of a residential building in Gaza City’s Rimal neighborhood, wounding three.

- Israeli forces shot and wounded two more Palestinians east of Deir al-Balah.

- Four Palestinians were wounded by Israeli fire in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis.

- Additionally, Israeli forces destroyed the Dar Al-Muttaqin Mosque in the Yarmouk area of central Gaza City, leveling tents sheltering displaced people beside it, and issued several forced displacement orders in Deir al-Balah and Gaza City preceding Tuesday’s wave of strikes.

- Israeli settlers, forces continue to ravage the occupied West Bank:

- Israeli forces demolished a house in the town of Naalin, west of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to Arab48.  The house, which was constructed during the late Ottoman era, was more than 120 years old.

- Israeli forces demolished at least 13 Palestinian homes across the West Bank this week alone, according to the IMEMC news agency.

- Israeli authorities confiscated more than 22 dunums—an area roughly equal to the size of four football fields—of Palestinian land near Jenin in the northern occupied West Bank, the Palestinian Information Center reported on Tuesday.

- Israeli settlers destroyed a vehicle belonging to a Palestinian man in Beit Ula on Tuesday, kidnapping him and another passenger, WAFA reported.

- In a separate incident on Tuesday evening in the Bethlehem district, Israeli settlers set fire to a Palestinian man’s vehicle after attacking his home.

- Israeli undercover forces disguised in civilian clothing shot and wounded a 55-year-old Palestinian man in the abdomen and foot during a raid on the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, on Wednesday, according to WAFA. The forces also surrounded a home in the area and arrested a Palestinian man.

- Israeli settlers cut down 20 citrus trees on a Palestinian farm in Wada Qana on Wednesday morning, WAFA reported.

- In the Tubas area, Israeli forces began to destroy an artesian well used by Palestinian families in the area, WAFA reported. The well had previously been rendered inoperable by Israeli attacks, endangering the agricultural endeavors of the area, which are suffering under Israel’s “Crimson Thread,” a project to build a military road and separation wall in the area.

- UNHCR: Attacks by Israeli settlers “hitting an all-time high”: The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights said attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers and the expansion of settlements and outposts are “hitting an all-time high” in the occupied West Bank. “We are alarmed by the Israeli government’s announcement to further increase the number of settlements and outposts, and open calls by Israeli leaders for revenge and collective punishment against Palestinian communities, accompanied by threats to turn the West Bank into another Gaza,” Ravina Shamdasani, UNHCR spokesperson said in a statement on Wednesday.

- Palestinian man accused of carrying out “shooting attack” was shot while unarmed, video shows: Sheikh Farouk Ramadan, a Palestinian whom Israel labeled a “terrorist” after he defended himself during a confrontation with armed settlers in the occupied West Bank village of Tal on Friday, was shot dead while unarmed, an analysis of four videos by +972 Magazine and Local Call found.

- The report confirms that Ramadan did wrestle away a settler’s rifle and that he fired it during their interaction.

- Videos then show him walking slowly towards soldiers, unarmed and with nothing in his hands, before dropping to the ground. He was shot dead in this position, possibly by a settler, minutes after the gun had left his hands.

## Lebanon

- Israeli ceasefire violations continue in southern Lebanon:

- Israeli forces set fire to homes in the village of Qantara in Marjayoun district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.

- Israeli soldiers also shelled the Ali Al-Taher hill on the outskirts of Nabatieh Al-Fawqa.

- In Tyre (Sour) district, Israeli forces detonated and demolished the remaining homes in villages across the western sector before dawn, particularly in the Al-Masha area of Mansouri.

- Israel accuses Hezbollah of ceasefire breach: Israel accused Hezbollah of committing a “blatant violation” of the Lebanon ceasefire, alleging the group launched an explosive drone at an Israeli military engineering vehicle in the Ali Al-Taher area of occupied southern Lebanon overnight, The Times of Israel reported. The Israeli military said no injuries were reported and that its troops would continue operating in the area. Israel is currently deliberating a response to the incident, according to security officials.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## U.S. News

- Senate advances bipartisan Russia sanctions bill: The Senate voted 86-12 Tuesday to advance a bipartisan measure imposing sweeping sanctions on Russia and Iran, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died earlier this month while working to secure the bill’s passage.

- The bill imposes harsh new penalties on countries that purchase oil and other energy products from Russia and expands existing sanctions against Iran.

- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy watched from the gallery after meeting with senators.

- 11 Democrats and one Republican voted against the bill.

- ICE document confirms forced feeding of hunger striker in detention: An ICE Health Service Corps document reviewed by The Guardian confirms the Trump administration forcibly treated at least one immigrant detention hunger striker between October and December of last year, using methods that could include force-feeding, hydration, or involuntary catheterization or blood draws.

- The disclosure, produced in response to Senate appropriations committee reporting requirements, comes as hundreds of detainees have staged hunger strikes at facilities including Delaney Hall in New Jersey and Adelanto in California.

- Forced feeding has been condemned by international human rights groups and medical associations as a form of torture.

- Senate confirms Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence: The Senate confirmed Jay Clayton, the U.S. attorney in Manhattan, to lead the Office of the Director of National Intelligence in a 51-47 party-line vote on Tuesday.

- Democratic support eroded after Clayton gave evasive answers during his confirmation hearing about whether President Joe Biden won the 2020 election.

- Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) said he hoped Clayton would prove more stable than acting director Bill Pulte, who claimed Tuesday to have executed a “5th and Near Final Round of TERMINATIONS” totaling a 30% staff reduction during his brief tenure.

- Fauci invokes the Fifth Amendment: Anthony Fauci, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination in response to questions from the Senate Homeland Security Committee Tuesday about his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic.

- Fauci, who was pardoned by President Joe Biden, accused Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) of having an “unhinged obsession with me.” Paul released 11,000 pages of Fauci’s unredacted personal diary over the weekend, in which his observations often directly contradicted his public messaging about the virus.

- Beshear calls out McConnell for concealing health status: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear publicly demanded that Sen. Mitch McConnell prove he remains capable of serving or resign, after 43 days without voting or directly addressing constituents following his hospitalization.

- After writing a letter to McConnell on Monday, Beshear called upon Sen. John Thune to “fully investigate” McConnell’s health condition and his ability to serve Kentuckians.

- August 3 may be the cutoff date after which Beshear cannot call a special election, Beshear noted during a Tuesday appearance on Bloomberg.

## Other International News

- Cholera outbreak in Sudan: Cholera has killed at least 170 people and infected more than 2,000 in Sudan since May, with the Kordofan region hit hardest, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

- Relief agencies are racing to respond despite severe obstacles set by the country’s ongoing civil war, setting up nearly 80 monitoring sites, 16 treatment centers, and eight rehydration facilities, and reaching more than 270,000 people with prevention efforts.

- OCHA warned the response is crippled by a funding shortfall, with Sudan’s 2026 humanitarian appeal raising just $1.1 billion of the $2.9 billion needed.

- Ukrainian drones strike refineries and logistics sites across Russia: Ukraine launched overnight attacks using long-range drones on oil refineries in Perm and Ryazan, a Ryazan logistics center, an export terminal and military plant in Rostov, and a Russian naval base in occupied Crimea, President Zelenskyy said in a statement announcing the strikes.

- A warehouse for the company Wildberries in Ryazan was evacuated after catching fire. The online retailer, known as the Russian equivalent to Amazon, said that a recent campaign of Ukrainian strikes targeting its facilities have damaged at least seven warehouses in recent days, eliminating roughly 10 percent of its storage capacity. Ukraine claims that the company provides components for Russian attack drones.

- Russia, meanwhile, struck Kherson, killing one person, and said its drones hit two vessels carrying weapons and military equipment near Odessa.

- Russia charges Telegram founder with aiding terrorism: Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) charged Telegram founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorist activity and placed him on an international wanted list, alleging that Ukrainian intelligence used a dating chatbot on the platform to recruit young Russians for attacks on security personnel and infrastructure.

- The FSB said 46 Russians ages 12 to 22 had been arrested over the past year after being recruited through the chatbot.

- Telegram is popular in Russia and used by Russian defense and government agencies for public communications, though Moscow has begun throttling access to the platform in response to concerns over its use for foreign espionage.

- UN report: Boeing 727s linked to U.S. contractor supplied RSF in Sudan: A draft UN report found that Boeing 727s linked to a business network involving former U.S. Army Special Forces contractor Steven Shaulis transported mercenaries, weapons and drones for Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces via an N’Djamena-Nyala air corridor, according to Reuters.

- The report also detailed the scale of support from an estimated 1,500-2,000 Colombian mercenaries known as the Desert Wolves, hired by UAE-based firm Global Security Services Group, who fought alongside the RSF during its siege of El-Fasher, violence the UN has said amounted to genocide.

- Five Kenyan security officers killed in clash with al-Shabaab: Five Kenyan security officers were killed Tuesday when a patrol team clashed with suspected al-Shabaab militants near Wantey Dam in Mandera county, close to the Somali border, according to Reuters.

- Police said they are pursuing the militants after a reinforcement team’s armored vehicle was destroyed by an improvised explosive device, though no casualties were reported from this attack.

- Thousands protest against third presidential term in Congo: Thousands rallied Tuesday in the M23-controlled cities of Goma and Bukavu against proposed constitutional changes that could allow President Félix Tshisekedi to seek a third term, Reuters reported, following Congo’s parliament approving a bill in June to submit such changes to a referendum.

- Demonstrators also called for the UN to lift sanctions imposed this month on AFC/M23 leader Corneille Nangaa, as government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya accused the rebels of forcing residents to join the protests, which proceeded despite an Ebola-related gathering ban.

- Turkey, Iraq discuss energy deal that could bring 1 million barrels of oil daily: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Tuesday that Turkey could receive up to 1 million barrels of oil a day under an energy cooperation plan discussed with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Ankara, the AP reported, with Turkey’s state petroleum company also acquiring a 15% stake in BP Energy Company of Kirkuk.

reads.title: Ansarallah strikes Saudi oil facility; Katz orders Israeli takeover of West Bank refugee camp; Chad pulls out of ICC
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: July 28, 2026
reads.body:
- A Palestinian boy sits on a concrete barrier near armed Israeli soldiers in the Old City of Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, on July 25, 2026. Photo by Mosab Shawer / Middle East Images / AFP via Getty Images.This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Attacks reported in Iraqi Kurdistan: Iranian forces reportedly launched a wave of drones toward Iraq’s Kurdistan Region on Monday night, with repeated explosions and interceptions reported over Erbil.

- Kurdish journalist Scharo Bajalan reported at least two impacts: one in the Alana Valley near Soran, where a Komala opposition camp is located, and another north of Erbil. He said drones were launched from both Iran and areas controlled by Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces.

- Footage circulating online appeared to show U.S. forces intercepting at least one drone over Erbil. The extent of any casualties or damage remains unclear.

- Explosions reported in Saudi Arabia; drone attacks on Jordan: Explosions were heard in eastern Saudi Arabia and drones attacked Jordan overnight, an Iranian state-linked outlet reported on Tuesday.

- At least 6 “powerful explosions” struck the eastern region of Saudi Arabia near oil and gas facilities, Nour News, an outlet affiliated with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, reported early Tuesday. The Saudi government has not confirmed the attack

- In a separate report, the outlet said local sources had described “extensive” drone attacks in the eastern desert of Jordan.

- Jordan’s military said it shot down a drone that entered its airspace over the eastern desert near the borders with Iraq and Saudi Arabia early Tuesday, without identifying its origin.

- Separately, the Israeli military said it intercepted a drone near the Jordanian border that did not enter Israeli airspace and that it was investigating where it was launched from.

- Hormuz talks continue as Oman reportedly puts forward joint management proposal: Iran, Oman, and Gulf states stepped up diplomatic efforts over the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.

- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held separate phone calls with Oman’s Badr Albusaidi and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud. According to IRNA, the ministers reviewed regional developments and stressed strengthening diplomatic cooperation to restore stability and address “insecurity” in the Strait.

- Oman presented Iran with a proposal for a joint regional mechanism to manage the Strait of Hormuz with voluntary user fees, Reuters reported. Under the proposal, which reportedly has regional backing, Iran would no longer exercise sole control over the waterway.

- Foreign ministers from Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries also held a virtual meeting on the ongoing U.S.-Iran negotiations on Tuesday. Oman’s Foreign Ministry said they stressed the need for closer coordination on freedom and safety of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz while prioritising political and diplomatic solutions to strengthen regional security and stability.

- Iranian FM spokesperson discusses U.S. “quagmire”: Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei spoke to reporters on Monday about the U.S.’ current position, saying that he did not believe they were “managing” the conflict well. “This war was supposed to force Iran to surrender,” he said “but five months later they remain trapped in a quagmire.”

- Baghaei reaffirmed that Iran would “not allow the United States to decide when war and peace begin and end.”

- The spokesperson also criticized Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who announced actions this weekend against Russian ships he claimed were being used to transport supplies to Iran. Baghaei compared Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s conduct to anarchists who carried out dramatic and dangerous acts before World War I, calling his actions “theatrical” and saying that they “exaggerated” his “limited weight in international affairs.” “Zelenskyy’s patrons must rein him in,” he said.

- Trump says that talks with Iran are “ongoing”: President Donald Trump told reporters on Air Force One on Monday that the U.S. was in “very deep talks” with Iran, and that there was a “good chance” of reaching an agreement, but that military action could resume if no deal is reached, saying that the U.S. would “go back to what we were doing two days ago.”

- Neither Tehran nor Washington acknowledged any direct meetings, but indirect talks primarily involving Iran and Oman, and secondarily involving Qatar, Pakistan, Egypt, and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, reportedly remain ongoing, according to Axios. The current negotiations are focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting talks on a comprehensive nuclear agreement, according to the outlet.

- Trump also said that the U.S. had “taken in billions and billions of dollars from Venezuela,” and threatened that he would do the same with Iran. The comments follow reporting from the Financial Times last week that of the $13 billion in oil revenue seized by the U.S., $7 billion remains unaccounted for. When asked about this by reporters on Monday, he said the money he was being used to “run the country.”

- Shipping remains severely constrained in Hormuz and Babl-Mandab: Windward recorded seven Strait of Hormuz crossings on July 27, two of these inbound and five of them outbound, all using the northern Iran-run corridor.

- 14 vessels entered the Red Sea through the Bab Al-Mandab and 21 exited on July 26, Windward reported. Inbound traffic into the strait  has collapsed by nearly 70%, and outbound traffic has fallen about 28%.

- Two more executed in Iran: Iran executed two men convicted on charges of killing police officers and damaging public properties during the mass protests in January, according to the state affiliated agency Mizan. The two men were identified as Abolfazl Sepahi Badjani and Amir Hossein Safari Hosseinabadi. Iran hanged two other men convicted in the same case earlier in July. Iran has executed dozens of people so far in 2026.

## Yemen

- Ansarallah claims strike on major Saudi oil facility in Abqaiq: Ansarallah claimed responsibility on Monday for a drone strike on Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq crude-processing facility, the kingdom’s largest.

- Abqaiq stabilizes the bulk of Saudi crude before export, making it one of the most critical nodes in the kingdom’s oil infrastructure. It was also the target of the September 2019 drone and missile attack that briefly cut roughly 5% of global oil supply, causing a major shock in oil prices.

- Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry confirmed the attack, but attributed it to Iran-backed militias operating in Iraq.

- Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, Iraq’s prime minister, directed security agencies to investigate Saudi Arabia’s claim, according to the Iraqi News Agency. The Iraqi government said it would be examining the evidence and would pursue legal action against anyone found to have been involved

- Saudi Aramco shuts down Jazan refinery after Ansarallah attack: Saudi Aramco shut down its 400,000-barrel-per-day Jazan refinery following an Ansarallah attack, Reuters reported, citing consultancy IR. The attack reportedly damaged the refinery’s integrated gasification combined-cycle (IGCC) complex and oil tank area, with repairs expected to allow an initial restart by August 15.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, four Palestinians were killed—three in new attacks and one due to wounds sustained in earlier attacks—and 14 were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,333 killed, with 174,023 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,207 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 3,914, while 803 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel attacks Gaza on Monday and Tuesday:

- Israeli forces killed three Palestinians and wounded several others on Monday, shelling the northern and central parts of the Strip, according to Felesteen Online.

- An Israeli drone attack on Monday also wounded three fishermen near the Gaza port gate.

- An Israeli military vehicle fired on Deir-al-Balah on Tuesday, wounding two Palestinians, according to WAFA.

- At least eight Palestinians killed since Thursday as Israeli raids and settler attacks escalate across the occupied West Bank: Israeli forces and armed settlers continue to intensify their attacks across the occupied West Bank following Friday’s settler attack in Tal. At least eight Palestinians, including a child, have been killed since Thursday, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reported. On Tuesday, raids, assaults, land seizures, and settler violence were reported across multiple governorates, according to WAFA, with at least 22 Palestinians detained by Israeli forces, according to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Affairs office.

- Bethlehem: A Palestinian was injured after Israeli settlers beat him with an iron pipe near Al-Minya village. Israeli forces separately raided Tuqu’ and Husan.

- Ramallah: Israeli forces raided Shuqba, west of Ramallah, on Tuesday morning and demolished a residential building, leaving the families who lived there homeless.

- Hebron: Israeli settlers assaulted Palestinians in the Khallet Al-Hamam area of Yatta, beating residents and firing tear gas. Israeli forces arrested a Palestinian father and his two sons after the attack. Forces also demolished two residential buildings.

- A Palestinian man in Masafer Yatta seized a weapon from a violent Israeli settler on Tuesday, becoming the third to attempt to do so in the last four days.

- Salfit: Israeli settlers established a new settlement outpost on Palestinian land in Yasuf, erecting a tent roughly 50 metres from residents’ homes. Read Zena Tahhan’s on-the-ground report from the occupied West Bank, which covers the attacks, the military raids, and the rapid expansion of illegal settler outposts here.

- Nablus: Israeli settlers uprooted thousands of trees near Madama, southwest of Nablus, the village council’s head reported.

- Occupied East Jerusalem: Israeli forces raided the UNRWA Qalandia Vocational Training Centre for the second time in less than a month on Monday, detaining dozens of students and staff inside the facility. Israeli forces also arrested the son of Jerusalem Governor, after raiding Silwan, south of Al-Aqsa Mosque, on Monday evening, the Palestinian Information Center reported.

- On Monday, Israeli forces demolished four homes, 18 shops, two inhabited apartments and a livestock facility in Jenin, Ni’lin and occupied East Jerusalem.

- Katz orders army takeover ​​of another West Bank refugee camp: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz issued instructions to expand the scope of the military assault on the occupied West Bank and to prepare to occupy another Palestinian refugee camp under the model of the army invasions of the Jenin, Tulkarem, and Nur Shams camps in early 2025. According to Israeli news outlets, Katz issued the order following a security assessment on Monday attended by military commanders and senior security and intelligence officials. Last year, Human Rights Watch found that Israel’s forced displacement of over 30,000 residents of the three refugee camps in the northern West Bank amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity.

- Sixty Palestinian prisoners released to Gaza, many showing signs of abuse: Israel released 60 battered Gaza prisoners on Monday after they had spent months in detention, with many showing signs of abuse. Red Cross teams transferred them through the Karam Abu Salem crossing to Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital for urgent medical examinations.

- The group included 40 Palestinians held under harsh conditions in the Negev desert prison and 20 Gaza workers arrested inside Israel after October 7.

- Rescue teams salvage additional bodies from Gaza wreckage: Rescue teams recovered the remains of 99 Palestinians from beneath a destroyed home belonging to the Abu Sharia and Al-Hasayna families in Gaza City’s Sabra neighborhood on Monday.

- The building had been struck in multiple Israeli airstrikes, including in October 2023 and June 2025.

- Crews said recovery operations are severely constrained by the destruction and Israel’s total ban on heavy machinery, with around 8,000 Palestinians still believed to be buried beneath rubble across Gaza.

- Israeli soldiers remove U.S. citizens from home in West Bank assault: Israeli soldiers forced two U.S. citizens from their home in Turmus Ayya, in the occupied West Bank, so troops could use it as a lookout position, their son, Dr. Said Shukri, told Drop Site News.

- The home belongs to Dr. Hassan Said Shukri, a neurologist based in Syracuse, New York.

- Shukri said soldiers carrying M16s pointed a gun at his 61-year-old mother and gave his parents one hour to pack. He contacted the U.S. Embassy, which said it could do nothing and refused to contact the Israeli military.

- His parents have since returned after the soldiers abruptly left. “It is only because of the public pressure that they were able to return to their home,” Shukri said. He said soldiers had occupied the neighboring family’s home for four days before moving directly into his parents’ house.

- Gaza groundwater too polluted to drink: Gaza’s groundwater is becoming too salty and contaminated to drink, the Gaza Ministry of Health said on Monday.

- Groundwater now contains an average of 3,588 mg of dissolved salts per liter, more than three times the level generally considered acceptable.

- 19% of municipal wells are bacterially contaminated and 40% are not effectively chlorinated, Gaza Health Ministry Director General said, noting that nearly half of reported diseases are now linked to unsafe water and environmental conditions.

- Hamas delegation heads to Cairo: A Hamas negotiating delegation traveled to Cairo on Tuesday to continue second-phase negotiations on the Gaza ceasefire agreement, senior Hamas official Basem Naim announced in a social media post.

- Naim said talks with mediators would focus on consolidating the ceasefire and implementing first-phase commitments, particularly Israel’s humanitarian obligations, before moving to phase two of President Donald Trump’s plan.

## Lebanon

- Israel continues military operations in Lebanon despite “ceasefire”:

- An Israeli drone strike Tuesday hit a residential apartment in Nabatieh Al-Fawqa, in Nabatieh, setting it ablaze, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.

- Israeli forces also carried out a large demolition in the village of Al-Qusayr in the Marjayoun district.

- In Tyre, explosions continued to echo into the morning as Israeli forces carried out demolitions in the villages of Majdal Zoun, Al-Mansouri, and areas of Bint Jbeil.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## U.S. News

- Deported couple found bound, shot dead in Guatemala: Nixon Giovanni Pérez Paz and Glendy Marisol González de la Cruz were found bound, gagged and shot to death in a sugarcane field in southern Guatemala weeks after González de la Cruz self-deported to join her husband, who ICE had deported from Missouri last year, according to St. Louis Public Radio.

- Their 14-month-old daughter was found crying beside her mother’s body and is recovering from dehydration, according to the Guatemalan news outlet ABC Stereo.

- “I felt that they took the thing I wanted most,” Paz’s brother said. “I felt a huge pain because it was my brother, my sister-in-law—people that wanted to work, to fight.”

- McConnell says he won’t return to Senate this week: Sen. Mitch McConnell, 84, who was hospitalized for six weeks following a fall at his Capitol Hill home last month, said Monday he won’t return to the Senate this week or attend Kentucky’s annual Fancy Farm picnic, an event he’s attended for more than four decades. McConnell’s extended absence has complicated Republicans’ narrow Senate margin, particularly on the Appropriations Committee.

- Venezuelan men sue U.S. aviation firms that flew them to notorious Salvadoran prison: More than 230 Venezuelan men expelled by the Trump administration to El Salvador last year are suing CSI Aviation and GlobalX, accusing the companies of helping carry out illegal “rendition flights” to the Cecot maximum-security prison, José Olivares reports for The Guardian.

- The lawsuit says the firms transported the men despite a federal judge ordering the planes to return and despite knowing they faced a foreseeable risk of torture. The men were held for four months and reported beatings, sexual assault, pepper spray and rubber-bullet attacks.

- CSI, ICE’s largest contractor, received $1.23 billion from the agency in 2025 and subcontracted the three flights to GlobalX.

- Mamdani announces plan to use city grocery stores to relieve rising prices: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled plans on Monday to sell essential groceries at prices 30% below typical retail rates through five city-owned stores, one in each borough.

- The discount will cover all fresh produce, meat, and seafood, along with 20 pantry, dairy, and refrigerated staples, including milk, cheese, and bread. Prices will be set at the beginning of each month and remain fixed throughout it, with no income restrictions for shoppers.

- The city has allocated $70 million to develop the stores and will cover rent and property taxes, while private contractors operate them. The first is expected to open in Hunts Point in the Bronx by late 2027, followed by La Marqueta in East Harlem by 2029. All five are planned to open before Mamdani’s term ends.

- The administration estimates the program could save an average household about $1,000 annually. The stores will not sell alcohol, cigarettes, lottery tickets, or hot food, partly to limit competition with neighborhood bodegas.

- ICE arrests over 12,000 after tips from child migrant agency, Reuters finds: More than 12,000 people, including unaccompanied migrant children’s sponsors and household members, have been arrested by ICE following tips from the Office of Refugee Resettlement since January 2025, according to internal government data reviewed by Reuters, which found ORR shared more than 460,000 “leads” with ICE during that period.

- Former ORR deputy director Jen Smyers said safeguards against such data sharing have been “completely reversed,” and accused the administration of “weaponizing a child welfare program for the purposes of more deportations.”

- Six House members bought SpaceX stock days after IPO: At least six House members or their immediate families purchased between roughly $83,000 and $245,000 in SpaceX shares within six days of the company’s June 12 IPO, CNBC found, with five of the buyers serving on committees overseeing aspects of the company’s business, including defense and AI.

- The trades, which include purchases by Reps. William Timmons (R-S.C.), Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) and Gil Cisneros (D-Calif.) themselves and by spouses or children of Reps. John McGuire (R-Va.), Dan Meuser (R-Pa.), and John James (R-Mich.), come as the House passed legislation Wednesday restricting future individual stock trading by lawmakers, though critics have pointed out the measure’s weaknesses, including its non-extension to current holdings.

- ACLU: LA immigration agents used racial slurs, targeted Latinos in raids: Body camera footage and text messages obtained through court discovery show ICE and Border Patrol agents in Los Angeles using slurs like “tonk” and “wet” to refer to Latinos, according to a 42-page motion filed Monday by the ACLU.

- The filing argues evidence “flatly disproves” government claims that stops were based on intelligence rather than race, describing a shift toward mass “collateral” arrests through “roving patrols” at locations like Home Depots and car washes, and asks a federal judge to bar agents from relying on perceived Latino ethnicity to conduct stops.

- Valdez endorses Lawrence: Claire Valdez, who recently won a Democratic primary in New York’s 7th district, endorsed progressive William Lawrence in his Michigan primary on Monday.

- Moskowitz refuses to debate Larkin: Rep. Jared Moskowitz has pulled out of Monday night’s debate with progressive challenger Oliver Larkin, hosted jointly by the Broward and Miami-Dade Democratic Black Caucuses.

- Larkin said he would still attend to address voters directly, declaring that he will be “debating an empty lectern.”

- His campaign accused Moskowitz of avoiding scrutiny of his voting record and noted that the incumbent has not held a town hall in Florida’s newly redrawn 25th Congressional District.

- Michigan Senate debate: Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens went head-to-head in a debate on Monday night, with both candidates vying for the Democratic nomination for the open Senate seat in Michigan. The primary is next Tuesday, August 4.

- El-Sayed pointed out the $60 million in outside spending backing Stevens’ campaign, saying she has been “bought off” by corporations that “expect to own your next U.S. senator.”

- Abdul El-Sayed also blasted the record $46 million in AIPAC money backing Haley Stevens, saying it was spent because “they know she’ll be a reliable vote,” pointing to her vote last week for another $3.3 billion in aid to Israel.

- More highlights from the debate are available on our X feed, here.

## Other International News

- Fresh clashes erupt in Pakistan-administered Kashmir: Clashes broke out Monday in Rawalakot, Pakistan-administered Kashmir, as thousands of supporters of the Joint Awami Action Committee tried to march toward regional capital Muzaffarabad, part of weeks of protests demanding electoral reform ahead of a three-phase regional election that began the same day.

- The protests have called for the reallocation of parliamentary seats reserved for Kashmiris living elsewhere in Pakistan to those actually living in Azad Kashmir.

- The J.A.A.C. claimed several of their supporters died in clashes with police, though the deaths could not be confirmed as of Tuesday, bringing the reported death toll since protests began in early June to at least 30.

- Dozens killed in air strikes on North Kordofan civilian sites: Dozens of civilians were killed across a series of air strikes in Sudan’s North Kordofan state between July 24 and 26, according to the rights group Emergency Lawyers, which reported drone attacks on a water station, a civilian vehicle, and a water well, health center and school, along with a bombing of a fuel-carrying vehicle in Um Badr. The strikes coincided with an escalation in clashes following an army ground offensive that cleared Rapid Support Forces from key routes.

- At least 30 killed in armed attack on Nigerian village: Gunmen killed at least 30 people, including eight children, in a nighttime raid on Naridon village in Nigeria’s Kaduna state early Monday, residents told Reuters.

- A local leader said attackers opened fire on women, children and the elderly before setting houses ablaze and fleeing, with security personnel arriving only hours later.

- No group has claimed responsibility for the attack.

- Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru’s president: Keiko Fujimori is set to be inaugurated as Peru’s president on Tuesday, becoming the country’s 10th leader since 2016 after narrowly defeating leftist congressman Roberto Sanchez in June runoff election

- Fujimori, who has expressed interest in joining Trump’s proposed “Shield of the Americas” regional security initiative, named former central bank board member Elmer Cuba as her economy minister on Tuesday, and Carlos Espa, a former U.S. embassy employee and presidential candidate, as her foreign minister.

- Fujimori inherits a fragmented, newly bicameral Congress where her Popular Force party holds the largest minority bloc.

- Chad pulls out of ICC: Chad pulled out of the ICC on Monday under U.S. pressure, complicating an ongoing probe into the genocide in Darfur.

- Chad’s Foreign Ministry said on Monday it had notified the UN secretary-general of its decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute, the treaty underpinning the International Criminal Court, calling the court’s record “limited and uneven” and focused on Africa.

- Chad said the request came from Washington, and that the U.S. deputy secretary of state for African affairs had urged it to reconsider its membership in a phone call last Thursday.

- The withdrawal could shield actors in the war in neighboring Darfur, where the U.S. and a UN fact-finding mission have both found the RSF committed genocide against non-Arab communities. Chad has been accused of serving as a conduit for arms reaching the RSF from the UAE.

- Chad is the fifth country to move toward withdrawal in recent months, after Venezuela on Friday and the September exit by Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.

- White phosphorus leak triggers brief evacuation near U.S. base in South Korea: South Korean authorities briefly ordered residents living close to Osan Air Base in Pyeongtaek, near Seoul, to evacuate Tuesday following a reported white phosphorus leak detected around 5 p.m., lifting the order hours later after decontamination was completed, the AP reported.

- The U.S. 51st Fighter Wing did not confirm a phosphorus leak but said it established a 1,000-foot safety cordon “due to a ground mishap and out of an abundance of caution,” denying reports of a general base evacuation.

- Afghan provincial official assassinated in Badakhshan: Zabihullah Amiri, director of Badakhshan’s Information and Culture Department, was assassinated Tuesday by two armed attackers near provincial capital Fayzabad, Afghanistan’s Interior Ministry said.

- Amiri’s guards killed one suspected attacker in a shootout while a search for the second continued. The ministry did not attribute blame to any specific group.
