reads.title: Israel Is Paying Millions to Train AI Chatbots How to Talk About Gaza. It's Working.
reads.subtitle: Former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale is overseeing an operation posting hundreds of blog posts on behalf of Israel, with the goal of infiltrating artificial intelligence.
reads.body:
- Brad Parscale, the former campaign manager for U.S. President Donald Trump,  on November 4, 2019 in Lexington, Kentucky. Photo by Bryan Woolston/Getty Images.Since October, former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale has been quietly overseeing an operation posting hundreds of blog posts on behalf of Israel. One article, titled “The Reality Behind Gaza’s ‘Journalists’: Terror Ties, Propaganda, and the Laws of War,” asserts that a majority of journalists in Gaza were linked to terrorist organizations. Another casts doubt on the killing of Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by the Israeli military in 2024.
The key intended audience of these sites is not concerned Americans, it’s not even humans—most of the sites average a few hundred unique visitors each month. Instead, Parscale and his firm, Clock Tower X, created them as part of a $46.5 million contract with the Israeli government to try and influence artificial intelligence-powered chatbots, tools like Claude or ChatGPT.
Parscale has made his goal of influencing artificial intelligence—often referred to as “LLM poisoning”—explicit. In his initial agreement with Israel, Parscale said that he would deploy “websites and content to deliver GPT framing results on GPT conversations” as part of the contract. More recently, his team even told Axios they are “seeing success” at getting popular AI systems to incorporate information from their sites, though they declined to provide data.
And it is working, according to disinformation experts who reviewed a Drop Site analysis of chatbot queries and training data, meaning tens of millions of Americans who use chatbots are increasingly likely to receive answers manipulated by Parscale on behalf of the Israeli government.
Investigations take resources. Subscribe or make a tax-deductible gift today.
When Drop Site asked Perplexity “Is it beneficial for the US to enhance military cooperation with Israel?” the chatbot responded with a one-word answer: “Yes.” The top source listed was Allyvia.org, a Parscale-created website dedicated to promoting the U.S.-Israel military relationship. Microsoft Copilot similarly cited Parscale’s websites.

-
- Screenshot from Perplexity.Allyvia is one of 10 different websites created by Clock Tower X, a boutique digital influence company owned by Parscale. Each website is dedicated to promoting a different Israeli narrative. FactSignal.org, for instance, fashions itself as fact-checking website tackling anti-Israel information, containing articles discrediting slain journalists as Hamas terrorists and rejecting the notion that Israel’s military actions in Gaza constitute a genocide. Paxpoint.org, meanwhile, promotes the narrative that Israel is a nation of peace.
All of Parscale’s websites contain a statement at the bottom which states “this material is distributed by Clock Tower X LLC on behalf of the State of Israel.” This statement is a mandatory disclosure requirement under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA). Despite this, when Drop Site asked prominent chatbots about the latest news from Paxpoint.org, Perplexity and Copilot did not flag that the site was created as part of an Israeli influence operation. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini did flag the caveat.
“Perplexity is built to give people cited, linked answers from a range of sources so they can go directly to the original reporting and reach their own conclusions,” spokesperson Beejoli Shah told Drop Site News when reached for comment.
Parscale’s websites—referred to throughout this article as the “Clock Tower network”—get cited by chatbots, but they also are successfully infiltrating the underlying training data.
The Clock Tower network started to get archived by Common Crawl—a nonprofit that oversees a massive repository of data used to train large language models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude—earlier this year. Common Crawl is the backbone of the artificial industry, training 80% of the tokens of OpenAI’s GPT-3, making it a useful proxy for understanding if malicious actors successfully infiltrate AI training data.
READ MORE from Nick Cleveland-Stout at the Quincy Institute: “The Eighth Front: Inside Israel’s $1 Billion Influence Campaign.”

## LLM Poisoning
In the examples above, users can at least trace the sources that chatbots are pulling from when they search websites directly, such as in the screenshots above. Infiltrating the training data itself, on the other hand, can lead to Israel-influenced responses that are nearly impossible for users to trace.
To measure how deeply the network had penetrated the data used to train AI models, Drop Site used Claude Fable to query Common Crawl to count how often Parscale’s sites appear in its monthly snapshots. According to that analysis, a sample of which was manually fact-checked by Drop Site, between January and June 10 sites were crawled by Common Crawl 912 times. While this is a drop in the bucket of Common Crawl data, emerging research suggests a very low number of documents can successfully manipulate AI chatbots, no matter the data volume.
The 10 sites are:

- Paxpoint.org (crawled 220 times): Website dedicated to showcasing the narrative that Israel is a nation of peace. “Paxpoint highlights Israel’s ongoing commitment to peace and coexistence, sharing historical accords, humanitarian initiatives, and grassroots projects that bridge divides.”

- Allyvia.org (crawled 158 times): Website dedicated to strengthening the U.S.-Israel alliance. “Allyvia showcases how the US and Israel alliance directly benefits Americans through joint security, cutting-edge technologies, job creation, and shared values of liberty.”

- Factsignal.org (crawled 108 times): Mission is to “prove that Hamas’ terrorist designation reflects global consensus and undeniable evidence of violence, not conspiracy”

- Cognitura.org (crawled 106 times): Website claims to be a “research and education platform” dedicated to exploring how extremist groups such as Hamas operate.

- Justorium.org (crawled 93 times): Website dedicated to arguing that Israel’s military actions in Gaza “follows international law and reflects the democratic ethics shared by the US and Israel.”

- Culturavia.org (crawled 76 times): Website focused on celebrating cultural ties between U.S. and Israel.

- Compassionpulse.org (crawled 57 times): Website dedicated to sharing stories, data, and eyewitness accounts of “how Israel protects civilians, delivers humanitarian aid, and upholds moral values shared with the US.”

- Econora.org (crawled 49 times): Website dedicated to highlighting U.S.-Israeli trade relationship.

- Innovascope.org (crawled 45 times): Website dedicated to highlighting U.S.-Israeli technology partnership.

- Feedingyoufiction.com (crawled 1 time): Website featuring videos that claim footage coming out Gaza is staged and denying famine.
These sites are being crawled more and more. In January 2026, the sites were only crawled twice. In May, the sites were crawled 376 times, before a notable dip in June. To check the accuracy of Claude Fable, Drop Site manually searched for a sampling of 50 of the Clock Tower X URLs archived in Common Crawl’s CDXJ index, and did not detect any errors.
Hervé Letoqueux, Chief Executive Officer at Check First, an organization that combats digital disinformation, explained that Common Crawl’s status as the go-to source for training chatbots opens it up as a target for manipulation. “Common Crawl is widely used in the world of data science for training LLMs, which also means that actors want to manipulate the answers in their favor, which some studies have indicated are fairly easy to do.”
It only takes about “250 malicious documents to produce a ‘backdoor’ vulnerability in a large language model—regardless of model size of training data volume,” according to an October Anthropic study. The authors of the study note “this means anyone can create online content that might eventually end up in a model’s training data,” and that malicious actors “can inject specific text into these posts to make a model learn undesirable or dangerous behaviours, in a process known as poisoning.”
The Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab published a similar study earlier this year on Russia’s disinformation network’s attempts to influence LLMs and noted an important caveat. Because artificial intelligence companies have their own process of quality control when they incorporate data, “Inclusion in Common Crawl does not guarantee inclusion in any given model’s training data.”
Drop Site also performed a demo alongside Letoqueux to test five different chatbots—Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude AI, and Perplexity—on whether they could produce articles using only their training data. Of the five, the Parscale network consistently appears in the training data of Gemini and Copilot. Claude and ChatGPT did not appear to contain the websites in the training data, though these chatbots can still search Clock Tower X websites when responding to queries. Perplexity, meanwhile, appeared to be trained on some of the Clock Tower X websites.
Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini did not respond to a request for comment for this article.
‘It is easy to prove that these models were trained on the Clock Tower X websites, though it is difficult to know the degree to which that influences the response a chatbot gives to a query,’ said Letoqueux.

## Optimizing for AI
Parscale’s team has credited their success with a softer approach to selling Israel’s narrative. Scott Stouffer, Chief Technology Officer of Market Brew—a company that specializes in influencing LLMs that Parscale invests in—told Axios that information written in a “factual tone and tightly organized” is more likely to be cited in AI platforms. “What you can do is make sure that your information is structured, sourced, and aligned in a way that those systems are more likely to retrieve it when someone asks a question. It’s less about changing the conversation and more about making sure your facts are eligible to be part of it.”
Many of the blog posts on the Clock Tower network contain at least a few sentences of nuance, which disinformation researchers say make it more palatable for chatbots. For instance, the FactSignal blog post about how journalists in Gaza are supposedly secret terrorists states that, “Distinguishing between legitimate reporters and militant operatives is not always simple, but accurate reporting requires careful investigation and transparency.”
The author of many of the blog posts is Israel-based digital marketer Mark Ginsberg, according to the source code. Ginsberg, who registered as a foreign agent for Israel in March, advertises his expertise in Generative Engine Optimization—or LLM grooming—on his Linkedin profile. In a June article for The Times of Israel, Ginsberg laid out the argument for Israel investing in efforts to influence chatbots. “Israel needs to invest seriously in the defense of truth…It means ensuring that accurate information appears not merely in government archives but in search results, educational resources, encyclopedias, social media feeds, podcasts, documentaries, and AI training datasets,” Ginsberg wrote. Trying to influence AI training data, Ginsberg argued, is not “embracing disinformation” but rather stating “reality itself.”
Letoqueux, who reviewed the Clock Tower network sites, confirmed that because chatbots have a built-in preference for presenting a balanced view, websites that are sourced and present a lighter touch might be more successful. “These websites could probably be quite useful at doing damage control on questions such as ‘Is Israel committing a genocide?’ because they provide the Israeli narrative, which chatbots can then repeat as representative of one side of the debate,” said Letoqueux, who is the former head of operations at VIGINUM, the French agency responsible for identifying foreign digital interference.
Alice Lee, an analyst at NewsGuard, a disinformation tracking company, explained in an interview with Drop Site that the Parscale network sites have all the hallmarks of sites that would be successful at influencing chatbots. “The websites have bullet points, key takeaways at the top of the page, aggressive sourcing, digestible information, all of which increase the likelihood that this content is picked up by AI chatbots.”
While Russia’s Pravda network overall is far larger, Parscale’s sites have a far higher rate of successfully being archived. The Clock Tower network contains 900 different pathways—individual blog posts, fact sheets, etc—and 85% of them have been archived in Common Crawl, compared to Russia’s network at an average rate of around 2.5%.
Lee, who specializes in Russian disinformation, explained that whereas Russia is churning out easily debunkable propaganda at scale, Israel’s more targeted approach appears to be geared more toward conveying the Israeli narrative on half-truths, opinions, and disputed facts, which is more difficult for LLMs to dismiss. “It’s harder to put guardrails around opinion,” she explained.
Parscale appears to have created several other websites related to Qatar that did not end up being published. On the same IP address as the Clock Tower network, Drop Site identified domains for websites including “qataritracker.org” and “qatarfacts.com.” These sites are currently inaccessible.
The Clock Tower network is responsive to Israel’s shifting priorities. When the sites first launched in October, many of them posted frequently about how Israel is a peaceful nation. “While critics portray Israel as resistant to compromise, history shows the opposite: Israel has repeatedly made territorial and strategic concessions in exchange for peace, only to face renewed hostility,” reads one website page published in October, cited by Microsoft Copilot below. That page was archived by Common Crawl twice.

-
- Screenshot of Copilot citing a Clock Tower X site.Part of this effort included shaping the narrative over Israel’s military actions in Gaza. For instance, a page on Justorium.org titled “How Israel Reduces Civilian Harm in War Against Hamas and Hezbollah” claims that Israel went above and beyond international legal requirements to reduce civilian harm. The post says that Israel “used short warning strikes on rooftops, known as roof knocking, to signal imminent danger without causing casualties.” The New York Times has reported that Israel “significantly reduced its use of so-called roof knocks” from the first day of the war, and has often opted for 2,000 pound bombs that cause greater damage rather than more precise munitions.
That post has been archived by Common Crawl once, and is also cited below by Perplexity.
Screenshot of Perplexity citing from a Clock Tower X site.Most recently, as debate in the U.S. erupted over a Congressional measure that could further intertwine the U.S. and Israeli military sectors, the Clock Tower network published a series of posts framing the move as a positive development. The House version of Section 219, as it’s known, passed as part of the annual defense spending bill this week.
When Drop Site asked prominent chatbots a question containing similar language from one of the Parscale sites, “how does technology collaboration between the U.S. and Israel benefit both nations?” Gemini, Copilot, and Perplexity once again cited websites from the Clock Tower network without noting these sources are created on behalf of the Israeli government.

-
- Screenshot of Gemini citing a Clock Tower X site.
-
- Screenshot of Copilot citing two Clock Tower X sites.

## $4.5 Million a Month
Public opinion of Israel has cratered in the U.S. after its U.S.-funded military siege of Gaza has killed over 70,000 Palestinians, including across key demographics such as conservatives and evangelicals that have long supported the U.S.-Israel relationship.
According to a new Quincy Institute report by the author of this article, Israel has spent well-over $100 million on foreign lobbying efforts under FARA in the U.S. since 2023, hiring 17 new firms in 2024 and 2025 alone. Although Israel has historically avoided hiring official contractors under FARA, it is now on track to become the largest single spender in 2026.
Parscale, who gained national attention as Trump’s campaign manager for hiring the controversial microtargetting firm Cambridge Analytica, is the largest recipient of Israel’s massive influence investment. Parscale’s intention to influence chatbots was first reported by Responsible Statecraft in September, when he signed a $1.5 million a month contract with the Israeli government to integrate pro-Israel messaging into conservative media, carry out a mass texting campaign, and influence chatbots. Since then, the contract has tripled in size to $4.5 million a month.
Despite this increased investment, Israel does not appear satisfied with Parscale’s results so far. “We pissed at Brad Parscale,” one Israeli official familiar with the contract told Time. “We have paid him lots of money. But what did he do with it? Things have only gotten worse,” they said.
Stephen Walt, author of the “Israel Lobby,” suggested to the Quincy Institute that Israel is not seeing a return on investment because these kinds of influence operations are counterproductive. “Once a country gets the reputation for spinning constantly, and gets repeatedly caught making things up, then doing ever more of it just sends the message to listeners that more BS is on the way,” Walt said.
Parscale and Clock Tower X did not respond to a request for comment for this article.
The Clock Tower network serves another purpose. Parscale is also leading a mass texting campaign that reaches out to Americans under the auspices of supposed “peace” organizations. “Hi, I’m John with Friends for Peace. Quick question for folks in Illinois about Israel and Iran. Got a second?”
Then, after a back and forth, these chatbots frequently send links to the Clock Tower network, websites like Allyvia.org.

-
- Text messages from “Friends for Peace.”
-
- Text messages from “Friends for Peace.”“Friends for Peace” is not a registered nonprofit or LLC and does not appear to exist as an organization, meaning Americans wanting to know who is behind the text operation would have to click the link and scroll to the bottom of each page to see the disclaimer that it is an operation funded by the Israeli government.
When the Wall Street Journal asked Parscale about if “Friends for Peace” was a real organization, Parscale replied, “What do you define as an actual organization?”

reads.body:
Armed Israeli settlers backed by the military and government have continued to escalate attacks on Palestinians living in the West Bank in recent weeks, attacking villages and towns amid an ongoing push to assert Israeli sovereignty over the territory. At the same time, there are indications that the “wall of fear” among Palestinians in the West Bank has begun to crumble—as individual Palestinians have engaged in increasingly bold efforts to defend their homes and communities against armed attacks.
On this week’s stream, Murtaza Hussain and Maysa Mustafa discuss the situation in the West Bank with Abdaljawad Omar, a professor at Birzeit University in the West Bank.
Later in the show, Murtaza discusses the youth-led, “Cockroach Movement” protests in India against corruption and economic inequality with guests Akshay Marathe, former national spokesperson for India’s Aam Aadmi Party, and journalist Meghnad Bose.

reads.title: Leaked Saudi Cables Reveal the Shadowy Committee That Oversees the Kingdom’s Policy on Yemen
reads.subtitle: In 2012, then-Saudi defense minister Salman bin Abdulaziz instructed the Special Committee of the Council of Ministers to engineer a rift to target Ansarallah.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- Then-Saudi Defense Minister Salman bin Abdul Aziz looks on during the King Faisal International prize awards ceremony held in Riyadh on March 6, 2012. Photo by Fayez Nureldine/AFP via Getty Images.Story by Shuaib Almosawa and Jeb Boone
SANA’A, Yemen—In January 2012, Saudi Arabia’s then-defense minister, Salman bin Abdulaziz, issued a directive advising a shadowy Saudi government committee to widen Yemen’s northern war. In broad terms, the plan entailed engineering a rift between northern Yemen’s Shia majority and Salafi Sunnis when one previously had not existed.
The order came at a time when Yemen’s internal power structures were in disarray following a 2011 popular uprising against the longtime rule of Yemeni president Ali Abdullah Saleh. Saudi Arabia, which shares a 812-mile border with Yemen, had long managed delicate relations with its southern neighbor and now looked with growing concern at the chaos unfolding within the country. By 2012, Yemen’s army had splintered into rival factions both camped inside the capital city, Sana’a. Saleh had stepped down after 33 years of power and his former vice president Abd Rabo Mansur Hadi stood prepared to take the reins through a single candidate election—hardly the legitimate figure the fractured political landscape demanded.
Worst of all for Saudi Arabia, its old rival Ansarallah—which was based in Yemen’s northern highlands with a stronghold in the city of Saada—stood poised to take advantage of the chaos.
Known as the Houthis, Ansarallah grew out of a revival movement among Yemen’s Zaydis, followers of a branch of Shia Islam that ruled the northern highlands for a thousand years until 1962. Zaydism sits closer in doctrine to the four orthodox Sunni legal schools than to the Twelver Shiism of Iran, and in the early 2000s most Zaydis hadn’t yet joined the Houthi cause.
Salman’s plan was essentially twofold: to arm the Yemeni tribes fighting the Houthi movement, most of them ultra-conservative adherents of the Salafi school of Islamic jurisprudence and educated in the kingdom’s own Wahhabi current; and to drive a wedge between Ansarallah and the wider Zaydi community.
A January 2012 cable directed to a secretive special government committee handling Saudi Arabia’s relationship to Yemen stamped “Extremely Secret, Very Urgent” with Salman’s signature at the bottom outlines the plan: “The Special Committee of the Council of Ministers should discuss and study supporting Yemeni tribes hostile to the Houthis if they fail to commit to reconciliation with Ahl al-Sunnah [Salafists] in Saada, enabling multiple fronts against them, fostering discord between Houthis and Zaydi followers, while ensuring the fighting does not appear as a Sunni-Shia sectarian war in Yemen or that the Kingdom is behind it.”
Salman did not want it to appear sectarian because a war between Ansarallah and Saudi Arabia framed as a purely sectarian conflict, Sunni vs. Shia, would drive northern Yemen’s majority Zaydi Shia population toward support for Ansarallah out of a sense of religious duty or alignment with the cause.
The kingdom’s proxy fighting force in northern Yemen at the time, the Salafist Sunni tribes, were just one part of their plan. In order to isolate Ansarallah from Yemen’s wider Zaydi Shia community, fighting needed to look like a local quarrel. If violence appeared to be carried out by Saudi-backed Sunnis against local Shia communities, the Houthis would quickly become the defenders of the sect rather than a local nuisance.
Salman’s plan to “foster discord” between the Houthis and other Zaydis meant drawing a sectarian line in Yemen where none yet ran. Saudi Arabia would fund the fight from one side of that line and keep its name off it.
But this attempt to carefully curate the narrative would ultimately go on to fail when Saudi Arabia launched an air war backed by the U.S. against Ansarallah in 2015 that began decimating Saada soon after Salman was appointed king.
The secret cable is part of a trove of classified Saudi cables obtained by Drop Site News. The cables were issued by the Special Committee of the Saudi Council of Ministers, the agency that has run the kingdom’s Yemen policy since 1962. Riyadh created the committee the year republican officers backed by Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser toppled Yemen’s thousand-year-old Zaydi imamate, and charged it with managing “all matters related to Yemeni affairs.” The committee reports directly to the Saudi Prime Minister’s Office and the Saudi ambassador in Sana’a sits as a member. Its name does not appear in any official media in either country.
For more than half a century the special committee has been the kingdom’s primary instrument in Yemen. It helped organize strategy toward Yemen and kept individual files on Yemen’s tribal sheikhs, religious leaders, military commanders, and politicians in government and opposition alike. It also ran allowances—monthly stipends paid out to keep powerful Yemenis loyal to Riyadh. The secret cables date from 2010 to 2012. They record payments and informant reports, the wars the committee funded, and the terms it set for the men on its books.
Single pages from the set of cables obtained by Drop Site have been previously published by Wikileaks and by local media in Yemen, corroborating the larger tranche’s authenticity. Drop Site contacted several Saudi government offices to ask for comment on the cables but did not receive any response.
This is the first in a series of reports based on the Saudi Special Committee Cables by Drop Site News. We are publishing the cables in both Arabic and English here.
The cables help shed light on Riyadh’s machinations in Yemen at a time when Saudi Arabia and Ansarallah appear to be hurtling toward open conflict once again. An attack by Saudi Arabia on Sana’a earlier this month sparked retaliatory strikes by Ansarallah followed by a declared naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Bab al-Mandab strait. The latest developments threaten to completely upend a four-year-long ceasefire that could ultimately play a role in intensifying the U.S. war with Iran. The roots of the conflict between Ansarallah and Riyadh can be found in part in Saudi Arabia’s attempts to foment internal strife within Yemen.

## The Plan to Open Multiple Fronts Against Ansarallah
The same January 2012 cable names two men tasked with carrying out Salman’s plan. The cable claimed Sheikh Mohammed al-Imam, who ran a Salafi institute in the city of Dhamar, “prepared 300 armed men to target Houthi positions” to relieve pressure on the Salafis of Dammaj who were battling the Houthis, though the claim could not be independently verified. Located in the Saada governorate of northwest Yemen, Dammaj was the base of Saudi-influenced Salafi seminary built in the Zaydi heartland in 1979, and by 2012 it had become the symbolic front line of the war. The cable also said that a serving Yemeni army officer, the artillery brigade commander Hussein Khiran, smuggled the fighters their ammunition.
It is not clear from the cables that Drop Site obtained whether these specific actions were taken, but Saudi Arabia did back, arm, and fund Salafi fighters to battle Ansarallah.
The cable also said that Ansarallah leader Abdulmalik al-Houthi sent envoys to two estranged Zaydi figures, Mohammed Abdulazim and Abdullah al-Razami, to plead for fighters. “We now cannot resist the Wahhabis,” Abdulmalik al-Houthi reportedly said, referring to the Salafi tribes. “If you do not support us we will hand Saada over to them, because we cannot continue.” Abdulazim refused the request, while Al-Razami sent seventy men, according to the cable.
A separate cable records the money. Saudi Prince Mishal bin Abdullah, then governor of the border province of Najran, signed an Interior Ministry cable dated May 7, 2012 under the subject line “Regarding the Houthis and the Sunnis.” The cable states that Mishal’s office received an installment of five million Saudi Riyals (about $1.3 million) and passed the money to the Dammaj and Aahim fronts before requesting a second installment of funds. The cable also reports that the kingdom’s men armed and supplied the Aahim front in the province of Hajjah and were arranging to open a third front in Rahub. It also endorses a plan by a Salafi sheikh named Musleh bin Hamad Fanis Al-Athla to build a new branch of the Dammaj institute, calling it “a good thing” that “helps weaken the Houthi movement.”
Saudi Arabia had been financially backing anti-Houthi Yemeni border tribes for years. Before Salman’s 2012 plan to engineer a rift in the north, a special committee cable dated March 15, 2010 signed by King Abdullah authorized the immediate release of 50 million Saudi riyals (around $13 million) to arm, supply, and financially support the tribes battling Ansarallah along the border.
A March 2012 report from the General Intelligence Presidency (GIP), a powerful Saudi intelligence agency, signed by intelligence chief Muqrin bin Abdulaziz describes former president Ali Abdullah Saleh secretly funding the Houthis as a counterweight to Salafi forces. By the report’s account, he steered some 12 billion Yemeni riyals (roughly $55.8 million) their way over an undisclosed time period, because the movement “poses an obstacle to the Salafi current in Yemen.” While Saleh did support the Houthis at various times, the Saudi intelligence assessment claiming billions of Yemeni riyals could not be independently verified and may have been exaggerated by informants in a bid to prompt Saudi to provide more funding to counter it.
Saudi Arabia armed one side. Saleh backed the other. The Zaydi north absorbed the war that both were funding and the damage was catastrophic. Fighting in Dammaj continued from October 2011 to January 2014 and spread to other Houthi strongholds in Saada, Hajjah, Amran and al-Jawf. Casualty numbers and damage reports appear throughout the Saudi cables, quoting Houthi commanders and often citing “large [casualty] numbers from both sides.”
The Red Cross documented more than 100 dead in the first siege of Dammaj in late 2011, among them four children. A report from Yemen’s health authorities counted 199 killed, 29 of them children, and 594 wounded in the final hundred days alone. When a ceasefire was implemented in January 2014, three hundred buses evacuated roughly 10,000 people, evacuating foreigners and those who sought to escape what was understood to be another round of inevitable fighting.
In early 2014, the Houthis overran Dammaj and expelled the Salafi students Riyadh had paid to protect. By September 2014 they had taken over the capital, Sana’a.
The covert war escalated into a full blown conflict in March 2015 when a Saudi-led coalition of Gulf nations, with American military, intelligence and logistical support, began a years-long bombing campaign of northern Yemen. While Salman wanted to ensure the fighting did not appear as a Sunni-Shia sectarian war, the kingdom did ultimately play on sectarianism to rally Salafist Sunnis to join its campaign against Ansarallah.
The bombing campaign lasted eight years across over 25,000 strikes, nearly a third of which struck civilian sites. The accompanying naval and air blockade contributed to the world’s largest cholera outbreak in history, and what the UN for years called the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. By the end of 2021, the UN put the war’s toll at 377,000 dead, most of them from hunger and disease.
Ansarallah, the movement Salman’s ministry once hoped to fracture, has remained in control of most of Yemen for the past decade. It has fired sporadic missiles at Israel in solidarity with Gaza and targeted commercial ships in the Red Sea, most recently declaring a blockade on all Saudi vessels through the Bab al-Mandab strait. The cables show how Saudi Arabia tried to sideline and weaken Ansarallah by sowing division in northern Yemen only to escalate into an all out war that also ultimately failed to drive the Houthis from power. The Special Committee still operates as Saudi Arabia’s secret body that is running the kingdom’s policies toward Yemen.

reads.title: Elon Musk is helping to destroy the West
reads.subtitle: He isn't saving the West. He's doing the exact opposite
reads.body:
- The world’s richest man is a thin-skinned megalomaniac defined by his ignorance, deceit and bigotry.
The interview Elon Musk gave to The Economist was certainly revealing. It helps underline why the West is in crisis - which it is.
The interview was conducted by the magazine’s editor-in-chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes. Musk evidently realised it had gone disastrously, because afterwards he denounced her as “a traitor to the West, plain and simple”.
Now, I would not describe anyone as a “traitor to the West”. As it happens, the elite faction represented by The Economist has played a significant role in plunging the West into crisis: championing an economic order which enriches a tiny minority while hollowing out communities, cheering disastrous wars and treating Israel’s genocide in Gaza as an unfortunate public-relations problem.
But Musk and the far right have promoted the biggest lie of our time: that Muslims, migrants, refugees, trans people and the so-called “woke left” are responsible for the West’s decline.
They are not.
Muslims did not design an economic system which sucked wealth and power upwards while leaving millions condemned to insecurity and falling living standards. Refugees did not invade Iraq, destroy Libya and devastate Afghanistan, humiliating Western military power and spawning chaos across entire regions. Trans people did not deregulate finance, smash trade unions or privatise essential services. The “woke left” did not arm Israel as it obliterated Gaza, completing the West’s moral collapse before the eyes of the world.
To help us expand our challenge to the mainstream media, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
The West’s elites did that - including Elon Musk.
The far right which Musk actively promotes is now manipulating the resulting anger, directing it away from those who possess wealth and power and towards people who lack either. At the same time, the authoritarian apparatus forged by the so-called “war on terror” is rebounding against Western societies themselves, with dissent increasingly criminalised and democracy placed under threat.
This is what I explore in my forthcoming book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It. The subtitle has a deliberate double meaning. The West’s rulers have lost their dominance - and, as Musk demonstrates, many of them appear to have lost their minds, too.
Share

## Musk’s civil war fantasy
A running theme of Musk’s interview was that Britain is overwhelmed with violent disorder.
He denied stating that Britain was collapsing into apocalyptic disorder - and yet has repeatedly tweeted that civil war in Britain “is inevitable”.
Notably, he tweeted this during the August 2024 violent uprising by far-right and racist extremists in the UK:
@stclairashley Civil war is inevitable","username":"elonmusk","name":"Elon Musk","profile_image_url":"https://pbs.substack.com/profile_images/2053244804520427520/m8mdWZCG_normal.jpg","date":"2024-08-04T03:07:47.000Z","photos":[],"quoted_tweet":{},"reply_count":5076,"retweet_count":4194,"like_count":32266,"impression_count":10021062,"expanded_url":null,"video_url":null,"video_preview_media_key":null,"belowTheFold":true}" data-component-name="Twitter2ToDOM">Then, there really was violent disorder - driven by those who views on migrants, refugees and Muslims not dissimilar to his own.
This was when these elements jumped on the horrific Southport murders - and attempted to burn asylum seekers alive in hotels, attacked mosques, assaulted people of colour in the street, tried to drag migrants from cars, attacked the homes and businesses belonging either to minorities or people suspected of being migrants - we could go on. It was a pogrom.
Subscribe now
In a speech broadcast to a protest organised by far-right criminal Tommy Robinson, he said:

> This is a message to the reasonable centre, the people who ordinarily wouldn’t get involved in politics, who just want to live their lives. They don’t want that, they’re quiet, they just go about their business.
My message is to them: if this continues, that violence is going to come to you, you will have no choice. You’re in a fundamental situation here.
Whether you choose violence or not, violence is coming to you. You either fight back or you die, that’s the truth, I think.
How can this not be understood as incitement?
But Musk’s portrayal of Britain as falling into violent bedlam because of migrants, refugees and minorities is false.
Homicides in England and Wales have fallen to their lowest level in almost 50 years.
The murder rate in London is at the lowest level ever recorded. Admissions to hospital because of assault, knife assault, bodily force, blunt objects and firearms have plummeted.
Violence is much lower than in the US. There it has fallen, too, albeit from much higher levels.
Britain has certainly experienced a massive increase in immigration and become far more diverse over the last few decades. Yet, at the same time, violence has plummeted.
The real danger is that the far right persuades enough people that society is being overrun by violent foreigners, whipping up the fear and fury which produces actual mass disorder.
Musk accuses Minton Beddoes of living a “cloistered existence”. That’s almost certainly true - yet what world does he believe he inhabits? He is literally the world’s richest man, and admitted he hasn’t even visited the UK for years.
Subscribe now

## “Normal people”
When challenged about his support for the far right, Musk insists that these are simply “normal people” who want “secure borders, safe cities and sensible spending.”
Yet this completely erases the actual reality of the far-right movements he supported.
Consider Restore Britain, the far-right party led by Rupert Lowe which Musk has enthusiastically promoted.
Restore proposes deporting legally resident foreign nationals if they live in social housing, claim benefits, cannot speak English or supposedly “fail to integrate” - an disturbingly elastic category which could mean almost anything. Lowe has declared that “millions and millions” must leave or be made to leave.
He has also threatened to use the state retrospectively against officials, judges and politicians who he claims placed “dangerous third world savages” in British communities.
Prominent members of Restore include neo-Nazis, Hitler sympathisers and advocates of ethnic cleansing.
These are not “normal people” being unfairly maligned by elite journalists.
They represent a mortal threat to democracy in Britain and across the West.
Subscribe now

## A straightforward question
Minton Beddoes asks Musk a very simple question: is he anti-Muslim?
He could simply answer “no”.
Instead, after pausing at length, he says that he opposes people entering countries with “antithetical views”, and then announces that he is against rape and murder.
What is he saying here exactly? Asked whether he is hostile towards around two billion of his fellow human beings, he immediately jumps to talking about sexual violence and killing.
Musk says he opposes people with beliefs he says are “antithetical” to Western values. But his beliefs are antithetical to mine. I believe in democracy, equality, solidarity and the redistribution of wealth and power. He promotes authoritarianism, far-right extremists and racialised conspiracy theories.
So how do we define these shared Western values exactly?
The vast majority of human beings oppose rape and murder, wherever they were born and whatever faith they hold. Many of those arriving in Western countries are fleeing such violence - including violence that was unleashed or intensified by Western wars.
Yet Musk takes two crimes overwhelmingly condemned across humanity and attaches them, without prompting, to a question about Muslims.
Subscribe now

## Loathed
When Minton Beddoes tells Musk that people loathe him, his response is to cite his quarter of a billion followers on X.
YouGov’s British tracker finds that just 21 per cent of people like Musk, while 62 per cent dislike him - a net rating of minus 41. According to YouGov in the US, 33 per cent viewed him favourably and 53 per cent unfavourably, putting him 14 points underwater.
Musk suggests that actually it is the media who are hated.
There are very good reasons to be angry at the Western media. Media outlets are mostly the playthings of a tiny number of rich moguls. Elite journalists routinely present the interests of the wealthy as basic common sense. Much of the media cheer on disastrous foreign wars, economic policies which benefit the rich at the expense of ordinary people, and redirect anger away from those with wealth and power towards migrants, refugees and Muslims.
But that makes the media very much like Elon Musk.
He is not angry because establishment journalism serves the interests of the powerful. After all, he is one of the richest, most powerful human beings on earth.
He is angry because he doesn’t believe that they go far enough in promoting the bigotry he promotes.
The West really is in crisis. Its economic model has imposed stagnation, decline and misery on millions. Its military adventures have produced disaster after catastrophe. Its ruling class has forfeited its authority, while its complicity in Gaza has destroyed any remaining illusions in its moral leadership.
But Muslims are not to blame. Refugees are not to blame. Trans people are not to blame. The left are not to blame.
The West’s own elites are to blame - and now rich men like Elon Musk are exploiting the ruinous consequences.
In doing so, he promotes far-right movements which threaten already deeply compromised democracies.
Elon Musk is not a prophet warning us about the fall of the West.
He is helping to bring it about.
BattleLines with Owen Jones is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

reads.title: Drone Strikes Are Destroying the Infrastructure of Survival in the Heart of Sudan
reads.subtitle: In El-Obeid, RSF drone strikes are destroying fuel, electricity, and water that keeps the most fragile patients alive.
reads.body:
- Components from drones that struck the night before on Sunday, March 29, 2026 in El-Obeid, Sudan. Faiz Abubakr / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images.Story by Mohamed Wad Al-Sak
Ahmed Mahmoud’s sister, Nafisah, died last month in the city of El-Obeid, another victim of a more than three-year long war raging across Sudan already considered one of the deadliest conflicts for civilians this century.
But like a growing number of Sudanese victims of the war, Mahmoud’s sister’s death was not the direct result of an airstrike, or gunfire. Instead, she fell victim to the near-total collapse of basic infrastructure in the country as a result of calculated attacks aimed at depriving Sudanese civilians the necessities of life.
The war in Sudan has now killed somewhere between 150,000 to 400,000 people according to outside analysts, with people dying from a combination of direct violence, hunger, and lack of access to healthcare.
In June, the 21-year-old Nafisah suddenly fell faint and needed urgent hospital care; she had been managing the impact of an under-treated blood clot in her left leg since 2024. With El-Obeid under constant drone attack and bombardment conducted by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), receiving prompt medical care for basic conditions was nearly impossible.
“We called the ambulance and waited a long time for any tuk-tuk or private car. Then we were told that movement was difficult because of the conditions and the fuel shortage,” Mahmoud said. Blood clots can be life-threatening without immediate medical treatment. “After that we started looking for any car or way to move her. But time kept passing, and her condition kept getting worse.”
When they finally did reach the hospital, the facility was facing resource and personnel strains due to the war and overwhelmed with patients. “When we arrived we found the doctors trying to help everyone, but the pressure was immense and resources were limited. It was clear they were working under extremely difficult conditions,” he said.
His sister died several hours after arriving at the hospital. Her death still haunts her family members, who believe that the delay in arriving at the facility and receiving treatment contributed to her death.
“After she died, I kept thinking: if the ambulance had arrived faster, or if the services hadn’t broken down, maybe my sister would still be with us,” Mahmoud said. “People think war only kills those struck by shells. But the truth is it also kills when it prevents a patient from reaching treatment. My sister was one of them.”
Drop Site is supported by readers. Subscribe or make a gift today.

## War on Infrastructure
The crisis that has overtaken hospitals and other infrastructure in El-Obeid is the product of a calculated military campaign waged by the RSF that has directly targeted civilian infrastructure and imposed a de facto siege.
In recent months, the RSF, which receives arms and other support from the United Arab Emirates, has begun using bombardment by foreign-supplied drones to destroy critical infrastructure, attack supply lines, and force the capitulation of the city’s population.
El-Obeid itself remains under the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF). Its 5th Infantry Division is headquartered in the city, which serves as the army’s main operational base in North Kordofan, after being pushed out of the Sudanese capital of Khartoum, and falling back toward its western strongholds in Darfur last year, the group no longer has the manpower or heavy equipment to mount a direct ground assault and seize the city outright.
Lacking the ability to launch a direct assault, the RSF has reverted to besieging the entire city—cutting supply lines into El-Obeid and striking infrastructure with drones on a regular basis. El-Obeid has experienced a spike in aerial attacks since mid-June, according to the global monitor group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED).
Those findings are echoed by local residents who say that drone attacks by the RSF have intensified against the city, targeting fuel and water infrastructure while making many roadways too dangerous to cross. For five consecutive days in the middle of this month, strikes hit fuel stations in El-Obeid. On June 19, a strike on the main power transformer cut off electricity entirely.
The price of food and fuel is skyrocketing as supplies disappear, while families have resorted to digging wells in a desperate attempt to access water of dubious safety. Nour al-Din Hajj al-Lain, 37, a transport worker in El-Obeid, said that in the wake of the fuel station attacks, fuel prices have reached approximately $30 per gallon with passenger fares rising by up to 2,000 pounds. “Many people are now walking to work,” he said. “El-Obeid is a principal transit point—when transport here is disrupted, the impact extends across a wide area well beyond the city itself.”
Adam Hamid, who has been working in El-Obeid’s main market for about 15 years, said most residents continue their daily lives despite mounting anxiety, but that uncertainty and insecurity has already altered economic behavior. Before the drone attacks made daily life in the city unsafe, the market was much busier, Hamid said. His small shop, which sells household basics, used to receive around 50-70 customers a day. That average has dropped to less than half—dipping further on days following attacks, or when there are reports of possible new strikes.
“Most customers now focus only on essential goods such as food and basic necessities, while postponing non-essential purchases or larger expenses,” he explained. Traders are similarly cautious and have stopped buying large quantities of goods or are reducing their operations. On June 24 members of Congress urged the State Department to secure an agreement to lift the siege, which it said the RSF and its allies have used to “collectively punish civilians and maximize death and destruction.”

-
- A man stands in a hole filled with drone components on Sunday, March 29, 2026 in El Obeid, Sudan. Faiz Abubakr / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images.

## Healthcare Disruptions
Emergency first responders in El-Obeid today describe a nightmarish situation in which shortages of fuel have left them unable to reach civilians in distress, while drone attacks on major roads make it treacherous for ambulances to travel even when fuel is available.
“Before, we used to move the moment we got a call. Now the first question we ask is: is the road safe?” said an ambulance driver at a health facility in the city, who asked not to be named for security reasons. “Often we delay or take longer routes to avoid areas that might be targeted [by airstrikes], which means the patient waits longer before help arrives.”
For patients with hemorrhaging or blood clots—like the sister of Ahmed Mahmoud—that delay can mean the difference between life and death.
Abdelmajeed Mohammed, a neurosurgeon in El-Obeid, said that the escalation of attacks has transformed how the city’s referral hospitals operate. “In a single minute, 50 patients can come in, and life practically stops with the shelling,” said Mohammed.
Drone strikes, he added, have paralyzed every step of the medical system.
“Ambulances struggle to move because of fuel shortages and security risks, medical staff are delayed getting to the hospital, and medical supplies are disrupted,” he said. “And if the power goes out or the generator fuel runs dry, vital equipment—monitors, oxygen, operating rooms, dialysis machines—all stop. That’s why we say life inside the hospital nearly comes to a halt.”
The strikes on fuel stations have also further crippled hospitals, which rely on them to operate generators amid nationwide blackouts and strikes on electrical power stations.
“Two days ago we were forced to suspend some emergency admissions because of a power outage, and before that, surgeries were postponed because generator fuel wasn’t available,” he said. “Fuel is the lifeline of the hospital for us. Patients who need oxygen depend on machines that don’t work without electricity, and even the machines that read vital signs don’t work without electricity and fuel. And if you can’t see the vital signs, you can’t treat the patient.”
El-Obeid’s Al-Jameeh Dialysis Center is one of the last medical centers offering kidney dialysis in western Sudan after war shut down services across the area. But now, it too is teetering.
Ayman Abdulrahman, one of the center’s medical staff, said machines are breaking down at a rapid clip because of the relentless flow of patients. At the moment, all they can do is scale back services. “In the past we used to give the patient two full sessions, but with the pressure and the machine shortage we were forced to cut the session length so we could give other patients a chance too.”
A similar wave of strikes in June 2023 wreaked havoc on the dialysis unit, with at least 12 patients dying as a result. So far there are no officially documented figures on how many deaths have resulted at the center from the latest strikes.
“The work day now starts with the question: do we have electricity? Is there enough fuel to run the generator?” said Esraa Awad, a doctor at the dialysis center and its former director. “A patient hooked up to a dialysis machine can’t simply have their session stopped because of shelling or a power cut. Any sudden interruption puts us in front of real medical risks.”
Awad explained the fuel crisis extends beyond generators to patient transport and the arrival of staff and supplies: “Dialysis isn’t just a machine, it’s an interconnected chain. If the fuel or electricity is cut, or a patient or supplies can’t get through, the whole link collapses—and the patient is the first to pay the price.”
After the RSF stepped up its strikes on fuel-stations in June, it cut even deeper into critical energy supplies for the city’s hospitals, said an emergency room nurse at Al-Daman Hospital, who asked not to be named for her personal safety. “We now start every shift not knowing whether the power will hold, or whether there’s enough fuel to run the generator until the end of the day,” she said. “These are questions that weren’t part of our job before the war.”

## Drone Warfare
In addition to the impact on civilians, the RSF strikes on infrastructure are also changing the balance of the war around El-Obeid. A member of the Joint Forces, an armed group aligned with the SAF, told Drop Site on condition of anonymity that the military was having difficulties moving troops and supplies as a result of RSF attacks on fuel stations and roads in the area.
The region now being contested by the two sides has become vital to the larger war. The area under siege separates the army-controlled east of Sudan from the RSF-controlled west. That makes it the main corridor through which the warring parties move troops, weapons, fuel, and supplies.
For both sides, drones have become an important tool for combat, as well as a means to punish and pressure the civilian population. In the first four months of 2026, armed drones caused more than 80% of civilian deaths, killing at least 880 people nationwide, with the Kordofan and Darfur regions hardest hit, the UN said in May.
The drones themselves come from outside Sudan. According to international investigations, the RSF’s fleet—including Chinese-made CH-95 and Wing Loong II drones—reaches the battlefield through a UAE-linked supply network routed through Chad and Libya.
The SAF’s drones, including Iranian Mohajer-6 and Ababil-3 models and Turkish Bayraktar TB2 and Akinci aircraft, reportedly arrive with the support of Egypt, which has provided the army with aircraft, ammunition, and military coordination throughout the war.
The current wave of attacks on El-Obeid accelerated after the historic capital of  the massive Darfur region, El-Fasher, fell in October 2025—an event that was also followed by a horrific massacre in the city according to local witnesses and international monitors.
On January 4, RSF drones hit El-Obeid’s city’s thermal power plant. The attack came as part of a wider wave that also struck the Merowe Dam and Kenana airbase in the city. On January 30, roughly 20 RSF drones struck government buildings in a rare daytime attack.
The UN has said that drone attacks are now expanding beyond Kordofan and Darfur into the regions of Blue Nile, White Nile, and Khartoum itself. A strike on Khartoum International Airport on May 4 grounded all flights, raising fears that hostilities could return to the capital after a period of relative calm.

## “Total Collapse of Everything”
Civilians in El-Obeid are struggling to maintain the surviving infrastructure in the city. A pediatrician at El-Obeid Teaching Hospital described the situation as a “total collapse of everything,” with the breakdown of supply chains and power infrastructure depriving children of life-saving interventions. He said he’s seen numerous cases where children have died because of the indirect impacts of airstrikes.
“The child needs blood, and we don’t have any. He needs oxygen, but the generator has stopped. He needs to be transferred to a higher-level hospital, but no ambulance dares take the road,” said the doctor, who asked to be identified by the initials MT to protect his safety. “The drone didn’t strike this child directly. But it killed him.”
The dire conditions are compounded by the rising number of displaced people arriving from other regions as refugees. “El-Obeid is hosting growing numbers of displaced people, while at the same time its own residents are suffering from repeated attacks on their livelihoods, infrastructure, and basic services,” said Majdi al-Naeem of the Sudan Human Rights Monitor.
Al-Naeem said the attacks on infrastructure do not, in his view, serve any clear military objective, but instead impose direct burdens on the civilian population. “In my assessment, these attacks don’t serve a military purpose so much as they affect civilians’ lives, and targeting civilian objects is prohibited under international humanitarian law,” he said.
On Monday, the Sudanese army and allied groups recaptured Bara, Al-Baraka, Um Sayala, Jabrat Al-Sheikh, and other areas on Sunday after heavy clashes with the RSF, according to military officials cited by Sudan Tribune. Officials said 73 RSF vehicles were destroyed, others seized, and numerous fighters killed. The advance opens a new supply corridor to El-Obeid, strengthening its eastern defenses.
For the past few weeks, talk has been spreading of a possible RSF offensive once the city and its defenders have been sufficiently weakened by the siege. The SAF reclaiming the highway into El-Obeid will likely disrupt the RSF's momentum toward El-Obeid, restricting the movement of fighters, supplies, and reinforcements.
Zahra Nurain, a mother of five living in the Karima neighborhood in the city’s northeast, said the talk of a potential large-scale battle has been a daily source of anxiety but has not pushed her toward leaving—a reflection of the limited choices available after more than three years of war.
“We hear the news and rumors every day, and sometimes we follow the sounds of aircraft and explosions. But where would we go?” she said. “El-Obeid has become a refuge for many people during this war. We hope it does not become another battlefield.”
Mohamed Wad Al-Sak is a Sudanese freelance journalist and multimedia producer covering conflict, displacement, and human rights across Sudan and East Africa.
