reads.title: Iran war pauses; Yemen and Saudi go “siege for a siege”; Dr. Fauci’s diary
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: July 27, 2026
reads.body:
- Sailors from the navy of Yemen's Aden-based Saudi-backed government aboard a vessel patrolling a shipping lane off Hanish Island in the Red Sea on July 27, 2026. Photo by Khaled Ziad / AFP via Getty Images.Monday, July 27, 2026 – U.S., Iran pause strikes. New York Times: President Donald Trump to avoid major escalation in Iran, for now. Iran, Ukraine accuse each other of involvement in each other's wars. Ship explodes in the Strait. Iran claims full control over Hormuz. Pentagon removes four U.S. troop deaths from official Iran war casualty tally. Saudi Arabia says Iran-backed groups in Iraq launched drones at oil facilities. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to meet Trump. Ansarallah launches strikes deep inside Saudi Arabia. Saudi strikes hit Ansarallah positions. Yemen’s transportation minister tallies damage from strikes. Netanyahu threatens further West Bank escalation. Israel attacks Gaza over the weekend. Israel strikes journalists’ gathering spot near hospital. Israel kills Gaza police chief on Saturday, internal security officer on Sunday. Israel greenlights multinational force in Gaza. Israeli attacks are blocking residents’ return to devastated southern Lebanese town. Progressives campaign for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Minnesota State Sen. John Hoffman accuses Angie Craig’s senate campaign of seeking endorsement while he was in ICU. Military boat strikes haven’t reduced U.S. cocaine supply, U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency assesses. Troy Jackson formally wins Maine Democratic Senate nomination. Border czar Tom Homan says ICE reviewing vetting after Maine agent’s domestic violence accusations. ICE plans deportation blitz targeting Haitian migrants. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorses Haley Stevens over El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race. Anthony Fauci’s diary. U.S. congratulates Venezuela for leaving ICC. UN urges removal of Syria sanctions. Sudanese army recaptures key North Kordofan towns near El-Obeid. Police kill suspect in deadly Berlin Pride car-ramming attack. Russian and Ukrainian attacks kill 10 as peace talks stall. Congo’s Ebola death toll surpasses 1,400 as vaccine trials begin. Flávio Bolsonaro launches 2026 presidential bid as Milei sparks diplomatic row.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- U.S., Iran pause strikes: The U.S. ceased its two-week-long campaign of strikes on Iran on Friday evening, with no strikes announced or confirmed by the U.S. on Saturday or Sunday.

- U.S. Central Command said on Saturday that its blockade of Iran remains in full effect, with 12 commercial vessels redirected, two disabled and two boarded as of July 25. The blockade was reimposed on July 14.

- Iran said Sunday it had stopped its retaliatory attacks across the region after the U.S. refrained from striking Iran for a second consecutive night and third day.

- “Over the past two nights the Americans have stopped their attacks,” army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said, adding that because Iran’s strategy was “essentially retaliatory,” it had halted its own operations in turn.

- A senior Iranian source told Reuters that Tehran would keep holding its fire as long as Washington maintained the pause, however, the source said Iran remained skeptical of U.S. intentions, with the prevailing view that the halt was “tactical rather than genuine.”

- Mike Walz, the U.S. ambassador to the UN, told Fox News on Sunday that Trump had paused the strikes to open “some space” for diplomacy.

- Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Monday that Tehran has not requested a resumption of negotiations with the U.S. Speaking at a press conference in Tehran, Baghaei also rejected U.S. involvement in managing the conflict, saying, “This is not war management. Repeated war crimes and boasting about them are merely attempts to escape a disaster they created under the influence of the Zionist regime, and they will inevitably pay the price.”

- NYT: Trump to avoid major escalation in Iran, for now: Trump has temporarily abandoned his plans for a major escalation of the U.S. war against Iran after advisers warned it could dangerously drain depleted Patriot interceptor stocks and trigger a wider regional war, the New York Times reported on Saturday.

- According to the Times, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine reportedly told Trump that renewed large-scale combat was possible but would severely reduce CENTCOM’s remaining air defenses. The Pentagon has used more than 1,200 Patriot missiles, costing over $4 million each.

- Officials also cited threats to Gulf allies, rising energy prices and doubts that heavier strikes would force Iran back to negotiations.

- CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper advised ending the U.S. bombing campaign around the Strait of Hormuz, saying it had reached the limit of its effectiveness and most designated targets were exhausted, according to a separate report on Sunday from Axios.

- Iran, Ukraine accuse each other of involvement in each other’s wars: Iran’s Foreign Ministry accused Ukraine on Saturday of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, saying an explosion killed one sailor and wounded another, according to a statement carried by Iranian state media.

- The Ministry called the strike a violation of the UN Charter and “an act of aggression,” and said responsibility for the consequences would lie with Ukraine “and its supporters and instigators.”

- Iran’s accusation followed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s announcement on Saturday that Ukraine had struck Russian warships and cargo vessels in the Caspian that it said were transporting military cargo between Russia and Iran.

- Ukraine’s Security Service, quoted by RFE/RL and United24, named two ships, the Port Olya 2 and the Begey, both under Western sanctions, and said it also hit a Lukoil offshore oil platform and a Russian missile boat. Neither government’s account could be independently verified.

- Zelenskyy separately alleged, in comments on X, that Russia has been passing satellite imagery of Gulf states and U.S. military bases to Iran, claiming a correlation between Russian surveillance and Iranian strikes on four air bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait on July 19 and 20.

- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke by phone with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Saturday about the attack, and called for a firm response from the UN Security Council, the European Union and the wider international community.

- Ship explodes in the Strait: An oil tanker exploded in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday after striking a naval mine, according to Iranian state-affiliated media, which said the vessel had strayed from the shipping route designated by Tehran. No details about the vessel were immediately available.

- Iran claims full control over Hormuz: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Sunday that its navy had consolidated complete control over the Strait of Hormuz, claiming no vessel can now pass without accepting Iranian-imposed rules, according to a statement carried by the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency.

- The group also reported that it had forced six ships to drop anchor and accept Iranian instructions after receiving warnings on Saturday.

- Iran’s Baghaei said Monday that the “vital waterway for global energy supplies and maritime shipping” remains closed by Iran.

- Iran and Oman held several rounds of talks in Tehran between their deputy foreign ministers on Friday and Saturday over managing safe traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, Baghaei told Tasnim. Baghaei called the talks productive and said technical discussions were ongoing.

- Pentagon removes four U.S. troop deaths from official Iran war casualty tally: The Pentagon removed four U.S. soldiers killed during the recent fighting with Iran from its official Iran war casualty count, instead listing them under a newly created “Overseas Operations” category, according to the Associated Press, raising questions about the true human cost on American soldiers.

- The Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System also removed dozens of wounded troops from the tally. The new category lists the four Army personnel by name along with 207 wounded service members, although it is unclear whether all of those injuries are linked to the Iran conflict.

- Saudi Arabia says Iran-backed groups in Iraq launched drones at oil facilities: Saudi Arabia said several drones were launched from Iraq targeting its oil facilities in the country’s Eastern Province and the Riyadh region, accusing “militias affiliated with Iran in Iraq” of carrying out the attack, according to a statement from its Defense Ministry.

- Netanyahu to meet Trump: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will travel to Washington on Monday and meet President Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, Israeli Army Radio reported. Netanyahu said he would discuss “all the issues on the agenda, first and foremost, Iran.”

## Yemen

- Ansarallah launches strikes deep inside Saudi Arabia: A senior Ansarallah media official said the group launched an intensified wave of missile and drone strikes deep inside Saudi Arabia overnight Friday, posting footage he said showed fires burning in the kingdom’s south.

- Strikes were reported on an Aramco facility in Jizan, as well as on Yanbu, Dhahran, Khamis Mushait airbase and areas near an airport. Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attacks.

- The barrage came hours after Saudi airstrikes on Yemen’s Hodeidah province and Kamaran Island.

- A senior negotiator for the group, Hamid Assem, said on Saturday that Ansarallah’s attacks on Saudi Arabia would continue as long as the kingdom maintains its blockade of Yemen, in an interview with the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency in Sanaa.

- Ansarallah announced further attacks targeting oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia on Monday, with military spokesperson Yahya Saree saying the group targeted “sensitive facilities and points” along the crude oil supply and transport route from eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.

- Saudi strikes hit Ansarallah positions: Attacks were reported on Ansarallah positions in the Marib and Al-Jawf provinces on Saturday, according to Yemen TV, the broadcaster of the Saudi-backed government.

- The channel did not identify the source of the strikes but said they destroyed missile launchers, a Katyusha rocket-launching site and weapons depots in the al-Jubah, al-Safra and Majzar districts. It claimed several Ansarallah members were killed.

- An Ansarallah official reported that Saudi strikes on Saturday targeted two pharmaceutical factories in the country.

- Later on Saturday, clashes between Saudi-backed Yemeni groups and Ansarallah forces were reported in Al-Jawf.

- Yemen’s transportation minister tallies damage from strikes: Ansarallah’s Transport and Public Works Minister Mohammed Qahim said on Sunday that Saudi airstrikes destroyed cranes and docks at Hodeidah Port, and threats against ships and blockade restrictions had reduced annual imports into the country from six million tons to one million.

- Qahim said no container ships had entered for nearly five years, some goods have been banned for 12 years. He estimated the total loss to the country at $12 billion since the Saudi blockade began in 2015.

- Hodeidah now receives only 400 to 500 containers, compared with more than 300,000 annually before the blockade.

- Ansarallah announced a blockade on Saudi shipping through Bab Al-Mandab last Monday, as part of a “siege for siege” policy.

## Palestine

- Netanyahu threatens further West Bank escalation: Israeli forces imposed sweeping arrests and movement restrictions across the occupied West Bank after settlers killed four Palestinians in the town of Tal on Friday. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel is prepared to expand military operations across the occupied West Bank, telling a cabinet meeting Sunday that troops had been ordered to “enter villages, search them, seize weapons, and make arrests,” and that Israel would “act more broadly against terrorist strongholds,” per the Times of Israel.

- Israeli settlers set up an outpost in Tal less than 24 hours after the attack on the town, with a UK-sanctioned contractor uprooting hundreds of olive trees in the area. Settlers claimed, as they recorded the construction, that “the retaliation [against] the murderous people’s village has begun.” Read a breakdown of the first 24 hours following the attack from Drop Site contributor Younis Tirawi here.

- Israel ordered military gates and checkpoints leading toward Nablus and Ramallah to be closed on Saturday evening.

- One Israeli checkpoint delayed an ambulance carrying a Palestinian woman who was six months pregnant and suffering from heavy bleeding, according to WAFA. Soldiers held the ambulance for more than 30 minutes at Nablus, searched the woman despite her condition, and ordered the crew to switch off the vehicle’s engine, shutting down its medical equipment. The woman survived after reaching hospital, but lost her baby.

- Israeli settlers were filmed on Saturday smashing Palestinian vehicles near the entrance to Al-Nashash, south of Bethlehem, Al Jazeera reported. Settlers also reportedly attacked a Palestinian resident from Deir Jarir and vandalized his truck near the Silwad–Ein Yabrud road.

- Israeli forces fired tear gas canisters and set fire to Palestinian property in Kafr Malik on Saturday, northeast of Ramallah, as part of an ongoing raid.

- Israeli settlers attacked the northern West Bank town of Qusra on Saturday evening, setting fire to a mosque and spray-painting racist slogans on its walls. On Sunday, another group of settlers set fire to a mosque in the Tulkarem area. Drop Site spoke with residents of Qusra about the attack in a video report available here.

- Israeli forces arrested more than 120 Palestinians in Nablus, Tulkarm and Hebron over two days as part of a systematic campaign of collective punishment, the Palestinian Center for Prisoners Advocacy said.

- Israeli forces also demolished nine homes and two other structures across the occupied West Bank on Monday alone, including in Jerusalem, Ramallah and Jenin.

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, three Palestinians were killed—two in new attacks and one due to wounds sustained in earlier attacks—and 12 were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. One body was also recovered from under the rubble.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,329 killed, with 174,009 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,203 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 3,900, while 803 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israeli attacks on Gaza over the weekend:

- Israeli attacks on Gaza on Saturday killed at least nine and wounded at least 36 others.

- Israeli forces fired on the Nuseirat refugee camp, wounding a Palestinian woman in the head.

- Israeli forces also carried out demolitions east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza. Three explosions and multiple strikes were reported in the area earlier, with at least two killed in the incident.

- An Israeli strike on Khan Younis on Saturday killed a newly graduated high school student on his way to buy sweets for a celebration marking the accomplishment.

- A second Israeli strike on Khan Younis hit the roof of a family home, killing two.

- Israel strikes journalists’ gathering spot near hospital: The Israeli military struck the area outside Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital in central Gaza on Saturday, next to a public workspace where journalists routinely gather. The attack wounded at least 10.

- Footage captured by Drop Site contributor Mohamed Ahmed shows the bloody aftermath of the attack.

- “We were sitting here because we believed this was a safe place in front of a hospital,” one journalist said. “There is no safe place in the Gaza Strip.”

- Israel kills Gaza police chief on Saturday, internal security officer on Sunday: Israeli forces targeted and killed Col. Abdel Nasser Al-Maqadmeh, 54, director of police for the North Gaza governorate, in a Saturday airstrike on Gaza City’s Sheikh Radwan neighborhood, according to Gaza’s Interior Ministry. Several others were reportedly wounded.

- Israel killed Col. Wael al-Ladawi, the head of Gaza’s internal security service in central Gaza, and a second officer as they drove through Deir Al-Balah on Sunday, according to Gaza’s Interior Ministry.

- The UN human rights office has documented at least a dozen Israeli attacks on Palestinian police in 2026, including officers directing traffic and patrolling markets. “The pattern of attacks raises concerns that Israeli forces apply no distinction between police personnel and fighters,” it said.

- Israel greenlights multinational force in Gaza: Israel’s security cabinet approved the entry of a multinational force into Gaza on Sunday as part of Trump’s “Board of Peace” plan.

- The International Stabilization Force, roughly 200 personnel at this stage from what an Israeli official called “friendly countries” such as Uganda and Morocco, will operate only in areas outside Israeli military control and “in full coordination” with the Israeli army.

- The cabinet ruled that only Israel will approve which countries take part.

## Lebanon

- Israeli attacks are blocking residents’ return to devastated southern town: Residents began returning to Zawtar Al-Gharbiyeh in southern Lebanon on Friday to find more than half the town destroyed, after Israeli troops withdrew and the Lebanese army deployed under a U.S.-brokered framework, Reuters reported. At least four bodies were recovered from the town as rescue operations continue.

- The town is one of three “pilot zones” under the deal, which requires Hezbollah to disarm in designated areas as Israel withdraws in phases. On Sunday, the Lebanese army said Israel was obstructing the handover through “systematic destruction and bulldozing of homes, bombardment and sweeps with automatic weapons in several southern areas.”

- Lebanon’s Army said Israeli soldiers were “opening fire near army positions in Kfar Tibnit, Nabatieh Fawqa and Zawtar Al-Gharbiyeh, which hinders the implementation of its missions.”

- Israeli forces still occupy a strip up to 10 km inside Lebanon, where they continue to systematically raze villages in violation of the agreement and international law.

- Israeli attacks continued on Monday with artillery shelling reported near the outskirts of Tallousa and Markaba, sparking fires in the area, while Israeli forces demolished buildings in Markaba, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## U.S. News

- Progressives campaign for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan:  Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) campaigned for Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Ferndale, Michigan, just north of Detroit, on Saturday.

- “It is pretty simple, we want someone who is going to be there for working people,” he told the room.

- Van Hollen is among several national Democrats stumping for El-Sayed this weekend, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Pramila Jayapal. El-Sayed faces Rep. Haley Stevens, who has received more than $30 million in support from the pro-Israel lobby, in the Democratic Senate primary on August 4. El-Sayed also got Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman’s endorsement Monday.

- Hoffman accuses Craig campaign of seeking endorsement while he was in ICU: Minnesota state Sen. John Hoffman said Rep. Angie Craig’s campaign sought his endorsement for her U.S. Senate bid while he was in intensive care recovering from a June 2025 assassination attempt, an account confirmed by a close friend of Hoffman’s.

- Craig, who is running against Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan to replace Amy Klobuchar, has received more than $800,000 from AIPAC and its associates since she first ran for Congress in 2018.

- Military boat strikes haven’t reduced U.S. cocaine supply, DEA assesses: An internal DEA report reviewed by The Washington Post found that U.S. military strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats have not reduced cocaine supply in the U.S., instead prompting traffickers to shift toward larger boats hugging coastlines and aircraft routes through Guyana and Suriname.

- Based on the price of cocaine, the supply may have increased, according to the Post, with the price of a kilogram in Florida dropping by roughly 50% over the last five years.

- The findings contradict President Donald Trump’s repeated claims that the strikes, which have killed at least 221 people since September, cut maritime drug trafficking by “97-98%.”

- Troy Jackson formally wins Maine Democratic Senate nomination: Troy Jackson won Maine Democrats’ nomination for Senate 566 to 5 at a convention Saturday, replacing Graham Platner.

- Jackson, a progressive and former state Senate president, will face incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November’s general election.

- Homan says ICE reviewing vetting after Maine agent’s domestic violence accusations: Border czar Tom Homan said Sunday that ICE’s vetting and training processes are “under review” after reports that David Brouillette, the agent involved in the fatal Maine shooting of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, had a history of domestic violence accusations that should have flagged him during vetting.

- Homan told CNN that changes have also been made to vehicle-stop procedures, including new guidance requiring at least one body camera on such stops, following that shooting and a separate fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston days earlier.

- ICE plans deportation blitz targeting Haitian migrants: ICE has made internal plans to ramp up arrests and deportation flights targeting Haitian migrants, including in Ohio communities like Springfield, ahead of the termination of Temporary Protected Status for more than 300,000 Haitians, CBS News reported.

- The operations could begin as early as this week following a Supreme Court ruling upholding the TPS termination, with DHS telling those losing status “it’s closing time” and urging self-deportation, and with advocates describing Haitian communities as gripped by “extreme trauma, fear, and terror.”

- Whitmer endorses Stevens over El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Rep. Haley Stevens over Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary on Friday, in a video posted to Stevens’ X account.

- A report from The Lever noted Whitmer’s family and financial ties to Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan, whose former CEO was her father.

-  El-Sayed, a longtime Medicare for All advocate, poses a threat to the health insurance industry. For more on this possible explanation for the endorsement, read the full article from The Lever here.

- Dr. Fauci’s diary: A Senate investigation conducted by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) revealed that Anthony Fauci kept a diary throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, in which his observations often directly contradicted his public messaging about the virus. The junior senator from Kentucky released Fauci’s entries from December 2019 to December 2022 in a thread on X over the weekend. On January 26, 2020, roughly two months before the American public entered quarantine, Fauci wrote, “Now we know the market was not the source, it was the amplifier,” referring to the Wuhan market at which many speculated COVID-19 originated.

## Other International News

- U.S. congratulates Venezuela for leaving ICC: The U.S. State Department welcomed Venezuela’s withdrawal from the International Criminal Court on Saturday and called on every member state to follow, calling the court “corrupt and worthless” and saying the US-installed government of Delcy Rodríguez had joined “American-led efforts to dismantle” it. “It is time to dismantle the ICC,” it said in a statement.

- On the same day, staunchly pro-Israel lawmaker Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) posted photos with Rodríguez from what he called the first congressional delegation to Venezuela in a decade. He credited “President Trump’s decision to remove Maduro” with making the country “a key ally” and “an energy powerhouse.”

- UN urges removal of Syria sanctions: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged the immediate removal of all sanctions imposed on Syria under ousted ruler Bashar al-Assad, wrapping up a two-day visit to Damascus on Sunday, according to AFP.

- Western states including the US have begun lifting sanctions since Assad’s fall in December 2024, though investors remain wary, and the World Bank estimates reconstruction could cost $216 billion.

- Sudanese army recaptures key North Kordofan towns near El-Obeid: The Sudanese army and allied groups recaptured Bara, Al-Baraka, Um Sayala, Jabrat Al-Sheikh and other areas on Sunday after heavy clashes with the RSF, according to military officials cited by Sudan Tribune.

- Officials said 73 RSF vehicles were destroyed, others seized and numerous fighters killed. A senior Sudan Liberation Movement commander was also reportedly killed in the offensive.

- The advance opens a new supply corridor to El-Obeid, strengthens its eastern defenses and could help restore direct ground access to Omdurman.

- Police kill suspect in deadly Berlin Pride car-ramming attack: German police shot dead 21-year-old Abdul Ballout on Sunday, ending a 24-hour manhunt after he allegedly drove a van into crowds near Berlin’s Pride celebrations, killing one person and injuring 29.

- Police said Ballout charged at officers with a blade when they located him at an allotment complex in Spandau. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the ramming as an apparent “Islamist terror attack,” saying Ballout had previously been convicted of preparing an act of violence after attempting to join ISIS.

- Russian and Ukrainian attacks kill 10 as peace talks stall: Russia launched seven ballistic missiles and 136 drones across Ukraine, killing six people in a new wave of attacks on urban centers, according to Ukrainian authorities, while Ukrainian strikes killed forces in the occupied region of Horlivka and Russia’s Belgorod.

- The attacks come days after a deadly bombing of a drone technology exhibition near Kyiv that was struck by Russian ballistic missiles after being publicly advertised in promotional materials online—an attack that killed ten and wounded dozens more.

- The Kremlin separately said it had received no concrete information about new peace proposals ahead of Tuesday’s meeting between Trump and Zelenskyy in Washington  with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissing reports as “media speculation.”

- Congo’s Ebola death toll surpasses 1,400 as vaccine trials begin: The Democratic Republic of Congo has recorded 3,200 confirmed ebola infections and 1,405 deaths since late April, according to local authorities. Nearly 90% of cases are in conflict-ravaged Ituri province, though the epidemic has spread across five eastern provinces and the true toll is believed to be substantially higher.

- With no approved vaccine or specific treatment for this strain, Oxford University has begun testing an experimental vaccine, while other candidates are being fast-tracked.

- Flávio Bolsonaro launches 2026 presidential bid as Milei sparks diplomatic row: Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his 2026 Brazilian presidential campaign as the Liberal Party’s candidate, stepping into the spotlight as his father Jair Bolsonaro’s political heir while facing intense legal scrutiny and a tight electoral race against President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

- The launch event included a video endorsement from Netanyahu and an in-person embrace from Argentine President Javier Milei.

reads.title: Israeli Settlers Set Up At Least Six New Colonial Outposts After Friday Killings in the Occupied West Bank
reads.subtitle: Israeli soldiers and settlers have unleashed a campaign of terror on Palestinians across the occupied West Bank with home raids, shootings, assaults, mass detentions, and house demolitions.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- A Palestinian man sits on a couch in front of a building containing shops and flats that were demolished by Israeli forces in Anzah, south of the Palestinian city of Jenin in the northern Israeli-occupied West Bank, on July 27, 2026. Photo by JOHN WESSELS / AFP via Getty Images.RAMALLAH, occupied West Bank—In the aftermath of Friday’s killings in the village of Tal, hundreds of armed Israeli settlers and soldiers launched a campaign of terror targeting Palestinian towns and villages across the occupied West Bank, with reports of home raids, shootings, assaults, mass detentions, and demolitions of property—including residential buildings, mosques, cars, agricultural equipment, and farmland.
It began when armed settlers raided Tal, which is southwest of Nablus city in the northern West Bank, at around 7 a.m. local time and opened fire. They were confronted by Palestinian residents of the village who were attempting to protect their homes and land. Just a week earlier, armed settlers had raided Tal and set fire to a Palestinian home. The family managed to escape before the house was consumed by flames.
During Friday’s attack, one of the Palestinian residents, Farouq Ramadan, a father of five, managed to seize the machine gun of an Israeli settler in a moment captured on camera. Ramadan then shot one of the settlers. Ramadan, and three of his cousins— brothers Jawad and Ibrahim Ramadan, and their cousin Imran—were then shot dead by settlers and soldiers, while two settlers were killed.
“This was self-defense. Farouq was defending himself, his uncle and his cousins. Farouq is well-known in our village—he has never gone out to confront the occupation and its forces and settlers. Had the settlers not been close to his sister’s home in the village he would not have gone out,” Firas al-Saifi, a local Palestinian journalist from Tal, told Drop Site. “The situation is that they raid Palestinian villages and homes and point their guns at residents, and expect them to be killed in silence.”
Four others were shot and wounded at the scene by settler and soldier fire, including Orwa Ramadan, the brother of Jawad and Ibrahim, who was shot in the shoulder. Shortly after the attack, Israeli soldiers abducted Orwa from his hospital bed at the Nablus Specialty Hospital, where he was transferred for treatment. He remains detained along with another one of his brothers, Majd Ramadan, who was at work and uninvolved during the attack.
The arrests came amid a sweeping campaign of mass detentions by Israeli occupation forces, with more than 100 Palestinians taken into custody and interrogated from Tal alone—more than 20 remained in custody as of Monday—and dozens more arrested across the West Bank, according to local officials.
Israeli forces also raided Ramadan’s home, taking measurements in preparation for the planned demolition of his family home and that of his parents, who live on the lower floor of the same building. Armed settlers, accompanied by the Israeli military, established a new illegal outpost on the site of the attack—installing caravans after uprooting hundreds of Palestinian-owned olive trees in the area.
It is one of at least six new colonial outposts reported on occupied Palestinian land as Israeli settlers take advantage of the mass crackdown they incited, in addition to the expansion of existing outposts over the past few days alone with the support of the Israeli army. Other outposts established by Israeli settlers over the weekend in Palestinian villages include in Umm Safa and Sinjil in the Ramallah governorate; in Deir Istya and Deir Ballut in the Salfit governorate; and Asira al-Shamaliya in the Nablus governorate. Multiple other outposts are being expanded.
MORE: Video obtained by Drop Site of the new settler outpost at Tal

## Expanding Attacks and Colonization
Once the news of the two killed Israelis emerged on Friday, hundreds more settlers attacked at least 30 different villages and locations between Friday and midday on Monday. The Israeli army not only supported the settlers but launched its own military raids.
Dozens of Palestinians were wounded, including many through live ammunition, rubber-coated bullets, rocks, pepper-spray, and physical assaults. At least seven homes, two mosques, a quarry, many cars, and farmlands were set on fire and burned, while many other properties faced arson attempts but were blocked by residents.
Reports of attacks came from numerous villages, including Tal, Surra, Qusra, Urif, Madama, Asira al-Qibliya, Burin, Iraq Burin, Qabalan, Jalud, Qaryut, Aqraba, Beita, Lubban al-Sharqiya, Wadi al-Sha’ir, Khirbat Tana al-Fawqa, Beit Furik, As-Sawiya, Tilfeet, and Huwwara in the Nablus district; Jit, Fara’ta, and Immatin in the Qalqilya district; Kur in the Tulkarem district; Sinjil, Beitillu, and Ein Samiya in the Ramallah and al-Bireh district; Surif in the Hebron district; and al-Maniya in the Bethlehem district.
Compounding the attacks, the Israeli army imposed a suffocating lockdown on Palestinian cities and severed movement between towns and villages, effectively trapping residents as the attacks were underway. Because of blocked access to essential services, according to local medics, there have been at least four cases of Palestinian women being forced to give birth at military closures and checkpoints over the weekend, with ambulances blocked from evacuating them. On Monday, one woman tragically delivered a stillborn after enduring severe bleeding due to the closures by the Israeli army. Soldiers held the ambulance for more than 30 minutes at Nablus, searched the woman despite her condition, and ordered the crew to switch off the vehicle’s engine, shutting down its medical equipment. The woman survived after reaching hospital, but lost her baby.
Bashar Qaryouti, a volunteer medic and activist from the village of Qaryout south of Nablus city, explained that the current period marks a clear shift. “We used to be afraid of the night—we called the settlers ‘bats’ because they used to carry out their attacks under the cover of darkness. Now, they commit all their crimes in broad daylight without a care in the world,” Qaryouti told Drop Site.
Following the killings, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who is also in charge of the building of illegal colonies in the occupied West Bank, called for the destruction of Palestinian villages and the transfer of their residents, and demanded the expansion of Israeli colonies. A similar statement was made by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, who announced a series of measures, among them the building of new colonies.
While most settler attacks in recent years have focused on Palestinians living in Area C—the area comprising roughly 60 percent of the occupied West Bank and excluding the built-up areas of Palestinian cities and villages—settler violence is now increasingly moving into Areas A and B, where the majority of Palestinian villages are located.
“We are in a new stage. The settlers and soldiers have emptied about 99 percent of Area C through their attacks and by forcing residents out, and now the settlers are moving into the villages and attacking them. They have begun taking over homes on the edges of villages and launching attacks deep inside our towns,” Qaryouti said.
One of the new outposts is in Deir Istya, a historic Palestinian town in the Salfit governorate in the northern West Bank. “The place where they established [one of the new outposts] is the only remaining open space available for the people of Deir Istya to expand their construction in the future. The area they have taken control of covers 44 dunams (around 10 acres),” Izzat Mansour, the mayor of Deir Istya, told Drop Site on Monday. “They set up tents there last night, and since three o’clock this morning Israeli army forces have been present there. All the surrounding areas of Deir Istya are already enclosed by settlers.”
“We see that what happened to our people in 1948 is now being repeated in the West Bank,” Mansour added, referring to the mass expulsion of 750,000 Palestinians from their homes by Zionist militias in what is known as the Nakba, Arabic for ‘catastrophe.’ “There is continuous and systematic daily harassment from different directions by settlers. We are using every means available to us to continue living on these lands, to resist displacement, and to prevent them from gaining control over these areas and imposing a new reality.”
Routine attacks by Israeli settlers and soldiers on Palestinians in the West Bank have been taking place for decades, but over the last few years, particularly since the genocide in Gaza began in 2023, they have significantly increased and become more organized. The Israeli military also increasingly shows up to support the settlers’ actions.
Sinjil, a Palestinian village northeast of Ramallah, was close to one of the new outposts established this weekend. “Before the events of Tal—two or three days before—Sinjil was attacked by dozens of armed settlers. They fired live ammunition directly at people…The settlers have gone far beyond all limits. Their attacks have escalated to the point where they enter people’s homes, vandalize shops, vandalize houses. These are systematic attacks. They steal money—anything they can get their hands on,” Mohammad Ghafry, a resident of Sinjil. “Since the events in Tal, they have tightened the closure of Sinjil. All of the town’s entrances have been completely sealed off.”
“In addition to that, they established a new settlement outpost in the eastern plain,” Ghafry added. “These lands belong to al-Mazra’a al-Sharqiya, not Sinjil, but the outpost is located at Sinjil’s eastern entrance. The settlers in this outpost have effectively become like the army’s eyes.”
Before the attacks on Tal, more than 80 Palestinians had already been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers in the occupied West Bank so far in 2026, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry
The coordination between armed settlers and Israeli occupation forces is painfully clear, Qaryouti said. “They have worked together for a long time, but now they do it openly.”
“Both the occupation authorities and the settlers are deliberately pushing Palestinians towards an explosion because it serves their broader settlement plan.”

reads.title: India’s Cockroach Protests End as Modi Government Bows to Demands
reads.subtitle: Hundreds of thousands of young protesters assembled in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar every day to demand the resignation of the education minister and accountability from the Modi government.
reads.body:
Drop Site is reader-funded — no corporate owners, no outside influence. Your support is what keeps this journalism independent and free. Please consider making a tax-deductible donation to support our work.
Subscribe now

-
- Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, speaks in a protest march towards Parliament from Jantar Mantar on July 20, 2026 in New Delhi, India.  Photo by Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times via Getty Images.DELHI—Protesters occupying the central parts of Delhi, India were triumphant on Saturday evening after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government accepted all demands raised by the movement’s leaders, including the resignation of the country’s education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The protest was spearheaded by the newly formed Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)—a wordplay on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The word “cockroach” is attributed to the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, who in May referred to the youth of the country as “cockroaches” during a court hearing.
Ministers of the Modi government’s cabinet sat for talks with CJP representatives on Friday and Saturday. At the end of the talks on Saturday, the CJP announced that the government had agreed to all their demands.
Accepting all the protesters’ demands was a rare surrender to popular dissent in Modi’s 12 years of being in power, during which the Hindu nationalist leader has built his image as a strongman that does not back down or take criticism kindly.
“This is just the beginning of a larger movement that will restore basic governance and will work for the people of this country,” said Sauraav Das, a spokesperson for CJP.
Hundreds of thousands of these cockroach protesters had been assembling for over a month at Jantar Mantar, which is less than half a mile south of Connaught Place, the central market in the heart of Delhi. They were demanding the resignation of Pradhan, who is also a senior leader in India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, the party of Modi. The protesters at Jantar Mantar consider Pradhan to be responsible for failing to prevent “paper leaks”—the unauthorized release of highly competitive national college entrance examinations, often hours and sometimes minutes before the exam is due.
The Jantar Mantar movement emerged in May in response to a leak of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), the countrywide medical entrance exam. Reports suggest at least a dozen students across the country died by suicide after the tests were canceled. Protesters claim the number is over 20. The protestor’s demand that the families of each of these students be paid ten million Indian rupees was accepted by the government on Saturday.
After Delhi’s police and other armed forces cracked down heavily against protesters on Monday, the market became a pale shadow of its usual self. Traffic was redirected. And at least half a dozen metro stations around it were shut. Instead it was full with a young, Gen Z crowd who were there to register their dissent against the Modi government in growing numbers and spirit unseen in recent years.
Betu Yadav, a 26-year-old post-graduate student from Uttar Pradesh was hit on the back of her head with batons by male police officers on Monday, leading to intense bleeding that required seven stitches. As news of the government agreeing to the demands emerged, Yadav, still wearing a bandage over her head, said that she can finally celebrate the fruit of her month-long struggle.
“The fight that we fought has transformed into a big success. And today, on the 25th of July, Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned. Along with the resignation of Pradhan, the struggle to overthrow the BJP government will also be achieved by the same youth and the same crowd,” she said.

-
- Crowds of supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party gather at Jantar Mantar to Join the ongoing protest, on July 23, 2026 in New Delhi, India. Photo by Vipin Kumar/Hindustan Times via Getty Images.

## Police Brutality Backfired
Many of the Cockroach protesters had poured into Jantar Mantar from various parts of the country since Monday, when leaders of CJP called for a protest march to the Indian parliament demanding Pradhan’s resignation.
As protesters began their march on parliament, the Delhi Police and other armed forces cracked  down heavily, jamming the internet in central Delhi, using tear gas, beating students with batons, and in some instances shooting them with pellet guns. At least one person has been reportedly left with a permanent disability due to the use of pellet guns.
Multiple students were detained, many of whom have been since released and charges were pressed against some.
“I was shoved to the ground and pulled across,” said Sachin Rawat, a software engineer who came from Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. Rawat incurred injuries on his forehead, shoulder, arm, and legs on Monday. “I consider this as the love of Delhi Police,” he said satirically, adding, “whenever there is a revolutionary struggle, there will be such signs of it being repressed.”
Video evidence has since gone viral on social media showing a senior police officer slapping a young woman, and other male officers groping and attacking women.
The brutalities witnessed on Monday pushed more students to join the movement, with lines to enter the central area of the protest site reaching several blocks at any point of the day in the past week. Since videos of police action against students went viral on social media, protests spread to a dozen other cities around the country.
Apart from Pradhan’s resignation, the leaders of the CJP also demanded that all charges pressed against peaceful protesters be withdrawn. A spokesperson for CJP who was present at talks said that the government has agreed to withdraw all charges against protesters across the country.

## A Broken Education System
“I had to appear twice for the same exam. It was really stressful. I still don’t know which university I will be admitted to,” said 17-year-old Mohammad Kashan, whose dream is to study at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi. Earlier this year, Kashan had taken the Central University Examination Test (CUET), which admits students into federal government-owned colleges across the country. Each year, over ten million students appear for this exam.
Kashan came to Delhi with a friend on July 22, on a low-cost train ticket from Patna, the capital city of Bihar, a state in eastern India. Kashan said the police brutality against students he saw on social media for simply demanding accountability pushed him to join the protests. He has no friends or family in Delhi and was sleeping on the sidewalk since he arrived with a thin cloth for a bed and his back-pack as a pillow.
Twenty-one-year-old Shalu Yadav also took a train but traveled even further, from Hyderabad, in the southern Indian state of Telangana. She is studying law and said she fought with her parents to be present at the protest.
“Our education system is completely broken, it does not guarantee a seat in an institute nor does it guarantee a job. I saw the call for the protest and I decided I need to attend it,” Yadav said.
Since Modi took office in 2014, the budget of India’s Ministry of Education, as a share of the national budget, has dropped by nearly half, even as overall spending has increased, according to a recent investigation by The Indian Express.
Protesters pointed out that the government is instead privatizing education rapidly. “The entire exam system gets outsourced to private contractors. So there is no accountability for paper leaks. Funding for universities and research has been cut down. We are against this entire education policy,” said Priyam, a master’s student at Delhi University and a member of Collective, a progressive students group.
“This is bigger than a protest, it is a movement. There is no future in this country right now. I won’t leave till the government resolves our issues, including the resignation of the education minister,” Yadav said on Thursday.
Many like Yadav are now packing their bags to finally head home after a week, or in some cases after almost a month, of volunteering at the protest site.

## Solidarity with Students of Gaza
For 21-year-old Tubassum, a Master’s student at Delhi University, the movement symbolizes solidarity with other struggles. Although she has two cousins who had to re-appear for the medical tests and were depressed through the entire ordeal, showing up for a protest means a lot more for Tubassum, who came sporting a keffiyeh over her burqa. She was in ninth grade when her mother and aunts joined the Muslim women’s protest at Shaheen Bagh, Delhi, in 2019-20, against a citizenship bill that discriminated against Muslims.
“I remember how people showed up for each other in 2019 at Shaheen Bagh against the Modi government. I want to extend the same solidarity to my peers. And while we raise our voice for our education, I also stand with the students of Gaza who suffered a genocide. Whose education has been ripped due to the genocide” she said.
The Modi government, which has systemically targeted Indian Muslims through immigration laws, regulating food habits, and revising voter rolls, is one of Israel’s staunchest allies.
Bhumi, an undergraduate student at Delhi’s Ambedkar University, and a member of Collective, a progressive student group, was also wearing a keffiyeh and has been attending the protest since last month. “No one is free until everyone is free. This struggle is not only about education but also about basic rights. Not only about paper leaks, but also about rights of workers, farmers, and transpeople. And this solidarity extends to Gaza,” she said.

-
- Crowds of supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party gather at Jantar Mantar to Join the ongoing protest, on July 23, 2026 in New Delhi, India as the police crackdown on protesters at Jantar Mantar and neighbouring areas rocked both Houses of Parliament. Photo by Vipin Kumar/Hindustan Times via Getty Images.

## Modi Loses the Narrative
While the central demand of the Jantar Mantar movement was the resignation of the education minister, protesters did not hesitate to direct their attention at Modi.
Since Monday’s police action, the most popular slogan heard through the protest site chanted in Hindi translates to, “Whenever Modi gets scared, he sends the police in front.” Gen Z protesters speaking the language of viral Instagram reels and memes were also often heard chanting nasty slogans that ridicule Modi.
“We cannot forget that the ruling party BJP is responsible for this. We cannot forget that Home Minister Amit Shah is responsible for the brutalities. We cannot forget that this is ultimately Narendra Modi’s government that perpetrated the paper leaks and the police brutality,” said Neha Bora, national president of the leftist group All India Students Association, during a speech from the center stage of the protest site on Thursday night. Bora went on a hunger strike for 23 days, ending on July 20, demanding the resignation of the education minister.
In response, Modi has promised to set up fast track courts that address the paper leak issue. On Thursday night, he released a statement in a vertical video format on his social media—seen as a way to be more Gen Z friendly—promising that his government will take imminent action against paper leaks. On Friday night there was another video with a similar message. And on Saturday, his government bowed down to the demands.
Rahul Verma, an election analyst and a professor of politics at Shiv Nadar University, argues that many from within Modi’s Hindu nationalist base also appeared to support the movement, placing him on the defensive.
“Unlike many previous mobilisations against the BJP this movement draws hugely from groups that have constituted an important part of the party’s electoral coalition,” he wrote in a column. “A large number of these young, aspirational Indians and their parents on the protest site may have even voted for BJP in the recent past. They are protesting because the systems through which they hoped to advance appear increasingly unreliable.”

Share

reads.title: The Last-Minute Million-Dollar Ad Spend Against Will Lawrence Is Coming From a Major Pro-Israel Group
reads.subtitle: Democratic Majority for Israel is routing the contribution through a CBC-linked PAC—producing a one-of-a-kind irony.
reads.body:
- Still from the attack ad by Rolling Sea Action Fund against candidate Will Lawrence in Michigan’s 7th district.Democratic Majority for Israel is behind a million-dollar effort to slow the momentum of populist candidate William Lawrence in the closing days of a three-way primary in mid-Michigan’s 7th congressional district, according to two sources familiar with the arrangement.
Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, is running primarily against data center buildouts in the district, but has also made opposition to Israel’s genocide in Gaza and the war in Iran core parts of his campaign. He has two well-funded centrist challengers. The winner will take on Republican incumbent Tom Barrett.
DMFI is using a vehicle called Rolling Sea Action Fund PAC to move money into the race. It is unclear if DMFI is funding the ad buy with a transfer or whether DMFI donors were being directed to Rolling Sea, but Joel Wanger, DMFI’s chief political officer, is organizing the effort. It’s a PAC affiliated with the Congressional Black Caucus, but it is regularly used by big money interests as a pass-through to cloak the true source of spending. “Rolling Sea exists as a place to wash money,” as one consultant working on the race put it to Drop Site. The ad buy began with $899,000 being put behind it.
DMFI, Rolling Sea and CBC PAC didn’t respond to requests for comment.
There is a rich irony in the nature of the attack ad from DMFI. The ad takes a shot at Lawrence for a 2024 podcast interview, in which Lawrence talked about the way that the progressive momentum is often countered by a party establishment that co-opts the moral legacy of the Civil Rights movement and repurposes it as a weapon in its own defense. A pro-Israel PAC shrouding its activity in the veil of the Congressional Black Caucus would be exactly the kind of co-optation that Lawrence was warning against. It is much easier in a Democratic primary to take on a pro-Israel PAC directly than it is to take on the CBC, which was the precise point Lawrence is being attacked for making.
Drop Site needs readers like you to make it run. Subscribe for free or make a tax-deductible gift today.
On the podcast Black Internationalism, Lawrence was being interviewed by host Khury Petersen-Smith, who brought up President Joe Biden’s commencement address at Morehouse College. “The fact that Biden gave his commencement address at Morehouse College was pretty painful to watch, as a Black person, as a Black leftist, the Morehouse administration, in such a crass way, to lend its platform to Biden,” Peterson-Smith told Lawrence. “It was just so cynical, to say, We know that the majority of Americans want a ceasefire, we know that young people in particular are absolutely appalled by U.S. support for Israel, but this place that is kind of the crown jewel of historically Black colleges, the fact that Biden can give this commencement address is a gesture toward the idea that this is a progressive administration and so that is something for us to grapple with.”
Petersen-Smith argued that Morehouse and Biden knew exactly what they were doing. “We recognize the political significance of the moral authority and credibility of the Black freedom struggle. It’s not just that we recognize that, but power recognizes that. Biden recognizes that, the White House recognizes that, and therefore that’s a contested space that we need to show up to,” he said.
Lawrence agreed, but noted that as a white person he wasn’t the best to carry such a message, an insight borne out by the subsequent attacks on the comments that came next. “It’s not something I can talk too much about, because I’m white and it’s not my struggle,” he said. “That being said, the extent to which the older generation of Black political leadership are such a pillar, frankly, for establishment, capitalist, imperialist American power through their role as this kind of traditionalist, establishment-ist pillar of the Democratic Party, it’s a big problem. It’s a big problem for left politics in this country. And it gets us every single time. It really defangs the white left and puts us in impossible positions, really. It’s very effective politically.” They later discussed Jesse Jackson’s RAINBOW coalition as a model for “a Black-led, multiracial political agenda for all poor people and for Palestinians too.”
DMFI’s attack ads, meanwhile, zero in on Lawrence’s use of the phrase “the white left,” but not in defense of Israel, or in defense of U.S. support for Israel, Instead, DMFI uses the Rolling Sea PAC to do what Petersen-Smith had identified as an effective tactic, to exploit “the moral authority and credibility of the Black freedom struggle” in service of a competing agenda.
It stands to reason that CBC leadership would be bothered by the Lawrence remark, but neither the CBC nor Rolling Sea has the sort of cash on hand to drop nearly a million dollars in a single race between three white candidates in a district with a Black population of roughly 6%. Rolling Sea had just $103,000 cash on hand at the end of June.
The Crush MAGA PAC has already spent nearly $1 million against Lawrence; an affiliate of Crush MAGA, called Save Democracy, took $100,000 transfer from AIPAC’s Super PAC, United Democracy Project, in May.
Lawrence has gotten $400,000 in outside support from National Nurses United and is now getting the backing of an anti-AIPAC PAC. The super PAC Vote Vets has gotten heavily behind Matthew Maasdam, running heavily on his service as a Navy SEAL. A third candidate, Bridget Brink, is splitting the establishment vote. Consultants involved in the race say that recent internal polling shows Lawrence with a significant lead ahead of the August 4 primary.
Internal polls also show Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ahead in the mid-Michigan region. American Priorities, the anti-AIPAC PAC, started spending this week in a joint effort in the area to boost both El-Sayed and Lawrence together, replicating a strategy rolled out in New York City, in which the same ad would elevate both Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, since both were running in separate districts in the same media market.
The intervention comes as the Haley Stevens campaign grapples with the revelation that its most prominent consultant, Caitlin Legacki, was also working secretly as a Palantir consultant. Palantir supplies substantial intelligence and technological support for Israel, and is also integrated to the operations of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency better known as ICE.
After Drop Site asked the Stevens campaign for comment on Legacki’s role, her role was terminated. “Haley was unaware of Ms. Legacki’s work for Palantir. Her contract with the campaign has been terminated. She is no longer consulting for the campaign,” a Stevens spokesperson told Drop Site.
Stevens is relying primarily on AIPAC spending to boost her campaign; the group has spent more than $30 million so far backing her.
The spokesperson went on: “Haley believes ICE is out of control, putting Michiganders in danger, and needs an immediate overhaul. That’s why she’s voted against giving them another cent without serious reforms, including prosecuting any ICE agents who commit crimes and abuse their power, forcing ICE agents to wear proper ID and prohibiting them from wearing masks to conceal their identities, and taking away their $75 billion slush fund.”
Legacki complained that Drop Site is “more interested in my sources of income than Abdul El-Sayed’s, the actual candidate in this race who hasn’t filed his personal financial disclosure.”
El-Sayed spokesperson Roxie Richner said that the problem runs deeper than a single consultant. “Congresswoman Stevens said she’ll stand up to ICE, all while she took talking points and advice from a compromised corporate apologist now revealed to be a key advisor in Trump’s deportation machine,” Richner told the Michigan Advance. “Perhaps it’s why Stevens voted to thank and fund ICE. Abdul has been clear and consistent on his stance since 2018: Abolish ICE.”
On Friday, in a major boost to Stevens, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced she would be getting off the sidelines and backing Stevens, saying the congresswoman “will always put Michigan first.”
